You're playing a movie - utilising the illusion of choice - that is trying to distract you from the fact that you can never leave the rails with shoe-horned activities that were included in an attempt to remedy a vacant world with minimal meaningful player interaction. I am lucky enough (now poor enough) to run max settings at a steady 110+ fps on 1440p.  I bought Cyberpunk during a 60% sale.  [b] TL:DR [/b] a brilliant but imperfect experience with constant reminders of cut content, weighing in at a reliable but slightly disappointing [b]B+[/b].  [u] Story & writing: B+ [/u] The first 5hrs are a total mess.  Things settle down in the middle section.  The writing is a hodgepodge of deep storytelling and badly written US crime drama, carried by excellent voice acting.  [u] Quests: B- [/u] A broad mix of action and dialogue quests, interrupted by mundane objectives and “walking sim quests" here and there.  The yellow side quests are better than the main story.  I was disappointed the Trauma Team only appear once for 30 seconds during an early mission, despite their prevalence in the lore as a crack team of specialists.  [u] Action: A+ [/u] This is where it really shines.  Weapons, perks, and flexible builds.  Fluid movement and cover mechanics.  The only missing element is the complete lack of airborne combatants.  Hover drones (ground units) don't count - I'm talking about the helicopter & minigun that never makes an appearance.  [u] Music & sound: A- [/u] Guns and weapons feel great and the soundtrack is awesome.  But, ambient background sounds on foot are overcooked and repetitive (I've heard the same shopping area music 2000 times now).  The car horns also sound like a Fisher-Price toy.  Everything else is top-shelf.  [u] Graphics: A- [/u] It's great, but not outstanding.  Characters, weapons, and clothing are incredibly detailed.  The open world environment is less detailed, with some patchy textures and a kind of "blockiness" to the building design.  [u] Driving: D [/u] The weakest part of the gameplay.  Roads are not wide enough to zip through traffic.  Pedestrians dive out in front of your car while you are cornering because they are coded to "dodge" in the wrong direction (they leap out into the road from the pavement).  The sat-nav isn't clear on motorway ramps, and off-roading is a painful experience.  Ultimately, cars don't handle well.  [u] Bugs & crashes [/u] Around 7-8 crashes in my 64hrs, but re-loading the game was no biggie.

There are no game breaking bugs, perse, but there are some little tiny ones that I noticed: -items sticking to an NPC's hand even though they put it down, in which it then breaks the physics of the object and it slowly drifts around the room in motion with the NPC's hand -Car falling from the sky when called -Some questlines are bugged to where you have to do some finagling to get the quest to start, AKA Kerry not calling you even though its been 24 HRs, rest assured, he will call eventually, just gotta do some random fast traveling or time skips to get it to happen.  Those were the most consistent bugs i noticed, other than that, it played beautifully, the level of detail in this game, honestly puts many other RPG's to shame, the world feels lived in, there are secrets to be found. You feel like a living, breathing, part of Night City. The story is IMMACULATE, even the DLC is compelling, you find a reason to get attached to every character in this game. The only character I feel could have used a lot more flushing out and more time with was Jackie, he is a phenomenal character, but you don't spend enough time with him to get the full weight and impact of the moment.   Cyberpunk 2077 is going in my top 3 RPG's of all time, it is a phenomenal, and if you haven't played it, you absolutely should.

One of my absolute favorite games of all time, criminally underrated even with its overwhelmingly positive reviews.  I'm absolutely infatuated with this world and its presentation, I've got 5 full playthroughs and 320 hours under my belt and even now it still feels like theres more to see in Night City.  Great gameplay with excellent build variety encouraging replays, extremely immersive world and incredibly written characters, absolutely [i] incredible [/i] story. Phantom liberty is just as good if not ever so slightly better than the base game as well, elevating the complete package even further.  My only knock against the game is that the male voice option for V is kind of garbage, he really doesn't give any emotion at all and keeps a flat, soulless, macho facade up for the entire game. Choose female in the character creator for the complete opposite with one of the best video game performances I've ever heard, Cherami Leigh understood the script and story perfectly and is responsible for this being one of the only pieces of media to ever make me cry by the end. You can really feel her "growing up" in her performance as the plot progresses.  9.7/10  Minor spoilers ahead, I'll be describing a few key points of this game that I particularly love that I feel are overlooked too often: [spoiler]Cyberpunk 2077 strikes the perfect balance between dystopia and the resilience of the human spirit, nailing the core concepts of the genre. A lot of cyberpunk media often misses the entire point, in favor of focusing entirely on futuristic eyecandy, but 2077 avoids those common pitfalls and instead does a great job portraying the punk side of the genre by having Johnny and his experiences in life be such a key part of the emotional core of the story, providing key insight into what life in this world is really like for someone who wants to make a difference.[/spoiler]   [spoiler]Act 1 is cleverly written to lull you into a false sense of security, to put you in the same naive shoes as V and trick you into thinking this is just a futuristic GTA clone, before suddenly tearing that all down and introducing Johnny to further ground you in the reality of Night City and the true gravity of this plot. Act 1 separates the, for lack of a better term, larpers, from those who are willing to actually give this great story the time of day. This design motif of rewarding those with proper investment in the world and story is furthered by the insane amount of work put into all the "side content" within the game, I'd go far enough to say that there are [i]no[/i] underwhelming quests in this game period short of a few mercenary gigs, practically all of the quests are worth seeing if you truly care about this world and its inhabitants. You can really tell who "played" this game compared to who actually sank their teeth into it and finished it, the entire game is finely crafted to be highly rewarding to those properly invested in its world and characters.[/spoiler]   Absolutely perfect game for the right type of person whos looking for a cyberpunk game with proper depth, characters, and understanding of the genre.

SCORE: 9/10  It's true this game's launch was awful. But at the time of writing this, the game is absolutely incredible. If you even find the setting of the game mildly interesting, you should give it a try. The level of polish between now and when the game launched is night and day.   The roleplay elements are super extensive and the variety you can have in the story and the gameplay is massive between the huge amount of dialogue, guns, cyberware, eta. Not to mention the DLC is also amazing with the new ending options and the characters and their choices are incredibly compelling.   The game is still not perfect, I did run into some bugs during my most recent playthrough however non of them were game-breaking like they were at launch. Performance is also a hitch for low to medium end PCs, I would suggest getting used to DLSS and frame gen if you are on an RTX card although I can't speak for AMD users. I will also say that CDPRs take on a FPS is a little clunky at times and can be quite noticeable when doing stuff like sliding. And finally this is an RPG at heart so if you don't like large amounts of straight up just talking and picking dialogue choices you may find yourself bored or frustrated sometimes.   However as a person who mostly plays FPS, the content of the story was sufficient to keep me from being bored, especially as someone who really likes the setting and genre of Cyberpunk. So if you like that too you should give it a try.

I anticipated, played, and repeatedly completed  Cyberpunk 2077 at release (via GOG). I even took two weeks off work to fully take in the experience on PC, using my then brand-new RTX 2060 Super. It was certainly an experience, but a mixed one. The game had various bugs and glitches and wasn't stable at all. With a little humor, I was still able to have a great time and ignore most of the technical issues.  Almost 6 years later, I gave it another try and HOLY MOLY it's a completely different game. It has fully reached the potential people saw back then. Even more than that, the developers turned it into a masterpiece.  The game can run on a wide variety of systems thanks to its highly customizable graphics settings. I tried out every setting to make it run as smoothly as possible on my build. That experience alone was fun as heck. I truly understand why this game is one of the great benchmark titles for PC hardware. It looks absolutely stunning, especially considering its age. There isn't much more that needs to be said about the graphics and performance.  The skill system seems to have been massively overhauled. Combined with your cyberware, the game now lets you create genuinely distinct builds with depth. I chose to play as a gunslinging cowboy, focused on ridiculous headshot damage and a high cool attribute. There are also many dialogue options tied to your attributes. Having certain attributes at a high level unlocks a surprising number of unique dialoge options, encouraging multiple playthroughs. In some way, this has always reminded me of Fallout NV, which is a huge compliment. I also see great potential in a Netrunner build for my next playthrough.  The story and the overall pacing are peak. I love how naturally the relationships between V, Johnny and all the other main characters develop. Keanu is a real gem and the star of the game. The choices you make genuinely matter. The world feels believable and immersive enough to lose yourself in for hours. I also love how the police and wanted system was overhauled, too.  My only gripe with the game is the long introduction [spoiler] that builds your relationship with Jackie. By my x-th playthrough, I started noticing- and hating- how hard the developers try to make him as sympathetic as possible, just to make you care even more when he dies.  Bro... I'm tired of getting my heart broken.  RIP, Jackie.[/spoiler]  It is, without a doubt, a masterpiece. Have fun playing it!

h1]Cyberpunk for me was one of the most immersive and engaging open world videogame experiences i've ever had[/h1] ,  While this might sound like a pretty loaded statement I stand behind it.  There are other games that of course felt sort of similar to me.  But the whole package here makes something that is greater than it's parts.  I still remember my first time playing Cyberpunk2077.  Little things like entering a car and having the cutscene play out [b]in the car and in first person[/b] while driving through an open world listening to the car radio.  Everything at 1/1 scale.  And everything is [b]huge[/b].  I couldn't remember another game where the buildings are literally as tall and wide as mountains from metal and painted with neon. And they managed it to make them feel like you are sort of scouring through them by walking through underpasses and tunnels, over and under bridges, up and down elevators and ladders etc.  Or just walking through Urmland Street, walking through your small part of the Megabuilding, visiting Lizzies, the first time at Clouds all these things are so vividly realized and felt so tangible.  The character models are incredibly high fidelity, the materials of the clothes, the cyberware the way they animate [b]chefs kiss[/b]  Also I really appreciate the story of both the main game and the DLC.  The world building is superb and I think that the MO of CDPR licensing already established IPs and making a game from it while also having world class writers writing high quality stories and characters for it is beyond genius.  Depending on how you play, your gameplay experience can also be surprisingly varied.  Either covert hacking from a distance or hacking in combat.. or even both. Want to simultaneously use tech weapons with it? no problem.  Or do want it to be more action orientated with down to earth shotguns, revolvers and SMGs?  [i]How about no hacking?[/i]  Scared the cameras could ruin your ninja run?  Just install Sandy and Camouflage. Level up your engeneering perk a bit and run directly in front of cameras to turn them off and dash back to your hiding place while the world stands still.  Finishing off the remaining enemies with throwing knifes and katana before they even notice.  I love what they did here gameplay wise.  The addition of the forward dash and double jump was also a big brain move for traversal. This makes it feel a tiny bit like a parkour game in some aspects because the architecture encourages you to climb through it.  Exploring the open world and finding interesting notes, quests, weapons and upgrade materials in unconventional places really encourages you to look at every corner of this beautifully realised ♥♥♥♥ hole of a cyber city where the machine of capitalism went out of control.      After all that praise I have a nitpick though.  Given that this is a huge open world game with lots of moving parts there is bound to be some wear and tear.  One thing I notice every run is that when you see your own character in a cutscene like in the very beginning or very end of the game it always looks inferior to the characters you meet along the story.  Especially the face animations.  Makes some sense because you can style your character in many different ways but it always stands out to me like a sore thumb.  yeah.. other than that I have not many notes considering how much they already patched.  I mean there is always something one could criticize but at some point I feel there should be acceptance of things that are not bugs.  And I'm sure that when CDPR goes in the second round with Orion, there will be changes made that will fix, expand and improve upon alot of things that me and other people would appreciate for Cyberpunk.      So yeah after 6 years playing Cyberpunk2077, first on PS4 (for 1 hour) then realizing its broken and waiting for the free PS5 upgrade pretending in the meantime it didn't launch yet.  Immediately loving it on PS5 and then a few years later playing it at least 3 times on a high end PC with PT because of major updates and the story DLC, feeling like I played a proper remake or something  I finally brought myself to write a review.  This is a journey I never experienced with any other game.  And maybe that's a factor, despite the unconventional nature of it, why it is so high on my list when I think about [u]excellent open world single player games that I can get lost in for hundreds of hours without having the feeling that i'm wasting my time[/u]

Un juego que tuve mucho tiempo pendiente por su mala reputación inicial: problemas de rendimiento, falta de contenido, bugs constantes. La realidad actual es completamente distinta.  Es un juegazo. La historia tiene un nivel narrativo perfectamente adaptable al cine, con personajes memorables como Johnny Silverhand, Jackie Welles, Judy Alvarez y Panam Palmer. Incluso los secundarios y terciarios están muy bien construidos, algo que ya es marca habitual de CD Projekt.  Gráficamente es impresionante. Con una RX 9070 XT, jugando en ajustes altos con ray tracing en nivel medio, el rendimiento fue excelente: más de 120 FPS estables durante prácticamente toda la experiencia. En ese aspecto, el juego está muy bien optimizado actualmente.  Sobre los bugs: sí, existen, pero en mi experiencia no fueron determinantes. Me encontré alguno cada par de horas, generalmente menor y sin afectar seriamente la partida.  Después de terminarlo, queda claro que el trabajo de redención ha sido sólido. Ahora mismo es un título totalmente recomendable.  Tengo muchas ganas de empezar Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty, que según lo que he visto mantiene (o incluso supera) el nivel del juego base. Probablemente actualice esta reseña cuando lo termine.

Currently only my second full playthrough. For what was once a horrible, undercooked game at launch, now, this is arguably one of the best RPGS I have ever played.   Phenomenal world building. Amazing and memorable characters with fantastic writing. The legendary Johnny Silverhand. Jackie. Judy. Panam. All incredible and are just the first that come to mind. Speaking of which, the romance options, whilst limited, are wonderfully written.  Excellent character customisation, cyberware implants and ability upgrades mean that no playthrough will be the same. The mantis sword arms are a personal favourite! I also recommend using Nexusmods to make the experience even better if you want to expand your appearance options.   The multiple endings are brilliant and you really get to decide the fate of your character. The multiple factions and opportunities to change your experience are extremely varied and offer many different outcomes.   As much as I love this wonderful game; isn't perfect, however. The game had a VERY rocky launch back in 2020 with multiple glitches and bugs, unfortunately some of which are still present and do pop up. Luckily it is fully playable and they are nowhere near as common as they used to be (i did encounter a lot of bugs in my first playthrough in 2024 but my second in 2026 I have only seen a couple thankfully). Some characters and locations also can look either detailed and stunning or ugly and unappealing.  If you're unsure about jumping into this amazing game (It is a very large and long experience) then I highly recommend watching the anime Cyberpunk Edgerunners, which is canon to the game and is set roughly a year before. That's what I did before I played for the first time and it really paid off.  Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 is a fantastic and extremely immersive RPG that deserves all of the praise it now has. A very strong and well-earned 9/10

Verdict: 8.5/10 — A breathtaking, deeply immersive powerhouse that successfully overcame its historic launch flaws to become a defining RPG of its era.  The Setup: Welcome to Night City You step into the shoes of V, a cyberpunk mercenary scratching out a living in Night City—a sprawling, neon-drenched megalopolis ruled by mega-corporations, street gangs, and chrome-infused violence. After a high-stakes heist goes sideways, V finds their mind tethered to a digital ghost: Johnny Silverhand (portrayed by Keanu Reeves), an anarchistic rockerboy with a personal grudge against the corporate elite.  What follows is a race against time as V and Johnny’s consciousnesses slowly merge, driving a narrative that balances high-octane action with surprising existential dread and emotional weight.  The Good: What Makes It Shine A Visually Stunning, Immersive World: Night City remains an architectural and atmospheric marvel. From the corporate towering heights of City Center to the dusty, sprawling badlands outside, the environmental design is rich with ambient detail, neon glare, and verticality that rewards pure exploration.  Rewarding Build Variety & Combat: Whether you want to play a stealthy Netrunner who hacks enemies' brains from afar, a speed-blitzing close-quarters combatant slicing foes up with katanas and a Sandevistan, or a heavy-gun-toting brute, the combat systems offer incredible power fantasies.  Exceptional Side Content: True to CD Projekt Red's pedigree, the side quests and "gigs" often outshine the main narrative. Characters like Judy Alvarez and Panam Palmer are brought to life with phenomenal voice acting, nuanced facial animations, and writing that makes you genuinely care about their fates.  The Bad: Where It Still Stumbles Open-World Reactive Limits: While Night City looks alive, the background crowds and non-scripted NPCs can feel a bit rigid if you spend too long observing their routines. The police system, though heavily patched from its disastrous launch state, still lacks the intricate depth found in other sandbox titles.  Structural Pacing: The core narrative’s middle act hits a few pacing speed bumps, and the initial life path choice you make at character creation still has less impact on the overall story than its heavy marketing initially implied.  Lingering Quirks: Though major technical instability has been largely ironed out, you will still occasionally run into physics oddities, minor UI annoyances, or pathfinding glitches.  Final Verdict Looking back at its rocky history, Cyberpunk 2077 stands as one of the most notable redemption arcs in gaming history. What launched as an over-promised, bug-riddled mess has matured into an ambitious, deeply absorbing sci-fi epic. If you love rich storytelling, visceral action, and exploring one of the most meticulously crafted virtual cities ever built, it is well worth diving into.

This is one of those reviews where i really wish i could click on a [b]mixed[/b] option, I waited a long time to play this game after the horrible launch and long road of bug fixes, finally decided to go ahead and play it through  [h2] Big Cool Review [/h2]  Cyberpunk is definitely one of the biggest games ever made, the city is large and beautiful, especially so if you can experience it in all its glory on a powerful device and the same goes for outside the city in the desert views and wastelands. The gameplay offers plenty of ways to go about making a build you like, with a very large skill tree and available body upgrades, however for me it felt way too grindy or hard to achieve the skill combinations or enhancements I wanted before already reaching the final missions and end of the game  As for the story, the main plot is good with a bunch of storylines and side missions with interesting characters and great voice acting, and obviously Keanu Reeves was BREATHTAKING :D  But unfortunately it overall suffers from its execution, I found myself very lost at the plot in many occasions, why we were doing this and that again. Mostly due to the amount of traveling around the map to do all sorts of different storylines and missions with all its dialogue options since there are just so many. So when I finally returned to another one I had forgotten the 1 or 2 conversations I had with that character up until this point.. that can all just be me being forgetful but I haven’t been this lost in a story before which really cut off the immersion for me  Another thing cutting the immersion to this day is still the bugs that still appear in the animations too much to be ignored or written as a one off funny moment, characters resetting, walking through walls and driving in and through all possible traffic during a scripted drive.   While this game also had plenty of good storylines, sometimes certain characters development(s) felt rushed and/or storylines too short. For the finale, I did 3 endings myself, after a quick googling I found out there are 6 so I did half and cannot speak for all of them, but for some reason they just felt a bit… anticlimactic so to say. It may have just been because I had not immersed myself into the story too deeply but they just felt very quickly cut (except for the Temperance ending) which had a bit more to it before cutting credits  While I may be getting a bit nitpicky here since I’m already going on about the negatives, but the story doesn’t feel like it supports the gameplay either, the whole main plot is about [spoiler] V trying to get rid of the construct that is killing her, being on limited time and we can see her/his health quickly deteriorating especially as you advance In the main story, however the gameplay and open world actively encourages you to do other side missions, explore the world, and do storylines that at times completely forget about the fact that V is actively on the verge of dying.. and once you finally go do a main story mission again V just immediately collapses on the ground 3 times reminding you of that again [/spoiler]  Honestly I don’t think I’ve perfectly captured my thoughts on this game here, and even though I speak more of the negatives in this review then the good there is still a LOT of good here. It just pains me to see all the potential of this game not executed to the vision it was seeking out to be   [h2] TLDR / Summary [/h2]  All the pieces of an amazing plot, gameplay and world are already there to make this one of the best games of all time, unfortunately it just was not executed to perfection and suffers from its unorganized vastness and messy plot. It is still a good game worth your time but it just doesn’t get to the heights it has all the potential to reach

I guess this review has been long overdue.  I picked up this game just for the heck of it. I didn't play much of The Witcher 3. I liked it, but it never really captured my adventurous spirit, so I didn't have much praise for CD Projekt Red. I did know The Witcher 3 was considered an amazing game, though.  I bought Cyberpunk 2077 during a sale after seeing some trailers for Phantom Liberty. I thought, "Maybe I should give it a try." I even remember being offered the bundle discount, but I decided not to get it because I thought I might not like the game and would just be wasting money.  Man... was I wrong.  At first, I was a little confused by everything, but after about five hours, especially after meeting my boy Jackie, I was completely hooked. By the time I was 60+ hours in, I really started to regret not buying the bundle, so I ended up getting the DLC at full price. Absolutely worth it, in my opinion.  I played this game at a time when I genuinely thought I was "growing up." I'd play a few games here and there, but they could never hold my attention for very long. After about an hour, I'd usually lose interest and never touch them again. I honestly thought I had outgrown gaming.  What this game proved to me was the exact opposite. I didn't lose interest in games. I just hadn't been playing any "good" games, especially story-focused ones, for a very long time.  I always dismissed the notion that "old games are just better." I thought it was just nostalgia talking. But in reality, there was some truth to it. A lot of the newer games I'd been playing just didn't have the same soul as the games I grew up with. [h1]I couldn't rate this game out of 10 if I tried.[/h1] Not because it's just [i]that[/i] good or anything. If you're into FPS's or stealth games, you'll get a lot of enjoyment out of this one. However, if you're not into those genres, I don't think the RPG mechanics and other elements would save it for you. [hr][/hr] [h2]Crushing it in Combat[/h2] Combat and stealth are so integral to this game that there are very few missions that don't have you doing at least some. You're going to be taking down thousands and thousands of baddies and there's an alright variety to be had, what with the different factions and different classes of weapons they use. There's a dozen different "capstone" abilities you can mix and match across the different skill paths that all play differently, and you're free to combine a few of them across your playthrough to see what works the best for you. Similar to Skyrim, however, "stealth archer" is always what I find myself drawn to. Fortunately Cyberpunk makes that a ton of fun.  You'll find yourself in a lot of situations where the game wants or even requires you to do it quietly and never be spotted. This means you'll need to carefully manage enemies, take over the cameras to scout ahead before shutting them off, jack into security systems to shut off traps, and carefully take down and dispose of enemies one at a time so you don't raise an alarm. This feels awesome every single time, and nothing was better than clearing a mission without being seen. Even if you go in guns ablazing, the actual combat feels very satisfying with it's wide variety of punchy guns. However, the game's not perfect enough to facilitate that experience 100% of the time.  [h2]It's Glitchy (to rock your mind)[/h2] There's no denying that this game is about on the level of Bethesda games in terms of bugs, and that's coming from someone who typically never notices glitches. Menus misbehaving, UI elements disappearing or displaying wrong information, lighting and texture glitches, framerate hiccups, and untimely crashes, the list goes on and on. Granted, I was in the habit of quicksaving, so I never lost hours of progress, but this game just straight up isn't stable enough to maintain anything close to pristine. The worst of the bunch were when enemies glitched out before/during combat, either becoming aggressive unusually fast or seeing me through walls or just have botched animations, it was always a toss-up if something was going to work right or not.  This couples with the minor gripes I have about all the menus and equipment in this game that are horrible to sort through and manage. You'll be hitting your inventory limit all the time and the game will grind to a halt every half hour or so for five minutes while you fumble with the lack of usable sorting options and clunky interface, with unintuitive dives through the nested menus. Eventually I felt like I had a handle on it, but that was 80 hours in, which I don't know if that reflects worse on me or the game. This isn't helped by the notification for picking anything up being so small and quick that I never saw what I was picking up unless I studied it beforehand, which with there being anywhere from 15 to 100 things to pick up in any one area, I quickly abandoned the practice.  [h2]Smiting the Writing[/h2] I think that the writing is alright. It gets the job done. A few lines made me chuckle, some of them were deeply cringe, but what game at this scale doesn't have that mix of dialogue? A lot of, if not basically all but a handful of the side quests are incredibly forgettable. They all boil down to one-sentence descriptors, typically involving one person who's bad and you need to go stop them. To put it into perspective, I thought they were randomly generated at first because a lot of them felt so generic. Granted, when the game wants to, it'll put on a show for you, but I found myself skipping over the voice actor's decent to excellent delivery of lines just to get through some of it faster. The worst writing comes with a lot of the romanceable characters. They're gender-locked, which while realistic, should've impacted their writing more. All of them will act as though you boned down and that you're the love of their life even if you reject them or, even worse, aren't their preferred gender of partner. It's even more awkward when they are actively seducing you, you go to do a sexy dialogue option, and they put up their hands and say "WOAH I'm not gay bro" (I paraphrased) before then letting you "spend the night" where you wake up in their bed. Coming off of a game such as Baldur's Gate 3, where they're down to let anyone be with anyone, coming into this one was probably gave more whiplash than your typical player as I played heterosexual whack-a-mole trying to avoid the painfully awkward and sometimes even unskippable sex scenes.  The main storyline also doesn't feel as sprawling as games like CDPR's other headliner the Witcher is. I could actively see how my choices were being acknowledged 99% of the time, sure, but insofar as to just let me know that I did indeed decide something. Often I'd have V, the player character, say something, and realize that based on the response of the NPC that regardless of what I said, they'd've said the same thing. Some games hide it better, but this one certainly doesn't. It helps that the voice actor for V (at least the male one) is phenomenal.  [h2]But hey, 100 hours is a 100 hours.[/h2] I won't deny that there's a lot of stuff to do in this one. I could write a whole multi-hour video essay over all the aspects to this game that are done well, like the combat, the driving, the [i]shockingly[/i] good photo mode and clothing options, the main quest line, the characters, and on and on. And the city, good lord Night City is one of the most well-executed cities I've ever seen in a video game. I just loved existing in it, and it pains me to keep the praise on it brief, because honestly the asking price (especially on sale) is worth it just to walk around and take in the incredible work that's been done.  But just as many words can be said about the awkward and sluggish menus that take up way more hours of the game time than they should or all the glitches and edge cases that weren't accounted for. But, obviously, I recommend this one. There's a lot to hate on when it comes to Cyberpunk 2077, but there's also a whole lot of preem stuff in there.

I played and completed this game on release. It was exceedingly mid. This has been a labor of love by CDPR to fix it and make it closer to the game we had envisioned. It's still missing some of the promised features and most of the choices you make don't matter. It's odd that in a futuristic world where transhumanism is a thing that our companions are sex locked when people can easily modify their body to change their sex, but if we like a certain companion we are locked out if we are playing as the incorrect sex. It's a bit of a nitpick, but it really feels out of place in this world. The main story itself is not particularly special in my opinion. I found it interesting that you could approach missions with quite a few different methods depending on your own creativity.   The side stories are where a lot of the interesting lore and the best stories are told. Even the really good Phantom Liberty DLC (despite loving it) where the characters felt solid, the endings felt quite shoe-horned and forced. Spoiler free but it feels like it changes a lot of characters' personalities or is just forcibly melancholy.  The RPG elements and systems feel more interesting and fun after the reworked systems. Gunplay is solid. You get some interesting builds with melee, netrunner/hacker, and several gun types.   My main problems in the game are that the game still feels like there's a [i]lot[/i] of missed opportunity, particularly that the choices don't matter 99% of the time, and the 1% that do you don't know how or why without looking up a guide. I think that's lame storytelling. You should [i]feel[/i] as though your choices matter and actually impact the world. For example, Witcher 3 I found to be a much better game despite in terms of storytelling despite, in my opinion, the combat being significantly worse than it is in this game.  I'm torn between if I thought this game was a solid 8 (8.5?) or a 9 so I think I'll give game an enjoyable 8.5/10 and Phantom Liberty a 9/10.

[h2]This game is a literal masterpiece, and a candidate for best RPG of all times.[/h2]  [h3]Overview[/h3] I actually bought this game on release day, purely on the strength of the demo they'd released and my desire to vote with my wallet for the kind of game I want to see made. I know it had issues at release but I didn't get around to seriously playing it until 2025 so my opinion is based on only experiencing the current ("fixed") state of the game.  It is a complex game with a lot of subtlety that is all kind of stuff thrown at you at once when you first play and I recommend just shutting off your brain, going with it and see what happens. You'll figure it out. My first run was somewhat typical for me in RPGs...he was a kind of stealthy corpo assassin who tried to use a cyberdeck but wasn't great at it. It wasn't until late in my first run that enough of the quickhack stuff clicked and I finally "got it." So I played again explicitly going full-on netrunner and it was almost a different game. Massively fun and I got emotionally invested in the entire story in ways that surprised me. Just finishing my fourth run and I'm still discovering new things, hidden references or rewards, character interactions I'd never seen, different romance stories, etc.  [h3]The Game[/h3] An expansive Cyberpunk role-playing game based heavily on Mike Pondsmith's Cyberpunk tabletop RPG. And no screwing around it is a very faithful adaptation. It's a computer game so some stuff will get streamlined, some stuff ignored, but having experience with both I can say that it's clearly an adaptation of the TTRPG. The setting, characters and world are all consistent. And all horrible. There are no happy endings in Night City and that's another aspect of storytelling I can enjoy here. Characters are so well fleshed out that you can really start to hate them, or want to protect them. But more often than not they'll die. And you'll be at fault. If you insist on exclusively goody-twoshoeing your way through RPGs you'll find Night City a great wake-up call. Sometimes you have to make choices and it's rare for everyone to have a good outcome.  Combat is engaging and varied. You can set yourself up to rely on your cyberdeck to hack your environment and enemies, be a stealthy assassin that was never there, or enable a kind of bullet-time mode where time is slowed for your opponents but not for you while you apply shotgun or katana, or become an invulnerable baseball bat-wielding psychopath who drops on her opponents superman style smashing everything around them.  [h3]TL;DR[/h3] Story is awesome. The actors are uniformely great and I got very attached to them. Missions are excellent and varied with some reaching the pinacle of cool design. I would consider the Project Liberty content mandatory. It is top notch, and slots into the existing story very well. Combat is amazing. Modding it can be fun, particularly for clothing.  The only thing I'd note is that "storyline missions" can feel quite "on-rails" at times, and it's a very different feeling from general side jobs or other activities. A minor compaint for a game that offers so much.  [h2]10/10[/h2]

I finally gave Cyberpunk 2077 another proper chance after my first experience with it on PS4 at launch, and I think that original release definitely left a sour taste in my mouth.  After playing it now, I can honestly say it's a good game—but I don't think it's the masterpiece that a lot of people make it out to be.  The main story is enjoyable and kept me interested throughout, but where the game really shines is with its side characters and the stories that come with them felt far more memorable than a lot of the main plot. Those side quests had some of the best writing in the game.  That said, the longer I played, I seemed to encounter more bugs and glitches later into my playthrough than I did at the beginning. Nothing completely game-breaking, but enough to pull me out of the experience.  Another issue for me was the amount of repetitive side content. The NCPD scanner missions (which I am still working through) and quite a few of the gigs start off fun, but after a while they become a checklist rather than something you're actually excited to do. By the end, I was doing them more out of obligation than enjoyment.  So, is Cyberpunk 2077 a bad game? Absolutely not. It's a solid RPG with a great story, memorable characters, and an incredible world to explore. But is it the generation-defining masterpiece that some people claim it is? I don't think so.  For me, it's a really good game that falls just short of being truly great.

When I first installed Cyberpunk 2077, I expected to become a legendary mercenary, take down corporations, and shape the fate of Night City. Instead, I accidentally became the city's most dedicated food critic. Somewhere between my first mission and the next main quest, I realized I was spending more time examining vending machines than my skill tree. The story is fantastic, but every time I saw a food stand with steam rising from a fresh bowl of noodles, my priorities completely changed.  The amount of detail put into the food is honestly incredible. Every snack, drink, and meal has its own unique packaging, name, and design. Most games throw a generic "Health Potion" into your inventory and call it a day. Cyberpunk gives you dozens upon dozens of different foods that actually look like products people would buy in a futuristic city. Even when two items serve the same purpose, they still have their own identity. It sounds like a small detail, but it makes Night City feel like a real place instead of just another open world.  The vending machines deserve their own award. I don't know how CD Projekt Red managed to make me stop every few blocks just to browse digital snack machines, but they did. Every glowing screen tempts you with some new mystery drink or suspiciously colorful burrito. I started every mission by saying, "This time I'm going straight to the objective," only to get distracted by a vending machine selling a drink I'd never seen before. Somewhere along the way, I accepted that I wasn't playing an action RPG anymore—I was just grocery shopping with occasional firefights.  The restaurants and food vendors scattered around the city add so much personality. Walking through Japantown, grabbing noodles from a street vendor, or passing tiny cafés packed with NPCs enjoying their meals makes the world feel alive. It isn't just decoration; it creates the feeling that people actually live here instead of existing solely to hand out quests. Even when I wasn't buying anything, I found myself stopping just to look around and appreciate the atmosphere.  My inventory eventually became less of an arsenal and more of a convenience store. Sure, I had legendary weapons capable of eliminating an entire room of enemies in seconds, but I was equally proud of carrying fifteen different flavors of soda, multiple coffees, enough burritos to feed a family, and an alarming amount of packaged noodles. Did I need any of it? Probably not. Did I still refuse to sell any of it because "I might want that later"? Absolutely.  Then there are the advertisements. Every giant holographic billboard screaming about the newest beverage or synthetic snack somehow fits perfectly into the world. The corporations don't just sell products—they sell lifestyles, and even the food feels like part of the culture. It's hilarious, over-the-top, and somehow believable. After enough hours in Night City, I genuinely started recognizing fictional brands the same way I recognize real ones.  I also appreciate that the food reflects the diversity of Night City. You can find everything from classic comfort food to futuristic processed meals that sound like they were invented by an AI after reading one cookbook. Some of the item names made me laugh, while others actually made me wish they existed in real life. Then there are the mystery foods that raise more questions than answers. Whatever half of these products are made of, I don't think I actually want to know—but my character sure wasn't picky.  People always ask me about my favorite part of Cyberpunk 2077. They expect me to say the combat, the graphics, the story, or the incredible soundtrack. Instead, I tell them about the time I spent twenty minutes comparing vending machine inventories because I wanted to collect every snack I hadn't seen before. At some point I realized I had become emotionally invested in fictional convenience store products, and honestly, I have no regrets.  Cyberpunk 2077 succeeds because every little detail contributes to the illusion that Night City exists whether you're there or not. The food isn't just a healing item; it's part of the world's identity. It tells stories about the corporations, the culture, the economy, and the people who live there. Few games put this much care into something most players will barely notice, and I think that's worth celebrating.  So yes, the game has unforgettable characters, emotional quests, incredible world-building, gorgeous visuals, and some of the best atmosphere I've experienced in gaming. But if you ask me what kept pulling me back for hundreds of hours, it wasn't the guns or the cyberware—it was wondering what ridiculous snack I'd find around the next corner. I came to Night City looking for glory. I left with a backpack full of burritos, enough soda to fill a warehouse, and an appreciation for fictional fast food that I never expected to have. 10/10. Came for the cyberware. Stayed for the snacks.

I'm usually late to the party. I rarely jump head first into newly released triple a titles that cost a fortune and have yet to be fully optimized. In the case of Cyberpunk 2077 this was undoubtedly a boon, given its supposedly disastrous launch state. The Cyberpunk 2077 I played ran like a dream on both my desktop and LegionGo (Steam OS on Linux). But at this point, the technical aspects feel largely beside the point. Cyberpunk is more than the sum of its technical accomplishments. It's a pulsating, neon gut punch of sex, violence and moral ambiguity. It's everything I've always wanted from GTA but that GTA has never been able to give me. It's the general direction the Fallout series should have been aiming for after New Vegas. The characters, the acting. All the different ways you can approach the same mission, the builds, the city. Most of all Night City. Alongside Witcher 3 Cyberpunk surely establishes CD Projekt Red as  the best in the business when it comes to creating teeming environments that truly feel alive. Just driving around the various neighborhoods is a blast. Plus, if you go for Phantom Liberty, which you absolutely should, you get to spend some time with Stringer bell, which is never a bad thing. I played out every possible ending to the main scenario and each moved me in a different way, leaving me with a sense of loss and sadness and incredible beauty against the odds. Honestly didn't expect to enjoy this as much as I did. I bounced off it back in 2020 like everyone else, but coming back after Phantom Liberty and all the patches, it barely feels like the same game.  What works: Night City is still incredible to just exist in. Every district has its own personality and I found myself slowing down just to look around. The writing is way better than I remembered too, especially the gigs and the personal side stories, some of them hit harder than the main quest. Combat finally feels good, hacking is fun instead of tedious, and building your character actually changes how you play. Phantom Liberty on its own is worth the price, the whole spy thriller arc with Solomon Reed is one of the best things CDPR has ever written. Soundtrack is great, voice acting is great, and the game still looks stunning even years later.  What doesn't work as well: the cops still just materialize out of nowhere if you sneeze near a crime, driving feels stiff more often than it should, and you'll still run into the occasional weird bug even now. A lot of the map filler quests feel like they exist just to pad your playtime next to the genuinely good stuff. And after all the buildup the endings wrap up faster than they probably should.  Still, this is a redemption arc I wasn't expecting to root for. If you dropped it years ago it's genuinely worth going back to.

Technical issues were never the biggest problem.  And that's coming from someone that first played the game to completion on PS4 almost 5 years ago.  As a fan of CDPR games like The Witcher series, and of the original Cyberpunk 2020 tabletop RPG, I truly wanted to enjoy this game.  ...what, you didn't know this game was based off a TTRPG?  That was the original concept of this game: a video game adaptation not unlike CRPG's like Baldur's Gate did for D&D.  That's why back in 2012, CDPR "promised" things like: * a "mature RPG...set in a rich, futuristic world"  * a "gripping non-linear story filled with life and detail" * "advanced RPG mechanics based on pen & paper RPG system" * "varied selection of different character classes"  If only.  Night City could have, and should have, been one of the most expansive interactive, raw, gut wrenching environments ever to exist in gaming history.  The TTRPG even says that Night City should basically be its own character with everything it has to offer.  But instead, you get city block after city block of empty buildings, non-functional store fronts and window dressing.  A detailed world of which very little can be interacted with.  Most NPC's barely have anything more to say than a zombie would, and blend in with the background.    One of the fixers tells you not to spend all your money on "glitter and XBD's".  Which would be hilarious if it was not so sad already, because in this game there is no glitter or XBD that you can buy in any meaningful way, in contrast to what the TTRPG offers.  The world of Witcher 3, by comparison, offers far more of a "rich world" with "life and detail".  And then consider games like Deus Ex and Daggerfall which came out decades before Cyberpunk 2077 did, and yet had far more interactive worlds by comparison.  The game is basically GTA set in the future: loot, shoot and run.  Some of the new quests added in the expansion are literally just stealing a car and driving to the target destination, while escaping from the police and any other aggrieved parties.  Quests are still mostly linear and handheld with waypoints.  Only practical variation seems to be dialog choices which seem surface level at best.  One of the "new quests" added in this edition is literally just repeatable recycled dialogue and animations, not even updating as you progress in Phantom Liberty.  You have a choice of lifepath when you create your character, being either a nomad, street rat or corpo, but these only affect the first hour of the game, and then anything afterwards is just the occasional unique dialog choice.  There's no unique equipment, missions or endings based on your lifepath.    There are no "classes" in the traditional RPG sense in this game.  There's a skill tree, and you can invest in different stats which come with different skills to specialize in specific weapons or playstyles, but there's no choosing a class at character creation like a solo, netrunner or fixer like the TTRPG.  The Phantom Liberty expansion adds a single new area: a previously inaccessible area of Pacifica called "Dogtown".  This place is a run down, almost post apocalyptic neighborhood, so it doesn't really add to the "cyberpunk" theme of this game.  If anything, it's almost poetic how reflective this is of the state of Night City: mostly empty and a shell of itself compared to what could have been.  Compare how much extra content The Witcher 3 expansions "Heart of Stone", and "Blood and Wine" added.  To give credit where it's due: the Phantom Liberty expansion does add one new ending to the base game, based on certain choices you make in the Phantom Liberty storyline.  But without regard to story choices made in that ending, there's no final mission, no final boss, or any build up; just your usual follow the waypoints, talk to characters, move on, maybe get some dialog choices, etc.  So it's very unrewarding.  While I'll admit this game is a bit of a guilty pleasure for me, there's just too many flaws to the game's design that no amount of expansion will solve.  CDPR knows how to make good RPG's with the Witcher series, and games like Baldur's Gate 1 and 2 perfected the CRPG genre decades ago with a tiny fraction of the technology available when this game was made, so there's no excuse.

Few games capture the imagination quite like Cyberpunk 2077. Set in the sprawling metropolis of Night City, CD Projekt Red delivers a world that feels alive with towering skyscrapers, neon-lit streets, and unforgettable characters. Blending a compelling narrative with deep role-playing mechanics and breathtaking visual design, the game immerses players in a futuristic society where ambition, technology, and humanity constantly collide. Following years of improvements and updates, Cyberpunk 2077 has evolved into the experience many hoped for at launch, standing as one of the most immersive and visually impressive RPGs of its generation.  This game developed by CD Projekt Red shows that a great open-world RPG is not only about its main story but also about its side missions. The optional quests make the game more interesting, meaningful and lengthen your whole run in this game. Even though the game has some bugs, its exciting missions and emotional moments more than make up for it.  In the game, you play as V, a mercenary living in Night City. After getting shot in the head early on in the story, V was implanted with a special bioship called the “Relic”. The chip contains the digital personality of Johnny Silverhand, a famous rock star and rebel played by Keanu Reeves. As the Relic started taking over V's mind, Johnny began appearing in V's head, which allowed him to start appearing in front of him  and to talk to him in his head. At first, Johnny and V do not get along, but over time they build a stronger relationship. Their journey together is one of the most important parts of the story.  The structure of this game is different from many other RPGs. After only a short time in the main story, you already have many side missions and gigs (from various fixers) to choose from. In the future, people often call you on your phone to offer new jobs, so you do not always need to search for quests yourself. This means the game gives you many choices early on. While your progress may not always feel bigger over time, there is always something interesting to do.  One important thing to mention is that, if you make use of the Fast Travel option, there is the possibility of certain questlines bugging, which means that you will not receive an important phone call for the next mission. This happened to me during the Panam and Judy questlines on an older save. Because of this, I recommend driving around the city and completing short activities such as NCPD missions while waiting for important calls instead of using Fast Travel too often.  Night City rewards careful exploration. If you move too fast, you will miss many interesting details. You can shape your character through your skills and dialogue choices. Your decisions affect both V's story and the lives of other characters, making every playthrough feel unique.  The combat in Cyberpunk 2077 becomes more enjoyable as you play. At first, the enemies can feel too strong, but as you unlock new skills, weapons, and cybernetic upgrades, combat becomes much easier and more fun. You can use powerful weapons, slow down time, double jump, or fight with Mantis Blades or an Electric Baton, which lets you pick up an enemy and toss them through the air or against a wall, which is extremely violent. These abilities let you choose your own fighting style and make every battle more exciting.  One of the best parts of the game is its unique Iconic weapons. These special weapons have different abilities and can be upgraded, so they stay useful throughout the game. Some weapons have special effects, while others are simply fun to use. This system lets players keep their favorite weapons instead of replacing them all the time, making combat more enjoyable and rewarding.  As you become stronger, the game lets you choose how to complete missions. You can fight enemies directly or use stealth to avoid them. Many areas have hidden paths, useful items, and computers that can help you by opening doors or turning off security cameras. Even though the stealth system is simple, it is fun to plan your route and use Quickhacks to distract or stop enemies.  Quickhacking is one of the most interesting features in Cyberpunk 2077. It lets you hack enemies by overheating them, causing them to detonate a grenade, making them suffer from cyberpsychosis, or temporarily blinding them. This makes both stealth and combat more exciting. By using Quickhacks and hidden paths, you can complete some missions without fighting anyone, giving players many different ways to play the game.  Unfortunately, the amount of bugs I experienced really does need to be mentioned. Sometimes characters move in strange ways, objects do not appear correctly, dialogues overlap, and certain questlines can get stuck. I also experienced visual glitches, such as missing hair on my character or V being stuck in a T-pose inside a car. Although I had to reload my saves a couple times, these problems never stopped me from enjoying what is probably the most content-rich single-player game I have ever played. The game's strong characters, huge variety of content, and well-written missions made these issues quite easy to overlook.  Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 is an outstanding open-world RPG with a beautiful and highly detailed world to explore. The story is exciting, emotional, and full of memorable moments. Although the main story is shorter than expected, you can turn the game into a very long experience by exploring everything it has to offer, listening to every dialogue, completing every side mission and gig, and unlocking all possible endings. I highly recommend completing every available mission before entering Embers to meet Hanako, because after that the story does not continue. Instead, the game returns you to the point right before the final mission through the "Sure, just one more gig" option, allowing you to finish any remaining content, but it just wouldn’t feel the same after having already completed the story beforehand. If you own Phantom Liberty, you should also complete it before the final mission, as it unlocks an additional ending that becomes available during the game's final choice.

Worth picking up if it's cheap and you like the futuristic setting.  Pros: - beautiful city that feels alive - great graphics - varied combat systems, with guns, swords and hacking - skill trees for different playstyles - runs well, short loading times and easy to jump in and out of - plenty of content in the city. Lots of stories, side missions and collectables.  Cons: - the story is boring and forgettable - the entire game is 1st person and you never see your character which makes it hard to identify with them - whilst the combat is varied, the actual gunplay is very basic. You soon become OP and there is no reason to use any of the guns you find instead of Iconic weapons - dialogue is weird. There's a lot of futuristic colloquialisms but the actual dialogue is just odd and easy to miss key details - the game expects you to know a lot about the setting and ignores the 'show don't tell' rule. There will be loads of times were you're like 'wait, who is that?' 'what is that?' 'why does my character know this when I don't?' - stakes feel very low and attachment to characters is odd. Everyone is a stereotypical Cyberpunk resident. My character seems to care loads for people she's just met, or form deep relationships with people she doesn't know.  Overall it's a nice looking game if you like the Cyberpunk/Bladerunner vibe, but the story is very poor, the gunplay is basic and there's just not much to do outside of the pretty aesthetics. NO SPOILERS IN THIS REVIEW  obviously the graphics are great and the story is great, but temper your expectations and look deeper into this game to actually appreciate it.  PRE LAUNCH  its gone through development hell. released in a horrible state, devs claim the entire development process was grueling and stressful. it didnt release so unfinished because the devs were lazy, its because CDPR gave them incredible expcetations in way too little time. they built it on a fully custom engine, meaning everything was made from the ground up, which can if given enough time lead to a better optimized game like doom eternal, but in this game, crunch was horrid and they skipped corners to get it out the door and please investors.  POST LAUNCH  backstory aside, cyberpunk has gotten the most crazy comeback ive ever seen. 2.0 basically fixed most valid criticsism anyone had with the game and its more than in a playable state now. its pretty incredible. huge map with an absurd amount of content, every sidequest and gig has a bunch of lore you can optionally read to get backstory and context as to why youre here doing this and who youre dealing with on each job, people claim gig are repetitive in this game, which can be true, but i feel they arent actually invested in the stories each gig tells.theres betrayal, character arcs, spy stuff, relationships and a web of motives and lies each gig uses to tell a bigger story of the gangs in each district. their motives, goals, individual gripes, issues and development, even gets tied with the politics of night city and influences some of the bigger plot points in the story.  STORY  the main story... although good for a couple playthroughs, doesnt have nearly as many path altering options as youd think compared to how CDPR advertizes the game. there are a couple moments that are really important, and it makes you wanna play multiple playthroughs, but theres for sure  limited amount of interactions.  GAMEPLAY  the gameplay is amazing, lots of guns, cyberware, quickhacks, stealth, everything youd want in a combat focused game. its a very deep system, with granular difficulty. so you can either play on easy and just use whatever you want, or play on hard and be forced to spec into a specific playstyle, however you like to play.  SOUNDTRACK  the soundtrack is good in this game, some of the radio stations are really good, and others kinda feel like filler techpop kinda of thing. i wish the whole edgerunners soundtrack was a radio station because that one would be my favorite. CDPR worked with some really good indie bands to make some incredible scores and general music specifically for this game and for the anime.   DLC  phantom liberty is better than the entire rest of the game. full stop. it has the deepest most unique gigs, coolest characters, most gut wrenching story, darkest most filthy area in the game, way better cosmetics, sidequests, just everything. phantom liberty is a 10/10 in a vacuum. every issue i have with the base game just simply isnt present in the dlc.  OVERALL exceptional comeback from a game i almost wrote off too soon. im very glad i gave it another chance.  WAIT WAIT WAIT  cyberpunk, although a cool fictional setting, isnt a future to aspire to. its a warning. its what happens when corporations with greed in mind keep stripping away our rights, slowly. we already live in a somewhat dystopian cityscape. massive corpos sell your data around without your consent just for a couple cents, your for you page is curated to keep you as addicted as possible just to show you a couple more as, surveyllance companies like palantir have tens of thousands of flock cameras around the country where they log your driving habits, face, location data, eating and shopping data, etc. they sell it to various private companies and law enforcement without EVER having you agree. massive data centers are using more water than is sustainable, all to further AI which is used to power surveyllance and corpo power creep.   cyberpunk is a cautionary tail of late stage capitalism, so play the game and let it inspire you to help stop this dystopia from becoming a reality.

You know that feeling you get when you finish a great story from your favorite book? You finish that show you've been meaning to watch and it was actually as good as everyone said it was, or that time you finished that movie that just spoke to you in the right way? You probably know that feeling I am describing, when you put down the book, turn off the tv or in the case of Cyberpunk 2077, sit there and watch the credits at the end of a 40, 60 or 100 hour long adventure.  What makes you sit there is a lot of things. Sadness it is over, joy at having experienced it, maybe some melancholy because you know there is never gonna be an experience with the game like your first. I have done 2 playthroughs of Cyberpunk 2077 and it's expansion Phantom Liberty. It's story, with minimal spoilers is about your character V going on a heist and being changed permanently because of it. V is for lack of a better way of putting it dying. You are playing a character who is facing down their own mortality and is trying to stop it. There is no grand "save the world" plot, instead the story is personal, intimate and grounded despite it's futuristic setting.  The first time I played I enjoyed it but didn't love it. Wrote it off as a good but slightly underwhelming adventure. But somebody in my family adored it. Convinced me to watch the anime too, and give it another chance. This same someone was also diagnosed with a brain tumor. Their own body turned on them and our family watched in real time as they deteriorated before us. This person ultimately passed away October 2025.  I write all this to say when I did my revisit in their honor, suddenly the story mattered a lot more. I saw the parallels, saw the deeper meanings and messages. This game became personal in a way I did not anticipate. I cried when it was over, and I cried because of Phantom Liberty. Do I recommend this game? I guess yes, yes I do. It has become a personal joy of mine to play and I will never touch it again. If we get a surprise DLC announcement in 10 years ala Witcher 3, then on that day I will change my mind and I will play it in your honor.  I love you Jeremy. "Today was a good day."

I originally played Cyberpunk a little while after it released. If you're unaware, the game had an incredibly rocky launch, being in an unacceptable state. While I avoided most of the worst bugs, the game felt lackluster. At best, it was an average RPG with a good story, and at worst, it was an unfinished and unpolished experience. I shelved it thinking I would never return, until about five years later when I bought the Phantom Liberty DLC. Now, I regard Cyberpunk as one of the finest RPGs, though not quite the greatest.  The game especially shines with how much player interaction there is. The ways missions reacted to my previous actions, such as decisions or completion of certain quests, is astonishing. Aside from the major story beats, my two playthroughs of this game felt incredibly different, despite me likely making similar decisions. Almost everything I did felt like it will be acknowledged down the line, whether that be through modified quest-lines, objectives, or dialogue. Each one of those moments, of which is present throughout the entire game, added greatly to my experience, no matter how small nor insignificant those acknowledgements turned out to be.  Beyond missions, Cyberpunk does a great job at feeling [i]alive[/i]. I love how I can walk into any shop and chat with the owner, especially bars. I love how I'm able to text or call characters after missions to debrief them or seek a second opinion. And more broadly, I love how much unmarked content there is. There are so many things in this game that I would have never encountered if I lacked explorative drive. From things as minor as dialogue or texts, to as major as really powerful items and entire side-quests. Amazingly, despite my recent ~100 hour playthrough, there's definitely still a portion of the game I have yet to experience. The abundance of content makes the game feel fresh and like it's a world at my fingertips.  In a similar vein, I greatly appreciate how much variety there is. There are tons of different builds you can pursue, each being very flexible in how you design it. For instance, fast-paced blades, heavy-hitting weaponry, stealthy glass canons, and any combination thereof. Within missions, there's always several ways to go about them and a plethora of optional objectives that can improve (or hinder) your primary goal.  However, as much as I regard Cyberpunk as one of the finest RPGs, I hesitate praising it too highly. While a strong entry in its category, it sits [i]just[/i] beneath the best, as there's a few criticisms holding it back. Most overtly, there's a strange absence of trans-humanism. In a world where one can modify any part of the body with cybernetic enhancements, and enter most stores to change one's phenotype on a whim, you would expect themes of identity, alienation, individuality, and the human condition to be present. At best, the extent of trans-humanism's presence is cyberpsychosis, quite literally psychosis induced by cybernetic abuse, and interaction with a few characters who hardly view themselves as human. How can a game based on a genre whose defining trait is trans-humanism completely omit it? Even something as minor as the occasional human with elf ears or otherwise unnatural traits would have satisfied this niche.  Another criticism is a small, yet significant, portion of writing for the protagonist, V. I appreciate that you have a great deal in customizing V, including their identity and backstory, as well as their behavior. However, I dislike that V has one constant underlying motivation: to make a big name for themselves. This made perfect sense for certain backstories, especially my first playthrough as a Streetkid, but made little sense for my playthrough as a former Corpo. Why do I have to always role-play as someone who ultimately desires fame and glory? What about something as simple as living comfortably or returning to a former lost life? While I concede that I am ultimately role-playing as V and not a self-insert, I dislike how Cyberpunk offers so much variety to customize V's character, only for their driving force kickstarting the story to always be exactly the same. Isn't this antithetical to the customization of V?  Despite these two, I still regard Cyberpunk among the greatest RPGs, though not at the top. In spite of my criticisms of the story, they only encompass a very small part of it. The story is definitely one of the better video game stories. Frequently, RPGs suffer from the amount of exponential writing needed to make it work, and I think Cyberpunk nailed both the execution of the main story beats, as well as allowing flexibility in responding to my play-style. It is well-written, and I personally enjoyed everyone's performances, especially Keanu Reeves'. The variety and volume of content is also impressive.  I also recommend picking up the Phantom Liberty DLC. It adds a lot to the experience and stands even higher than the base game. For brevity reasons, I moved all discussion of Phantom Liberty into its own review.

I adored this game during my first hundred hours—so much so that I purchased "The World of Cyberpunk 2077," a hardcover book that, now looking back at it, was probably released by Dark Horse as part of the public relations and marketing work of CD Projekt Red to increase hype and sales before launch in 2020. I hadn't been so smitten by a world since discovering Star Wars in early middle school. But somewhere after that 100 hour mark, the story and world began unraveling for me and I finished the game feeling rather hollow.  Cyberpunk appears to be a labor of love for the many involved in making it. Aesthetically, it's gorgeous. There were countless times where I stopped to take in and appreciate the models and textures that were around me. The artists and developers who made this are top tier, no question. Unfortunately, as I continued my time in Night City, I was struck with the feeling of just how massive an endeavor building this city was and just how many assets were reused in monotonous ways. Things began to feel imperfect and rushed, and those moments of awe that happened so frequently turned into me questioning just why the game had to be so big and why certain gigs had to exist. The game feels far too large to the point of feeling incredibly vapid. It made me yearn for smaller, more thoughtful stories and environments that are carefully tailored and handcrafted. You don't have to paint the entire world. Paint a few very interesting locations and allow the viewer to dream about the rest.  The story itself is at its strongest in the early main quests, when the player doesn't quite realize how terribly superficial all the endings will turn out to be. I felt like I had a stronger emotional connection to Jackie for four hours than compared to my 200+ hours with Johnny. I think this shows that CD Projekt Red tried to do far too much without a cohesive overarching narrative or goal. It left me feeling pushed and pulled in many different directions, confused, and frustrated that a game with this much potential could fall so flat. It's a good game and there are there are many things that I experienced while playing that will stick with me for the rest of my life, but I just wish that it was much smaller with more time and care put into crafting the details.

TLDR: Having been overhyped before launch and apparently released in a poorly optimised state, the game suffered initial poor critics. However, as it is now, it is a great, if only good to some, game. Does it compare to Witcher 3? No. Is it a completly different genre? Yes. So maybe quit comparing the 2 and enjoy it for what it is; a 2077 tale of how much can go wrong in a heist and how will you ever manage to fix it.  Story: As V, choose from 3 selectable backgrounds (which barely impacts the game), you decide you've had enough of your old life and decide to make it big in Night City. I'll try to skim the details and bite into the obvious fat; Johnny Silverhand, a.k.a. our dear Keanu Reeves. He does a good job, like amazingly so. He basically carries the whole story on his back. Honestly, if it wasn't for his annoying naggy personna in the game, I would've chosen many different dialogue choices, and from this comes the main gimmick of the game. Balance between the main protagonist, and Johnny.   Gameplay: Guns feel tight and there is variety, though most scopes look horrendous. While I was initially overwhelmed by the amount of details and possible interactions at any given time... I quickly realised that the actual worth of said interactions are minimal. So apart from looting chests and kills, hacking and interacting with NPCs related to quest, there's no reason to fiddle with everything. This is an obvious case of quantity over quality. Stealth is amazingly well done for how little they push it to be used... There are many ways to go about it; using TVs, cameras, vending machines, etc to distract enemies, turning off CCTVs with enough tech knowledge manually, by hacking it, or simply by finding the right terminal. You can knock out enemies if you catch them unaware and hide their bodies in lockers and dumpsters, and much, much more. While there is a level cap (both street cred and proper), I never saw an enemy's level. My guess is that this was changed in an update, and I'm unsure if it was the right call. It allows the player to go wherever and whenever, sure, but renders the whole experienced a bit disjointed.   Some objectives grant better rewards if you don't outright kill enemies, and while there are means to knock out enemies without killing them, accidentaly killing them is too easy. More specific weapons that don't kill with an extra bullet would have been nice.  There are well over 200 side quests (gigs, psychos and sidejobs). Depending on your backstory and previous choices, you may or may not have access to some, at least not on a singular playthrough. This is excluding the NCPD hustles... aaaand this is excluding the DLC. Yeah there's a lot to do. But not all is really worth doing. The character customisation at the beginning is pretty in depth, but the game is mostly 1st person (well it 100% is, apart from driving). I would still say it's worth it since you can view yourself in some critical moments. It hits different when you haven't seen yourself in around 60 hours. The cyberware section of the character is ''interesting'', as you can equip quickhacks (spells, if you like), and change some of your body up; enabling you to double jump, have blades coming out of your arms, equiping a thick boi skeleton and the likes. However it feels like a lot of the stats that the cyberware grants are superfluous.  The perks and stats points, imo, is where its at, as it will impact how you approach missions, dialogue options, extra moves and even which weapons you're more proficient with.  Graphics: Cyberpunk is very demanding, probably due to how many things are going on at once. There is no loading between areas and since the city is built vertically with neons signs everywhere who can be flickering, playing different TV stations, NPCs interacting with each other through dialogue or pure fighting... There is a never ending demand of things towards your CPU.  The game basically seems to have a hard time handling itself, much like Skyrim. Maybe their vision was too big for the tech of the time.  But back to graphics.. The game looks great, especially important characters. NC truly becomes something when night comes. But then again, everything looks better in the dark ;)  Audio: The voice overs are amazing. Even V, the main protagonist, which you hardly ever see, manages to retain a strong presence with just dialogue. I don't think people realise how hard that is!  The music is pretty good, however don't expect bangers. It's mostly industrial, tehcno and punk. While this might sound appealling, in kinda gets annoying and feels like just noise as it can get hard to isolate the music from the noise. There's no real chill moment, it's just noise, noise and noise. I remember a moment during a gig where the NPC in front of me was talking to me, someone phoned me and it automatically picked up, a small group of randoms were having a conversation next to me, my personnal radio (on the protagonist) was playing, a TV station was chatting on about some such and a portable radio was also playing. So... a quicksave was in order and I shot the place up. So yeah. sometimes too many dialogues are happening at once and can overlap each other.  NC is lively, too lively for lil' ol' me.   For a game that throws sex in your face all the time where there's romancing to be done, I had basically 4 options; to be gay, kinda gay, super gay, or straight with someone that keeps telling me to get ♥♥♥♥♥♥. I guess I'll deal with a nutcase but man... Really?! Was it that hard to have a 2nd option?! My car also got stuck inside the road, doodads could drop from the sky (tires especially, dunno why), and Jackie's bike was launched in the stratosphere after getting stuck in a fence. Enemies can also sometimes drop stuff through the floor so you can't pick it up. Bummer. Also, I dunno if it's just me, but for once the traffic works right in a game!!! While I may have sounded like the game is litered with bugs, it's really minor and my game only crashed once. All the other things are minor. There's also a ton of easter eggs, often very subtle. I also found Roach's minigame funny. Way too funny.
