[b]One of the Greatest Comeback Stories in Video Game History[/b]  I had started this when it first came out way back in 2020 on the Series X. Dropped off a few times as I was studying exams and lost track of the narrative and it remained benched.  Enter 2026! Cyberpunk 2077 is a triumph! What an insane experience to engage with this after the incredible amount of overhauling CDPR have done over the years. This, arguably is now the only way it should be played and I am SO GLAD I inadvertently waiting this long to play it.  CDPR have managed to turn something that was one of the most horrific openings of all time for a video game into something that is now in many circle regarded as a masterpiece.  The world is gorgeous and running on a suped up PC rig with path tracing is a true sight to behold. I'm over 100 hours in and still stop to admire the eye candy. More importantly is the story being told. Here we have a bleak view of the future where corporate giants rule the world crushing the environment with dangerous AI and other nefarious groups running amok. Sounds familiar right?  Cyberpunk is probably more relevant today than it ever has been. Listening to Johnny Silverhand, the incredibly cast Keanu Reeves, rant about tech giants obliterating farmland is somewhat scary as we are watching that very same thing happen in 2026 with these new large data centres.  The game pulls on so many sci-fi influences, the love it have for Neuromancer and Gibsons work is evident and there are so many little awesome easter eggs if you are already initiated. [b]Summary[/b] [hr][/hr]  I've had people recommend this game to me for years; now that I've played it I'm just utterly confused as to how anyone can find fun in this title.  It runs like it has congestive heart failure even if you have the hardware, and the gameplay is so hands-off you may as well just watch the anime.   [b]Performance[/b] [hr][/hr]  Short version, it's terribly optimized and getting consistent performance (60+fps) is impossible.  I've spent 4 hours in the actual game, the rest of my 'play time' has been benchmarking performance and trying to fine tune the controls so they aren't fighting me.  I just cannot find a way to stop the game from randomly cratering into the 20fps range.  The assumption at this point is that I'm on an i7700k (above mininum, below recommended) and that's the bottleneck.  The GPU is a 3070 (above recommended) and there's 32gb of RAM.  Even without any ray/path tracing enabled the game will never stay above 60fps for more than a few seconds.  With DLSS enabled there is brutal artifacting and ghosting, whether in the benchmark or the game proper, so that's not an option.  Basically, the system requirements mean nothing.  The game can go higher than 60fps, but it will regularly tank into the 20s regardless of settings without warning.  I set everything in the options to either off or low - even the level of detail and crowd density - at 1080p and it will still randomly tank into the 20s.  It'll hang in the 20-30s for a couple seconds, spend another 5-10s in the 40s, before 'stabilizing' between 50-60fps.  After a few minutes it will randomly hang again and struggle to recover.  The benchmark says I'm not dropping below 60fps at minimum everything settings, but the actual game experience is very different.  I get the same benchmark result at 720p with medium texture resolution as I do 1440p with high texture resolution (my 4K display maxes out at 60hz and i have the game capped at 65fps).  This is the biggest indicator of a CPU limitation.  Unfortunately, there are no settings for this outside of 'Level of Detail' and 'Crowd Density'.  In other words, I either live with it or move onto something else in my backlog.  Pretty easy choice.   [b]Controls[/b] [hr][/hr]  This was actually the most disappointing part of the entire experience.  Even if this game could get to a minimum 60fps I have my doubts about it would ever feel good to navigate.  The movement and controls are somewhere between non-functional at worst and feeling like you're under water at best.    Walking is slow, running is slow, carrying a body gives you plenty of time to consider how you could be better spending your time.  Dashing by default is an absolute mess, and driving by default is worse than that.  In fact, driving is so bad there's an auto-drive option.  Also, it's pretty much the first thing you do after character creation.  When you're at 60fps the game feels decent, but it's usually bouncing between 50 and 60 or tanking entirely.  That variability isn't helping the controls, but even when the game is hitting that 60fps they still don't feel great by any means..   [b]Gameplay[/b] [hr][/hr]  The play experience is more akin to a visual novel than an FPS.  I know it's supposed to have RPG elements but I was really unprepared for how little game there is to play.  You mostly listen to other people talk, which can't be skipped and more frustratingly is broken up where characters will expect you to say something.  Sometimes you don't have to, other times they'll pester you until you respond (quips such as 'are you listening?' and the like).  You can't even walk down the street without hearing some random NPC polluting your ears with useless drek.  It all becomes noise very fast.  When you do get to do something other than respond to dialogue, it feels like executing a checklist.  Remember how people hated always having to go into detective mode in Arkham Asylum?  Here it's called scan mode and it's equally annoying.  Want to open a door?  You'll probably have to scan it and do something else first.  It's easier to steal a car - which hilariously also involves opening a door - but doing that would involve driving.  It rarely feels like you can just do something, there always seems to be a process attached to it.  The combat is fine, which is as much a criticism as much as it is a compliment.  You have guns and can shoot stuff.  The game really expects you to employ a variety of stealth and hacking techniques to overcome a lot of the challenges.  Once again, that's a process and it is rarely as simple or quick as violence.  This is probably why the combat feels so tepid.  A feature that's oddly missing is a custom radio channel.  You need a mod to have a custom radio channel, which is a feature indie companies with a fraction of the budget have integrated without issue.  I guess they really want to make sure all the money spent on copyrighted music was worth it (music is subjective, but I feel they wasted their money).  My big critique - outside of some more options to ease the strain on the CPU - is the field of view slider maxing out at 100.  This is unacceptable and makes the game feel claustrophobic regardless of where you set it.     [b]The Good:[/b] [hr][/hr]  The game does have its positive elements; they simply don't matter when the overall experience is so poor.  The graphics are nice, even at low details, and I particularly really like all of the neon colours.  The character models are nice (especially with the graphics kicked up to high), and the voice work is quite well done for them.  I wish more games had an options menu as extensive as this, it's generally quite comprehensive.  At this point I don't think any amount of tweaking will ever make this game feel good to play, but I really do appreciate the vast options.     [b]Conclusion:[/b] [hr][/hr]  Ultimately then, I guess there are two things that this game accomplished.  The first is that I spent enough time trying to get stable performance and proper controls that I'm no longer eligible for a refund - something I wasn't even thinking about initially as I was expecting to enjoy this title.    The second accomplishment is that freeing up 70gb of hard drive space means I can install some games that aren't fighting me every step of the way to do the most basic of things.  They might even be fun.

I'm not much of a guy for story games, but this is genuinely one of the greatest games I have ever played. [hr][/hr] [h1]GENERAL RATINGS: [/h1] [h2]Story: [/h2] Incredibly well-written. The story is genuinely so interesting that even side missions, gigs, or those random data chips with archived conversations are worth looking into. In fact, even though I'm a guy who usually spams the skip button, I like to occasionally take the time to learn about Cyberpunk, it's lore, and even some of the more nitty-gritty details with things like Maximum Mike, the Cyberpunk 2020 TTRPG, etc.  [i] - Side note: You should 100% check out the anime/show Cyberpunk Edgerunners. In game, I also recommend setting your radio to 107.3 Morro Rock Radio, as it's basically a podcast of theories by "Maximum Mike," voiced by Mike Pondsmith, the original creator of the Cyberpunk Series. [/i]  [h2]Graphics: [/h2] Top-tier with an amazing environment to simply roam around in, but slightly rig dependent if you want something truly amazing. Still, it can look amazing even on the lowest settings.  [h2]Gameplay Loop and Upgrades: [/h2] Pre-2.0 I heard that the gameplay loop wasn't the greatest, with a stale upgrade system that never gave anything meaningful. Now, it has been fleshed out so that almost every single major module makes it feel like you didn't waste time grinding for a higher level.  [h2]DLC: [/h2] Genuinely amazing. I consider this one of the best DLC/Expansions made for a game. It's a true expansion with a new part of the map that flips the experience of Night City on its head while still keeping the dark cyberpunk vibe. Ending was open-ended, which some people consider bad. Personally, I think it was one of the better endings. [hr][/hr] [h1]MISC. RATINGS: [/h1] [h2]Complaints: [/h2] The only thing that is truly missing here is maybe some depth with a few fixers around the map, as I would have loved to see more from fixers like El Capitán. Gigs were awesome overall though (however, some of the NCPD scanner missions did get stale after a little bit). Still though, the game only feels like a grind if YOU choose to grind.  [h2]My Experience in a Nutshell: [/h2] Currently, I have around 90 hours on it and I have almost 100% finished the game aside from 2 of the DLC endings, of which I plan to complete on my new second playthrough. This game is able to perfectly balance a linear story that you can quickly complete, as well as an immersive open-world that you can spend tens if not hundreds of hours in if you choose to.  [h1]Final Remarks: [/h1] This game may not be perfect, but no matter what people say, I can confidently say that this game will not be a waste of your time if you simply give it a try (and that includes the absolutely amazing DLC that is Phantom Liberty).

When I first played the game, the bugs utterly killed any interest I could have had for it. A crafting error wiped my entire nine hour save and I had no interest in playing it again. Then Phantom Liberty dropped a few years ago, and people were calling it one of the best games of the decade; I remained unconvinced, because I’m a stubborn bastard. Then, recently, I reinstalled it on a whim when there was a lull in my backlog. I figured if they fixed all the major bugs, there’s no harm in giving it another shot, right? I don’t lose another sixty dollars.  That turned out to be one of the best decisions I’ve made in my entire life. I say this to you, dear reader, with no hyperbole, no sensationalist overhyping or overselling of facts: Cyberpunk 2077 is one of the greatest games I have ever had the pleasure of playing.   Mike Pondsmith’s gritty, dark and morally-corrupt neon-concrete playground comes truly alive. It’s simply one of those games that you can completely lose yourself in; I spent about a five hour stretch just walking through Night City, no car, just strolling one end of town down the other and back, walking down the street and taking in the sights and vibes. I didn’t even realize I did it at first until I heard birds chirping outside my window, and my first thought wasn’t “holy crap, it’s morning now”, it was “wait a minute, there’s no birds in Corpo Plaza”.   It isn’t just the visuals or themes that completely sell me, the narrative is utterly gripping. Even the most unassuming side quest will suddenly grab you by the throat and make you question your ideals in a city that thrives on grinding them into paste. I went from disassociating after dealing with a vile serial killer, to playing laser tag with my friend’s kids at a cookout, and the very next day I talked a sentient car off a ledge after disposing of some corpo’s body for the Japanese mob. Take your time and do all the side content you can, because all of them have little nuggets of gold in them. You will completely regret it if you just do the main story. When you do work at the main story, I strongly suggest you get to know Johnny Silverhand; he’s a remarkably deep lake of insight and character development where I initially saw a jerkass puddle of self-importance. He steals the show in literally every scene he is in - which is a lot, considering he can jump into them at any time he feels like.  You do yourself a disservice if you don’t dedicate a portion of your time to this game. I’m not ashamed to admit it’s life-altering, and the kind of person that comes out of the other end of NC is based solely on your choices, which is refreshing in an industry seemingly built on the illusion of choice.  Welcome to the City of Dreams. You won’t regret it.

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ I bought Cyberpunk 2077 expecting to become a chrome-plated mercenary who would cruise through Night City in style, make millions of eddies, and look cool doing it. Instead... I spent the first hour admiring my character in every mirror, accidentally punched a random civilian trying to open a door, got flattened by a car while crossing the street, and somehow still felt like the coolest person alive. Night City has a funny way of making you feel unstoppable one minute and completely insignificant the next. One mission has you blasting through enemies with an arsenal that would make an army jealous. The next has you sitting on a rooftop, talking to someone about life, regret, and the choices that brought them there. And that's when the game quietly sneaks up on you. I came for the explosions, the cyberware, the fast cars, and the overpowered builds.  I stayed because of the people.  Every character feels like they have a life outside of your story. Some make you laugh, some frustrate you, and some leave a mark that stays with you long after the credits roll. Even the smallest side gigs often tell stories that are more emotional than entire games.  Then there's Johnny Silverhand.  At first, he's the last person you'd want living in your head. Sarcastic, arrogant, constantly reminding you that your life isn't exactly going according to plan. But somewhere along the way, without even realizing it, the arguments become conversations, the conversations become understanding, and the understanding becomes friendship. I never expected to care so much about someone who technically shouldn't even exist.  Night City itself deserves its own award.  It's beautiful, chaotic, cruel, loud, vibrant, and strangely comforting all at once. Every alley has a story. Every neon sign hides another tragedy. Every district feels alive, whether you're racing through it at full speed or simply walking with the radio playing in the background.  For all its violence and chaos, Cyberpunk 2077 constantly asks one simple question:  **"What kind of person do you want to be when the world is trying to turn you into something else?"** Very few games have made me laugh as much as this one. Very few games have made me stop moving just to listen to a conversation. And very, very few games have left me staring at the credits, not because I was waiting for a post-credit scene... but because I wasn't ready to say goodbye.  Cyberpunk 2077 isn't just about saving Night City.  It's about finding pieces of yourself in a city that never stops taking from people. I thought I was buying an open-world RPG. I ended up with memories I'll probably carry for years.  **10/10.**  *"Goodbye, Night City... and thanks for reminding me that even in a world full of chrome, it's still the human moments that matter most."*  And one more thing the both games from CD projekt games (you know what is another one) are amazing at first fells somewhat boring, if you continue your journey you can fell the story, character, narration. Superb game. From the multiple endings and choices/dialogue matters (especially with Johnny), the visuals, the degree of customization in gameplay (weapons, cyberware, attributes, skills...), you can truly make this game's story yours. The endings really make you think hard about your choices and your beliefs as well, which I love in a game. Lots of interesting choices to make as well. Often, all choices are grey, nothing is black or white in this world, which makes everything so much more real and believable.  Enormous amount of stuff to do, whether it be main storyline or beyond that (100h of gameplay and I am nearing the end of all side quests now + finished DLC).   The gameplay is incredible, there are so many different ways to play and fight depending on what you like, so any gamer should find a way (if not multiple) to play that is satisfying for them. Quite a few combats were hard (especially boss fights) where I'd have to give it a few try, but nothing is extremely out of your reach or requires hours on the same fight, at least, on normal mode.   Phantom Liberty DLC: Really recommend playing it. First, you get so much more opportunity to talk to Johnny, which could help you within the main story and what choices you make with him (I played the dlc after the main story so it didn't help me particularly, but I wished I did for that reason). The DLC story on its own is really good as well, with yet again some hard choices to make. Also, Mr Hands by far my fav fixer, lol. I like that it unlocks the Relic too, it gives additional skills to work for. DLC completed in 30h (all quests and side stuff).  Visuals on high settings on my current specs, no lagging, looked really beautiful as well. Took quite a few screenshots to make my wallpaper! Music as well is incredible (shoutout to the Choke Hold instrumental when you play Hansen, what an absolute bop).  Really want to read the book now!  Context: Finished the main game about 2 years ago, and just downloaded the DLC and finished it now.  Finished all missions, storylines and side gigs of the DLC, and almost finish on side gigs in the main game. I didn't play when the game came out and was super buggy, so I avoided the worst of it! In the state that I played it, I didn't really see any bugs. If they were some, they were small, and could easily be bypassed.

The storyline of Cyberpunk 2077 is absolutely gripping from beginning to end. It's packed with intense action, emotional moments, memorable characters, and major plot twists that keep you invested throughout the entire game. Every main mission feels meaningful, and the story does an excellent job of balancing fast-paced combat with quieter moments that help build the world and the relationships between characters.  One of the game's biggest strengths is the amount of player choice. Your decisions throughout the story can affect how certain events unfold, how characters react to you, and ultimately which ending you receive. With multiple different endings available, each playthrough can feel unique, encouraging players to replay the game and make different choices to experience outcomes they may have missed the first time.  Even after completing the main storyline, there is still an incredible amount of content to enjoy. Players can continue exploring Night City, complete side jobs, discover hidden locations, take on gigs from fixers, purchase vehicles and apartments, upgrade cyberware, and uncover countless secrets scattered throughout the world. The side content is so well developed that it often feels just as engaging as the main story, adding even more depth to the overall experience.  Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 delivers a thrilling and highly replayable story. Its combination of action-packed missions, meaningful player choices, multiple endings, and a huge amount of post-story content makes it a game that players can continue enjoying long after the credits roll.

I saw the memes and funny glitches from the first release of the game (hardy-har-har npcs go brrrrrrr), and that in itself was quite entertaining. I was lucky enough that my friend bought me this as a Christmas gift when the game was polished enough. I'd watched many tutorials and thought of some fun builds before I even launched the game for the first time.  Aside from all that though- let me ask you something: Who are you when you're near the end of your life, and what does it mean to leave a legacy behind you? How does that affect your views on family, on fame and fortune, on forgiveness and second chances, and on your values and what you choose to fight for? Cyberpunk 2077 answers many of these questions BEAUTIFULLY. I'll put money down to say this is one of the best written narratives in gaming history. The storylines, NPCs, and diverging paths are all written and detailed so so well! And thats just for the story! HA! As for the combat? OH GOOD GOD THE COMBAT!! You can stealth, throw knives, fire big-ass machine guns, hack your enemies, lure them to  a gas tank and blow it up, or slice and dice with Mantis blades- There's so many awesome weapons and cyberware that you'll find your own incredibly satisfying ways to flatline an average Maelstrom gonk down in Watson, zero some Tygers in Japantown, or clear out a Maxtac Squad! Do what you want- there really are no bad picks to fighting as long as you have the skills, upgrades, chrome, and eddies. NOW let me get to the best part of Cyberpunk itself, in my opinion- Night City. Where legends rise and fall every day. There are all sorts of little side missions scattered around, but if you really want to experience this game for yourself- get your favorite vehicle and gear and just explore. Search every nook and cranny- or sit next to a campfire in the wastelands if the noise is too much for you. CDProjectRed studied actual city layouts and dynamics, making the enviornments here some of the most immersive and beautiful you will ever see. I like to stand at a balcony over Japantown or find some other cozy overlooks. I promise you will find some spectauclar views, restaurants, and places to chill. Remember to use the in-game camera mode to really save your memories and spectacular views with this game! I really could go on ENDLESSLY gushing here. Since playing I've watched Edgerunners and purchased the No Coincidence novel. Might even buy some enamel pins for my outings. This truly is one of the greatest franchises in gaming. Please save up your money experience this game. Tell me about it if you can!  Lastly- CMAC, if you're reading this, you're one of my best Chooms. Thanks for this gift. If the game ever updates with multiplayer or something like that, I'll drive us down to The Afterlife for a drink.

Over the past six years, I've played countless singleplayer games, but very few have ever convinced me to come back for a second playthrough. Yet here I am in 2026, starting my fourth run of Cyberpunk 2077.  What sets Cyberpunk 2077 apart is the incredible amount of detail poured into Night City. If you slow down and simply walk the streets instead of rushing missions, the world tells its own story. You can see the effects of poverty, unchecked corporate power, and political corruption everywhere you look. It's a bleak but incredibly believable setting that feels alive in a way few games ever achieve.  I bought the game on day one, and I'll be the first to admit it had a rough launch. Performance issues and missing systems (infamous police spawning out of nowhere) which hurt the immersion and overshadowed what was already a fantastic foundation. To CD Projekt Red's credit, they've spent years improving and refining the game into the masterpiece it was always capable of becoming.  In my opinion, Cyberpunk 2077 is one of those rare single-player experiences that I can revisit again and again without getting bored. It stands alongside games like Fallout: New Vegas, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, and Abiotic Factor as one of the most detailed and immersive worlds I've had the pleasure of exploring.  TLDR: Cyberpunk 2077 has grown from a rough launch into one of the most immersive and replayable single-player games I've ever played, with a world that rewards every moment you spend exploring it.

[h1] Cyberpunk 2077 is a gem everyone should try. [/h1]  I'm going to preface this review by saying yes, it had a very rough launch. But it has had massive overhauls and the game feels how it was meant to on release. The bugs are now little to none.  [b]Night City is a masterpiece of art.[/b] Driving through the neon streets is an experience I have not felt in any other experience of media. It truly feels alive, with so many people, side jobs, gigs, NCPD scans you can do, there is so much content to experience.  The 2.0 update and cyberware changes solidified the combat as [b]satisfying[/b] and [b]rewarding[/b]. You can tailor it to how you wish to play, whether you wish to be a net-runner, a cyber-samurai or go in guns blazing, the game allows you to. For most (~90%) of missions in the game you can pick how you want to play and will not need to worry about being stealthy or having to go in loud if you don't want to. The combat is a blast to play.  [b]The story is gut wrenching.[/b] The characters, especially those like Johnny feel very real. It's a gripping story that will take you through the difficult journey of V's life as to how they became what they are. There are many ending choices for this game, and many of them are very good and provide a very satisfying ending for V's story. [spoiler] Not the suicide ending, that one sucks [/spoiler]   [h1] Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty [/h1]  The DLC adds a large amount of new story content for you to play, also fun new gigs and missions. Going through the journey with Reed and Songbird is a new experience every new and old cyberpunk fan should experience.   After the significant changes, updates and the Phantom Liberty expansion, Cyberpunk 2077 has turned into a polished and immersive story driven experience within a well designed Night City. [b]You should play this game.[/b]

I'm obviously a few years late to this, but for $20 on discount this an amazing value. It's a perfect mix of Deux Ex (Human Revolution) and Fallout, but with actually good gunplay. Like Fallout there is a lot of inventory management (and obsessive looting!), there's a quickhack system that works at lot like VATS, and there's an encouragement towards stealth but really only as a means of landing big critical hits. And like DEHR you can customize the cyberware all over your body in pretty much the same ways and it shares a lot of subject matter and themes (also borrowing HEAVILY from Neuromancer). DEHR is, I think, a much more literate approach to this subject matter but Cyberpunk is a much more cohesive and entertaining final product.  The roleplaying element is honestly quite light - attributes and perks can be reallocated at any time - and it's easy to quickly become so over-leveled that the combat presents absolutely no challenge. Often to an amusing or frustrating degree, as a mission may spend 15-20 minutes of dialogue and prep in advance of what is built up as a big, difficult battle, and then it turns out to be like 8 guys who you can 1-shot. Cyberwear quick hacks honestly feel like they are game-breakingly unbalanced, as you can kill multiple enemies just be looking at them in your scanner.   If the game has a major weak spot, its in the vehicles/driving. Combat in vehicles stinks (especially the on-rails sections from the main quest), All the vehicles handle terribly, and you'll have to do a lot of driving because Night City is very big. It's also quite empty. I know that it would have just been too much of a technological burden to make it more crowded, but you'll often be the only car on the road. You can drive at top speed in a straight line on the highway without even having to swerve. There's an obvious comp to GTA here; cars and driving are much more integral to the core gameplay in those games than they are here. I wound up using the fast travel nodes as much as possible.  The main appeal is the main quest, which deals with a lot of ideas and tropes from the cyberpunk genre. In some ways this feels like a HOPEFUL vision of the future, and in most ways it's very much the opposite. The writing and performance is overall quite strong. I did think a few characters felt a little off - Panam especially. She sounds way too educated and articulate for a streetwise desert nomad. V (the male version) also seems to alternate in and out of an east coast streetwise accent. Overall, small complaints. The big miss in the acting is Keanu Reeves. He is who he is at this point, and he's just a very low-energy, monotone kind of actor. He gives that same sort of performance here and, like the driving, it's not very exciting.

To be fair, I'd recommend checking this game out on a deep deep sale, as it's more like "an interesting phenomenon". I don't think it's a good game in traditional sense.  The whole thing is rather barebones and janky, but it poses as something much bigger, using smoke and mirrors, and the good old bluff. The facade of beautiful environments, film set lighting, and great music hides a non-reactive world, poorly re-cut (version 2.0) dialogue, and illusion of choice and consequence, where all the major decisions and relationships can be turned around in the last mission (depending on who you choose to help you). Stealth is janky, as is climbing and driving. RPG systems are poorly explained, crafting and upgrading is meaningless, as differences in tiers are in tenths of a percent. Some things, like quickhack vendors, aren't explained at all.  By the way, fans who are trying to frame the DLC and fixes as similar to No Man's Sky comeback story are kidding themselves. Hello Games actually sat down and wrote the systems they lied about prior release. CDPR fixed missing assets, added a few minor features like multiple apartments, and that's mostly it. You can see a shadow of collosal ambition of the creators here, in both the scale of the open world, art direction, and the themes within the narrative. Remember, at some point CDPR said they should be capable of reaching RDR2 level of quality. Maybe that's why it is interesting phenomenon, more as a record of collective delusion, an internal (and possibly mid-life) crisis in CDPR ranks.  As a game, it will leave you frustrated, more often than not, because you'll be tricked into thinking that you can do much more, and have much more choice than you actually have.

I'm glad I waited to pick this up. The game is far from the tragic mess it was at launch, and I really enjoyed my time in Night City. I spent entirely too much time making outfits. I saw pretty much everything I wanted to; I did almost all of the side quests and gigs (didn't go out of my way for the NCPD jobs), plus Phantom Liberty. Some of the side quests were really cool, and honestly more interesting than some of the main story missions. The game asks you to make some *tough* choices, and in the end, you're still not sure if you made the right decisions.   I did get some ludonarrative dissonance. You're supposed to be in a bit of a rush after Act 1, but there's [i]so[/i] much you can do, and [spoiler]there won't be consequences for taking your sweet, sweet time. I wonder if there's a way they could have added some pressure outside of story missions? Maybe actual debuffs from random malfunctions? I felt a bit too healthy.[/spoiler]  I played a stealth netrunner build, going for nonlethal takedowns when possible, and shotgun blasts when not. By endgame, I felt kind of unstoppable. Big contrast to early game when I was just a dude with a gun and had nothing in my toolkit to deal with enemy cyberware. Some of the higher tier quickhacks have super cool combinations with each other. Some of the mechanics weren't terribly well-explained, though, and I had to spend more time outside of the game than I think I should have to figure them out. For example, some quickhacks get cheaper after reducing enemy trace progress; I still don't know how to do that lol.  Some of the RPG systems felt underutilized or half-baked. Lifepaths and dialogue choices rarely made a difference. Crafting never felt particularly worth it (besides a few iconic blueprints; Yinglong rules). By the time you could craft higher tier gear, they were already dropping as loot. It's weird that we couldn't customize the look of the weapons, either. You can pick up a sick, hot pink Mox-themed weapon off the street, but you can't choose which "skin" the stuff you craft gets? Bummer. Having nearly every box contain Tier X crafting components felt a bit lame, but at least I didn't need to maintain a "shopping list" of required materials like I did for Horizon Zero Dawn back in the day. Lots of literal junk, too; maybe those could have had lore attached to them, Dark Souls style. That said, there was already [i]so[/i] much lore laying around. I don't know how much of 230 hours of playtime was skimming data shards, but I'm sure it was a lot.  Performance was mostly fine, for me, if a bit CPU heavy. I was able to stay around 60 FPS with RT medium and HDR (with RenoDX) at 4K with FSR 4 Performance upscaling, and the game looked fantastic with those settings. There were bugs (invite [spoiler]Kerry[/spoiler] to the Glen apartment for a surprise), and I did have more random crashes than I would have liked (photo mode was rough), but the game saved frequently enough that it was usually only an inconvenience. There seemed to be some VRAM leaks, however, and I'd occasionally get nasty overflow hitches when opening or closing the map.  Anyway, thank you for reading my rambling. Cyberpunk 2077 was fun, and if you're at all interested, I think it's worth your time and eddies.

Compared to CD Projekt Red’s other blockbuster game, The Witcher III: Wild Hunt, I feel that Cyberpunk 2077 is a worse RPG, shorter, and less complex. Despite all of this, I had more fun playing Cyberpunk than The Witcher. I will start with what I considered the weaker parts of the game, and work up to why I enjoyed playing Cyberpunk more than The Witcher.  I felt that the story wasn’t all too interesting. An alright concept to give your character a set time limit to give the player a sense of urgency, however the game does not incorporate an actual time limit on the player. Despite the story telling you explicitly that you have a short time, you are free to do whatever you want, for however much time you want. One of my favorite games is The Legend of Zelda: Majora’s Mask, and it’s core gameplay gimmick is the 3-day time cycle. You are not able to save everyone in one run, thus making the choices you make on a cycle-by-cycle basis have more weight. I would’ve liked to see something similar here, just on a larger scale. Especially given one of my favorite aspects of the game that I will get into greater detail later.  I adored the world/setting, as well as the secondary characters way more than the core story. It is such a brilliantly vivid world with incredibly detailed, well-written, and superbly voice acted characters with defined goals and personalities. Very few games got me to legitimately care for it’s characters as effectively as this game did. I was devastated whenever a character I liked was either killed or faced difficulties.  Moving on from the narrative points, let me touch on the gameplay, starting with the core gameplay loop. I found leveling up way too fast and easy. I made it to the max level (50) after about 3 hours after just driving around doing minor events (NCPD Scanners, Cyberpsychos, and Gigs [Which, on a side note, were incredibly repetitive and boring. They all boiled down to simply going to an area, and either killing everyone, or stealthing through to retrieve something or someone, and that is all.]).  By this point I still didn’t even know how I wanted to play the game, what build to aim for, as I was still experimenting with the mechanics of the game. This wouldn’t be much of a problem if the game had a way to redistribute (or respec) your skills/attributes to test out different builds to determine which suits your playstyle, but it doesn’t seem to (at least not in base game, as I do not own the DLC). Despite all of this, my balanced, directionless build was overwhelming overpowered, mowing down anyone and everyone in my path at normal difficulty. I had to increase the difficult because the game just got way to easy after about 5 hours of gameplay at normal difficulty.  I also had way more in-game currency (Eddies) than I knew what to do with. The game has 4 major things you can buy with your Eddies: Apartments, Vehicles, Weapons, and Cybernetic Upgrades. Only one of these are worth it; Cybernetics. Apartments provide no new gameplay mechanics, and you are never required to return to your apartment for anything, and the game showers you with free vehicles and weapons that spending any money on those is unnecessary.  On the topic of weapons, I think it’s finally time to move on to why I enjoy this game as much as I do. Sure there are still several nitpicks, such as the bugs that persist beyond it’s many patches, terrible NPC AI, clunky feeling controls in some places, and the narrative focus on first-person that I do not entirely agree with, but let’s not dwell on those, and get to the good stuff.  This game has such an immense variety of weapons that it rivals looter-shooters. Regardless of the playstyle you prefer, there is a weapon just for you in the game, all you need to do is find it. And even if you cannot find it, you can modify one and get close to your vision. This game makes collecting and experimenting guns such a blast, for lack of a better term.  Additionally, and quite possibly it’s most powerful aspect is it’s variety in builds. The game has so many different builds that allows absolute freedom in player expression. You can build a tank, a rogue, sniper, netrunner, melee-only, grenadier, etc. I am certain no two playthroughs will be exactly the same.  And these two major points – the looter-shooter-like gun collecting, and variety in builds – coupled with the fact that the game is somewhat short with multiple endings results in a highly replayable game.  Let me give you a small peak into my brain. Some of my most played games throughout the years (Gmod, Skyrim, Super Smash Bros Ultimate, The Sims, the Star Wars Battlefront series, Team Fortress 2, Fortnite, etc.) are all games that I call ‘power saving brain games,’ or ‘uber-casual games.’ Although for the most part I will not consider my favorite games, I still have clocked the most amount of time in them because of their low-commitment, and varied gameplay. Either through mods, or updates, I see myself coming back to these games when I have nothing else to play, or whenever I am bored and just want to hop into a game, burn some time, and hop out.  With this in mind, I adored my time in Night City, and certainly see myself returning sooner rather than later. I am putting off that return until I purchase the DLC as it seems to add a lot of additional content include several new endings. I have a lot of other games to keep me busy in the meantime.  I give Cyberpunk 2077:  8.3 Johnny Silverhands bragging about his penis out of 10  If you are reading this, and plan on getting this game, the I would definitely advise to put off the small events such as NCPD Scanners, Cyberpsychos, and Gigs. Let them either 1) occur naturally, or 2) when you need the levels or Eddies. Don’t just rush in and get them out of the way ASAP, as you will level way faster than the story intends, and you will find yourself with nothing to do later when the story requires for several days to pass before advancing.

I’ve unlocked all the achievements in Cyberpunk 2077, and I can honestly say it was an unforgettable experience. The game has so many meaningful side stories that add real depth to the main plot and make Night City feel alive. Some of these stories stayed with me even after I stopped playing.  What I enjoyed most was how often the game made me think about difficult moral decisions. I usually prefer playing characters with paladin-like qualities—loyalty, kindness, honor, and a strong sense of justice. However, we are still a mercenary trying to survive in a brutal world.  At times, I tried to act like a noble and honorable person, helping others and staying loyal to the people close to me. In other situations, the game made me feel more like a death knight from World of Warcraft—driven by anger, revenge, and the desire to punish those who had caused suffering. This contrast made many choices feel personal, because they reflected real-life struggles between doing what is right, protecting yourself, staying loyal, or giving in to anger.  The combat is fun and satisfying, although I wish more cyberware options were available to the player. Some characters have unique cybernetic arms, legs, hands, and other visible modifications that we cannot use ourselves. More cosmetic cyberware would make character customization feel even more personal and immersive.  Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 is a fantastic game with an emotional story, memorable characters, and choices that can genuinely make you reflect on your own values. I’m really looking forward to the sequel and seeing where this world goes next.

This game is a masterpiece. ☐ A broken launch turned into a legend ☐ Flatlined  THE REAL REVIEW Before anything, let me say this is my third playthrough of Cyberpunk 2077. This was the first game I ever pre-ordered. I played it on PC at launch, and even with all the problems, I still loved the story, music, characters, and world. I would have given it a 9/10 back then, but I always felt like something was missing. I played it again in 2021 and felt the same way, so I left it alone and waited for it to become the best version of itself, which honestly, in this industry, usually never happens. This year, I replayed it with all the updates and Phantom Liberty, and damn, it completely blew me away. Now I understand why people call Cyberpunk 2077 one of the biggest comeback stories in modern gaming.  BASE GAME: CYBERPUNK 2077 The strongest part of the base game is Night City itself. It feels alive, dangerous, beautiful, depressing, stylish, and hopeless all at once. Every neon sign, back alley, market, megabuilding, and corpo tower adds to the feeling that you are living inside a dystopian future controlled by corporations, gangs, technology, and survival. The story is one of the game's biggest strengths. Playing as V, you get pulled into a world of crime, ambition, body modification, identity, and desperation. The relationship between V and Johnny Silverhand gives the story its heart. At first, Johnny feels like a problem forced into your head, but over time, that dynamic becomes much more personal and emotional. Gameplay has improved a lot compared to launch. Combat now feels fast, stylish, and flexible. You can play as a netrunner, stealth assassin, gunslinger, melee fighter, or mix everything together. I chose a netrunner build, and hacking enemies, spreading quickhacks, controlling the battlefield, and combining cyberware with smart weapons made every fight feel different. The music is probably my favourite part. I genuinely believe music can make or break any game, movie, or media property, and Cyberpunk 2077 absolutely gets it right. The score by Marcin Przybylowicz, P.T. Adamczyk, and Paul Leonard-Morgan becomes part of Night City itself. It gives the city its pulse, sadness, aggression, and identity. Tracks like The Rebel Path, V, Outsider No More, Been Good to Know Ya, and Bells of Laguna Bend carry so much emotion. The radio music is also incredible. Songs like 4ÆM, Never Fade Away, Delicate Weapon, Major Crimes, Kill Kill, PON-PON ♥♥♥♥, and I Really Want to Stay at Your House make Night City feel like a real place with its own culture and sound. Even the gang and faction themes are amazing. Scavenger Hunt sounds dirty and uncomfortable, the Valentinos themes have style and rhythm, Maelstrom sounds violent and industrial, and Militech feels heavy and tactical. The gangs do not just look different; they sound different.  PHANTOM LIBERTY - THE BEST DLC/EXPANSION I HAVE PLAYED Phantom Liberty makes Cyberpunk 2077 even better. It adds a spy-thriller story that feels darker, tighter, and more mature than many parts of the base game. The story is full of tension, betrayal, difficult choices, and morally grey characters. It constantly makes you question who you should trust. Dogtown is a brilliant addition. It feels more lawless, unstable, and dangerous than the rest of Night City. The missions are more focused and cinematic, with a strong mix of stealth, action, hacking, exploration, and decision-making. It does not feel like side content; it feels like an essential part of the full Cyberpunk experience. The music in Phantom Liberty is unbelievable. The score by P.T. Adamczyk and Jacek Paciorkowski perfectly matches the spy-thriller tone. It feels tense, emotional, mysterious, and dangerous, almost like James Bond filtered through Cyberpunk's darker world. I'm a Netrunner, Contra la Luna, Force Projection, Hardest to Be, Gate K9, Just Another Weapon, and Phantom Liberty are all bangers.  ISSUES Cyberpunk 2077 is still not perfect. My main issue is that random NPCs can still feel a bit bland. Night City looks alive and immersive, but some NPC behaviour does not always match the quality of the world around them. It is not a huge problem for me, but I noticed it.  FINAL THOUGHTS Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 has had its ups and downs, but playing it in 2026 with all the updates and improvements, it genuinely feels like a masterpiece. It has incredible world-building, strong characters, stylish combat, emotional storytelling, unforgettable music, and one of the best cities in gaming. It may have started as a disappointment for many people, but today it feels like the game it was always meant to be. For me, after three playthroughs, it has become one of the most memorable gaming experiences I have ever had. Cyberpunk 2077 is not just a great comeback story. It is now one of the best open-world RPGs I have played.  Base Game: 9.5/10 Phantom Liberty: 10/10

Hey Chooms,   I was one of those people who wrote this game off years ago after its disastrous launch. It took lots of convincing from multiple friends for me to finally give this game a shot (once the game + DLC went on deep sale). I am glad I waited all these years for the game to be ironed out and fixed, but I also feel like I have missed out on something the past few years. I have just completed the game + DLC after 75 hours, and left a lot of side missions and gigs on the table in the base game and have been told there are a lot of small things I missed, but that content can wait for a second playthrough eventually.  It took me awhile to get into the game, roughly 10-15 hours before it finally hooked me and made me want to come back and keep playing. The characters are fun and enjoyable to speak and interact with. I do wish there were more characters to develop friendships/relationships with but there are still plenty by modern game standards. I think Mass Effect has just ruined my expectations in terms of relationships/companions in video games. There is a heap of side characters that give you side jobs/gigs and some of them are genuinely really funny and interesting. The main story has plenty of twists and turns depending on how you do things in what feels like a way most games nowadays do not do, which gives this game probably hundreds of hours of replayability to those who really sink into this. I think there is something along the lines of 7 or 8 endings for this game so, there are plenty of ways to tackle the main narrative of the game.  The game's build variety is top notch. I feel like I barely scratched the surface of the possibilities. I opted to do a more run and gun shoot first and ask questions later style. The gun play is smooth and all of the different ranged/melee weapons feel unique and different with various upgrades and attachments. I ended up using the same few guns for most of my playthrough but mainly because I just enjoyed them so much. The hacking in the game is something I wish I invested in a bit more for my first playthrough, as there are some seriously game breaking whacky stuff you can do with it. Exploring the hacking more will have to wait for my second playthrough.   The game has plenty of vehicles and character apartments to choose from and purchase. Admittedly I did not really spend time exploring this stuff because I was just enjoying playing the game but now that I finished the game and am rich, ill go back and take a look at all of that stuff. Driving in the game feels just ok? Its nothing to write home about. Feels very GTA-like. The cops in the game are a complete afterthought which is disappointing. A lot of the time the cops just spawn behind/in front of you once you get wanted which just feels bad/lame. Feels like a missed opportunity to have cool chrome-juiced cops tracking you down or doing anything other than trying to chase you. If you break line of sight, they forget about you very quick. The cops really only care once you start killing civilians or once you ram a cop car. Speeding and breaking road laws right in front of them does nothing.   This review is already really long. If you like immersive RPGs, big open worlds, cyberpunk aesthetic and large branching narrative games you will enjoy this game. Getting the base game + DLC on sale for roughly $30 feels like a really good deal. This is not a game without faults, but its a good ride.

I’m only around 13 hours into Cyberpunk 2077 so far, but I’m already properly hooked.  Night City is easily the best part for me. It genuinely feels massive, crowded and alive, and I keep getting distracted from the main story because there is always something happening nearby. I’ll set a waypoint for a mission, then somehow spend the next hour doing random gigs, buying cyberware or just driving around looking at the city 💀  A few things I really like so far:  - Night City looks absolutely incredible - The story and characters are actually keeping me interested - Gunplay feels satisfying once you find weapons you like - Cyberware gives you loads of ways to customise your build - Side missions feel like proper content instead of filler - The soundtrack and radio stations fit the world perfectly - Driving around at night with all the neon lights looks unreal - There are loads of different ways to approach fights  The amount of choice in how you build your character is probably what has surprised me most. You can focus on normal weapons, hacking, stealth, blades or just run directly into everyone and hope for the best. I’m still figuring out what kind of build I want, but experimenting with different abilities has been really fun.  The characters also feel much more memorable than I expected. Absolutely.  Cyberpunk 2077 has a brilliant world, interesting characters and loads of freedom in how you play. After beating the game like four separate times, I'd say this: It railroads you hard, and tries to make it seem like it doesn't, and that's frustrating. The game is full of "press button to advance plot" sections and it gets annoying. Most of the life path dialogue options are just flavor. At most an NPC might say one addition line of dialogue and then say exactly what they would have said if you chose any other option. Most of the skill-related dialogue options are the same as above. Most of the skillchecks in general are redundant. Have 20 body stat? You can pry open a door to get into a room. Or you could walk 10 feet to the left and crawl through a hatch to do the same thing. Nearly every quest, be it main quest or side quest, has this false sense of urgency attached to it. Characters make it seem like you need to hurry up or you'll miss the quest, but there are only like 3 quests in the entire game that are actually time sensitive.  The combat is really fun though. There's a ton of side content to do. Different playstyles give completely different experiences. A lot of the characters are really well written, and NPC dialogue is really good.  Though V's dialogue can be very melodramatic at times. It's a bit jarring.  All-in-all, this game suffers from a lot of issues, but it's a fun experience if you take it at face value. Do not be under any illusion that you are going to be able to make any real meaningful choices in this game, because outside of a few quests, you have no real options. Nothing you can do affects the story in any meaningful way. You are on a rollercoaster ride. It's fun, but your cart is running on rails. Wait for a sale, don't buy it at full price.

This is possibly one of the best games I have ever played, completely immersing yourself in the world of Night City and making myself a walking GOD was an incredible experience.  I have to admit though, I played my second playthrough with mods and I was blown away by how much missed potential this game has. Imagine if you could ride the metro or that the hacking system can be optimized to be as fluid and dynamic as possible?  How about fixing the DAMN DRIVING? I was able to make the driving so smooth but it required a bundle of 8 mods to fix it. In a game that rewards exploration, the driving mechanics really work against your favor and it's a shame that I missed out on so many things on my first playthrough. I didn't had that problem on my second because I added the Welcome To Night City mod collection and the forementioned driving fix mod pack.  It went pretty great but because of the amount of mods (321 total) running at the same time the game would start dropping in frames after playing for ~1 hour. I would have to turn off the game and come back to it, no big deal but just makes me think how if these features were just included in the base game I could be playing without interruptions. Despite all these things the game is still very worth playing and attempting to get 100%. If given the opportunity, I would've loved to get more immersed into my character by having a hardcore option like in FNV (this mod exists, it's called Dark Future) where you have to eat, drink, and sleep throughout the playthrough as well as being able to get addicted and get Cyberpsychosis. There are so many things that the WTNC mod pack does to improve the game that I can't fit into this review.  My biggest example of how frustratingly great playing with mods was when I went for the secret ending. I had completed every mission and gig up until that point and I was ready to do it but my game started crashing every time I started the mission because of the mods. Then I turned off all the mods and tried playing vanilla but the Netrunning was so awful because I was used to hacking with number key binds and many other fixes that were done to the balancing of Netrunning and Cyberware. I kept getting my ass kicked so I had to go back and turn off like about 100 mods just to get it to work and then miraculously it worked!  Why must I struggle though? Why couldn't this be part of the base game anyways? If only there were a financial incentive for the mods to come back and add yet more stuff they did to the game when they redeemed themselves after the botched release.  The base game has so many dumb issues that you have to either go out of your way to fix or just suck it up and play. However, after all that being said I think this games deserves a 10/10 for the story alone, Johnny Silverhand might me hands down my favorite character in all of media and Mike Pondsmith is a genius. It would be amazing if the developers were able to take a look at the wonderful work fans of the game have done for free and implement it into the game. Hopefully on the next game they take all of these community content additions into consideration.

Set even further into the future than the 1988 TTRPG it was based on, Cyberpunk 2077 pays homage to not only Mike Pondsmith's work, but the whole Cyberpunk genre that pervaded the United States and Japan in the late '80s and '90s. This title, therefore, plays out more like a "classic" RPG than the marketing might have you think, although there are plenty of modern twists to make it feel new.  What any prospective player must understand about this game is that the central focus is not V, Johnny Silverhand, or any of the supporting cast of characters. It's the setting itself: Night City. This game relies quite heavily on the setting and atmosphere to keep you engaged, and while the narrative and character stories are quite good despite that, they serve as more of a mechanism to keep you coming back to Night City over and over again. To get the most out of it, you, as the player, ought to take a lot of initiative to seek out and find what the world has to offer, even if the game doesn't reward you for doing it, because you want to be in that world. Yes, the main story can technically be completed in less than 15 hours, but you're really selling yourself short and not giving this game enough time to show its hand in that amount of time.  You'll get no spoilers from me; Cyberpunk 2077 has many completely different endings, with lots of variation between them and hours of missable content. Night City is a grinder that chews people up and spits them back out, so your experience with the game and its story is directly tied to the content you chose to explore in your playthrough and the decisions you made. You decide what happens, and you decide who it happens to.  That said, if you're expecting a strong single-player narrative and power fantasy, some players will likely be disappointed (Not true for the Phantom Liberty expansion). If that's what you're looking for, there are plenty of other games I would recommend instead. Play Cyberpunk 2077 because you want to be in the world of Cyberpunk, and you will likely have a fantastic experience. You get more out of this title the more you put into it. Expect to invest at least 50 to 60 hours.  Many of my complaints with the game are rather simple. I found some of the characters far more interesting than others, but a lot of that is a projection of my own moral values onto their respective arcs, and the decisions I therefore made within them. However, I would remiss if I didn't add that Johnny Silverhand may very well be Keanu Reeves' best performance in his entire career. Not a major issue: the game is very dialogue heavy. You will spend a lot of the narrative's runtime leaning against a table while a series of characters use sometimes dense jargon to contextualize what's happening for you. Unlike Baldur's Gate 3, Cyberpunk 2077 does not tackle everything its universe has to offer. This game picks a couple things and does them really well; the majority of the perks you unlock and the Cyberware you install are stat increases related to firearms or melee weapons, which do not dramatically transform your gameplay, with few exceptions.  Obviously, it's a technical marvel that this game even runs following its disastrous launch, and it runs well on my hardware; 1440p DLSS Quality, Ultra Settings w/o Ray-Tracing, and I stayed above 100 fps in most areas of the game. Nearly all of the game's features and systems have been overhauled or entirely reworked since its launch as well, which improves playability substantially. Even so, I did experience a few hard-crashes to desktop, glitched enemy encounters that soft-locked my game, broken characters models or A.I., and several audio-visual bugs throughout my time with the game. Maintain a habit of saving regularly, and these will be less of an issue, but brace for some bumps along the way.  I guess the tl;dr is to play this game because you want to, then immerse yourself completely, and stick with it. I've often said that Ghost of Tsushima is one of my favorite Assassin's Creed games I've ever played, and while they're notably different from one another, I feel similarly that Cyberpunk 2077 is my favorite Bethesda game of all time. This has been, hands-down, the best experience I've ever had in its niche, and it excels at worldbuilding, but does little to push the RPG genre forward in terms of gameplay. I still haven't done everything I want to do in this title, but would strongly recommend it to anybody with a patient interest in what it does.

The negative review is for this: Do not buy it at full price, especially not if you have a mid-range PC like mine AND especially if you are a completionist like me. I tried to experience all the content the game had to offer in a single playthrough, which led to me "optimizing" it (meaning completing all side jobs, fixer gigs and NCPD scanners). Here is my extensive review:  Six years after its original release, I thought the game would be in a pretty great state, but it is still pretty disappointing. I think most people who praise it, they do so because they compare it to the dumpster fire it was on release. But the game still feels unpolished, even unfinished, and it's still riddled with bugs. Not game-breaking ones, but they are still there. I had to install numerous mods in order to get to a decent playable state (fix for junky melee combat, pedestrian behaviour, quality of life elements for HUD and menus, like filters etc, de-scaled skill checks which were impossible after leveling up)  Gameplay wise, the RPG elements are minimal, the dialogue options are mostly different flavours of the same choice, the combat is repetitive and the enemy AI is extremely stupid, even in Very Hard difficulty. The side content (gigs and NCPD scanner jobs) are all duplicate brain-dead quests (read flavour text, go to location, sneak/shoot, loot chest, read flavour text). And no, the city is not immersive at all for me. All the places feel the same.  Its only redeeming quality, the story and characters, are overshadowed and diluted by the immense amount of mediocre side content that continuously distracts you (text messages, calls, etc) and forces you to engage with it ("wait for a whole day until the next mission objective", "find something else to do until [character] contacts you").   As always, I think the level design would have benefited if was a more linear and condensed experience, allowing the player to progress through the map gradually and learning to organically traverse through the levels, instead of blindly following quest markers.  I'm considering playing it again and focusing only on the main mission, just to experience the story in a more condensed way, but I am dreading the thought of having to go through all the tedious character progress and repetitive combat.  EDIT: I played the game again, and engaged only with the main quest. It was a far more enjoyable experience for 2 reasons: 1) I was already accustomed with the in-game universe (slang, concepts, characters) and I realized this was part of why I felt lost all the time during my first playthrough, and 2) I was not distracted by the side content and I was able to focus on the story and characters).  Bottom line: Cyberpunk 2077 is a good game but its held down by the open world elements that feel they were forced and rushed by the devs, because apparently these are the minimal expectations for a AAA release.

One of the most disappointing big-budget games I've ever played. The main missions are 90% dialogue and 10% gameplay. Almost every mission consists of traveling to a location, talking to a character, then traveling somewhere else to talk some more. That wouldn't necessarily be a problem if the story stayed engaging after Act 1, but it quickly loses its momentum.  Almost the entire plot revolves around figuring out how to safely remove the biochip that's slowly killing V, yet there's never any real sense of urgency. The story falls into the same repetitive structure for dozens of hours with V doing mercenary favors for a handful of characters, who then promise to give him a lead on removing the chip. You simply follow these breadcrumb trails from one character to the next, with every mission padded by lengthy conversations that have no real meaning. The game constantly pauses to let you choose how to respond, but outside of the ending, very few dialogue choices have any impact and most conversations play out the exact same. For a game that prides itself on player choice, the RPG mechanics are incredibly shallow.  I've played dialogue-heavy games like visual novels and JRPGs, so Cyberpunk simply having a lot of dialogue isn't the issue. The presentation and writing are just so boring and bland that it's difficult to sit through. Every conversation is just you looking at the other character speak in first person, making them all feel the same and drawn out. There are no traditional cutscenes, no cinematic camera angles, and very little physical character animation when talking. The dialogue itself also starts to feel repetitive because almost every character talks the same way. Everyone constantly throws around the same handful of phrases like "preem," "delta," "zero," "choom," and "gonk." The game leans so heavily on its slang that many characters end up sounding interchangeable. A few stand out, but most of the cast feels surprisingly one-dimensional.   For a game that's so heavily driven by dialogue, the English voice acting is also a letdown. Male V constantly delivers lines in that stereotypical gruff AAA protagonist voice - "gotta find a way to jack in," "maybe there's another way through"... Once you notice it, it becomes hard to ignore. I found Gavin Drea's performance terribly flat, especially considering how much dialogue V has throughout the game. Keanu Reeves doesn't fare much better. His performance often sounds overly restrained, like he's trying to channel John Wick in every scene by speaking in an exaggerated rasp. It's unfortunate that the two voices heard in nearly every conversation are among the weakest performances in the game.  Now, during the 10% of the main missions where you're actually playing a game instead of talking or driving between checkpoints, Cyberpunk is genuinely fun. The gunplay and stealth mechanics are solid, and there's a good variety of weapons and playstyles to experiment with. The stealth gameplay reminded me a lot of the PAYDAY series, with mechanics like marking cameras, distracting enemies, and silently taking guards out one by one. I just wish the game rewarded stealth more often, since carefully clearing an entire area usually takes twice as long as simply shooting everyone for the same outcome. Outside of combat, though, you're mostly walking, waiting for elevators, or searching for power boxes to open doors so you can continue walking.  If you want more gameplay, you're expected to spend time doing side gigs. They're enjoyable at first, but after a handful you've essentially seen everything they have to offer. The same goes for the cyberpsychosis encounters, which amount to fighting dozens of bullet sponge enemies with a large health pool and very little mechanical variety. None of the side content ever becomes particularly challenging or memorable.  Cyberpunk 2077 is an extremely disappointing and repetitive game that loses its appeal shortly after the first act. Its amazing premise and story is buried beneath dozens of hours of repetitive dialogue, terrible voice performances, and excessive padding. While the combat is enjoyable enough, there simply isn't enough of it to carry the experience and it feels like watching a TV show packed with filler.

!--->The Good<---!  It is a beautiful game. It occasionally bugs out, but what can you do? Practically no game nowadays is as good as they used to be in the golden era.  <>Gameplay & Combat:  The gameplay is nice and the gunplay is interesting—almost like Borderlands, but more realistic.  <>True RPG:  Your choices actually matter here, unlike in Mass Effect 3 or Fallout 4 where every path eventually leads to the same ending.  <>Progression:  It is straightforward and rewards exploration, innovation, and how you approach any mission or enemy. Character development is insanely well done. No matter where you put points, you never sacrifice one ability for another; putting points into Intelligence instead of Strength doesn't make you feel weaker, you just get a different type of peak performance.  <>Mod Support:  The modding scene is amazingly unrestrictive. Whether you cheat your way to the top or progress naturally, you still get achievements. It’s fun either way.   !--->The Meh<---!  <>Driving: It's not the best driving experience, but not the worst. Personally, I don't quite like it because the cars feel unwieldy and the speedometer shows a higher speed than you are actually moving. There is a mod to fix this which I heavily recommend.  <>Intro:  Whenever you start up, you can't skip most of the game's intro logos and cinematics.  !--->The Bad <---!  <>(Performance & Quirks)Dogtown FPS Drops:  Whenever you transition into Dogtown (IF YOU BUY THE DLC, which I heavily recommend because it’s basically its own game with tons of extra stuff), your FPS drops hard and fast. About as fast as a piece of buttered bread landing butter-side down. It’s that nasty. Make sure you have at least 16GB of RAM or get ready to get cucked by your own system.  <>Random FPS Drops:  Your frame rate will randomly tank when you do almost anything outside of standard combat. It drops when you visit a ripperdoc, change clothes, configure your skill tree, change your car color, call a vehicle, change radio stations, buy from vendors, or consume food/meds from the inventory instead of the quick slot. I am not even joking—it drops if you drive a little too fast, shoot, walk, or breathe. Basically, do anything besides the main quest, and expect to lose frames.  <>The Cop AI:  You will constantly have to fight cops because you accidentally clipped a civilian, while whole enemy gangs can wipe out an entire block and the police don't do ♥♥♥♥. The funny thing is, if you have stars and run near an NCPD side gig, the cops will stop chasing you and finally do their jobs by attacking the gang instead. If you're good enough, you can literally bait them into doing their jobs for you.  <>Glitchy Cyberware:  Sometimes your cyberware locks up and straight-up stops working. You have to quicksave and quickload just to get your abilities back.  <>Weapon Mod Restrictions:  I hate that you can attach muzzle devices to guns but you can't swap out weapon mods (like crit chance or lower recoil). You can craft these mods, but once they are in the gun, you can't take them back out.  <>Swimming:  Do you like swimming? Me too, but this game will make you hate it. You know how other games just block you from water or kill you? Cyberpunk makes you feel suicidal the second you go for a swim. You will start hating water like an Indian person seeing soap.  !--->What I Hate the Most<---!  (The Corporate Lie)They blatantly lied for 48 minutes straight during that E3 gameplay trailer. They promised so much and heavily under-delivered, cutting massive features and replacing them with stupid filler. They also promised it would run great on older-gen consoles, but if you tried to run this on a base PS4 or Xbox One, you got 20 FPS at best, and 30 only with a miracle.  They weaponized an 8-year marketing timeline to build investor confidence and hype, but benched the project for years and only actively coded it for about 4. It’s like a carpentry company telling a client, "Yes sir, we are working on your house," making you wait 8 years, and delivering a half-built house with a caved-in roof. When you complain, the boss says, "Well, we spent 5 years planning and only 3 years building." You would be outraged. The launch disaster wasn't on the fans for having high expectations—this was entirely on corporate deception.  [So in general, do I recommend it?] --- Hell yeah! [But do I like it?] ------------------------- Kinda... [Do I think it's good?] ----------------- Well, that's up to taste. [Should you buy it?] ------------------- Read the things above, but keep in mind that it's the first of its kind, and if you like or even love Deus Ex, I assure you, you will love it.

After finishing Cyberpunk 2077, I can confidently say it's one of the most immersive RPGs I've ever played.  The campaign is the heart of the experience. It's a deeply personal story about identity, survival, and what it truly means to live when your time is running out. The characters feel authentic, their relationships evolve naturally, and many choices leave you thinking long after the credits roll.  The lore is equally impressive. Night City feels alive because every district, gang, corporation, and side character has its own history and purpose. Simply exploring the city often tells stories without a single line of dialogue, making the world feel believable and rich with detail.  Combat is another standout. Whether you prefer guns blazing with LMG, slicing through enemies with katanas, hacking entire squads from a distance, or combining all of them into your own unique playstyle, the gameplay stays engaging from beginning to end. The freedom to build your character however you want makes every fight feel personal.  My biggest criticism is the vehicle handling. While the cars look incredible, many of them feel overly slippery, clunky and imprecise, especially at higher speeds. Driving often lacks the responsiveness you'd expect, making races and city navigation more frustrating than enjoyable.  Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 has become an incredible redemption story. Its unforgettable campaign, exceptional world-building, and satisfying combat far outweigh its remaining flaws. If you enjoy narrative-driven RPGs, this is an experience that's absolutely worth your time.

If you're still judging it by the 2020 launch, you're missing out on an incredible experience.  Pros:  Night City is one of the best open worlds ever created. The soundtrack absolutely slaps. Combat never gets old. Hacking someone's cyberware until they self-destruct while their friends panic is peak entertainment. The characters are so well written that you'll actually miss them when the game ends. The side quests don't feel like filler. Half of them could've been main missions in other games. The graphics are ridiculous. Sometimes I forget I'm supposed to be playing and just start walking around looking at everything.  Cons:  I now compare every other RPG to Cyberpunk. Keanu Reeves has permanently raised my standards for digital companions. I keep telling myself "one more gig" and suddenly it's 3:47 AM.  CD Projekt Red took one of gaming's roughest launches and turned it into one of my favorite games of all time. That's not something you see often.  If you like RPGs, great stories, satisfying combat, or just getting lost in an incredible world, do yourself a favor and play this game.  Wake the f* up, Samurai. We've got a masterpiece to play.**

My Top 3 Game of All Time  I won’t go into CD Projekt Red’s original plans for Cyberpunk, its initial launch, or its state at release. The game looks fantastic now: I played on patch 2.31, clocked 99 hours on Steam, and about 66 hours in-game. I’ve completed both the expansion and the main story with all endings, unlocked 100% of the achievements on Steam, and completed every quest I could.   I really enjoyed the game. I love The Witcher 3, and Cyberpunk is just as much of a favorite for me as The Witcher. I played the game on console at launch, and it was pretty good—I didn’t run into any bugs back then, but I saw that many others did.   Now the game has been polished: the progression system is excellent, any playstyle is allowed and rewarded—I played using stealth kills plus a katana, a pistol, and a submachine gun, and I was very satisfied, but I could switch up my build and change my playstyle at any time.   The gameplay is awesome; I especially liked the contracts, which I didn’t actively pursue the first time around. For me, they served as a sort of sandbox this time—something like the missions in Hitman, where you have to find the entrance and choose how you’ll carry out the mission—it’s a bit of an immersive sim.  It isn’t particularly deep, but it was a lot of fun to play that way. I liked the story; the characters are the key to the success of CDPR’s games, in my opinion. Whether in The Witcher or Cyberpunk, the characters make this game one of the best of all time, in my view.  The DLC is also excellent: story-wise, I liked the main game’s narrative better, although the contracts featured in the expansion were executed perfectly; I also enjoyed the new location, weapons, and implants.  On the downside, I’d mention the FPS drops. I’ve seen many people with Ryzen processors report that their graphics card is only loaded up to 70% and doesn’t deliver its full power after a few hours of gameplay. I don’t know how to fix this—maybe there’s a mod out there. It’s a rare issue; not everyone experiences it, and I hardly ever had it myself, and when I did, it didn’t really bother me.   And there are still some bugs, like characters or vehicles falling through textures, but these are rare and don’t significantly impact the game.   If you’ve never played Cyberpunk or any CDPR games before, you should definitely give Cyberpunk 2077 a try. It’s a great game for the ages. I’m really looking forward to the sequel and The Witcher 4, and I really hope that CDPR will correct their mistakes from releasing the game in an unfinished state so that we can enjoy a great product right from launch.  Rating: 97/100
