Following its sweeping updates and the narrative-defining Phantom Liberty expansion, Cyberpunk 2077 is now the genre-defining sci-fi RPG it was always meant to be. Night City offers an unmatched, immersive PC experience with stellar storytelling, overhauled skill trees, and bleeding-edge visual fidelity.  Visuals & Performance  Night City on the PC remains one of the most visually staggering achievements in gaming. With high-end hardware, ray tracing and path tracing push graphical fidelity to near-photorealistic levels, while DLSS keeps performance remarkably smooth. The PC version also features superior crowd density and environment responsiveness compared to older console generations.  Gameplay & Combat  The total overhaul to the game's mechanics fixed early balancing issues, creating a deeply rewarding progression system.  Cyberware & Perks: Armor is now tied directly to your cyberware rather than clothing, allowing for full aesthetic customization without sacrificing stats.  Build Variety: Whether you prefer hacking from the shadows as a Netrunner, darting around with katanas, or going in guns-blazing, the redesigned perk trees allow for highly flexible and creative playstyles.  Narrative & Quests  The writing is a triumph. The core journey of V trying to survive the Arasaka Relic alongside Johnny Silverhand (brought to life by a compelling performance from Keanu Reeves) is emotional, tense, and gritty. Paired with the Phantom Liberty expansion—a masterful, paranoid spy-thriller—the game delivers some of the best cinematic storytelling in modern RPGs.  The Verdict  While the open world isn't as dynamic as a Grand Theft Auto sandbox, and vehicle combat can still feel a bit floaty, these are minor blemishes. On the PC, Cyberpunk 2077 is an absolute must-play for open-world and sci-fi fans.

After putting in the time to 100% complete Night City, I can confidently say Cyberpunk 2077 is an absolute blast and worth every single penny. The world, the characters, the music, and the raw atmosphere are a straight 10/10. Night City is easily one of the most detailed and gorgeous open worlds ever made, and running it with DLSS and Frame Generation is pure eye candy it runs beautifully, even with a few minor bugs lingering around. The movement feels super fluid and the side gigs are fantastic, but the gunplay never fully clicked for me. It feels more serviceable than exceptional. Only a handful of hand cannons, snipers, and shotguns actually feel satisfying to shoot, while most ARs and SMGs just feel underwhelming. Plus, even on Hard, the game rarely gave me a real challenge looking back, I definitely should’ve bumped it up to Very Hard. My main gripes come down to some uneven pacing, a few noticeable plot holes, and a surprisingly short list of true, memorable boss fights. You just can’t shake the feeling that a lot of content was left on the cutting room floor. But honestly, those flaws only stick out because the rest of the game is so damn good. They just make you realize how heartbreakingly close this came to being a completely flawless masterpiece. Throw in the Phantom Liberty DLC, which is absolute cinema from start to finish, and you’re looking at one of the best RPGs ever made. It’s not perfect, but it’s still a masterpiece in its own right, and an experience I won’t forget anytime soon.

I did not play the game when it initially launched, so I cannot comment on its state at the time. My first playthrough happened sometime after the Phantom Liberty launch and the game was still buggy here and there, but in my experience, there were no showstoppers in the form of blockers, crashes or anything of the sort.  At its best, what we have here is a dream come true for fans of the cyberpunk genre in a video game form. You play as a lowlife with access to body altering high-tech, the world is owned by mega corporations, there are references to other cyberpunk works like Ghost in the Shell, Bladerunner and many many more. The vibe, setting, visuals and audio are excellent.   Exploring the Night City, whether on foot or by vehicle, with the radio on, gives a Grand Theft Auto like experience on top of regular open world RPG exploration and side quests. You flow naturally from one activity to another and get immersed in the world.  What greatly helps the immersion is the first person perspective and how the many cutscenes were designed while keeping this in mind. The way NPCs act around you means that wherever you are looking, there is always something interesting happening and you can partly direct the cutscene yourself and focus on what you want to see.  The way the main quests are structured is pretty interesting as well. The campaign is cut up into a bunch of arcs that weave in and out as you spend your time in Night City. The story concludes with a number of different endings. The Phantom Liberty expansion offers an even more exciting spy adventure with a tighter story and plenty of cinematic moments.  Overall, while the technical state is still not perfect, this is a great cyberpunk experience for fans of the genre with a deeply immersive world. The highs are very high and the story stays with you forever.

I can't speak for how it was at launch, but it sure feels like it's worth every penny now. It feels like everything Starfield WISHED it could be.  Pros: - A very large open world to explore, with little dead space; think GTA V in terms of map size, but with more verticality. Almost every block in the city has SOMETHING to do, whether it's a main story quest or just some guy who's black market prosthetic... "body part" is causing him pain. - Stellar roleplaying and immersion: It's not very often anymore I truly get sucked into a game and start feeling like I'm LIVING in the world I'm playing in, but this game got it right. Every mission leaves me wondering what's going to happen next. - Satisfying combat mechanics. It doesn't do anything revolutionary here, but the weapons all feel like they have a good "punch" to them, and, outside of mechanical enemies or bosses, your opposition isn't lined up with bullet sponges (looking at you, Borderlands), which does nothing but making fights unnecessarily longer in my opinion as well as making me feel like all my weapons are made of rubber and completely useless. The one thing that makes things a little more unique in this game are the cybernetic implants, which act in some ways as your "spells" or "powers," but with a plausible modern source. - Beautiful graphics... I wish I had a 5090 to truly enjoy maximum settings, but even on medium or high, the aesthetics and visuals in this game are amazing. Seriously, the graphic artists for this game did great, especially when you consider every little detail that seems added to scenes like the items on shelves, the trash littered about, or the bright glow of lights on everything that should have it.   The main gripes I can think of are:  - Subpar modding support, which is definitely a bigger issue as someone who loved dumping 200+ mods into Bethesda games. Despite releasing an official mod kit, the game has no official way of "loading" mods, and instead relies on you either learning the game's file structure or relying on a 3rd party program to handle mods for you. On top of this, the mods can cause serious performance issues or just downright crash your game, even when doing seemingly innocuous things such as changing tooltip text or auto-scrapping items. - Occasional scripting oddities; there are occasions where NPCs will just awkwardly pause and stare at you before realizing they're supposed to advance a quest for you, but this mainly seems to happen with the boxing quests. I haven't noticed it much outside that. - The hacking minigame's RNG; I've spent an ungodly amount of time sitting in front of a breach before starting to try and solve all 3 challenges, but sometimes the game just doesn't give you a solvable puzzle, so you have to exit and reload it again to get a new one until it decides to play nice.  Overall, if you like Bethesda games, great stories, or even just a good shooter, this is a solid recommend. Can't wait to see what CDPR do next (assuming they don't botch the launch again lol)

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of those rare games that not only entertains but also immerses you completely. Night City feels alive in a way that most open worlds do not achieve. The city watches you, tempts you, overwhelms you, and sometimes quietly breaks you.  The 2.0 overhaul has transformed the game significantly. Combat is now sharp, fluid, and expressive. Whether you’re slicing through time with a Sandevistan, causing chaos through hacking, or going full chrome with cyberware, every character build feels meaningful. The gunplay carries weight, melee combat feels brutal, and the city reacts to your presence.  The story is the real draw. V’s journey is personal and existential, avoiding the typical “save the world” formula. The dynamic between Johnny Silverhand and V is messy, magnetic, and unforgettable. The side characters feel like real individuals with genuine stakes, rather than mere quest markers.  Phantom Liberty takes everything to its peak. Dogtown is dense and dangerous, the choices you make carry more weight, and Idris Elba’s performance as Solomon Reed is outstanding. The new endings add emotional depth that lingers long after the credits roll.  Visually, the game is stunning, especially on a powerful PC. Path tracing makes Night City resemble a neon cathedral. The soundtrack embodies pure cyberpunk with its industrial, electronic, and atmospheric qualities, perfectly complementing the experience.  Cyberpunk 2077 may not be flawless, but it is undeniably powerful. It is stylish, brutal, beautiful, and profoundly human beneath all the chrome.  For me, this game is not just a playthrough; it’s an experience that stays with you.

Can't really have no fun interactions with the environment or the NPCs.  Beyond that though, this game definitively confirmed to me, together with my previous excruciating attempts at playing The Witcher 3, that the developers at CD Project Red have no idea how to make an entertaining videogame.  This game's story is bad. It's generic, it's pompous, event though it has no right to be, since it's a dookie. It's filled with exposition dumping from a bunch of talking heads with stiff animations that explain to you why you should care and why it's essential for you to shoot 30 more guys for the story to progress. The story tries to touch on all your typical dystopian topics like corrupted corporations and governments, the violence, the meaning of life, but it fails to say anything meaningful or impactful.   The main character is arrogant and unlikeable. Their immature desire to hit the "big leagues" coupled with the overdone voice acting and terms like "delta", "nova", "choom" etc. really didn't evoke any emotion other than embarassment. I wanna emphasize just how much they dropped the ball with the story and the delivery of the voice lines, because I didn't feel this way about Cyberpunk Edgerunners, which used those same made-up slang terms, but didn't feel nowhere near as cringe, and it also succeeded at delivering a better story and showcasing the beauty of Night City much better.  The gameplay is there and it's just okay – and that is not okay, you know what I mean? There is nothing special, no scratch that – even remotely engaging about the gameplay. It's your typical "choose your own approach" game (similar to the Far Cry or Hitman games). Shooting is generic, driving is generic, stealth is generic. It's all serviceable, it's there, but it leaves you not being able to shake off the feeling that you're playing something you've already played dozens of times before. And let me be clear, I don't mind generic, it's just there's no fun gameplay loop here.  I could sit here a bunch more nitpicking about various things that rubbed me the wrong way about this game, like all the times I was tasked with finding a circuit breaker to restore power to progress a mission, or how a manual save system really doesn't fit an open world game like Cyberpunk and losing minutes of progress from accidentally dying while messing in the open world isn't fun. But I think it's time for a conclusion.  For all the hype that was created around this game before its release, even after all the patches it's nothing special. It didn't innovate, it didn't push games to a new level in any way. From where I'm standing, this game isn't worth the money that's being asked for it. And I bought it during a sale, so that's saying something.

Another fantastic game from CDPR. While The Witcher 3 remains at the top for me, this game does showcase incredible build variety, meaningful player choice, and multiple endings that make replaying it genuinely appealing if only to 100% it.  Night City is undoubtedly the main attraction. It's one of the most visually impressive open worlds I've explored, and simply driving around, taking in the neon-lit streets and atmosphere, never really gets old.  That said, I do have a few complaints.  Since I wasn't familiar with the Cyberpunk universe before playing, the chronology of Phantom Liberty was confusing to me. I accidentally started the expansion and stopped playing it at first available moment thinking it was post-game content only to come back to it after I was halfway done with my ending.  My usual approach to open-world games is to work my way up in excitement: NCPD Scanner missions -> gigs and cyberpsycho sightings -> side quests -> main story. While that progression worked for the most part, many quests have hidden trigger conditions or require waiting for phone calls, so there were long stretches near the end where I had nothing meaningful to do except skip time until someone finally contacted me. It made the otherwise engaging progression feel a bit disjointed.  [spoiler]Another disappointment was the hidden ending. I had a high relationship percentage with Johnny Silverhand, so I assumed I had met the requirements. Only later did I learn that a few very specific dialogue choices during one conversation determine whether it's available. Considering how significant that ending is, the game does a poor job of communicating what actually matters. This led me to reload to an earlier save before finishing the game, and having to sit through the unskippable goodbye call again which I gladly opted out of during my third time.[/spoiler]  Finally, while Johnny Silverhand is easily one of the game's strongest characters, V never quite clicked with me. As the story goes on, it starts to feel like it's more about Johnny than V (of course you can ignore all missions related to Johnny). I really enjoyed seeing Johnny grow and change, and many of the game's best moments come from his interactions with V.

Cyberpunk 2077 — 25.3 hrs  Played on: Windows 11 Pro (26200) · 12th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i9-12900K · 128 GB · NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 · NVMe SSD My time: 25.3 hrs  Fun 9 · Skill Ceiling 7 · Onboarding Tax 6 · Jank Tax 8 · Dad Tax 6 The Verdict: 7.5/10 — "Worth the sleep debt."  I remember exactly where I was for the 2020 launch — watching a $400 million game get pulled off a storefront like a bad build that never should've hit prod. I run a company. I know what shipping broken looks like from the inside, and I had zero interest in being someone else's beta tester on a $60 purchase. So I waited. Years, actually. Turns out patience is a stat I have plenty of now that I don't have free time to spend on anything else.  What I finally installed is not the game that launched. Update 2.0 rebuilt the skill trees, the police, the cars, the cyberware — it's a different product wearing the same box art, and it plays like one. Night City at night, headlights smearing off wet chrome, is still the best "just fifteen minutes before bed" screensaver-with-a-plot I've bought in years. I'm only 25.3 hours in, which for a game this size means I've barely left the tutorial gang territory, but every one of those hours felt earned rather than padded.  This is the rare AAA open world that doesn't punish you for having a life — side content is genuinely good instead of copy-pasted, and the main thread respects that you might only get through one job a night. I haven't hit a single crash, which after everything I remembered from launch day felt like its own small miracle.  👍 — a genuine comeback story, worth diving in now that the worst of the wreckage has been cleared; just don't expect to see the ending before your kids graduate.

I played finish Cyberpunk 2077 and I found the writing decent but also not outstanding. I feel that the game focuses more on the aesthetic of cyberpunk rather than the philosophical and psychological implications of society being in such a state towards humanity both on an individual and collective scale. The dialogue tends to resort to quoting philosophers in order to appear deep while hiding an inherent lack of depth. The world of Cyberpunk is really existentially empty. Those who are not elite live in extreme poverty and capitalism drains the life out of everyone and yet Cyberpunk ignores this sickening emptiness of existence. Johnny Silverhand is quite interesting at times but all he is is a walking talking ideology such that he appears shallow rather than complex. He appears to be just as dogmatic and narrow minded as those who accept the status quo. I would say the gameplay beats RDR2 but it is definitely has a much weaker story. Each character felt more like a trope, a kind of caricature rather than real. I don't believe anyone can live in the world of Cyberpunk without experiencing severe mental illness. It is a sick society and the game pushes colorful narratives upon us, beckoning us towards an adventure that is ultimately insignificant in the grand scheme of things. It just focuses on hype moment after hype moment rather than delving into the world which they have created which simply put is on the pinnacle of decadence. Disco Elysium is infinitely superior in writing about spiritual decay in relation to political ideology. However, the gameplay is highly addictive and the world is immersive and beautiful.

After putting 82 hours into Cyberpunk 2077 across three different devices, I can confidently say this game is an absolute blast and 100% worth your time.  Here is my breakdown after a massive playthrough:  [b] 1. Cross-Device Performance & Tech (The Cool Part) [/b] I actually played this game on my Desktop PC, Laptop, and a Handheld device, meaning I got to test all three major upscaling techs:  -PC (AMD GPU): Used FSR, ran super smooth. -Laptop (Nvidia RTX): Used DLSS, flawless performance. -Handheld (Intel): Used XeSS, surprisingly playable and smooth.  After tweaking the settings across all devices, I found out that even if you drop the settings to Low (as long as you keep it at 1080p), the game still looks visually stunning and handles amazingly well. You honestly get the full 100% experience on any decent hardware now.  [b] 2. Build & Lore Immersion [/b] I went with the Corpo life path for my first run, building a Netrunner mixed with a Stealth Handgun playstyle. Breaking into places, hacking everything, and popping heads silently is incredibly satisfying. The atmosphere of Night City is top-tier-fantastically immersive and beautiful. Plus, if you’ve watched the Edgerunners anime on Netflix, the game hits different. Recalling specific locations from the show while exploring the game (and vice versa) just adds a whole new layer of appreciation.  [b] 3. The Bugs & Stability [/b] Is it perfect? Not entirely, but it's very solid now. The only real bugs I encountered were vehicles occasionally spawning randomly or slight, weird teleportation glitches while driving (which sometimes caused funny collisions with pedestrians or objects). Performance-wise, I had exactly 2 random crashes on my PC, but surprisingly, my laptop and handheld ran perfectly without a single crash.  Verdict: The game has come a long way. I've tried GTA and other open-world games many times throughout my life, but none of them ever hooked me the way Cyberpunk 2077 did. I wasn't around for the horrible launch, so I'm reviewing it as someone who only experienced the final, polished version.  The world is incredibly detailed and immersive. I was completely invested in the story, and ended up loving Johnny, Panam, and V even more than the well developed characters of the anime like David and Rebecca. It's rare for a game to have a story and cast that resonate with me more than a great TV show, but this game here managed to do exactly that.  I'm also constantly surprised by how much care and effort went into the side missions, including the Fixer jobs. Some of them really feel like they could be part of the main story.  There are countless buildings you can enter that are fully detailed, often with multiple floors to explore.  The cars and bikes are awesome, the combat is fast, satisfying, and endlessly fun, and I love all the RPG mechanics and the variety of builds you can experiment with.  Even when I'm not doing missions, I have a great time simply riding around Night City and taking in the  great views.  I can't wait for the sequel, and I hope GTA 6 can scratch the same itch in the meantime.

Joguei Cyberpunk 2077 pela primeira vez em 2020, no Xbox. Mesmo com os bugs da época, eu gostei bastante do jogo. Naquele momento joguei de forma bem rushada, praticamente focando apenas nas missões principais para zerar o mais rápido possível.  Agora, em 2026, resolvi jogar novamente, dessa vez no PC, e a diferença é enorme. O jogo melhorou muito em praticamente todos os aspectos. A gameplay está mais refinada, o desempenho é muito melhor e a experiência como um todo é bem mais agradável.  Mesmo assim, ainda existem alguns pontos que me incomodam. Night City é linda visualmente, mas muitas vezes parece uma cidade sem vida. Os NPCs quase não interagem com o jogador nem entre si, e a IA da polícia continua sendo um dos pontos mais fracos do jogo, já que é extremamente fácil escapar de perseguições.  Outro problema, na minha opinião, é o ritmo da campanha. O início é excelente e prende bastante, mas da metade para o final a história perde um pouco do ritmo. Em vários momentos você precisa esperar ligações ou mensagens de NPCs para continuar a campanha, e acaba fazendo missões secundárias apenas para passar o tempo. Isso dá a sensação de que essas pausas existem mais para aumentar artificialmente a duração do jogo do que para melhorar a narrativa.  Ainda assim, Cyberpunk 2077 conseguiu dar a volta por cima. Apesar dos defeitos, continua sendo um RPG com uma história muito boa, personagens marcantes, ótima ambientação e um combate divertido. Se você deixou de jogar por causa do lançamento conturbado, vale muito a pena dar uma nova chance.  7.7/10

Absolutely stunning.  There is just so much to do, and CDPR really focus' on the details.  The main story is good but that's not where Cyberpunk shines, it's in the side content. I swear there were times I'd play 10 hours of side content in between main missions, and the pacing felt completely natural. All the different relationships you make during a playthrough are a prime example of why you MUST play the optional stuff in a game like this, because otherwise you miss so much of the "why". The missions you do with your friends or "chooms", really help you to understand why each character is making the choices they are, and literally shows you their origins, meeting the people they hold most dear. And even though there are limited dialogue options I never felt as if there was something I wanted to say and couldn't.  I have to also talk about the world itself. Night City. Such a well-built world from top to bottom. All of the different districts and subdistricts are laid out very well for the type of dystopian world Cyberpunk is set in, without straying too far from what we know a city to be. Night City is a dark, gloomy, plastic metropolis where class division is almost impossible not to see consistently, leading to subtle familiarities of real-life peeking through the cracks. It feels as if it is a character itself, constantly changing and having and impact on your story no matter what.  Lastly, I wanted to touch on the combat in this game. Wow is it ever fun! There are what feels like endless choices as to how you want to approach combat. Throughout my playthrough I tried a bunch of different approaches, and they all felt so good. I especially loved the throwing knives, and I loved them even more with double jump and air boosting. By the end of the game, you start to feel invincible, which is great because at the start you feel like EVERYONE is stronger than you. It makes you feel like your work paid off.  If you haven't played it yet and you are a big open world RPG fan, I would definitely recommend playing it at some point. But wait for it to go on sale and pick up the ultimate edition with the DLC. I played the main game before picking up the DLC and it was great, but after I got it, the game felt more complete.

A mile wide and an inch deep perfectly describes this game. To call it an RPG is, which technically true, feels wrong given that it makes the same cardinal sin that FO4 mad and has a voiced PC that completely kills most immersion the second they start talking, not to mention it also hilariously makes the same mistake of dialogue options being vague and sometimes completely different to what the PC actually says.   The world LOOKS nice, they did a fantastic job making it look like a complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥(I'm not being sarcastic, its a well made ♥♥♥♥♥♥ American city), but that's the only thing I can really say was good about it. The inhabitants might as well not exist, they either do nothing(civvies) or are the horde of mindless npcs to kill with no consequences. The police are a nonissue(which has always been a running theme in these kinds of games) and become even more so after finishing the DLC. Gangs in general feel like an after thought and set dressing than anything substantial besides from giving the fixer related to them a basic personality.   Missions are another problem in that outside of the story ones, its almost always just "GO here, kill these people, get item/person" Sure there's SOME good ones, but the VAST majority are copy paste kill this variety of goons, move on to next set. It tries to give you interesting non-combat stuff but fails when it becomes so obvious they put so little effort into the non-combat stuff. Non-lethal take downs and hacks feel pointless then there's no consequences for killing when I can easily avoid all consequences. I'm sure that's a message but it falls flat after the 100th (except for the cyber psycho quest obviously, and the reward is just another ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gun.)  The story itself was ok, predictable admittedly, but it wore its inspiration on its sleeve unabashed so I cant fault them for that.  Johnny was an ok character, a bit on the nose at times and his and V's relationship felt jumbled at times like the game forgot I was on good terms with him and randomly have V act like he suddenly hates him. NPC romances were a joke, but that's because they were NPC romances, no one but loosers take those seriously.  The DLC was surprisingly good story wise, gameplay wise was more of the same. At least it felt like my actions actually mattered this time rather than not.  Oh and the bugs ARE still there, they just arent game breaking anymore, just funny, like Bethesda bugs.  a solid 4/10, horribly disappointing for what they promised.

Yet another generic open-world game, good game if it's the first open-world game you ever played 6/10  Pros: Graphics  Cons:  1) BUGS: Still has multiple bugs after almost 6 years after release, MOSTLY VISUAL bugs, on one occasion wasn't able to pick an item to proceed with a side quest, found the exact same issue from a post 5 years ago - still isn't fixed. 2) Side Quests:  A) 90% of them are kill/steal/grab a person or body and leave. Generic objectives = generic story.  B) Side quests are spawned in a weird manner, coming in trickles, instead of spawning all of the options at once. While more "realistic", wastes the time to drive and teleport between cities one time after another to the same street. C) SPAM: Too much spam in speeches, phone calls and SMS - even if there was something interesting in the 5% of them, I am not gonna read all of it because most of it are fillers.  Side activities except driving: none PARKOUR: only jumping. so many body modifications but can only upgrade jump height - disappointing. CYBERWARE ("hacker abilities"): not many options to choose from, and the ones you do own aren't very interesting in their usage - disappointing. DIFFICULTY: Easy on "very hard" difficulty. ECONOMY: Finished the game with 1.3M dollars because there is nothing to spend it on except body upgrades. No way of obtaining them for free, higher tiers are locked behind your level, making you to buy newer tier and sell the lower tier and wasting extra money instead of buying the higher tier (even though it's an RPG, it makes less sense when you can higher tier just appear out of nowhere just because you level up) DRIVING: of the cars I have used, only cars that I received from quests don't have oily wheels. No chance of obtaining and driving an Air Vehicle? disappointing. COMBAT: as simple as it gets, some enemies look differently but don't require drastic change of measures  to deal with them, simply shooting anywhere them will do. No thermal vision in 2077? too bad AUTO-SAVES: on the face.  Summary: Questionable game design, flat story (even the main story feels short), basic combat and gameplay. all budget went into graphics

I first played Cyberpunk 2077 back when it launched on Xbox One X and completed it twice. Back then, despite seeing its incredible potential, it was hard to ignore the technical issues that held the experience back.  Coming back to the game today on macOS, it genuinely feels like playing a completely different product.  The world of Night City is still one of the most immersive and believable open worlds ever created. Every district has its own personality, the atmosphere is unmatched, and the cyberpunk aesthetic is simply breathtaking. Walking through neon-lit streets while the soundtrack plays never gets old.  The gameplay is fast, fluid, and incredibly satisfying. Gunplay feels impactful, movement is smooth, hacking, stealth, melee combat, and character builds offer a huge amount of freedom. Every encounter gives you multiple ways to approach it, making combat consistently exciting.  The story remains one of the game's strongest aspects. Memorable characters, emotional moments, excellent voice acting, and meaningful side quests make Night City feel alive. Many side missions are just as engaging as the main storyline.  What impressed me the most is how much CD Projekt Red transformed this game over the years. Countless improvements, gameplay refinements, quality-of-life updates, and overall polish have turned Cyberpunk 2077 into the experience it was always meant to be.  The macOS port is an impressive achievement on its own. It's fantastic to finally see a modern AAA title of this scale running natively on Mac, and it opens the door for more high-quality releases on the platform.  If you were disappointed at launch, I strongly encourage you to give Cyberpunk 2077 another chance. It deserves it.  Highly recommended.

Summary:  This game was incredible from start to finish. I am a heavy story game player, it is what I primarily enjoy. Assassins Creed, Borderlands, Ghost of Tsushima, pretty much any game that is rich in story and adventure, I will play it. This game fit the bill and then some. I will say, it starts out slow. The first main story mission turned me away from the game at first. I felt like you got attached to one of the main characters and then lose him off rip (spoiler) which makes it somewhat difficult to want to continue to play. I took a 2 month break from the game after completing the first mission, then came back and quite literally played through the entire main questline in the span of 24 hours (yes, concurrently in a single session). I enjoyed the fact that your in-game decisions affect the overall outcome of the story, it adds an extra layer of cognition to the game. You can run around and be mindless, or you can carefully think through your decisions. Regardless of what you do, there's an ending to the story as a consequence to those decisions. On top of the story being rich, there is TONS of side content to keep you busy, and much of it is purposeful. It doesn't feel like a waste of time when you go and do side quests, it feels like it adds to the lore and helps you understand some of what is going on a bit better than if you just skipped past it. The side quests are also entertaining, which is something a lot of story games lack. Some side quests are even longer than just a single mission - some of them are their own questlines which is sick. I cannot wait for the next addition to this franchise.  The GOOD: Graphics - Graphically speaking, the environment is incredible. I ran this game on Ultra settings once I built this rig and it was insane. Deeply immersive graphics. The map is MASSIVE. You can get lost in Night City - there are so many roads, alleyways, and buildings to explore. While there are fast travel points, the map is inviting enough that you would almost rather use a car to get around and explore than fast travel unless its for a mission.   Characters - the main characters in both the main game and Phantom Liberty were well-developed, they do not feel lackluster or boring in the slightest. You 100% develop attachments to some of them, and also enmity and aversion for others.  Combat - Combat feels challenging when you want it to be. It does not feel like it's overly punishing like a lot of adventure games can be. I can count on 2 hands how many times I died during the course of each boss fight to give you an idea. The environment is so well-built that if you are dying a ton, it truly means you are not observing what is around you to figure out how to win the fight. If you observe first and fight second, you will usually win. In other words, you are rewarded for thinking before fighting.  Story - The story feels developed and concise, nothing feels forced or feels like it shouldn't be there. The main quests are all conducive to furthering the development of characters or the storyline itself. You don't feel like any of the main missions are a waste of time.  The BAD  Glitches - I played this game post-rebuild/update, and there are glitches galore. Between time-based missions not triggering, checkpoint glitches, enemy and observation glitches, etc. it got pretty frustrating at times. Sometimes I would have to completely restart a mission from the beginning because the glitch couldn't be corrected by reverting to checkpoint.  Story - I am nitpicking by putting this here, but it is something I feel like I need to mention. For a game as rich in side content as this game is, I feel like there could have been way more content added to the main storyline. Give V more of a backstory leading up to the situation he is currently in - give the player more of an epic climactic buildup before the main story finishes. I feel like I shouldn't be able to complete the main story in a day's worth of gameplay but then spend weeks playing all of the side content. If there was more of a focus on building up the main story, it would have just made the game better than it already is.  OVERALL: BUY THIS GAME! If you enjoy story-rich open world games, you will LOVE this game. Everything about it is extremely addicting - I am almost saddened by the fact that I played through it as fast as I did. I wish there was more to the main story to explore - but regardless, it is fun and immersive, you will not regret the purchase.

I never reviewed this??? It's a masterpiece. Flawed, but what masterpiece isn't? The worldbuilding is glorious. The architecture tells its own story. The narrative is chef's kiss. The voice acting is top notch. The music is perfection. It's the kind of game where, when the credits roll, I sit in a stunned stupor after the game ripped me apart to my bare atoms and left me to deal with it. There are many different endings so be prepared to be broken over and over. It's one of those games that's clawed around in my mind and left marks that will last forever.   Think of every negative thing in modern media and crank it up by 1000% while the world is limping towards a total collapse, and give it more tech. That's Cyberpunk 2077's backdrop.   I didn't expect the story to revolve around V with a dead rocker boy in her head. I was annoyed by it at first. Silverhand pissed me off. I played on PC at launch so I ran into very few bugs.  My car got stuck under the map when I called it, and I once looked away from my parked bike for a second and it launched into V like it was possesed and slammed into a vending machine. Those are old bugs I haven't seen again.   The immersive city and stories are everything. The world is too close to reality and it knows it. The satire on current society is spot on from the ads, the TV commercials and shows, the trash, the districts themselves, healthcare, police, and more. The casual background TV shows are fascinating satire. Each channel pushes a different narrative in the interest of a different corporation. Like fox vs cnn. The host always controls the narrative. When it seems to be slipping from him, he reins it back in like a noose to align with the show's narrative and protect that channel's corporate aligned interest. If it puts someone's life in danger then damn them without a thought. Neither side has the publics interest in mind. It's all personal corporate interest that will destroy everything in its path until it eats its own tail.  The game is depressing. There are no happy endings. V's narrative isn't about saving a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ world. Raging against the Cyberpunk society thus far has only gotten people killed and changed nothing. It's about what personally matters to you and how you choose to live. Even if that choice is to rage for one moment before being snuffed out. Helping someone else live a little longer, going quietly into the good night, or making a deal with a devil. I love it because it leaves a mark and sticks with me far longer with resounding thoughts than a neatly wrapped happy ending.

8/10. Love the smell my PC has when running it, reminds me of a 2000s internet cafe.  It’s funny, because 90% of this review could stand up if it was posted at launch, minus the game-breaking bugs, of course. The core game is mostly the same as it was on day one, and  that is okay.  On a personal note, this game will always hold a special place for me as one of my pandemic getaways. After a lot of delays, it finally dropped right around Christmas of 2020. I played through the absolute mess of bugs at launch, and  underneath all that jank, the experience was still amazing.   Credit where credit is due, a major point has to be made for the business model and the developers' commitment. In an era plagued by battle passes and cash shops, the absolute lack of microtransactions here is incredibly refreshing. You buy the game, you get the game. Furthermore, CD Projekt Red actually stuck with it. Instead of cutting their losses and abandoning ship after a disastrous launch, they spent years grinding out patches to fix and sharpen the game. That shows a level of honesty and integrity that is increasingly rare in the modern AAA industry.  At its best, the game is a graphical benchmark. It has all the latest bells and whistles, and the overall vibe of Night City is incredible when you’re driving around taking it in. Story-wise, it shines. I love the ethical dilemmas it puts you in. The game makes a point of showing that you can never have your cake and eat it too. There is always a trade-off for every big decision, which keeps the narrative for the most part grounded. But when you get off the beaten path, the illusion breaks down. It feels like a funfair excursion: awesome while you’re looking at the main attractions, but step behind the storefronts and you see it’s just a movie set. I know the comparison is overused, but this game just lacks the polish of RDR2. In that game, the NPCs have routines and are detailed in their scripts, which sells the world as "real." Here, the NPCs act as background props. The world is inviting, but just not as alive as it could be.  I love the fact that the city is walkable with a ton of pedestrian pathways, but in this regard, I really wish it had more verticality. I look up at these massive buildings and I want to be able to actually climb them using in-game tools, rather than just taking inside elevators.  The quest rewards largely feel like sidegrades rather than true upgrades. The gear lacks meaningful, transformative stats. This issue is only made worse if you try to up the challenge: playing the game on Very Hard just makes the NPCs bullet sponges rather than actually giving better loot. I really wished the rewards scaled with the difficulty to actually give you a reason to do it that way. Even the cyberware options feel limited in scope: you get a few genuinely game-changing abilities like optical camo, double jump and various hp/ram giving items, but everything else is just a passive "+10% to this or that" stat bump. It makes looting feel like chore. Diablo does the same thing so why does it feel not as rewarding to get an upgrade?! Because in this game the gear doesn't really matter. This is more story and visualy driven.   Mechanically, the game has a massive identity crisis. It’s stuck somewhere in the middle of a first-person shooter, a looter-shooter, and an RPG, without truly nailing any of them. The driving physics suck: you never really feel a "need for speed," and the car engine sounds are surprisingly underwhelming. Even the quickhacks feel like a mechanic tacked on at the last minute rather than a foundational system the "cyberpunk" world was built around. To be fair, there are highly viable builds, and I absolutely love the mobility the game gives you. But gunplay-wise, the weapons lack a sense of raw power: with the exception of revolvers and pistols that can one-shot. They also definitely painted themselves into a corner with smart weapons; the novelty of a gun that aims itself wears off fast, though honestly, how else could they have handled it in this setting?  A significant drawback is how technical limitations restrict certain playstyles. You want to run a long-range sniper build? Good luck. The view distance is so aggressively optimized that you're literally aiming at flat, ugly 2D sprites instead of rendering actual targets. Not that snipers actually feel that  powerful anyway.  The Ubisoft formula, overused as it is, has had success for a reason: that core gameplay loop is genuinely fun. As in it offers verticality and things to do on the open world. I feel like a version of that loop could have been implemented here to give open-world exploration purpose (the NCPD dispatch missions could have been expanded on).  Finally, the clothing. For a game obsessed with style, a lot more work could have been done here. Instead of looking like a legendary mercenary, the clothing options often leave you looking generic and NPC-ish for the most part.  As objective as I tried to be, this is still just my personal opinion on the game. On that note, a massive plus is the thriving modding community, which can essentially 'fix' anything you personally don't like. Just be advised that modding always comes with a dose of risk and added jank.  That said, I enjoy it: the game is visually striking, huge in scope, and there is nothing even remotely like it. It’s a must-play for sure, and at this stage in time, even better bought at a discount.

Unironically one of the best games I have ever played and will likely always have an effect on me. The game had a rough start years ago and I even stopped playing very early on because of that, but CDPR despite all the criticism did this game right in trying to constantly improve it, fix it, and push out more content - and it clearly reflects well enough for them to continue work on Project Orion. I've played dozens of story games, it's the main type of game I play, but no game has ever made me feel both the amazement and dread/sadness that Cyberpunk has - characters you only see a few times have personalities and stories compelling enough for you to actually care about them even if you see them just a few times, your interactions from start to game make you actually think - 'is this what I would do?' but more of 'What would my character do? Are they this type of a person?' - it's not just a straight forward game, it forces you to think about the world around you and your character as if they're a real person.  The game itself is absolutely stunning, and has a vast modding community that helps making the game so much more expansive and customizable if that's what you want to do. And, if you enjoy the anime itself, you'll love the small easter eggs from Cyberpunk Edgerunners: Season 1. Even if it's small, it's nice to see the nod. I'm extremely excited to see season 2, as it'll take place after the game and see the nods to V if we get any (I can't imagine not getting any.)  While the game seems extreme at times, it also feels like a possible warning for what could happen to our world given if corruptness keeps going and little care for the world happens, and about how easy it is to slip into a world of dismay if we're not careful - especially for Americans in which this is based in.  Phantom Liberty made the game even better than it was too; and makes you question morals and loyalty even more than the base game did, and I'm so glad they're continuing into Orion with the producer for Phantom Liberty.  10/10, probably my favorite game I have ever played and seen - literally every ending feels impactful, heartbreaking or relieving, and would recommend it a million times over. Well worth the money despite the bugs years ago. If you are looking for a story game to play, this is ***THE*** game to play.

Recommended Playtime: 250+ hours  Night City isn’t just a setting; it’s a character that wants to chew you up and spit you out as chrome scrap. After the updates and the expansion, Cyberpunk 2077 has finally become the masterpiece it was always meant to be.  The Atmosphere The city is hot and brutal. You can almost feel the heat radiating off the sun-baked asphalt in Santo Domingo and the humid, neon-soaked air of Kabuki. It’s a place where life is cheap, but the style is expensive. The contrast between the glittering skyscrapers of the corporate center and the decaying slums creates a tension that never lets up.  The Tech and Gameplay The combat is where this game truly shines now.  Wild Cyberware: You can turn yourself into a literal god of metal. Whether you’re installing Mantis Blades to slice through scavs or a Sandevistan to move so fast time stands still, the customization is insane. Smart Weapons: There is nothing more satisfying than using smart weapons—watching your bullets curve mid-air to find a target hiding behind cover feels like something out of a high-octane sci-fi movie. The Magic Net: Netrunning feels like digital sorcery. You can clear an entire building without ever firing a bullet, using the "magic" of the Net to overheat enemy implants, shut down their eyes, or turn their own turrets against them. Cool Cars: The vehicle design is top-tier. From the roaring engines of the Quadra Type-66 to the sleek, futuristic lines of the Rayfield Caliburn, driving through the city at night with the radio blasting is an experience in itself. The Content There is an overwhelming amount of stuff to do, and it all feels meaningful:  The Main Story: A gripping, emotional race against time that explores what it means to be human (and features a legendary performance by Keanu Reeves). Friend Missions: These are the heart of the game. Building relationships with characters like Panam, Judy, and River provides some of the best writing in RPG history. Fixer Missions (Gigs): These are your bread and butter. Each fixer has a unique personality, and their missions range from stealthy thievery to full-blown assassinations. Street Missions: Random encounters and side stories that flesh out the lore of the world. NCPD Missions: If you just want to test out your new chrome, these "Scanner Hustles" let you take down gangs and clean up the streets for some quick eddies and XP. If you haven't stepped into Night City yet, do it. Just remember: in this city, you either die a legend or live long enough to become a sellout.  10/10 – See you in the major leagues, choom.

Creé a V. Y pasé cuarenta y cinco minutos en el editor de personajes. Cuarenta. Y. Cinco. Minutos. Ajustando la mandíbula, el tono de piel, la cicatriz, el tamaño de cosas que el juego después va a mostrar en cinemáticas donde la cámara cortésmente decide mirar hacia otro lado como un caballero medieval del siglo XXI. Porque Cyberpunk 2077 llegó a Steam con la patch 2.0 y de repente todo funcionaba, y de repente la ciudad respiraba, y de repente CDPR nos miró a los ojos y dijo: ¿recuerdan cuando prometimos esto en 2020? Aquí está. Con propinas. Y contenido para adultos desbloqueables. Capítulo I: El Cuerpo como Arte, Como Arma, y Como Fuente de Malos Juicios a las 2am Night City entiende el cuerpo. Lo entiende mejor que tu ex, mejor que tu médico de cabecera, mejor que cualquier persona que te haya mirado y pensado que te conocía. Los ripperdocs te abren como carta de amor y te llenan de cromo y opciones de mejora que en la vida real costarían un riñón y aquí cuestan eddies que conseguiste atracando un convoy de Militech vestido con un abrigo neón que ningún adulto debería usar y que yo usé durante cuarenta horas porque me hacía sentir poderoso. Pero el cuerpo en Cyberpunk no es solo combate. Oh no. CDPR fue muy específico al respecto. Judy Alvarez existe en este juego y si eres del tipo de jugador que hace todas las side quests —y si no lo eres, ¿qué estás haciendo con tu vida?— Judy te va a llevar al fondo de un lago. Al fondo de un lago. Bajo el agua turquesa donde Night City no llega, donde el neon se queda arriba ahogándose en su propia contaminación, y ahí, en el silencio más bonito que un videojuego me ha dado, dos personas se miran y el juego hace algo imperdonablemente bello: te deja respirar. No hay misión. No hay marcador. No hay Silverhand opinando. Solo V y Judy y el peso quieto del agua y yo en mi cuarto a las 3am sintiéndome un completo idiota por tener sentimientos hacia píxeles renderizados en tiempo real. Sin arrepentimientos. Panam Palmer, por otro lado, es el tipo de personaje que el universo crea cada mil años para recordarte que mereces que alguien te mire como ella mira a V cuando crees que no está mirando. Nómada. Terca. Con más dignidad en un dedo que toda la junta directiva de Arasaka junta. La noche antes del asalto final, en el desierto de Badlands, cielo lleno de estrellas que Night City nunca te deja ver porque la contaminación lumínica es el costo de vivir en la ciudad más brillante y más oscura del mundo, Panam y V tuvieron una conversación que Steam clasifica como "contenido sugerente" y que yo clasifico como "la razón por la que no dormí esa noche". Técnicamente épica. Emocionalmente devastadora. Visualmente: CDPR claramente contrató animadores que tenían algo que demostrar. River Ward llegó para los que prefieren a V masculino con una misión que empieza como policial procedural normal y termina con uno plantado en una granja al atardecer preguntándose cómo llegó aquí y si puede quedarse. River es el hombre más decente de Night City. Y Night City lo trata como Night City trata todo lo decente: con indiferencia criminal. Kerry Eurodyne, el rockstar arruinado que todavía cree en algo aunque no recuerda exactamente en qué, existe para recordarnos que la fama es otra forma de soledad con mejor iluminación. Y Meredith Stout — Meredith Stout es para los jugadores que leyeron el contrato completo antes de firmar y firmaron de todas formas porque la vida es corta y los corporativos son fascinantes cuando los encuentras en el contexto correcto en el momento incorrecto en un motel que cobra por horas y no hace preguntas. Capítulo II: Las Misiones que Me Quitaron el Sueño y Algo Más Phantom Liberty. Dogtown. Idris Elba como Reed. Una misión de espionaje tan bien escrita que olvidé durante horas que tenía un chip mortal en la cabeza porque el juego me tenía completamente ocupado desconfiando de todo el mundo mientras intentaba descifrar quién iba a traicionarme primero. Reed o Songbird. Songbird o Reed. Dos personas. Dos razones válidas. Cero respuestas cómodas. La misión del teatro abandonado. La persecución bajo la lluvia. El momento en que el juego te mira y dice: no hay héroe aquí, cariño. Solo hay elecciones y sus facturas. CDPR cobró esa factura con intereses. La misión de Viktor. Pequeña. Sin explosiones. Sin corporativos malvados. Solo V y el ripperdoc que le salvó la vida sentados en una clínica que huele a antiséptico y secretos teniendo una conversación sobre deudas que no siempre se pagan con eddies. Cuarenta segundos de juego. Cuarenta minutos de yo sentado procesando que un videojuego me acababa de dar más emoción con una charla entre amigos que muchos blockbusters con cien millones de presupuesto. El Heist. La misión que lo empieza todo. La misión que lo rompe todo. Jackie Wells. Jackie. Si alguien lee esto sin haber jugado: encariñate con Jackie Wells. Encariñate mucho. Confía en él. Quiérelo. Déjalo que te llame hermano con esa voz que suena como si hubiera nacido para ser tu mejor amigo. Y luego llora en el coche de Delamain mientras el juego te cobra la entrada a Night City con la única moneda que esta ciudad siempre acepta: lo que más te importa. Capítulo III: Los Tres Finales y Sus Tres Formas de Destrozarte con Estilo La Torre — "Vivir es el Acto Más Punk" V elige su cuerpo sobre la leyenda. Se va. En coche. Sin fanfarria. Hacia ningún lugar específico con todo el tiempo del mundo y la pregunta enorme flotando como humo de cigarro digital: ¿y ahora qué? Es el final más silencioso. Y el silencio en Cyberpunk es el lujo más caro que existe. La Estrella — "La Familia que Elegiste Cuando la Tuya No Alcanzó" Panam. Los Aldecaldos. El desierto infinito. V escoge a las personas sobre la inmortalidad y el juego, por una vez, decide que esa elección merece un horizonte abierto en lugar de una tragedia pulida. Es el final más cálido. Lo cual en Cyberpunk 2077 equivale a decir que solo lloré un poco. El Diablo — "Vendiste el Alma y el Contrato Era Legítimo" Arasaka. Mikoshi. La oferta de la corporación más malvada del mundo que resulta ser la única que puede darte lo que necesitas. V entra al cuarto del diablo y firma. Y el diablo cumple. Y eso casi lo hace peor. Porque los finales donde el villano cumple su promesa son los que te persiguen más tiempo. El Sol — "Silverhand, Esta es Tu Canción" El asalto a Arasaka. Tanques. Militech. Todo en llamas. V y un fantasma de rockstar contra el mundo corporativo entero. Épico como portada de álbum de rock de los 80. Trágico como el último track de ese mismo álbum. Y al final, Rogue Amendiares, la leyenda, la mujer que sobrevivió todo, tomando una última decisión que el juego no te avisa que va a partirte en dos. Epílogo: Lo que Night City Nunca Pudo Vender Night City tiene precio para todo. Cuerpos con cromo. Memorias en chips. Identidades de reemplazo. Vidas de segunda mano. Amor por horas en cualquier distritio que prefieras. Pero hay una cosa que Night City no pudo empacar, no pudo tokenizar, no pudo vender en ningún mercado negro de ningún callejón de Watson: Lo que sentiste jugándolo. La primera vez que V caminó por una calle de Night City y la ciudad rugió alrededor como organismo vivo, y la música de Refused y Grimes y SAMURAI te entró por los oídos como electricidad directa al alma. Eso no está en ninguna tienda. Ni en Steam aunque tengas el GOTY edition, el DLC, los mods de nexus que no voy a mencionar por nombre pero que todos hemos buscado a las 11pm con una expresión que no orgullosa exactamente pero sí comprometida. Night City te destruyó. Te destruyó con neón y balas y personajes que no merecían sus finales y finales que no merecías ver llorar. Y mañana vas a volver. Porque así es como funciona esta ciudad maldita y perfecta: nunca te suelta del todo. Y tú tampoco quieres que lo haga. V vivió. V murió. V fue leyenda. Y nosotros seguimos aquí, con la cara iluminada por el monitor a las 3am, preguntándonos si Judy está bien. Está bien. Tiene que estar bien.

Genuinely one of the most fun and immersive games I've ever played, and I've been waiting to play this for years ever since I first saw the anime Cyberpunk: Edgerunners. The story, writing, and overall world is a dark yet strangely beautiful look into what results from corporations gaining too much power within a world that favors them over the people. The gameplay is exhilarating, with a variety of fun weapons, build customization, and weighty, powerful vehicles. The character customization is amazing and gives anyone the power to make the person they envision, and the overall graphics and art design are beautiful. However, the best thing out of all these things and the whole game is that you get to meet the actor best known for his role in Toy Story 4 as "Duke Caboom": Keanu Reeves. His role as Johnny Silverhand adds so much to the story, and the approach they took with him is unique and morally horrifying.  I will admit though, the game still doesn't run that great even on a Linux PC around the recommended specs without RTX, and the game is still pretty buggy. The game fluctuates a lot between 50-70 FPS, and in indoor/less detailed sections of Night City, the FPS went up to around 90. Furthermore, the last section of the game had the worst performance for me, as I sometimes saw my FPS drop down to the 40s, especially during the [spoiler] Adam Smasher bossfight. [/spoiler] As for the bugs, they're not too game breaking, but I experienced primarily visual bugs with lighting, animations, and cutscene transitions, along with NPC AI bugs relating to moving around places. These bugs didn't break my immersion too much, but were a bit of a surprise to see still happening years after the game's initially horrible release.  Would I recommend people to buy this game? Of course. It's still buggy and runs badly, but that's unfortunately a prerequisite for modern triple A videogames nowadays. I'd recommend to buy it on a sale, as the game frequently costs ≤30 bucks, and the most recent Steam Summer Sale had the game priced at only 18 bucks. The modding scene for the game is also active, and the game still gets updates here and there (likely to get another one soon with the next season of Edgerunners!)  9/10

Once you look past the surface the veil drops as quick as the disappointment hits you because there's hints of greatness everywhere, however the story as a whole, the little moments, the world and the gameplay just don't live up to the potential. [url=https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLv4LBJ7ubTUXF34qf_S6HSCKK7Ijc0kLX] Here you can find some of the bugs I encountered [/url] (I will be adding more clips as time goes on)   Even if that weren't the case:  The city, while pretty as I said, is empty. The activities are all the same, scale being the only differentiating factor and a great part of the stories (especially in side content) is told through logs / mails which is extremely lazy and makes everything feel samey.  The only deviation here are the races (only 4 in total) which are a joke and a repeatable fetch quest they added in the DLC. Except that side content... takes time, time you don't have yet V is completely chill just going on random misadventures with whoever asks something of him.  Credit where credit is due, there are some decent choices in some missions but it doesn't matter when you find none of it interesting.  This isn't even approaching how interesting and intricate the dialogue in Witcher was.  Also to add to my frustrations, ♥♥♥♥ the advertismenets. I haven't even gotten to how terrible the skill tree is but alas, the review is getting long as it is. I've finished two full playthroughs now. First as a Nomad, then as a Corpo, and completed Phantom Liberty both times.  After almost 500 hours, I can honestly say this is my favorite game I've ever played.  Sure, the story is incredible, the characters are unforgettable, and Phantom Liberty somehow raises the bar even higher. But what keeps bringing me back isn't just the quests. Even after hundreds of hours I'm still finding details I've never noticed before.  And the soundtrack... wow. There aren't many games where the music alone can completely change your mood while cruising through the city at night.  On a more personal note, this game means more to me than entertainment. I'm a full-time caregiver for my mom, who has dementia. Life can be emotionally draining, and whenever I boot up Cyberpunk, I get to escape for a while. Night City became a place where I could breathe, relax, and simply exist.  Not many games have ever given me that feeling.  CD Projekt RED didn't just build a beautiful open world, they built one that I genuinely miss whenever I log off.  Here's hoping we get to return someday.  See you in NC, chooms.

Man, where do I even begin with this game? I think my playtime alone says enough for an open-world RPG.  The launch was undeniably rough, especially on consoles. PC had a better experience, but the game still needed a lot of work. Over the years, though, CD Projekt RED completely turned it around. Today it's one of the most immersive and visually stunning RPGs you can play.  I remember people expecting this to be the next GTA, but that's where many went wrong. This isn't GTA, it's an RPG first and foremost. The story is engaging, the side quests are excellent, and there's plenty of freedom to build your character however you want. The three lifepaths at the start are a cool idea, even if they don't have as much impact throughout the rest of the game as I'd hoped.  And then there's Phantom Liberty. It's easily one of the best DLCs I've played in recent years and elevates an already fantastic game even further.  If you skipped this game because of its launch, you're missing out. CD Projekt RED deserves a lot of credit for turning one of gaming's biggest disappointments into one of its greatest comeback stories.

While the world is detailed, the character designs and overall aesthetic lean into a kind of generic, lowest-common-denominator modern style that lacks the distinct identity you’d expect from a cyberpunk setting. Every character, for the most part, was ugly and suffering from the worst tropes of the woke gaming era. This game WILL feel aged in just a few more years. More importantly, it just doesn’t feel like true cyberpunk - the soul, grit, and atmosphere that define the best works in the genre are missing here.  The story also failed to hook me early on, which is a major issue for a game this dependent on narrative and immersion. Without that pull, there’s not much left to keep you invested - especially, not for 60+ hours.  In the end, it’s a game full of ideas that sound amazing but don’t translate into an enjoyable experience. I wanted to like it, but after just over an hour, I was bored and ready to move on.  On paper, it is everything I want. In execution, it is duller than a plastic butter knife left on a burner.

If I could give a mixed recommendation, I would, including for Liberty City. Summary for folks who want the brief - the main game plot is supposed to be a ticking time bomb where the MC have a limited time to save themselves, despite the worldbuilding and the core gameplay design contradicting it. That's it, now for a more critical reflection below.  Unlike previous Witcher projects, the main storyline is relatively quick (20-30 hours). For people who defends the game with all the side quests and Phantom Liberty DLC, the gameplay doesn't reflect the ticking time bomb. There is no timer for quests, and since you are somewhat expected to reach multiple endings by playing through branching side quests, you actually lose the plot and momentum by doing everything else.  Imagine if you play Red Dead 2, but on the last arc - you feel like something is missing if you didn't experience the freedom and glorious adventures in the previous arcs. CPK have this issue, and it's terribly rushed with some characters' arc being noticably trimmed down. You either have to forgo the mentality of a ticking time bomb, or you get the worst and more unrewarding main story content if you choose to focus on it.  I play main as female V because she, like Kassandra from AC: Odyssey, have the better VA. V's background honestly feels underwhelming and only affects some of the choices you will make, like getting more money. For a corpo, she doesn't feel like it, and the decision to age her down from 28 to 23 does affect your believability of her.  The game also over-balanced itself after patch 1.6, removing many fun previous mechanics like shooting through walls, hacking through walls, putting silencers on other guns besides pistols, and more customizability. Now, it kinda forces you to balance your character and build, which isn't as fun.  Everything else besides the main plot, including the characters, world, and combat, are all very fun. It is basically the Witcher gameplay with sci-fi elements. You can feel the project is rushed before the scope of their destination is reached, and I love the world so much I feel like it ruins part of the experience for me. Hell, I'd argue the overbalanced nature of later patches was because the overall game, including sidequests, are maybe 80-100 hours in total content and it isn't nearly enough to have a bigger and more complex skill tree.  I also gave it a bad review because, like many cultured players, the decision to not add romance for both Aurore and So Mi cripples me for days and I had to install mods to regain small parts of my sanity. Despite this game promising a lot, the romance and a few quests felt short of, well, being short. There is something amazing here if they choose to tap into more, and I hope their Orion project sequel will deliver.

Five years post launch and I finally get it running, and it turns out beneath all the bugs there's a pretty great game here. Who knew?  So if you didn't know, this game had a disastrous launch.. It got incredibly overhyped due to being made by CD Projekt Red, the developers of Witcher 3, and even if it hadn't clearly had a very troubled production and a rushed launch there would probably have still been a lot of disappointment. It's definitely not Witcher 3 but with guns and neon. I'd say design wise the game series it most reminds me of is GTA, although full disclosure last time I played a GTA game was Vice City Stories 15 years ago so my memory is a bit fuzzy. The hallmarks are here from what I remember. Open world sandbox based on a single city, drive around a lot, lots of music and radio stations, plot focused on crime and inevitable crime sprees when you get bored and start shooting random people. Unlike GTA it's first person, is not funny, has RPG mechanics and really good combat.   Combat is probably where the game really shines and it's pretty fantastic. Lots of shooting naturally but the rpg skill trees add a lot of welcome depth and variety to it. You can spec into various different weapons, get various upgrades, and there's the opportunity to get cyber implants on top of that as well. You can set enemies on fire or drive them insane, get roided up mechanical arms or blades that pop out of your forearms and there's even a lot of weapons with homing bullets/ The game gives you enough skill points to spec into almost all the areas and you can respec most of them easily so you are never spoiled for choice, and it remains very fun throughout. Any wider criticisms of the game I may make, let me be very clear that the core gameplay is absolutely fantastic and more than enough to give the thumbs up alone.  Besides killing things, the game has a very solid setting and a decent story. It's set in the Cyberpunk Red universe, which besides rather blithely being named after the genre seems to be a pretty interesting setting. The US fell apart in the 90s instead of the Soviets, it's set in a city state in california dominated by megacorps which is a glitzy but horrible place to live, characterised by social inequality, heavy cyber augmentation and near constant violence. It is called "Night City" but I don't know why as it still experiences day.  I'm not sure how much is the RPG and how much is the game, but it's a really well designed and thought out world that has a ton of details that make it feel really grounded and believable, and it's one that feels really immersive to explore. Unlike GTA it feels like a lot of areas took being a pedestrian into account, so there's all manner of pedestrian bridges and tunnels, and it's really nice just wandering around on foot at times drinking in the atmosphere. Story wise it begins as a gritty crime drama, with a heist gone wrong that leads to the player character suffering from a strange terminal illness called "keanu reeves." Whilst I have quibbles with the story, on a whole it's pretty great, and the mo-cap and voice acting is largely fantastic throughout.   On to quibbles, whilst I did like the story, it does feel rather chopped up, and there isn't really a main plot between the beginning and the end. The RPG stuff also does not really extend to deeper roleplay beyond a few dialogue checks, which are mostly just conversational and often don't affect much. There are story choices but they are the exception rather than the rule. Most other open world games have a longer more connected story, whilst this one feels more like four shorter stories connected by the main character that do overlap but don't really connect.. Kerry and River's stories are completely miss-able because you need to do a side job that you have no idea is necessary to unlock that much gameplay, and both of their stories feel to have been considerably cut down. The vast majority of the side jobs are "go here, kill gangsters in an alley" and whilst there are some with more story, there are a surprisingly small amount for such a long game. I can't get too mad at CDPR for this because as said, the combat is fantastic, but the game does feel to have less depth than I'd have liked, especially given the generally good quality of the writing. Having had such a troubled development it's understandable and they absolutely took the right decision focusing on good gameplay over more story depth, but I'm still somewhat left wanting more.  Gameplay wise I should also disclose, that whilst it's nowhere near launch levels, it's still quite a glitchy game, although I'd say no worse than any other open world game that I've played (and a lot better than anything made by Bethesda). I died once because I fell through the floor of the world, and twice I had to tab out and force quit the game because combat just failed to end and I couldn't call a car or do most interactions (Perhaps a masterful musing on ptsd and not a glitch), but glitches were mostly minor immersion breaking stuff like 3d models clipping or clothing behaving weirdly. For me 3 gamebreaks in 100 hours was not too bad but I can see the frequent minor glitches really pulling people out of the experience.  Final point to talk about, the music. The non diegetic soundtrack is decent although nothing to write home about, but I do want to voice some thoughts on the radio tracks. So unlike real life, you can actually get good music on the radio in this world, IRWSAYH and Pain were probably the standout tracks for me, but there was also a lot of incredibly awful music. It was a really interesting design choice to put the best and the worst tracks on Body Heat Radio. The worst for me was probably the one where a girl says "here in night city" over and over again for what feels like five hours straight, or "I want who I want who I want," which is just obnoxious and really annoying. I can't work out why Crustpunk seems to be every other song on that channel and plays three or four times more than most other songs, especially when consists solely of a generic guitar riff that feels like it would play over a chase scene in a mid budget British cop drama. Also.. I have no idea if PonPon Sh*t is good or bad, it's what anime music sounds like to someone who doesn't like anime but I found myself liking it somehow, possibly due to stockholm syndrome. I mostly voice this concern as I liked the good songs enough to nearly buy the soundtrack, before deferring because there's probably more bad tracks on it than good and If I hear "here in night city" while driving irl I may do as I do in game and plough my car straight into the nearest river in a desperate attempt to make it stop.  A final note,  I would like to offer legitimate praise to CDPR for supporting this post launch. So many AAA developers put out barely functional games with the promise of post launch support and then abandon them 6 months to a year later, CDPR actually followed through and turned a disaster into a redemption story, and gave us a really good game for it. Day of writing they just passed 40 million sales, so well done CDPR.

When this game came out, it was a mess. Now, its almost unrecognizable... Even back then though, I enjoyed playing it.  This is a deeply immersive RPG, with fun combat mechanics.  There is a lot of diversity and option in the playstyle, and this game ranks near the top of my 'open world' 'first person' list.  In fact, it might be number 1.    Another standout feature of this game is the writing.  It can be campy and over the top, but it is pure 'cyberpunk' through and through. They absolutely nailed the setting. The characters are engaging and quirky, and the story could have come straight out of a Shadowrun adventure from the 80s (who knows - maybe it did...).    My only gripe, if i have one, is that night city itself is a bit of a mixed bag.  The world is huge and diverse, but it doesn't feel anything at all like a real city - especially a North American one.  The city feels like it was designed by an alien who read about cities in an encyclopedia but had never actually seen one or been to one.  The 'districts' are bizarre. They each have unique  architecture and their own vibe, and then you cross the street and its different entirely. The metro system is clearly just a hacked game mechanic as opposed to being an incorporated part of the world. Also, the world can feel a little empty, as almost all of the content is specifically indicated on the map, so exploring can feel like you are walking through dead space between icons. Still, this is not a dealbreaker, and the game works within this limitation.  Its a bummer that the development of this game was such a debacle.  My hope is that its ultimate success will lead to more games set in this world, because I can't get enough.
