=== Long Review – No Spoilers === Hi folks! This review will have a closer look at Cyberpunk 2077 (CP). Let’s have a look at the facts before switching to my subjective views: CP is an open-worldish RPG in the cyberpunk world of “Night City” – a huge complex full of megastructures, alleys, roads and slums. You take the role of “V” – a mercenary who is on a quest for glory and fame, trying to become a legend. In order to achieve your goal, you take on various assignments (or “jobs” and “gigs”) where you have to eliminate gangsters, infiltrate facilities of the all-powerful mega corporations or fight against para-military forces. Apart from a large number of side quests, there is also a main storyline in which V uncovers some of the best-kept secrets of Night City and tries to survive while being hunted by powerful enemies.  To ensure your survival, V can command a wide arsenal of weapons, ranging from sniper rifles to submachine guns, pistols and even melee combat. Additionally, V is augmented with cyberware, meaning that your character can utilize all kinds of technology: You can choose between different skills and perks and freely decide what kind of gameplay you would like to favor: Would you rather want to silently sneak up on enemies from behind and use takedowns to avoid detection? Or do you want to comfortably hack into enemies from a distance using your cyberware, simply frying their systems? Why not avoid confrontation by luring away the bad guys using distraction techniques? All that is possible!  You can obtain and use cars or bikes to travel across the vast region of Night City and the outskirts (in addition to a fast-travel mechanism). You can freely customize your character V to give him or her your personal touch - including appearance, gender and clothing. In addition to the main game, an expansion is available as DLC, but I will not cover it in my review.  Let’s switch to my subjective views and let’s focus on the aspects which I liked: -	The world itself is very convincing and quite large: It has been crafted with such detail and variety, that I find this to be one of the strongest aspects of the game. It is simply cool to leave your apartment in a megastructure, then drive through the crowded streets of the city on your trusty bike while rain pours down and finally reach the outskirts as the sun rises and the sky clears up. Truly amazing atmosphere. -	The graphics are very decent, especially when you play with a high resolution and high details. -	Gunplay, melee combat and character movement feel “just right”, especially if you focus more on agility and reflex-based skills. -	Using certain skills or weapon categories unlocks specific perks while progress is tracked per skill category. I found this very engaging. -	Voice acting is outstanding – especially Keanu Reeves as “Johnny Sliverhand” -	A crafting system is available and you can upgrade your weapons -	Hacking events with small puzzles can be used to gain more crafting material or netrunner skills  This is a very solid foundation for a good or even great game. Still, there are also some aspects which I didn’t enjoy or which could be improved in my opinion, so let’s focus on them here: 1)	The dialog system is nearly identical to Witcher 3, meaning that there is a visual clue as to which answers drive a conversation forward (yellow) and which ones are purely “fluff” to add more details (blue). While this makes skipping of any non-essential dialogue very comfortable, I do not like this approach – especially, because the dialogue structure itself is rather shallow: There are hardly any real branches in the dialogue tree and sometimes it feels that you do not really have that much to decide or that your choices really do not have that much impact at all. IMHO, CP would have gained a lot from more complex and well-written dialogues – the potential is absolutely there, since the world itself is truly interesting and allows for so much cool content. 2)	The level and skill progression feels off to me: I reached the max level cap (50 without DLC) rather quickly after having completed roughly 50% of all missions and main story line. That felt way too early and after that was no progression anymore at all. Granted, the DLC adds another 10 levels to the cap, but still, this does not feel right. You cannot maximize all your skills, either. 3)	The overall balancing feels odd: While in the beginning I was very careful about how I moved around, I quickly reached a mid-game phase where my char was so strong that I could basically just walk in anywhere, gun down or slash anybody and walk away with barely a scratch. If you like being superior, this might be your thing, but especially some netrunner skills and weapons are so strong that it often takes away any necessity for stealthy or planned movements. 4)	Though there are multiple endings which I won’t spoil for you, the overall story left me unsatisfied: There is such a strong build up, such a cool world and lore, yet it feels that only a tiny fraction of the potential here is truly realized (compare point 1). 5)	A lot of your playtime will probably consist of driving around in CP. While the world is truly a sight to behold and rather large, I found it strangely boring rather quickly: There is not really any strong need to actually explore the world: You’ll just drive from A to B highlighted on your map to do gigs and deliveries. Discovering new locations does not really have any benefit as such (e.g. discover a new shop dealer that sells unique stuff) which is more than a little sad, because the environment itself *is* rather unique and offers some of the coolest landscapes I have ever seen in a video game.  6)	The driving physics are not very realistic and sometimes flat-out ridiculous when you drive some of the faster cars (I deliberately chose to stick with bikes).  The verdict: Is CP worth playing? Yes, I think so. The world and atmosphere are really cool – especially if you are a Sci-Fi or cyberpunk fan. But would I consider CP to be a “truly outstanding” game? Sadly, no. I would rate it with a 7 out of 10, but not more. The reason is that CP focuses more on width than on depth: Dialogue, story, variety in missions, skill progression, balancing and finally the way in which you can make your choices and how they affect the outcome of the story – all these aspects are not badly designed at all. However, I had a constant feeling that the devs built such a powerful world and core mechanics, that they were utterly overstrained to fully explore the possibilities of their construct in the end.  There is so much potential, but only a small fraction of that has actually been realized. I would have loved more complex missions and dialogues. Why give the player such excellent netrunner skills to distract enemies and cool takedown mechanics when even halfway through the game you can simply decide to mow down all enemies with your SMG or your katana? Somehow, the devs wanted to make everybody happy by offering every possible kind of combat, but that comes at the cost of having less refined and engaging gameplay.   It is exceedingly more difficult to find a good balance for all these different playstyles (especially when they can also be combined) than focusing on a specific kind of gameplay and it is an odd choice to use such a low level cap, then. I wonder what the game would have been like if the player would have to decide and stick with only *one* specialization (e.g. only melee and netrunning skills) per playthrough: Not only would that have forced the player to come up with really good strategies on how to beat the missions, the missions would also have felt drastically different in each playthrough.   All in all, the parallels to Witcher 3 are striking and that game has some of the very same issues. I personally would have loved it if CP would have been a little bit more like the Deus Ex series here and there without just imitating the concept…

What can I say that hasn't been already said? Of all the good things, I want to talk about jank.  I really liked how the game handles characters, which combined with the 'ethos' of the setting (No Happy Endings in Night City) made for really compelling stories. All of the characters are weird and janky in some way, most of all Silverhand and Songbird. There's this constant tension between the 'eff you got mine' structure of the city and people genuinely trying to create a community.  The setting itself is vibrant and full of compromise - you can sort of see why people want to live in Night City, even though it is very dystopian. Again, things are extremely janky but not hopeless. There are bases of goodwill, people trying to do better (even though they are selfish in their own ways). The game doesn't fall into that cynical hopelessness that I feel a lot of dystopian fiction slides into.  I even like how janky things are sometimes, gameplay-wise (my car repeatedly slamming into the road railings, my silencers resetting into the lowest rarity ones).  In short: I love the jank. This game has good jank.

Instead, I ended up spending 140 hours and completing every achievement.  Night City is one of the most immersive worlds I've ever explored. Every district has its own personality, the side quests often feel just as meaningful as the main story, and even random gigs have memorable characters and stories. It never felt like I was checking boxes just to reach 100%.  The combat gives you so much freedom. Whether you want to hack everything, sneak through missions, or go in guns blazing, the game lets you play exactly how you want. I was constantly changing my build because every approach was fun.  Coming from the anime made the emotional moments hit even harder. Walking through the same streets, hearing familiar music, and finding all the little references made Night City feel alive in a way very few games manage.  Going for 100% never felt like a chore. There was always another story worth experiencing, another build to try, or another corner of the city that made me stop and just take it all in.  140 hours later, I wasn't ready to leave Night City.  One of my favorite games of all time. Easy recommendation.

I love CD Projekt. The Witcher is one of my greatest loves, and The Witcher 3 in particular, despite its notoriously messy launch, remains one of the defining games of my life. Noblesse oblige, however, Cyberpunk 2077 took that predicament to an entirely different level. Its release seemed beyond redemption, yet the Poles worked what can only be described as magic.   The result is a monumental work, one whose attention to detail borders on the pathological. It builds a world of extraordinary corporeality, an immersion unlike anything else the medium has to offer. Night City is a monster to be feared, one that inevitably takes everything from you while offering only fleeting shards of humanity in return. It is a city haunted by nostalgia for a present that is constantly slipping through its inhabitants' fingers, suspended between helplessness and hopelessness. What keeps people moving is the belief that, amid everything that is lost, memories, bonds, decisions, and actions can still endure. Beneath layers upon layers of steel, the only thing left worth preserving is identity.   It is no coincidence that the story revolves around the Relic. The Soulkiller represents libertarianism's ultimate fantasy: stripping human beings of their souls so they can be fully subordinated to capital, while those in power preserve themselves by erasing the last remaining limit to domination, mortality itself. Everyone knows this is the system they are condemned to inhabit, yet awareness doesn't necessarily imply submission. Night City devours people, and those unable to cope with its tremendous injustices gradually abandon their humanity, finding meaning in their suffering through wealth, power, and recognition. Cyberpunk 2077 is intellectually rich in its philosophical ambitions, but even richer in the way it communicates them: not through mere exposition, but by making you live them.   Sorrowfully, the gameplay has significant shortcomings. Several of its core systems may feel unfair, unbalanced, or simply underdeveloped. The driving is simply and utterly dreadful and, as someone who avoids fast travel whenever possible, it became one of the game's greatest obstacles, even if the wide variety of vehicles and their distinct handling characteristics soften the blow somewhat. Progression is unbalanced, trivializing everything far too soon. Looting is another unnecessary problem the game creates for itself, one that could have been solved in countless better ways, especially without forcing the player to rely so heavily on the scanner. Combat, meanwhile, never quite lives up to its potential. Even on the highest difficulty, it rarely feels demanding, and despite its impressive breadth of builds and playstyles, it lacks the mechanical depth and satisfaction I had hoped for. The sheer amount of freedom is admirable, but that freedom inevitably comes at a cost.  You might think it contradictory to praise Cyberpunk 2077 so highly while acknowledging such fundamental mechanical flaws, but great games are not always defined by the perfection of their systems. What impressed me most is not any individual component, but the extraordinary cohesion between them. Every artistic discipline serves the same emotional and thematic purpose: portraying a  vision of a world where identity itself could become a commodity. Its branching narrative, world-building, unforgettable cast, dialogue, animation, staggering level of immersion, and the unmistakable passion poured into every corner of the experience elevate it far beyond the sum of its mechanics. Its dystopian vision feels unparalleled, while its lore reveals itself through countless interconnected threads. It has the rare ability to leave you emotionally devastated before quietly offering comfort in the same breath. Its visual identity is outstanding. Phantom Liberty is exceptional. The soundtrack is phenomenal in both composition and implementation, and in the way it interacts with the rest of the work. Its thoroughgoing mise en scène extracts the maximum expressive potential from every scene. [spoiler]The Sun ending, with V gazing toward the Crystal Palace as the chorus of "Never Fade Away" begins to swell, made me think: "There goes something truly special."[/spoiler].  I absolutely love Cyberpunk 2077. It is one of the very few video games that left me with a profound sense of emptiness, the distinct feeling that I would never experience anything like it again. That is transcendence.  A thing of beauty, I know Will never fade away

Its not on par with Witcher 3 but it does come close. A solid 7.5/10 experience in its current state, 8.5/10 if including use of mods to improve the gameplay issues.  The open world is amazing, the choices we can make decisions wise, the cyberware decisions, the skill tree decisions, perk decisions, weapon decisions, the amount of cars we can purchase, all amazing. Made looting a whole lot more tolerable and not wasting my time manually clicking each loot item from each dead body. Did not require any other mods to enjoy this 100% experience, but if I do another playthrough in the future will definitely use a lot more mods to spice things up.  All in all the developers nailed it, just so sad that they botched the release. Hope they do not repeat these mistakes for Witcher 4, I will not be preordering and repeating the mistake I made with cyberpunk though, learned my lesson and tanked the loss as the game is a fraction of its cost now as compared to when I bought it and never got to play it at the time due to the bugs.  Phantom Liberty was a great expansion, hopefully they will give us another one in the future that is as good and adds to the experience.

First, let me say that I SERIOUSLY HATE MEGA DEVELOPER, MASS-AUDIENCE GAMES. Most are made by major labels that focus on making a buck over true player investment. I usually focus on smaller indie games, because you can see the amount of care the developer has put into it.   This game is the exception that proves the rule.  I bought this a long while back, but found the actual gameplay a bit clunky and somewhat confusing. I set it aside and only recently decided to read up about it, learn how to play it, and make an informed decision.  The problem with that approach, is that the whole opening section of the game has a LOT of story and lots of little time wasters (fun little side bits). The result for most people is that by the time the trial period ends you are still a little confused.   The result is that a LOT of people grab the refund and forget it. (BIG MISTAKE imho)  This game is visually stunning. The voice acting is magnificent. The writing is superb, and the vibe is out of this world. It's both a game and an immersive visual entertainment. The feel of the game is like a blend of The Matrix, Blade Runner, and Ghost in the Shell.   My best advice for new players is to play it to level 25-30, and then go back and restart with a new character, because you will have developed a feel for how you envision playing the MC. I am on my 3rd run through the game and each one added new understanding and new insights.  In addition here are more pros/cons.  Pro:  238 hrs played before completing the game. Ability to play multiple times with a variety of builds and outcomes. Visually awesome world. Immersive open world feeling. You feel connected with many NPCs  Cons:  It is almost impossible to fail at missions and some are ridiculously hard to mess up. The game does force outcomes despite their attempt to create the illusion of choices. The inability to fast forward through many narrative scenes despite previously doing them.  My Bottom line: It is amazingly stunning and immersive as hell. You get sucked into the game and it often feels as much like an immersive film, as it does a game. It may not be the perfect game, but it is pretty darn close.

The irony is staggering, and it is easily one of the greatest examples of real-world corporate hypocrisy in gaming history. The developer became the exact villain they were warning us about.  CD Projekt Red spent years marketing a story about a dystopian future where greed destroys lives, workers are treated like garbage, and corporate executives lie to the public for a massive payday—and then they turned around and did it themselves.  1. The Corporate Exploitation of Workers (Crunch Culture)  The Promise: The studio’s leadership publicly promised their developers that they would not use forced "crunch" (mandatory, extreme overtime) to finish the game.  The Reality: As deadlines approached, corporate executives mandated six-day work weeks, with many developers working brutal 16-hour days for months on end just to patch a broken product. They literally ran a human-grinder corporate sweatshop to ship a game about human-grinder corporate sweatshops.  2. The Multi-Million Dollar Lie  The Corporate Gaslighting: To secure millions of pre-orders and protect their stock price, the executives actively lied to the public and their investors. They claimed the game ran "surprisingly well" on older consoles (PS4/Xbox One) when they knew it was completely unplayable.  Review Manipulation: In true corporate fashion, they heavily restricted review copies. They forbade reviewers from using their own gameplay footage on older consoles, forcing them to use pre-rendered corporate B-roll. It was a calculated, anti-consumer media blackout designed to milk the consumer before the truth came out.  3. Turning Rebellious Art into Corporate Slop  The True Irony: Johnny Silverhand is a character whose entire identity is about bombing a corporate headquarters to fight the system. CD Projekt Red turned that punk-rock anti-corporate icon into a marketing puppet used to sell limited-edition Porsche cars, branded energy drinks, and gaming chairs.  Night City isn't just a fictional warning anymore. The way Cyberpunk 2077 was handled proved that we already live in a cyberpunk world—where a massive company can package the idea of "rebellion," sell it to us for ₹4,000, break their workers in the process, and still walk away with a massive profit.

Honestly, I don't think I can describe a bigger disappointment for me than Cyberpunk 2077. I know it's considered one of the best RPGs by many people, but after about 5 hours, my experience has been almost the complete opposite.  Let's start with the positives. Night City is absolutely stunning. The graphics are easily one of the best I've ever seen, especially with ray tracing enabled. The attention to detail is incredible, the hacking mechanics are fun, and the main story has been interesting enough to keep me playing. If I had to rate those aspects alone, the graphics would be a 20/10 and the story, so far, around an 8/10.  Now for the parts that disappointed me.  Driving feels awful. Almost every vehicle I've driven feels like it's sliding on ice. Cars, bikes, vans—it doesn't really matter. Taking sharp corners often turns into either massive understeer or drifting when I didn't even want to drift. Traversing the city ended up being more frustrating than fun.  The gunplay also didn't click with me. The weapons look fantastic and have great animations, but actually using them feels bland. Damage numbers often feel strange, and combat never felt as satisfying as I expected.  Another thing that didn't appeal to me was how heavily the game leans into sexual themes. I understand it's part of the world's identity, but after a while it felt like it was everywhere—from advertisements to certain side quests—and it became more distracting than immersive. Some side missions also felt random and forgettable rather than meaningful.  Performance was... acceptable. On my RTX 5060 Laptop GPU at 1440p with max settings and low ray tracing, I averaged around 40-80 FPS, depending on the area. However, cinematic cutscenes occasionally became extremely laggy for me, dropping to what felt like single-digit FPS regardless of whether ray tracing was enabled. I'm not sure if that's a hardware issue or something on the game's side.  I also wasn't impressed with the NPC AI. I frequently saw civilians walking into walls, repeating strange behaviors, or panicking in unrealistic ways whenever combat started. It broke the immersion more than once.  Is the game worth buying for around $12-$15? I'd say yes. At that price, there's definitely enough content to justify the purchase, especially if you're interested in the story and exploring Night City.  Overall, I don't think Cyberpunk 2077 is a bad game—it just wasn't the game I expected. While the world, visuals, and main story are excellent, the driving, combat, AI, and some of the side content kept me from enjoying it as much as everyone else seems to.  Overall: 6.8/10  Graphics: 10/10 (20/10 if your GPU survives)  Story: 8/10 (so far)  Driving: 3/10  Combat: 5/10  Optimization: 7/10  NPC AI: 4/10  World Design: 10/10

I made a stealth runner, stealth and magic, methodically crawling through dungeons, taking my time to not be seen, and by level 12 I was pretty good at it. Then for the next 31 levels nothing changed. When i turned to the internet to figure out why the downtime in my gameplay loop hadn't improved in 30 levels. I found that there were more efficient combos and perk choices that I could be making. So after some research and spending some of my in-game money, I improved my build. Or so I though. The downtime had gotten shorter, but not significantly so. So little, in fact, that I would argue that it hadn't changed. Then after more research, I found that certain resource-recovery perks were intentionally disconnected from the most popular stealth quickhack combos, without it being mentioned anywhere in the game. I can only assume this was done for marketing purposes? Because the first version of the game was such a failure (not that I had invested a lot of time into it back then, and personally dont have an opinion about early CyberPunk77) that they decided to allow only fast paced action builds to shine so that they could redeem themselves more quickly through paid youtube shillery.  Ok, fine. So i put together a Damage over Time build that used the whip to detonate the debuffs. But I found that the interaction between the skills was rarely happening and that fights would only be explosively fast. With yet more research I found that the whip's hit scan function was bugged and ultra thin, so when you were attempting to hit the also bugged hitboxes of mobs who were displaying debuff animations. So my whip attacks were hitting less than 20% of the time and enemies were dying slowly to the DoT's alone.  From my experience alone, it can be surmised that, either on purpose or on accident, no single part of this game actually works. Certainly if you don't want to play sandevistan/katana build you shouldn't spend money on it either.  The narrative is irritating. I get that V is a headstrung, insecure, dumbass, but how many story hooks can start with my character being forced by the game to do something dangerously stupid? Am I expected to believe that she grew up in night city? I've been here 15 minutes and can tell you those jerks are going to do something jerky.  Also as an accomplished netrunner, V constantly praising Songbird and "needing" her for hacking jobs felt bad. Luckily my V was a weak nerd though, because if i was a sandevistan using katana wielder, I would have been pissed that the game required me to constantly ask the help of a geriatric woman to open all the doors in that intro.  Ultimately I think I'm done with CDprokect Red for a while. Maybe they'll get their act together eventually, but at this point in time I think we can safely say that the constant development issues over there are a feature, not a bug.

Suggestion for a Legacy System in the Next Game – Passing V’s Gear to the Next Protagonist  Dear CDPR Team,  First of all, thank you for creating Night City and the unforgettable journey of V. I just finished my playthrough with the “Sun” ending, and it left me with a strong feeling that V’s story shouldn’t just end there – his legacy should live on in some way.  I have a suggestion that I believe would be both immersive and meaningful for players who have completed Cyberpunk 2077 and will go on to play the next game, whether it’s the Orion Project or a future DLC.  The Idea – “Legacy Transfer System”  For players who have completed the main story of Cyberpunk 2077 (and have a save file), the next game could detect that save and place a small homage in the starting apartment of the new protagonist.  Specifically:  1. A Locked Storage Container – In the new protagonist’s first safehouse, there could be a locked container or drawer that can only be opened via a code or a small side quest referencing the original game. 2. The Content – A Weapon and a Note – Inside, the new protagonist would find:    · A weapon that belonged to V (could be any weapon – a pistol, a melee weapon, or even the Mantis Blades).    · A handwritten note from V, explaining who they were and why they left this item behind. 3. The Note’s Content Based on the Player’s Ending – The note could change based on which ending the player achieved:    · Sun Ending – “I went to the Crystal Palace. I don’t know if I’ll come back. But this piece of me – this weapon – should stay in good hands. Don’t let it rust.”    · Star Ending – “I left Night City with Panam. I’m done with this life. But this weapon has seen more battles than I can count. Maybe you’ll need it more than I do now.”    · Temperance Ending – “I gave everything I had to a friend. This weapon is all that remains of my time in the city. Use it well.”    · Devil Ending – (optional) “They took everything from me. Except this. I hope you never have to go through what I did.” 4. A Customizable Weapon Transfer – If technically feasible, the weapon itself could be imported from the player’s own inventory from Cyberpunk 2077 – for example, the very first legendary weapon they obtained, or a weapon they used most frequently. This would make the transfer feel deeply personal.  Why This Would Be Meaningful  This would create a powerful emotional bridge between the two games. It turns the new protagonist’s journey into something more than just a new story – it becomes a continuation of a legacy. It acknowledges the player’s unique journey with V and makes them feel that their actions truly mattered in the larger world.  It also fits perfectly with the core theme of the Cyberpunk universe: “Legacy and Memory.” In a world where identities can be digitized and people are replaced by copies, the idea that a weapon and a note carry more weight than any contract or eddy feels deeply authentic to the setting.  Final Thought  I know that implementing a system like this would require save-file recognition and a fair amount of narrative design work. But I truly believe it would be one of the most rewarding experiences for long-time players – the moment when you open that container in the new game and realize: “V was here. V left this for me.”  Thank you for taking the time to read this. Night City changed my life, and I hope this idea can help someone else feel that connection in the future.  Sincerely, A fan who walked the path of the Sun.

Review: it plays like Fallout 4 meets Far Cry + cyber magic. Not the RPG game many of us were expecting, wish I could say it's New Vegas meets Far Cry but I still had some fun. I got my money's worth by replaying it with DLC and mods YEARS after it released (hey just like Fallout 4 lmao) I was like, wow there's cops now? haha. This game is why Cyberpunk: Edgerunners exist, gets credit for that.  Advice: don't use fast travel!  For some reason, there's fast travel points EVERYWHERE but don't do it. Night City is the real main character, fast traveling would be depriving yourself from the best part of the game. Even Mike Pondsmith said he'll just drive around Night City after work. I can't imagine what that must feel like, driving throughout an interpretation of a world you created.  Experience: I'm finally done. This was the last game I was seriously HYPED for. I was beyond excited, watched the dev logs and everything. I even pre-ordered it which I never do! I mean, this is the developers of Witcher 3, like, what could go wrong? lol Personally, what I looked forward to the most was the role playing aspect. It was heavily advertised that every decision lead down interesting and diverse paths. However, not including DLC, one of the early missions has the most depth and it was the one used for advertisement. This was a huge let down and that wasn't even including the horrific launch. It was so broken I couldn't even finish it. I had to put it down and wait for it to be finished. Recently came back after getting Phantom liberty on sale (my friend recommended it). Started a completely new game and finally finished it. It's been a journey with this game for sure but I had my fill and I'm finally done with it.

I will start by clearing up one thing, this game had a very rough launch, but since then everything was fixed, so to those worrying about bugs- don't. Quick chart for those wanting a quick review: Story: 10/10 - dlc: 11/10 Gameplay: 10/10 Characters: 9/10 - dlc: 10/10 Graphics: 10/10 Replayability: 9/10 Voice/Movement Acting: 9/10 Now the more detalied review: Story:  The main story in cyberpunk isn't amongst the longest but it is well-written, thorough and moving. Yet cyberpunk shines even more when it comes to side quests/gigs as they are fun, engaging and other deeply unsettling- just like the night city itself. If you want an even more impactful story you need to check out Phantom Liberty dlc(which i strongly recommend, since cd projekt red is known for extensions so good they feel like separate games). Its story is somehow even better than the main storyline to the point where internet is still full of heated debate on the choices offered to the player. Gameplay: When it comes to gameplay, I must say it is phenomenal. The skill tree feels balanced and meaningful. Moreover the game doesn't force you to walk a designated path. You are free to become anyone, anything. Become a ghost lurking in the shadows, a netrunner(hacker) scouting enemy lines  from afar or just simply become a tank, grab the hottest iron you can find and strike front door. This is further reinforced by the fact that missions are designed with multiple different ways to complete them. Characters: They are memorable, fun and feel human-like, which perfectly enriches the story. I won't get into details not to spoiler anything unintentionally. Visual/Sound Aspects: This, not surprisingly, facet of the game was also nailed. Night city is alive and full of details often overlooked even by the veterans- so there is always something new to discover. Furthermore, the motion/voice acting make cutscenes cinematic to the point where you truly connect with the world and characters within. Conclusion: If you like story-rich, futuristic or cyberpunk games, you will definetly enjoy cyberpunk2077 as it nails nearly all categories I wrote about above.

First and foremost, Lets get this out of the way, this is NOT and RPG. This is an ACTION game with a story. The story does not revolve around your character, it revolves around Johnny Silverhand, and your character is a meat taxi to facilitate that story being told, nothing more. Do not expect any variation in story, and the endings are really only minor spins on one another. Its more like reading a book with extra steps than living a fantasy, which is what is to be expected with an RPG. Think of yourself as a flesh Delemain and you'll be just fine.  With that covered: I've been playing this game over and over, from when hitting a speedbump blew up your car and launched you into space on that, quite frankly comical "we told you it wasn't ready" release, through levels not mattering because you were one shot sniping the most powerful enemies in the game through a wall for half a billion damage at level 10, through the various phases of clean up, polish, and the DLC. Now even with (probably) nearly 10 playthroughs, I'm about to play it again.  This game is incredibly visually immersive with just enough of a decent story to - mostly - get lost in for a bit of grade-A escapism. Yes, there are still bugs, and perhaps I am biased because I played through the worst of the bugs, but the current bugs rarely interfere with game immersion unless you start exploiting them, and if you really care, modding a fix is a cakewalk in this game. Welcome to Night City, the City of Dreams! As much was I was hoping to have a dream-like experience with this game it sadly fell flat it some areas. Night City is a gigantic city with a variety of districts, varying from poor slums to rich penthouses to badlands. The map itself is very impressive, flawlessly blending and combining these areas, being very bright and lively while also being dark and calm. The story is not bad either, while being relatively short you experience a ton of action, sorrow, meet a bunch of people and make new friends. You can really express yourself with the amount of possibilities you have with the combat, a ton of builds, covering every type of player. It is also the origin of the bangin' soundtrack "I Want To Stay At Your House". Preem, enough praise, let's cut to the, personally, unenjoyable part of the game. As I just mentioned, the combat. While you can put some insane stuff together, I think the way they implemented this is messy. You have a vast amount of options to choose in a skill tree and body tech, you can change your body tech whenever you want but you only get to change your core build once by resetting your skill tree. Both systems not sharing the same menu too, changing your body tech needs you to visit a Ripper Doc every single time and costs quite a bit of money too. Weapons, something I didn't know beforehand is that this is essentially a looter shooter, a genre I'm not very fond of. You also have a massive amount of side content to do, which at some point is just so overwhelmingly boring and suffocating that it's just not fun. Even after 5.5 years the game still has some bugs, which range from simple NPC distortions to story boss enemies being stuck midair and are not able to move. If we strip this down and make it very simple, it's a buggy GTA-like environment with the combat of Borderlands, which is just not my cup of tea. This game is by no means a bad game, it's just I think their ambitions were just too big, tried to stuff in as much content as possible, completely disregarding the fun factor. Ignoring the side content to a degree and not completing 100% achievements is, personally, the better way to enjoy this game.

I initially played Cyberpunk 2077 on its launch day. While it was already a generally good, or even great, game back then, it definitely did not live up to the almost cult-like hype surrounding its release. Five years later, I decided to sink into the game thanks to substantial updates and especially the release of DLC. What I got was an immersive, narrative-rich, and action-driven experience with stunning visuals and atmosphere.  There are still some criticisms to be made. Some of them are caused by the bad taste that the game initially left at release, some of them are genuine that still remain as small stains on an otherwise (now) excellent game. However, it's worth noting that many of these critiques exist because of what the game promised pre-launch, and what we thought it would be. If you can detach yourself from the "what could have been" mindset, Cyberpunk is actually a fantastic game and one of the best RPGs ever made. The game's visuals also deserve high praise. To this day, it serves as the ultimate benchmark for gaming hardware, and that is really telling.  I first played The Witcher 3 long after it had received all its updates and evolved into a highly polished experience, which was further enhanced by two incredible DLCs, leading me to give it my first-ever 10/10 rating. Would Cyberpunk receive the same mark from me had I first encountered it under the exact same circumstances? Probably not. Despite being excellent now, it is still slightly less polished, shorter, the quests are less varied, and it feels a bit less atmospheric (though modern audiences might disagree on that last point). On the other hand, some might find the gameplay loop and combat options here more engaging, or prefer its characters – though I personally preferred the world-building and character arcs in The Witcher 3. Nevertheless, my final rating doesn't necessarily mean Cyberpunk is an inferior game; it just means that the complete package of The Witcher 3, at the time I first experienced it, is incredibly hard to match.  [h1] 9/10 [/h1]  Pros: + Amazing visuals that truly make you feel like you're in a futuristic, dystopian city + Deep, well-written characters and a thoroughly thought-out story + Great build variety when creating and leveling up your character + Fun and engaging combat + Amazing DLC content  Cons: - Too many cut corners are still obvious. The game was initially marketed as "GTA in Night City," but it clearly couldn't achieve that level of sandbox simulation. - Night City sometimes feels like a movie set – when you start exploring a bit deeper, it becomes obvious that the game is more of a semi-linear experience set against an open-world backdrop (which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it again contradicts the initial marketing). - Side quests can occasionally get repetitive, sometimes feeling like fetch quests where you do the exact same thing, just in a slightly different environment.

[h1] Cyberpunk 2077 review [/h1]  First off I want to say that I didnt get have to endure the incredible buggy and broken State it came out with, which must have been a bummer to some people eager to finally play in and expierience the world of Cyberpunk 2077.  But after about 5 Years the developers finally had enough time to pull through and eliminate mostly all the bugs and issues that the game started with. And thats where I bought it.    [h3] Graphics [/h3] [list] [*]Just like imagined - perfectly fit for depicting the worlds narrative and capitalist nightmare futurism, sadly at the cost of your fps - Good specs recommended to be able to expierience the beauty of high graphics settings. (or mods to make it even more beautiful) [*]detailed where it needs to be [*]nighttime rain is incredible [*]realistic character skin  [/list]   [h3] Gameplay [/h3]  [list]  [*]many builds to try (just be careful to think about it [b] before [/b] upgrading the perk tree you cant reset it infinite amount of times [*]cyberware is amazing, though some slots in the body are reserved for only one type of (recommended) build path  [*]many sidequests you can either stumble into or get them marked on the map, less story relevant more detailled look at the people around you. Often many shards with text to get a context of the situation your put into. [*]the dialoge options are well thought through and aren't cryptic for the most parts of the game, sometimes they are locked through amount of points spend in the skill tree on a specific skill [*]Gunplay is satisfying especially the unique weapons are really worthwhile trying out, the default weapons kinda all feel the same in their respective category, with winners mostly being the ones with the best stats [*]Movement is almost limitless, you can scale buildings all you want, get a whole new angle on the mission you are on, barbed wire is a bit iffy sometimes [*]Fast travel only unlocks the option when you have been to the spot at least once already, in the city fast travel isnt as cool as driving through it anyways (in the outlands it can be a bit boring to drive) [*]Vehicles are working as intended, some have weapons build into some you can only find in the world or be given as a reward. If you call a vehicle to you (especially with cars) there is a bug with slopes that makes their spawn a bit weird and they either spawn too high in the air and fall down or too low in the ground and shoot out of the ground but its not as often as on release [*]scanning in missions is used often and I understand that but sometimes it just takes too long for my liking [*]hacking is well thought through and hacking through cameras and vehicles also makes it a good tool to mark enemy positions and a path you want to go if your not full intelligence build  [*]modding is made accessible and easy to do with things like Vortex mod manager, there are many mods to explore (flying vehicles!) just be careful to keep the 18+ filter on lol  [/list]  [h3] Story [/h3]   I wont be spoiling much of the story so I keep it short in this one  [list] [*]main game story good and has 5 endings to explore, one of them being secret and all of them are peak (the phone calls you get are soul shattering) [*]the Phantom Liberty dlc was outstanding story wise, throwing you into a full blown secret agent-esque story within dogtown (located at the big stadium next to pacifica). There are 4 endings to explore and they broke me even more then the main story endings. [/list]   [h2] conclusion [/h2]   Cyberpunk 2077 is a great game with great gameplay, it is absolutely worth every cent (especially with discount). CD PROJECT RED thankfully managed to turn the buggy mess of 2020 into a fully fleshed out masterpiece with hunderts of hours of playtime possibilities. I got captured by the story and the characters. Also go check out the anime Cyberpunk edgerunners, maybe you'll find someones shotgun somewhere ;(  [spoiler]If you read this all the way thanks :) oh and if there are any typos or weird sentences its because my room is 42°C right now [/spoiler]

This game had a really troubling launch but I was not around for when it launched- actually that's not entirely true. I was hyped for this game when it was coming out but the series of delays and other drama surrounding it basically killed my interest in the game and I never really planned to pick this game up after that disaster of a launch.  But you can probably guess what changed. I watched Edgerunners and got so enamored with the setting that I decided to take the plunge in the year of our lord 2026 so my opinions are formed entirely around the version that's playable now.  With that out of the way- would I recommend Cyberpunk 2077? Yes! This is far from a perfect game and if you're a fan of CDPR's other works maybe this won't fit the standard you have for them but I've never cared for their other games and I don't care about playing a perfect game.   Getting my negatives out of the way first in case these might be deal breakers for you: -Yes, the game is still a bit buggy. At the time of writing this I've got 218 hours logged and I've had a fair share of glitches. Nothing that broke that game entirely and only a few CTDs (i think 3 in total) but mostly were without issue. Most bugs revolved around driving (and yeah, driving is pretty bad, imagine every car has the tire traction of the Halo CE warthog) and anything too intrusive could be fixed by quicksaving and reloading.  -Performance issues. I have a pretty good PC and I want to say a lot of this isn't necessarily the game's fault, but the game will drop frames and stutter if you move too fast. I think a lot of this can be chalked up to my weaker CPU bottlenecking performance (intel i5-10400F) but I've seen others complain about the game loading textures slow and the occasional stutter so worth mentioning.  -Gameplay issues. I've seen people complain about the gameplay and how it lacks depth but I want to expand on that a little, because I think when it comes to options the game provides you you're given a lot of mechanical depth and interesting options to play around with. Most guns feel pretty satisfying and the different cyberware lets you lean into a lot of different play styles and I think when people complain about gameplay what I think is really happening is that the base game never really makes you use those tools that well.   As far as vanilla cyberpunk goes, enemy and level design is pretty bland. Most enemies even on harder difficulties are squishy cannon fodder types lead by 1-2 slightly spongier cannon fodder types, so it can be pretty disappointing going into most combat arenas. 2.0 Apparently made changes to how vanilla game bosses were handled but most importantly to how the final boss plays out. Now, I never did the final boss in the older versions but the newer version is definitely one of the best fights in the game now.  Phantom Liberty also fixes a lot of issue with enemy depth and level design- to the point it almost feels like you're playing an entirely different game. Which now leads into my positives about the game-  -Phantom Liberty DLC is so good it's almost worth playing just for this, I say *almost* because the dlc area is quite small but TRUST when I say the quality more than makes up for it. Everything from the main questline down to the odd jobs has so much more depth to it and makes your builds feel like they matter here and it's an immensely satisfying experience.  -The Story. Cyberpunk 2077's story is one that really hinges on how well you like/get invested in the characters and so if you like character driven dramas then I think this will speak to you. I normally get really swept up in the emotions of games but less often am I brought to tears multiple times throughout a playthrough. CDPR did an amazing job of introducing this character meant to piss you off and over the course of a playthrough making you bond with him and change each other as you learn to deal with each other. The story is bleak but not without it's hope and underlying optimism in a better tomorrow that I found really touching. And the vocal performances by the EN voice actors is incredible. Easily Cherami Leigh's best performance, imo.  -Visuals. I don't usually care much for graphics or wanking over how good things look but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is Night City a beautiful place. Genuinely one of the only game I've ever felt inclined to mess around with the photo mode in. It's beautiful and it KNOWS it's beautiful because your in-game apartments let you hang up photos of the screenshots you take in game. How OBNOXIOUS. I love it.  Anyways that's all I got. If you like 6/10 games like I do then this is absolutely the game for you.

That said, my biggest criticism is the excessive focus on sexual content. I understand that mature themes are part of the game's setting, but in my opinion, the nudity, explicit scenes, and sexual references are overdone. At times, it feels like they're included more for shock value than to serve the story or the world-building.  Aside from that, Cyberpunk 2077 is an excellent experience. The developers deserve credit for the incredible improvements they've made since launch. If you can look past the overemphasis on sexual content, you'll find one of the best open-world RPGs of recent years.  Recommended.

[b] Budget Gamer Verdict: Highly Recommended. [/b]  If you waited out the storm like I did, you are getting an incredible, stable, and deeply mature sci-fi RPG.  [i] 🖥️ Performance on a Budget Laptop  [/i]  My Specs: RTX 3050 Laptop (4GB VRAM), Ryzen 5 5600H, 15GB RAM.  Perfect Stability: Played after all the major patches and it ran beautifully. No crashes, Only bugs i've seen are ones typical in other games (dead body stuck on walls or concrete, cars glitches to the floor which only happened twice for me because i was intentionally hitting stuff)  Zero Crashes: The game never crashed a single time during my entire main playthrough.  Mod Warning: The first and only crash happened after I beat the game and added cosmetic mods but not sure if it's the mods doing or not.  Low-Spec Approved: If you have a similar 4GB VRAM budget setup, do not fear this game anymore.  [i] 👁️ Next-Level Immersion  [/i]  Lost in the World: The atmosphere is incredibly thick and genuinely make you feel like you're living in a futuristic world. there are tons of easter eggs too  Living Breathing City: You will easily find yourself just wandering the neon streets for hours completing the massive amounts of side jobs and gigs, upgrading yourself, buying guns and clothing. To me, no gigs or side jobs feels the same because you are given freedom and multiple ways to get to the objective.  Butterfly Effect Missions: What you do in one part of the game heavily ripples into others part  Dynamic Content: Some missions have entirely different intros or outcomes based on choices you made hours earlier, there's even random events that will happen, and the world will respond if you handle it a certain way.  Engaging Story and Replayability: The story is nicely written, you can definitely play this multiple times with different lifepaths, builds and choices you make, there are a more than a few endings to the game. but remember: there is no "good ending" in Night City.  [i] 🔴 The Downsides (With a Twist)  [/i]  Too Easy Late-Game: By the end of the journey, the combat difficulty drops off. however, you're supposed to be built and upgraded into a god by the end, so melting enemies feels earned, especially if you've watched the anime (i haven't and its still satisfying).  Lack of Base Customization: The vanilla character creation options felt a bit limited for a futuristic RPG, at least for me. Luckily, this is incredibly easy to fix with cosmetic mods once you finish the vanilla game.  Locked Romance: some romances are locked via gender, but again, easily fixed with mods

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of those games I just keep coming back to.  I still remember pre-ordering it and the disappointment I felt at launch. As a longtime fan of CD Projekt Red, I expected a much more polished and optimized experience. Despite the overwhelming number of bugs, however, I pushed through and completed my first playthrough.  Looking back, that initial experience was still something special. Even beneath the technical issues was a breathtaking glimpse into the life of V and the world of Night City. The introduction is fantastic, the story hooks you almost immediately, and V's motivations are written well enough to allow players to shape their own interpretation of the character while still maintaining a strong narrative.  The gameplay is also a lot of fun. While I personally prefer the melee combat over gunplay, both are enjoyable and offer plenty of build variety. My biggest complaint is that the game's difficulty scaling often relies on turning enemies into bullet sponges rather than introducing more interesting combat challenges. It's not a dealbreaker, but it can occasionally drag down the pacing.  Now, years later and one expansion after launch, Cyberpunk 2077 has transformed into something I would confidently call a masterpiece of the RPG genre. The game is far more stable, polished, and enjoyable than it was at release. There are still a few lingering bugs and some features that could have been refined further, but the overall experience is exceptional.  The €60 price tag is admittedly steep, but I do think the game is worth it. That said, I'd still recommend waiting for a sale. CD Projekt Red is known for offering some incredible Steam discounts, often reaching 80% off or more.  If you've been hesitant because of the game's launch reputation, it's worth giving Cyberpunk 2077 a second look. The game that exists today is vastly different from the one that launched in 2020—and Night City is absolutely worth exploring.

Cyberpunk 2077 is not the best game ever made, but what it does well, it does at an exceptionally high level. The game is wrapped in the stunning setting of Night City, a visually breathtaking metropolis filled with vibrant colors, towering architecture, and dense urban design. However, despite its visual richness, the world can sometimes feel oddly hollow, lacking a stronger sense of interactivity or the feeling that the player can truly live in it.  From a gameplay perspective, Cyberpunk 2077 offers a solid and flexible experience. It provides a high degree of player agency, allowing different playstyles through varied builds, approaches to combat, and decision-making. Whether you prefer stealth, hacking, or direct combat, the game supports meaningful experimentation, which significantly enhances replayability.  Where the game truly excels is in its characters and storytelling. CD Projekt Red once again demonstrates its strength in narrative design, delivering both main and side quests that are consistently engaging from beginning to end. The writing, performances, and emotional weight of character-driven moments stand out as some of the strongest aspects of the experience. This is even more evident in the Phantom Liberty expansion, where the overall narrative, pacing, and gameplay loop feel more refined and cohesive than in the base game. The expansion elevates the experience and showcases what the game is capable of at its best.  Visually, the game is outstanding. The graphical fidelity, detailed environments, and high-quality animations contribute to an immersive presentation. Lighting plays a crucial role, with neon reflections and ray tracing pushing the atmosphere to another level, especially in night-time scenes where the city truly comes alive.  Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 delivers a strong and memorable experience. Despite some shortcomings in world interactivity, it stands out thanks to its excellent storytelling, compelling characters, impressive visuals, and outstanding soundtrack. It is a game well worth playing, particularly for those who appreciate narrative-driven RPGs.

The Witcher 3 is my favourite game of all time, I chose not to play Cyberpunk on launch due to all the optimization issues and bugs involved at the time, despite having faith CD-P-R would deliver something worth my time. I finally got around to playing it and finished it today. I didn't enjoy it as much as the Witcher, copies of the same exact NPC will walk past each other in the same enclosed space, dialogues will overlap one another as though the characters are having an argument, sometimes even getting stuck in a loop. Debris and certain objects will spazz out and explode when you come into the slightest bit of contact with them.  But the story is riveting, the characters are memorable and quests are unique.  There are soundtracks that make you feel badass or make you bear the emotional weight of the moment as it plays.  Combat is good, the graphics are better, and urguably my favourite feature of the game is the texting system. Even after you finish a quest and expect to never see or hear from a character again they'll text you in gratitude or just update you on their life. Its that small but significant detail that makes Night City feel alive, like you're not the only one living out their story. If you haven't got around to it give this game a shot, it's well worth your time.

I haven't finished the game yet, but I absolutely love it so far. I enjoy the freedom you have to do whatever you want, it's unlike any game I've played before. I really like how seamlessly it can flip from being easy to challenging depending on what you're doing, it helps keep the experience fresh, especially since I can get bored very quickly and drop a game altogether if it becomes stagnant. I especially adore all the care put into Night City and it's residents. It truly feels like NC isn't just a place, but a character in of itself. It's residents all have their own characters, designs, voices, etc.., it's so refreshing. It's certainly not perfect, partly due to the state the game was in when it released, and I personally don't see any reason for specific choices, but it's still a great experience despite my small gripes. For example, I genuinely don't understand why Keanu Reeves is LITERALLY Johnny Silverhand in profession, voice, appearance, and even mo-cap of all things. There is no story important reason for this decision whatsoever. I also don't like how he (and quite a lot of characters) cuss and make sexual innuendos for no real reason other than "this is an adult game so let's cuss and talk about sex!!!!" It gets grating very quickly. I say that knowing I can be just as bad with cussing myself, by the way. I know I'm a hypocrite in that regard lmao.  Anyway, despite my gripes, I do love this game a lot, and I'm excited to finish it and see the other routes besides Nomad. I can't remember the last time I had *this* much fun with a game, and I'm glad it's the game that's helping me branch out into PC gaming so I'm not exclusively bound to my Nintendo Switch!

This game, despite its many flaws that were only corrected way too late into the life cycle, is incredible. The lighting is superb in almost all cases, there is a hearty fps boost to be acquired with FSR 3+ and DLSS 4+ integrations, and it is extremely customizable in terms of accessibility and graphics settings, and a slew of mods are available for it on the nexus (nexusmods.com). As far as gameplay and story, I'd chock it up to be a shockingly similar experience to Fallout 4. Enemies are occasionally bullet sponges without modifications, the gunplay feels as if there's something missing, and stealth is suboptimal at certain points of the game. Walk/Jog cannot be permanently toggled and often resets to a jog, and, generally, there are minor gaps in the game as far as customization goes. However, if I were to say the game is not one of if not the most astonishing and intriguing stories I have ever played., I would genuinely be lying my ass off. Despite your player character, V, not having too-too much of a say in what's occurring, it is very IMMERSIVE and drives you into a state where you'd feel desperate enough to bend to other's will even if there was an option not to. This is a game you can stop and be with for maybe 15 minutes at a time, but is best played over long periods of time. If it were not for its previous performance issues on my specific setup, I would probably 100%ed the game by now, it is that fun. Friend of mine told me there was fast travel in the game, but I'd always prefer to drive to places sometimes even walk. NPCs don't feel like passerbys and seem like they actually have a story to tell being in the city.  Got Phantom Liberty and coughed at how small the new area is (Dogtown). Was surprised that its density was hidden vertically with layers and pockets of places to explore.  The characters in the game was what made the game stick to me like caramel. You get an initial vibe from them, til you do their missions and you slowly start to see their true colors. The writing for each character is great that you'll either love them, hate them, or struggle finding out if you love them or hate them.  I played without subtitles to read peoples faces and eyes. Could see when people were lying, opening up, closing up.  Roleplayed as myself "what choices would I make if I was in this situation in Night City?". Made choices I regret and left things dangling on the clothesline that a min/maxer would've DM'd me for. But it taught me just how unforgiving Night City is. You scootch along anyway.  RPG of the decade (GTA 6 isn't an RPG right?). If you didn't play this, you're missing out.

Nach den zahlreichen Updates und Verbesserungen läuft das Spiel deutlich stabiler als zum Release und bietet heute ein sehr rundes Spielerlebnis. Die Kombination aus Action, Rollenspielelementen und Entscheidungsfreiheit sorgt für viele Stunden Spielspaß. Auch die Erweiterung Phantom Liberty wird von vielen Spielern und Kritikern gelobt.   Wer Open-World-RPGs mit einer spannenden Handlung und einer beeindruckenden Cyberpunk-Atmosphäre mag, sollte diesem Spiel unbedingt eine Chance geben. Die Kritikerwertung liegt bei 86/100 auf Metacritic, was die insgesamt sehr positive Aufnahme widerspiegelt.   Fazit: Ein mitreißendes Science-Fiction-Abenteuer, das sich nach den Updates zu einem der besten modernen Rollenspiele entwickelt hat.

Right, 400+ hours in Night City and I’m still clocking in like it’s a part-time job I never applied for. That alone should tell you everything.  Cyberpunk 2077 had one of the messiest launches I’ve ever seen in gaming. Proper chaos. Bugs everywhere, NPCs glitching like they were having a breakdown, cars spawning inside buildings, whole internet clowning on it for months. It was rough. Not even gonna sugarcoat it.  But here’s the mad part — underneath all that mess, there was actually a brilliant game trying to get out. And after all the updates, fixes, overhauls, DLC polish… it finally did.  Now? It’s a completely different beast.  ⸻  You play V, just trying to make a name in Night City. Simple enough on paper. Get rich, survive, maybe get out. Standard dream. Except Night City doesn’t do “simple”. It chews you up and laughs while doing it.  Everything kicks off with a job that’s meant to be clean, quick money. Obviously it goes sideways instantly — because of course it does. And that’s where Johnny Silverhand shows up in your head like the world’s most aggressive unwanted roommate.  And from that point on, the whole story shifts.  It stops being just “V’s story” and becomes this constant tug-of-war between two minds in one body. You want survival. Johnny wants chaos, revenge, and to burn everything down just for the vibe of it. You’re trying to hold yourself together while this rockstar terrorist ghost is constantly in your ear judging your life choices like he’s got any moral high ground.  And the best part? It doesn’t stay one-note. Their relationship actually develops. At first it’s pure hate and sarcasm. Then it becomes tolerance. Then this weird, messy understanding. And eventually… something in-between that’s honestly hard to label.  It’s not just “buddy cop in your brain”. It’s more like slowly losing parts of yourself while arguing with someone who refuses to shut up. Proper mental.  ⸻  Side characters? Genuinely some of the best written in modern gaming. Every major story arc feels like it actually matters. No filler nonsense just to stretch runtime. People in Night City are all trying to survive in their own way, and most of them are just as cooked as you are — they just hide it differently.  And the game is constantly reminding you: there are no clean endings here. Just different shades of bad and worse.  ⸻  Gameplay-wise, after 400 hours I’ve basically turned V into every possible flavour of unhinged.  Sneaky netrunner ghost build? Done it. Katana cyber-psycho sprinting through enemies? Done it. Walking tank with more chrome than humanity? Also done it.  Night City itself is still ridiculous. Neon everywhere, rain reflecting off concrete, ads screaming at you 24/7. It’s beautiful but in a slightly depressing, overstimulating way. Like a city that never lets you breathe properly.  AI can still act a bit cooked sometimes, not gonna lie. You’ll see some NPCs doing the most questionable behaviour known to man. But honestly at this point it just feels like part of the city’s personality.  ⸻  Here’s the weird bit — after that long, you stop playing it like a normal game. You just… exist in Night City. You know the streets. You know the shortcuts. You know exactly which gigs are gonna end in chaos before they even start. And yet you still do them.  Because it’s not really about progression anymore. It’s about the vibe. The atmosphere. The feeling of being permanently one bad decision away from disaster.  And Johnny in your head never shuts up. Ever. Commenting on everything like an uninvited backseat driver with anger issues.  ⸻  Cyberpunk 2077 isn’t perfect. Still got its rough edges, still janky in places, still occasionally does something that makes you pause and go “what on earth just happened”.  But when it hits, it really hits.  It’s a story about identity, control, mortality, and slowly losing yourself while pretending you’re still in charge.  And after 400 hours?  Yeah… I’m still coming back.  Because I swear down at this point I’m just simping for Johnny Silverhand and I don’t even have the energy to deny it anymore.

Amazing game that took me a bit to get hooked on. Initially the controls felt a little clunky, especially combat. I was expecting it to be more like "Doom" given the aesthetic. That said, they really created an amazingly deep world that you feel apart of. Even a lot of the side quests are just...kind of interesting small little rabbit holes rather than your basic "fetch" or "escort" quest. There are so many hours of well done voice actor dialog too. Night City is a great place to just wander around and do side quests in and feel like you live there. Like all these sorts of games, it does feel weird to do that though when there is "NO TIME TO SPARE" in the main story line but apparently you have as much time to spare as you want.  Cons for me -  1) The crafting system is annoying and largely useless outside of simply disassembling everything for upgrade components for your stuff. Like a lot of these types of games, you're frequently breaking immersion to run around and loot every possible thing and then flipping through your inventory screens to break all of it down. 2) Some of the quests and especially the end of Phantom Liberty really feel drawn out. I realized there was an item I forgot to loot off a thing because I was too focused on the story (see previous criticism), and when I looked at the Autosave it was 30+ minutes in the past. So I just don't have it because I'm not listening to all that again.

The gameplay is smooth, the controls are easy, Combat is decent (enemy health is kind of like The Division with the damage and HP bars), and FPS drops are nonexistent so far, even in the dense parts of the map. The game offers a benchmark test that takes you through the different densities of the map with a live FPS count before showing you the recommended settings for your build. When it comes to strengths, the game does two things incredibly well: world building and character building. It was easy to get immersed into this world, with great artistic vision and attention to detail, and then get invested in the stories of its people, both main character and NPCs, whose personalities are given enough space to shine. Feeling at times a bit slow during cutscenes or dialogues is a price worth paying for that, in my opinion. The combat and character development system are good, they deliver fun and sense of progression, and allow some variety in future playthroughs. The story was a bit too generic, but still enjoyable.  The game is not without flaws though. The most criminal offense this game does at present day is incredibly ♥♥♥♥♥♥ music (I'm talking about radio music which you spend most of your time with and which is blasting from every boombox and car radio in the game world, cutscene music is much better), I had to mod most of it out just to be able to enjoy the game. My second issue is that the game doesn't do a great job as RPG: too often I find myself limited, because in a quest I'd like to take some decision and the character would be capable of doing that, but the game does not offer this option (for example no option to turn a murderer to authorities, no option to talk a guy out of a heist or even decline taking part in it). When it comes to bugs, the one that bothers me the most is when I lose my car and suddenly the game won't let me summon a new one (any of them!), in the city I can't find any parked vehicle and stealing one that's not as slow as walking requires strength which my build does not have, so now I have to run for 2km to next objective. Speaking of cars, the driving system is bad, cars slide on every turn and not in a fun way (better get that Caliburn asap). The open world formula allows you to breathe in the world, which is awesome, but on the other hand it's filled with activities that are very generic and lacking in variety, which screams wasted potential. The story, while good, is much too short and there are too few side stories. I also noticed cases of clearly forced wokeness ("forced" in the sense that it doesn't stem naturally from the game world, doesn't add anything to the story and is not needed for role-playing purposes, but is just shoved in your face and then gone the next minute), which feels like "we didn't want to do it but without it we wouldn't be considered for some game awards so here we are".  Despite the flaws, it's still worth to immerse in this cyberpunk world and experience what the game has to offer.

I bought the game after Phantom Liberty so I didn't have to deal with the launch difficulties so my review is of the game at its best. Story wise its the one of best of the past decade IMO KCD2 & BG3 are up there as well but maybe its just me but the vibe chef's kiss. The RPG elements are strong the consequences of dialog choices are in some ways at the top of the heap Balders Gate 3 is the best RPG of recent times but that's comparing apples to oranges. However I will say that compared to Fallout 4 this is voiced MC done right I really love BG3 and it delivers great story, world, companions & more while doing it well voiced MC pulled off is just cool.  There are areas where improvements could be made but that's true of all games. Considering how great character creation is its a bummer that 3rd person had to be modded in. That's just a pet peeve of mine if my V is stunting I want the option to enjoy that while doing cool stuff. However one major area of potential improvement would be something like the Stelthrunner Mod opening up the RPG mechanics a bit more. With how broad the interaction ability is with NPC's rival factions or their key characters could offer more. In BG3 you offers dialog and the ability to persuade, trick or intimidate your way out of immediate agro status when confronting  new people even if you are working to undermine and confront them in the future. Cyberpunk 2077 is like being in a movie with a great great deal of agency while BG3 can be played however you want. There are tradeoffs in the creative process it would be cool if the world was bigger or you have the chance to build up a Nomad settlement, a politically subversive faction or a gang. Although a lot of this falls into DLC and or Modding territory. I'm happy to see some very interesting mods as well as continued updates because the potential is sky high. New Vegas is essentially a pro mod of Fallout 3 and Fallout 4's great strength is its ease of modding and the dedicated fanbase that has the ability to create in such a amazing universe Cyberpunk is an equally awesome setting.  Cyberpunk holds a special place in my heart I can't speak highly enough of my experience on my first playthrough. There hasn't been the same kind of cash grab attempts that many other beloved games have moved towards. It had big problems at launch but by Phantom Liberty the game lived up to the promise it held at launch. Though during the time the Devs were fixing the issues many modders could have ended up creating new and interesting ideas. If the support remains from the developers this may still come to fruition as many of the great legacy franchise's are struggling to stay in touch as the genre's they defined have matured and created newer and higher standards. GTA 6 is coming later in 2026 but a new Elder Scrolls is far off and a new Fallout is not even on the horizon while serious questions of ability to compete in this mature market have even diehard fans feeling jaded and skeptical.  It would be great to see the modding scene flourish on Cyberpunk to raise the ability to replay not that it isn't crunchy enough not to want to play again but to keep it alive and vibrant for years to come needs the support of modders. I would love to see this if the devs show care to the fanbase beyond just the ability to add in horse armor to keep the money flowing. With the failure of Starfield and the professional opinion of diehard Bethesda fans that it's not fixable without a complete rebuild Many A True Nerd spells it out well. Overall I’d give Cyberpunk 2077 a 3.5–4.0/5.  This was my first CD Projekt Red game, and the storylines were easily the highlight. The character arcs and companion quests reminded me a lot of Fallout 4 and Dragon Age II/Inquisition. My first playthrough focused on Panam and the Nomads, Johnny, Judy, and the main Relic storyline, and I found all of those engaging.  The amount of content is honestly overwhelming. I mostly stuck to stealth takedowns, silenced pistols, and Panam’s sniper rifle. I kept expecting takedowns to evolve into cooler assassination animations, but they never really did.  I eventually started experimenting with swords, air dashes, and mobility perks. They were fun, but not especially intuitive. It often felt like I needed to stop and watch tutorials or read guides to understand how systems were meant to work. I also skipped almost all netrunner skills and gameplay, saving that for a future character. My build was focused on Cool and Reflexes, with cyberware geared toward stealth, headshots, and critical hits.  The game gave me strong GTA vibes with the mission structure, driving, gigs, side jobs, and overall crime/underworld atmosphere.  My biggest takeaway is that Cyberpunk has a lot of replayability. I can already see myself returning for a completely different build, especially a netrunner or full melee ninja playthrough.

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of the best RPGs I have ever played. The world of Night City feels alive, detailed, and incredibly immersive. Every district has its own atmosphere, and the graphics are simply stunning, especially with modern hardware. The visual design, lighting, and attention to detail make exploring the city a pleasure.  What impressed me the most was the story. The main narrative is emotional, memorable, and full of great characters. The chemistry between V and Johnny Silverhand is exceptional, and Johnny is easily one of the most memorable and well-written characters in the entire game. It's the kind of story that stays with you long after the credits roll. The side quests are also surprisingly well-written and often feel just as important as the main story.  As an RPG, Cyberpunk offers a lot of freedom in how you build your character and approach different situations. There are many playstyles to experiment with, which adds a lot of replay value.  Getting all achievements is not too easy but not extremely difficult either. I would describe the achievement hunt as moderately challenging and enjoyable rather than frustrating.  Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 is a fantastic RPG with amazing graphics, excellent gameplay, and one of the best stories I have experienced in gaming. Highly recommended.
