Before i get into im not gonna harp on anything the game does bad in this cuz i feel that the good outweighs it so much more.  Let me just say the launch drama tricked me like fr I can’t believe I slept on this for so long I literally avoided this game for years because of the terrible launch memes. I finally bought it on Steam a while back but never played it until it took the last 3-4 days of my life the past couple days because i was grinding it and I’m actually blown away. I feel so stupid for waiting this long to play it. If you’re still hesitating because of stuff from 2020, just buy it. On PC, it runs super smooth (besides when i share my screen on dc), looks insane, and is easily one of the most immersive games out. Also if you have watched the anime boy are you gonna love this game  8/10 overall (Story is a solid 9/10 though)  Night City is a dystopian masterpiece The city isn't just a map it is a living character that suffocates you with its vibe. The scale is overwhelming you look up and see massive megabuildings casting shadows over neon drenched alleys packed with vendors, cyberpunks, and garbage. Kabuki and Japantown feel claustrophobic and alive with bright neon signs and dense crowds. Pacifica feels like a warzone completely isolated from corporate control.  The Badlands offer a massive, dust choked contrast where you can just throttle willy nilly on a bike. The environmental storytelling is everywhere with much more to find  then you think if you look around for stuff.  these are just a few of many places i listed.  as for the gameplay The gameplay hits a super satisfying rhythm because it stops playing like a standard shooter and lets you become an absolute monster. The gunplay is heavy and punchy, especially when using tech weapons that punch through solid concrete walls or smart guns that track targets around corners. The build variety is where the game actually excels  The Sandevistan build lets you activate a neural implant to slow down time, letting you run circles around enemies and slice them to pieces with a katana before they can even draw their weapons. Mantis Blades and Gorilla Arms turn your own body into a lethal weapon, making close-quarters combat incredibly brutal. Quickhack builds turn you into a ghost, allowing you to wipe out an entire building of guards without firing a shot by forcing their cyberware to self detonate or burn them alive from the inside out. or even kill themself  theres many more builds out there these are just a few  The side quests aren't just filler either major storylines involving characters like Judy, Panam, or River feel just as fleshed out and emotional as the main plot. Vehicle handling takes some getting used to, and some of the minor fixer gigs can feel a bit repetitive, which is why the gameplay is an 8/10 for me. But when you are fully kitted out with cyberware and sliding through a firefight, the power trip is unmatched.  One thing you notice pretty quickly is that the clothing options are totally unbalanced. If you play as a guy, the male fashion choices feel lowkey mid and kinda trash. Meanwhile, the female clothing options get all the drip everything looks amazing, stylish, and actually fits the futuristic cyberpunk aesthetic perfectly. It wasn't an issue for me at all because I always prefer playing as a girl in most games anyway, but if you’re a dude who wants to play as a male V and look cool, the lack of good male drip is definitely going to annoy you.   The absolute best part of the game imo is Johnny Silverhand. At first, I lowkey thought he was just a loud annoying terrorist. I hated having this toxic digital ghost constantly trash talk me and all my choices i made (even if you drive to fast) most interactions force you to choose to follow with or against his radical philosophy that could cost you your life. He felt like a nuisance stuck in V's head. He pops up as a hologram out of nowhere to talk ♥♥♥♥ on all the people you talk to. (they cant see or hear him) But the writing is and gets so deep that your relationship actually evolves. The more I played, the more I actually started to understand him. His tragic backstory and cynical worldview completely won me over. not to mention his amazingly curated personality  Hes an ego driven rockstar who masks his massive regrets with arrogance and dark humor and he holds up a mirror to the darkest parts of Night City, making you question who the real villains are. but the friction slowly turns into understanding. You watch this deeply flawed, egoist slowly lower his guard and show real humanity. The transition happens so naturally that you don't even realize how close you've become until it all hits you. He goes from a parasite wanting you dead to someone who genuinely puts his own existence on the line just to save your life. By the end, they share an unbreakable bond out of shared trauma and mutual respect. Their banter, their quiet moments of vulnerability, and that shift from bitter enemies to true brothers-in-arms (i played as a girl) is easily one of my favorite story arcs in video game history. Keanu Reeves and the writing team absolutely cooked.  Johnny Silverhand is now my favorite side character of all time and Honestly, calling him a "side character" feels like an insult. He is literally the co-protagonist. His dynamic with V is the beating heart of the whole story. Keanu Reeves ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cooked with this performance.

*Cyberpunk 2077* is one of those games that stayed with me long after I closed it.  At first, Night City feels exciting. The lights, the cars, the clubs, the implants, the advertisements, the gangs, the weapons, everything looks loud and alive. But the longer I stayed there, the more I felt that the city was not alive in a beautiful way. It was alive like a machine that keeps eating people. Everyone in Night City wants something: money, fame, power, revenge, survival, a way out. But almost nobody gets out clean.  V’s story hit me because it starts with such a simple dream. V and Jackie do not want to save the world. They just want to become legends. They want their names remembered at the Afterlife. That dream sounds cool at first, especially when Jackie is there laughing, talking big, and making the city feel less lonely. Jackie gives the early game its heart. He makes V’s ambition feel human. So when the Konpeki Plaza heist goes wrong, it does not just feel like a mission failure. It feels like Night City taking payment for a dream that was too big.  Jackie’s death is one of the moments that changed the whole game for me. After that, the city feels different. The neon is still bright, but it feels colder. V gets the Relic, Johnny Silverhand appears in their head, and suddenly the story is no longer about becoming famous. It becomes about time running out. Every mission after that has this shadow over it: V is alive, but not completely. V is fighting for a future that may already be disappearing.  Johnny is the best part of the game for me. At first, he is unbearable. He is arrogant, angry, selfish, and constantly insulting V. But the more time he spends with V, the more human he becomes. He is not just a rockstar terrorist ghost. He is a man full of regret, ego, rage, and unfinished pain. His hatred for Arasaka is real, but so is his fear of being forgotten. What makes his relationship with V powerful is that they begin as enemies sharing one body, then slowly become the only people who truly understand each other.  The side characters are what make Night City feel painful instead of just stylish. Judy’s story with Evelyn is tragic because it shows how the city destroys people who are already vulnerable. Evelyn tries to climb out, tries to use the system before it uses her, but Night City crushes her anyway. Judy’s anger and sadness feel real because she is not just fighting enemies; she is grieving someone the world treated like disposable flesh.  Panam’s story feels different. With the Aldecaldos, the game finally lets V breathe. The desert is still dangerous, but it feels honest compared to the city. Panam is stubborn, emotional, loyal, and sometimes difficult, but that is why she feels real. Her missions made me feel like V was not just chasing survival, but maybe finding a place where people actually cared if they lived or died. The Aldecaldos ending is so powerful because it gives V something Night City almost never gives anyone: a family and a road forward.  Takemura is also a character I ended up liking more than I expected. He believes in order, loyalty, and Arasaka, even after being betrayed by the system he served. There is something sad about him. He is honorable in his own way, but also trapped by the world that shaped him. His bond with V is not warm like Jackie’s or Panam’s, but it has respect. He feels like someone who could have been a friend in another life.  What I love about *Cyberpunk 2077* is that almost every major character is trying to survive their own version of Night City. River wants justice in a place where justice barely exists. Kerry is famous but still lost inside his own history. Rogue has power, but it came with compromise. Johnny wanted to burn the system down, but even he became a memory trapped inside technology. Nobody really wins here. They just choose what they are willing to lose.  The endings are what make the game unforgettable. None of them feel completely happy, and I love that. The Devil ending feels cold and terrifying because V puts their fate into the hands of the same machine that ruined so many lives. The Sun ending feels legendary, but also empty, like V finally becomes the myth they wanted to be while still running from death. The Star ending feels the most human because V leaves the city with people who care. The Temperance ending hurts because Johnny gets a second chance, but only by living in the space V leaves behind. Even the suicide ending is devastating because it shows how tired V can become when every road feels cruel.  *Phantom Liberty* makes the game even stronger. Dogtown feels like Night City with the mask ripped off. Songbird, Reed, Myers, and Alex all live inside a world where loyalty is never clean. Songbird is desperate for freedom, but she lies and uses people because she has been used her whole life. Reed is loyal, but his loyalty feels like a prison. The choices there are painful because nobody is innocent, but nobody is completely wrong either. The new ending where V survives but loses their old life is one of the saddest in the whole game. It asks whether survival is still victory if the person who survives is no longer the person who fought so hard to live.  That is why *Cyberpunk 2077* means so much to me. It is not just about guns, cars, cyberware, or neon streets. It is about people trying to matter in a city designed to erase them. V wants to live. Jackie wants to be remembered. Johnny wants revenge and meaning. Judy wants justice. Panam wants freedom. Songbird wants escape. Almost everyone is reaching for something, and Night City keeps asking for a price.  The gameplay is also incredibly satisfying now. Driving through the city at night, walking into a gig, hacking cameras, using mantis blades, sniping from a rooftop, or clearing a building without being seen all feels amazing. But the reason I love the game is not only because it feels cool. I love it because the coolness always has sadness behind it. The city looks beautiful, but it is built on broken people.  When I think of *Cyberpunk 2077*, I think of Jackie’s drink at the Afterlife. I think of Johnny sitting beside V, quieter than usual. I think of Judy staring at a world that keeps taking from her. I think of Panam driving into the desert. I think of Songbird looking at the sky like freedom is almost close enough to touch. And I think of V, still fighting, still afraid, still trying to leave some kind of mark before the lights go out.  Night City is beautiful, cruel, unforgettable, and impossible to trust.  That is why I love this game so much.

Has not Cyberpunk been one of the most prescient genres of this Information age? Not because it has the language of technology we use today but that it shows us the very real and probable future of technologically accelerated hyper-capitalism. So where does Cyberpunk 2077 stand lay in the halls of Bladerunner and Neuromancer? And more importantly, is it a good fcking game?  CP2077 starts off strong by blasting you with a world that feels viscerally alive. The news reels blaring from nearby screens, the idle chatter that is more detailed and contextual than your usual npc lines done ad-infinitum, the cohesive and yet real and chaotic aesthetic narratives present in the architecture, clothes and minutiae of life. This not so distant future pops like a pungent tart thrown at your face. In the best way possible, the sensory overload mirrors ours, the trails of thought apparent in the many vivid lines to follow in the game’s immersion.  Yet this overloading of the senses does not stop the cheer joy and beauty of this supposed capitalist hellhole. The mega-structures are incredibly animated and the level design lets you explore the nooks and crannies of the various different sections of the city more openly than other GTA-style games.  In fact CB2077 is primarily a GTA-style sim that vastly improves on the formula and one of the major reasons is that the third person perspective is eschewed for the first. I can see up close the hyper-reality and the guts of my enemies fly into the ether. Whilst the side missions of GTA 5 felt like chores for the most part (playing weak mini-games to maintain relationships, taxing yourself or others) here they are much more fun because the shooting, hacking and stealth gameplay loop is superb. Some of the side quests are also indelible in their presentation and the leaving of notes and recordings trying to explain or give some semblance of story carries them better than the bare-bone fetch quests of games like Witcher 3. The guided meditation by the monk was a personal favourite as well as the braindance of the prisoner’s crucifixion.  Gunplay is the best facet in the loop with each weapon handling differently with the customisation and crafting components adding further variability and fun to the mess. Every shot and number popping out of the gonks head feels damn good and collecting rare guns is addictive. Stealthing around and backstabbing people is also satisfactory but not to the same extent as the AI feels stupid enough that the victory feels hollow. Hacking can be though of as spells in other games but more adaptable and malleable to the environment than the usual ‘do damage to bad guys’. You can disable CCTV or hijack them, distract enemies using household tech, make things blow up or cause psychosis again adding to the multiplicity of accomplishing missions. The driving parts are not very smooth and I would have rather ridden in the auto taxi service in the game than drive those monstrously weightless cars which is a damn shame as the scenery along the way can be truly stunning.  The rpg mechanics of the game are well realised with stat points and perk trees that are fun to explore and mess around with and the different specialisation can lead to markedly different playstyles. I did use a mod to enable unlimited respeccing that let me try them all out. One criticism is that the perks and special abilities are often automatic when a certain different action is done and that can make it too easy or dull depending on your tastes. The melee combat is not to the calibre of the gunplay but the fact it is added on and has some viability in what most other games would keep to ranged weapons only is commendable.  Where the GTA 5 comparison hurts CB2077 is that the writing and satire and commentary of the former is much better written than the later. While the world of CB2077 is really well historically documented and fleshed out, the actual content and exploration of the themes doesn’t hold a mirror to society like GTA did or the other masterpieces of the Cyberpunk genre. Those sparkling skylines and cybernetic enhancements are more welcoming than ominous and the freedom and rush of becoming a mercantile mastermind envelops any sense of the dystopia inherent in such a world. The uglier parts of the city are there but they lack the emotional wallop that comes with intelligent and poignant storytelling that hammers home the corpo-feudalism. Not that these themes aren’t hinted at in the story of V and his surrounds but it is undercooked and digest it long enough you will get salmonella. There is no inspection of the commodified sexuality of women and others, no dive into the racialised Haitian netrunner experience, the backlash against the Japanese super corporation and the role of poverty that underpins all class consciousness.   The initial personal pathos of V’s path, in contrast to both the latter part of this game and GTA, is much more realised mainly because of the character of Jackie and his wholesome buffoon act. But V himself is a dull placeholder. Some of this is part of the genre of the RPG but the way he talks in any of the options is quite generic to say the least and reads like a throwaway Italian American gangster wannabee in some 80’s paperback. The male V has the accent to match too, this buttrock voice that got grating very soon.  This leaves the emotional hit to be carried by the characters around V and unfortunately Keanu Reeves, as perhaps the most overrated actor of his generation, cannot do it justice. [h1]Cyberpunk 2077 — A Masterpiece Worth Every Hour[/h1]  [hr][/hr]  [h2]Visuals & Art Direction[/h2]  Night City is the most visually stunning open world ever put into a video game. The neon-drenched streets, jaw-dropping character design, rain on every surface — every corner looks like concept art brought to life. [b]The word "beautiful" gets thrown around a lot in gaming, but this game has genuinely earned it more than any other.[/b]  [hr][/hr]  [h2]Story & Narrative[/h2]  This is my [b]all-time favorite story-driven game[/b] and my [b]second favorite game overall[/b]. What makes it extraordinary isn't just the main quest — it's that every single side story feels completely alive and purposeful. No throwaway missions. Every character has depth. Every decision carries real weight.  The endings are something else entirely: [spoiler]The Hanako path and the conclusion involving the stars left me completely speechless. I couldn't have imagined better endings if I'd written them myself. Both were truly amazing in ways I never saw coming.[/spoiler]  [hr][/hr]  [h2]Voice Acting & Performances[/h2]  V's voice actors — [i]both of them[/i] — give performances so natural and committed that the illusion never breaks, not for a single line. You would never be able to tell it wasn't a real person speaking at every waking moment. Johnny Silverhand is equally extraordinary — magnetic, complicated, and impossible to look away from.  [hr][/hr]  [h2]Soundtrack & Audio[/h2]  [b]One of the best soundtracks in modern gaming, full stop.[/b] From the pounding synth during firefights to the melancholy ambience of V's apartment, to the radio stations you catch while cruising the highways — every audio choice feels deliberate and perfectly tuned to Night City's soul.  [hr][/hr]  [h2]Vehicles & Combat[/h2]  The vehicles aren't built for realism purists — and honestly, [i]that's exactly right.[/i] Cranking a car to top speed, launching off an overpass, and landing in the middle of a cyberpsycho takedown is one of the most purely fun things you can do in any game ever made.  Weapons follow the same smart philosophy: [b]no cleaning kits, no durability meters to babysit[/b] — but enough mechanical variety and feel to make your loadout matter, especially on higher difficulties. It hits the sweet spot between accessible and genuinely tactical.  [hr][/hr]  [h2]Modding Community[/h2]  The modding scene is [b]extraordinary.[/b] Community creators have built [u]fully flyable helicopters and aircraft[/u] from scratch — something not in the base game at all. There are tactical gear and weapon mods that slot seamlessly into the existing balance without breaking immersion or difficulty. And if you [i]want[/i] the power fantasy, those mods exist too. The ecosystem is massive, creative, and still growing.  [hr][/hr]  [h2] Final Thoughts[/h2]  I haven't finished the game after [b]4 years[/b] — and that is [u]not[/u] a criticism. That's because I'm doing every side quest, every gig, every achievement before I let myself reach the end. [b]This game rewards that kind of attention completely.[/b]  [strike]Just one more side quest...[/strike] okay maybe two.  [hr][/hr]  [h1] Verdict: 10 / 10[/h1] [b]Buy it. Mod it. Get completely lost in it.[/b] [i]The embodiment of the word "beautiful."[/i]

Cyberpunk 2077 — A Modern Masterpiece  Cyberpunk 2077 is one of those rare games that feels less like a product and more like a fully realized artistic vision. Night City is not just a setting — it is a living, breathing organism, filled with ambition, decay, beauty, violence, and humanity. From the moment you step into its neon-soaked streets, the game pulls you into a world that feels both terrifyingly dystopian and strangely believable.  What impressed me most is how well Cyberpunk 2077 combines atmosphere, storytelling, character writing, exploration, and player choice. The main story is emotional, stylish, and deeply personal, but the side quests are often just as memorable. Many of them feel handcrafted, meaningful, and written with the kind of detail you rarely see in open-world games. The characters are outstanding, the dialogue is sharp, and the world constantly gives you reasons to care.  The gameplay has also become excellent. Combat is fast, flexible, and satisfying, whether you prefer hacking enemies from the shadows, going in with blades, using firearms, or building your own hybrid playstyle. The RPG systems, cyberware, weapons, and progression all make the experience feel rewarding from start to finish.  The DLC content only makes the game stronger. It adds more depth, more emotional weight, more style, and more reasons to return to Night City. Everything feels like it expands the world naturally rather than simply adding extra content for the sake of it.  Yes, the game had issues at launch. That is impossible to ignore. But judging Cyberpunk 2077 as it stands today, those early technical problems do not define the experience anymore. What remains is an incredible open-world RPG with unforgettable atmosphere, powerful storytelling, and one of the most immersive cities ever created in gaming.  For me, Cyberpunk 2077 is not just a great game. It is a masterpiece. A bold, emotional, visually stunning, and unforgettable experience that deserves to be remembered as one of the defining games of its generation.  Rating: 5/5 Absolutely recommended.

From the beginning, Night City chews you up and spits you out, then insults your corpse while you're lying there, broken. You set out to become a legend, but just find you're hanging on, trying to keep your head above water, and so many promising starts lead to dead ends. Telling the truth or making what seems like a "morally good" choice may get you killed, or ruin someone's life. You'll shoot up the "criminals", only to remember they were criminals because a heartless corporation branded them as such, for what would usually (mostly) be minor offenses. You're not a hero, you're a rat in a neon maze. A maze of insanity, corruption, violence, pollution. Slathered with screaming ads and the stench of human suffering and vice at every level. Yet you can't stop coming back to it. The streets call to you. The city calls to you. The few friends you have (if they are truly friends at all), call to you. Each personality is so well written, they feel like living breathing beings, even as they disappoint you, use you, leave you, or stab you in the back. (Perhaps those traits in particular are what make them feel so humanly real.) Night City chews you up and spits you out, but you're an Edgerunner. That is the life you've chosen Choom, and whatever end awaits you, you'll light the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on fire on your way out, just to remind it you were there. See you in the Afterlife.

This game is all over the place. In some instances it's fantastic, then it rips your heart out with how undercooked it is in other places and your immersion is quickly broken.  [h2]Story and narrative[/h2] The premise of the world is simple - megacorpos run most of the world in a world where governments inexplicably bent over to them nearly everywhere regardless of the system, yet it fails to deliver that feeling in the most corpo-driven city. For some odd reason, their presence is visible everywhere, yet felt nearly nowhere throughout the story, even in quests where you are screwing with the corporations, and I blame the writing and pacing here. Edgerunner immediately pulls you into a world run by corpos, whereas the game tries it in so many ways, and still falls flat. This corpo narrative began and ended with Meredith Stout. That was a fantastic introduction to what corpos can and would do, and then it just fizzles out. They quickly became a background noise even though your whole main quest is related to dealing with them. Gangs became the focal point and the pacing prioritized them and the result is tangible.  Narrative is also suffering from pacing and writing. Just like in Fallout, you need to fulfill your mission before time runs out. Here however, it does not run out, because the world is filled with side quests and we wouldn't want to miss out on that. A terrible mistake. Cake-and-eat-it-too kind of a mistake. On top of that, you are bombarded with endless phonecalls in the very first hour of gameplay, to the point you begin to lose track of what certain quests or side characters are about and you do not know what to do first. How this wasn't ever patched or why it was introduced in the first place is beyond me.  The first mission is the best example of this dissonance. It's an endless stream of information and cutscenes that attempt to pull you into the story but they instead leave you dazed and confused. You're meeting over a dozen characters within your first hour, which is filled with cutscenes that inform you about three subsequent missions. Incomparable to the pacing of Witcher 3's beginning. Absurdly terrible but am I glad I stuck through it, as I knew what they were attempting to do.  [h2]World and immersion[/h2] I don't think I've ever played a game so immersive and yet so shallow at the same time. Citizens are immersion-breaking, but then you get to live a second life within this world as long as you're not done with much of the story, but as you finish quests, immersing in it becomes less and less interesting to you. Why? Because CD Projekt Red is not Rockstar nor Valve. They've created a static world that tries to simulate a dynamic one. Compare the world to GTA's where the world is an actual, reactive sandbox. Everything is designed to react to a trigger - from the world, from the characters, from the physics. In Cyberpunk, you are the sole trigger, and the game reminds you of it every so often. In GTA5 you can't drink, car interiors are awful, apartments are lackluster and staticky, the interaction with the world objects is undercooked, CP77 builds on that in so many ways, but it just didn't have the funding, time and tech know-how to build a living world, and one feels and sees it.  The city itself is beautiful to look at. The more you explore though, the more you see the seams unfortunately, but it's well detailed. Not many interiors to enter, some interiors are only a one-time occurrence, some are notably undercooked.  [h2]Characters' reactivity[/h2] It's a heavily narrative-driven game, relatively loose where it can afford to be, but otherwise you are shoehorned into a particular V every single time no matter your background. However, your choices do matter when it comes to characters you come across - their fate, and the reaction to your actions, are a direct consequence of your doing. They act in juxtaposition to certain choices you make throughout quests or stories, which allows you to really ponder on the eventual outcomes, though some outcomes will certainly leave you confused as to why X happened, and will feel forced as a consequence. Again, writing isn't the strongest suit of this game, pacing exacerbates it, but the characters are well fleshed out and they thankfully salvage the entire game. They suffer from a few things though - terribly animated vehicle cutscenes where they're the ones driving, mistimed voice lines and sound EQ being all over the place. The loud and annoying ads sometimes cut through very emotional lines so awfully, it left me extremely annoyed.  [h2]The technical slavjank nightmare[/h2] No wonder why they decided to go for Unreal Engine 5. The accumulated tech debt became too great. They're not a large corporation yet still they built an amazing looking engine that does things it's set out to do relatively well. But it is indeed a pig with a lipstick in every way imaginable and you get reminded of it while playing quite often. I will not list them here.  [h2]Phantom Liberty DLC[/h2] Very happy they eventually fixed most of the issues plaguing the game and even released a fantastic DLC. They doubled down on a game they worked their asses off for nearly a decade. The writing and pacing there is immeasurably better and it shows what CP77 could've been had they simplified the whole premise and focused on building a reactive world. Instead, they branched the main story out and the further you strayed from the beginning the more it suffered. This is a non-issue in the DLC. It's a relatively simple and arguably much more linear approach to an immersive and atmospheric story with memorable characters and, finally, very few side characters you're supposed to remember after a dozen or so quests. I still remember Paco and his friend I smuggled out of Dogtown, the chippery merchant who kept spamming me with tidbits about events that happened a week ago in game for some reason.  [h2]Modding![/h2] Hell yeah. So many great mods that we will not get to use once the new installment is launched on UE5. Plenty of mods brought back cut content and fix bugs that are still present. Imho they are vital for those who really want a great experience, doubly so for replays.   [h1]Main game: 8/10[/h1] [h1]DLC: 9.5/10[/h1]  I watched Cyberpunk's development ever since 2013 teaser dropped, and finally got to play it in 2026. Boy am I glad I waited till it got sorted out. Kudos to CD Projekt Red devs for this fantastic piece of art, and screw the management, the idea of a publicly traded game company, and the crunch culture.   Bunch of ♥♥♥♥-for-brain gonks.

This is a really, really good game.  I remember first downloading GOG over 10 years ago and that's all they would advertise:  "Cyberpunk 2077!"  I was like, "Great, another future title is being over-advertised and over-hyped.  It will probably end up sucking."  Well, I was half-right, because it did suck initially when it was released.  I figured I wouldn't even give it a chance because have little faith in developers with investors who rush and over-hype everything, like No Man's Sky, for example, but I was talking to a friend about Cyberpunk 2077 a year or so ago and he said the game has improved significantly.  So, I decided to get it.  No regrets.  I had a ton of fun playing and re-playing this game.  There are so many main quests and side quests that intermingle with the main quests and side quests that don't intermingle with the main quest, but intermingle with other side quests and independent side quests and gigs and crimes to resolve and races, etc.  There's so much content it was almost overwhelming, but in a good "I am getting my money's worth out of this game" way.  The story is pretty dystopian and bleak.  I'm pretty sure the developers don't really believe in "winners" as we do in a lot of games.  Decisions can be very difficult to make, unless your ambition is to get the most gain out of it.  However, if you're trying to be a "good" person, this game makes it difficult to do, because most story-driven choices have good and bad sides to them.  I won't spoil anything, but you'll see when you experience it.  And it's not just the main quest, there are side quests that have this same dynamic.  It was morally challenging.  My only problem was that, with each ending I discovered, I felt like I was finally making the right choice, but then the writers throw a random wrench into the ending that kind of ruins it for me.  I got a little tired of that, but like I said, this game wasn't meant to be good vs bad.  Ok, potential spoiler ahead, but I can't resist.  I recognized Keanu Reeves the moment I saw him.  I hadn't realized he was in this game, but he did a marvelous job in his role and he's a great actor.  I think a big part of this game's success is because of him.  I won't lie, though, I hated his character my first playthrough, and I wanted nothing to do with him.  However, the game slowly and surely makes him seem decent and enables you to understand things from his point of view.  He's still a bit of a jerk, but as I mentioned before, this game doesn't cater to your whim.  Oh yeah, I almost forgot, developers are finally recognizing and representing straight-edge and sexually-abstaining persons.  I was getting so tired of games ruining characters for me by having them get drunk, do a bunch of drugs and sleep around like degenerates without giving me the option to avoid it.  I was glad to finally have the choice to graciously decline alcohol, cigarettes, drugs, promiscuity, etc. if I wanted.  Speaking of such, you can turn off any and all nudity in this game.  Female characters will have a black, bra-like texture over their bosoms if they're "naked" and they'll be wearing panties.  Male characters will always have boxers on at least.  However, if you want the nudity, you can even change the size of your ding-dong or rack.  Aside from the cosmetic viewpoint, I don't think this mechanic adds anything else to the game.  So, weapons, cybernetic implants, clothing and outfits and consumables are numerous.  I found myself always discovering something new or better than what I had.  There's also a huge amount of "written" dialogue, in the form of data shards.  This can also be a little annoying, because I could either be sneaking around, fighting enemies and looting stashes and corpses, etc. and I'd pick up like 18 different data shards that I'd have to go to my journal to read.  Normally, that's not so bad if you can ignore it, but each data shard shows up as a bolded item under an extensive list of categories.  The "other" category being the biggest culprit because I'd have like 75 unread data shards in there because I'm not going to pause my game every 5 seconds to read shard number 54 of the 87 that I somehow got from the 5 gangsters I just hollowed out, neither am I going to analyze every stash I search for every little thing I want to pick up or not.  It got a little ridiculous by the end.  Anyway, I'm happy to say that this game turned out great.  If you're looking for a new first-person action adventure, definitely play this.

I first bought this game on release. It was a terrible, broken mess.   I tried the game again after 5 years, and it was a totally new game. Great job from CDPR to fix it.   Some criticisms:  The game still has quite a few bugs, but most are harmless and sometimes funny. Not to be unexpected for a game this complex and big. However, considering the game's tone is serious, I do think it would be great to iron them out for the sake of preventing immersion breaks.   Personally, I didn't like the English voice acting for male V nor female V. Perhaps just me, but it just felt a bit goofy, lacking in emotion, etc. They also reused quite a few voice lines and at times it is noticeable.  The game's pacing is also very awkward. There is quite a lot to do, except the game feels like it rushes you to complete the main storyline as you are dying in a matter of weeks. It seems like it was a big mistake to make that such a prominent part of the story so early on. It is also very difficult to care about Jackie, as you basically experience none of their previous relationship. I almost wonder if it was cut content.   I won't get into the details, but the pacing of the main game was not good, and it also felt quite short. It would have been great to have some time being a regular merc with Jackie before everything begins to go downhill.  There are a ton of details that have not been attended to, and are only partially fixed by mods (reflection in mirrors, for example).  I think player customization is also quite limited, accessible building interiors are limited as well. As you get more cyberware, your character does not reflect it. A shame.   Some random things that really came to bother me are how CDPR approached buildings that don't have accessible interiors. Instead of designing a model for the player to view from the window, they simply emplaced a 3D drawing that looks terrible if you look at it for longer than a second. And it is standardized, so you seem the same pattern everywhere, and it is quite immersion breaking. I wonder if they did it procedurally, because there are several spots on the map that you CAN actually go inside, but when viewing it from the outside window, it is just painted over with the same 3D drawing. This creates impossible physical dimensions and mismatched interiors/exteriors, etc.  Same thing with NPCs. Play long enough (just 10 hours was enough to notice), and you will realize that there are a limited number of base NPC models, of which all other NPCs are just variations of. Incredibly immersion breaking.  Your decisions in the game, as well as the life path you take in the game, basically do not matter except for the very end. That was quite frustrating. I also felt it was very limiting. If I wanted to roleplay as a diehard corpo, even after getting discarded, it is impossible to do so as your dialogue locks you into a certain philosophy and playstyle.   The romantic options are generally all terrible. I didn't like any of the characters that you had an option to romance. Only Kerry was fine, and it just feels wrong to romance him while being half-Johnny.   A lot of times, the dialogue prompts are completely different to what is actually said by V. Not just semantically different, directionally different. Very frustrating and a confusing design choice.  There is still a lot more to complain about, but those are the things that immediately come to mind.  Some compliments:  The graphics are generally great for a 2020 release. It is a visually stunning game. The atmosphere, overall story, and execution are well done.   What really saves this game, in my opinion, is the Phantom Liberty DLC. What a fantastic addition. I think it is better than the base game by far. The story is dynamic, morally grey, your decisions have profound consequences, it just does everything you would like it to. The characters are well fleshed out, flawed, and make the story incredibly captivating. As much as I like Keanu Reeves, I think not having the DLC be as focused on Johnny allowed CDPR to make something really special. It's a spy thriller meeting the Cyberpunk world. It was truly awesome.  Replayability is also pretty decent. Combat is fun. The cyberware is fun. For the most part, especially if you are able to ignore details (I struggle a bit), the game is very immersive.   I am really looking forward to Cyberpunk 2 (Orion), and I hope that not having to focus on Johnny will allow them to really flesh out a great story.

The game offers a brilliant mix of compelling storytelling, unforgettable characters, and fast-paced combat that lets you play exactly how you want - you can even go full cyberpunk samurai and slice through enemies using just a katana. To be fair, it's still not perfect, and you will definitely run into some annoying bugs and glitches from time to time. But despite these flaws, the incredible atmosphere and emotional story make it completely worth your time. It’s a solid 8/10 that you shouldn't miss.

Alright I admit that I'm six years late but bear with me; I don't usually write reviews for anything really but I had to make an exception here. I finally played Cyberpunk 2077, and I can confidently say it's the closest I'll ever get to living in the future. Night City is absolutely gorgeous. Every street looks like a neon-soaked fever dream designed by someone who drank six energy drinks and said, "What if Blade Runner had even more advertisements?" I spent half my playtime admiring the scenery and the other half accidentally running over pedestrians while trying to figure out the controls. The story is fantastic, the characters are memorable, and Keanu Reeves somehow manages to be cooler than every other person in a city full of cybernetic ninjas. That's not fair, but it's impressive. As for the bugs: I played long after launch, so most of them are gone. Instead of game-breaking glitches, I mostly encountered minor weirdness, like NPCs staring into the void or physics deciding that gravity is merely a suggestion.  Combat is fun, hacking makes you feel like a futuristic wizard, and customization lets you create a character that looks either incredibly intimidating or like they lost a fight with a glow-stick factory.  Overall: 9/10. Cyberpunk 2077 delivers an amazing sci-fi adventure, and after all the updates, it's finally become the game we were promised. Also, it taught me an important lesson: if the future is anything like Night City, I'm staying indoors.

Is it particularly deep? No. Is it particularly fun? Yes!  If you can think of this game not as an RPG but as an action game with a narrative focus, and you dig that, then this game is for you.  The gameplay is fun and has three very distinct archetypes (melee, ranged, hacking) that makes each of them actually play and feel different, giving the game enormous replayability. The game is still, in the year 2026, the very best looking game there is. The voice cast is fantastic, with Cherami Leigh (female V) giving the performance of not just her lifetime, but of most people's lifetime. It is THAT good. Last but certainly not least, Night City itself might be the best, most immersive open world environment ever made (at least until GTA 6), chock full of stuff for players to discover and enjoy if they engage with it beyond the main quest which is, admittedly, short.  Is it a masterpiece like The Witcher 3? No, but it's a more than respectable 9/10. If it had launched like this, instead of the broken mess that it was, it'd have made GoTY without a shadow of doubt.  If you get it half off it is an absolute steal. My only regret is having waited as long as I did to play it.

A difficult game to write a review on.  IMO, if you're into this genre of games, you must play it. It's one of those pillars in gaming history. There simply so many good parts about it, the story, the characters, the side quests, the music, the graphics, the gameplay. I had a lot of fun playing this game.  However. I waited years before playing this game together with its expansion. I hoped for the smoothest, best experience. And that didn't solve the problems. Because this game is still a mine field of game breaking bugs. Of glitches, dropping through the floor. visuals not loading fast enough. driving on non existing roads. And parts of the world or game that feel, incomplete. It feels like they wanted to add much more, but couldn't. And that blueprint is still visible.  The story side also doesn't always contain everything you want. Often I feel I miss actions I want to take with V. Like saying goodbye to someone. Or explaining something in a different way. Most of the time it's okay. Sometimes it really feels like it misses that part.  The biggest thing I noticed though ? The main quest of the game is super short. I suspect you might be able to finish it in like 4 hours. The side quests are the real deal. And I suggest doing what I did. Finish every side quest first. Because it will help you live inside the story, learn the characters, the reasoning.  I believe this game deserves a sequel. CDPR somehow dropped the ball on this one. And I hope they figured out why and fixed that internal team issue. Because I can really see and feel the love they put into this game. It's a game with a soul, which is funny considering the story. But it's got huge problems still to this day.  So, keeping that in mind. Yes, you need to play Cyberpunk together with its expansion. You deserve the experience it will give you.

The character animations are nicely done and life-like. The quests or missions are super long compared to other games. You literally feel like you're hanging out with someone for 2-3 hours. With lengthy dialogues and animations. Also, whether you are picking someone up, driving to a location to gather supplies, checking out or gathering intel on an enemy base before entering, driving to a location to pick up your reward. And even after everything, sometimes dropping that person back off.  To make the missions faster and easier to navigate, you can either fast travel to your objectives or allow AI to drive you to your objective markers with auto-drive. You can also skip forward in time, which skips dialogue and animations for those who have to reload a save and don't want to go through it all over again.  The Phantom Liberty DLC is well worth the price as I thought it would never end. But in a good way. With much more content, such as additional missions, skill tree, tech, cyberware, vehicles and weapons. A new cast of characters and actors. Not only does the base game alone have multiple different endings based on the decisions you make in the game, but the Phantom Liberty DLC also has many different endings.  The only downside to the game for me is there's no vehicle garage or aircraft hangars where you can customize your vehicles. You can at least purchase many different types of vehicles and give them a custom paint job.  I recommend making a manual save for each mission you play as there are some missable achievements and you also may have not liked the choices you have made that will change the overall experience and ending. Cyberpunk 2077 takes place in Night City, one of the most beautiful and detailed cities I have seen in a video game. The city looks especially amazing during the night, with all the lights, signs, and atmosphere making it feel alive.  You play as V and explore the city while upgrading different parts of your body to unlock new abilities and combat options. The gameplay gives you a lot of freedom in how you want to fight and build your character.  Everybody knows how rough the launch of this game was. It was a complete mess for many players. However, after multiple updates and the release of Phantom Liberty, the game has become much better and is now a great experience.  The story is excellent, and the characters are one of the strongest parts of the game. Johnny Silverhand, played by Keanu Reeves, is an amazing character. His dialogues, personality, and role in the story made him one of my favorite characters in the game.  Your choices also matter throughout the story. The people you talk to, the decisions you make, and the way you handle certain situations can affect future missions and events, so it is worth paying attention to what is happening.  The soundtrack is fantastic and always feels right for the moment. Whether you are exploring Night City or taking part in a mission, the music fits perfectly.  Phantom Liberty is also worth playing. It adds a new area called Dogtown along with new missions and characters. I enjoyed it just as much as the main game.  There are still some bugs and sometimes they can affect gameplay. They are not as bad as they were at launch, but you will probably run into a few issues during your playthrough.  Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 is a fantastic game with a great story, memorable characters, fun combat, and one of the best open worlds I have explored in a game.

One of the best if not the best story games i have every touched.  The Graphics id give a  10/10, they are gorgeous even tho i am running it on mid level graphics and it still has at least 70 fpsat the lowest. The map building is also awesome, each part of the map is deeply in touch with the certain organization running it shown not only by the Architecture, but also by the people and the language they speak. TL;DR nice graphics even on mid settings  The fighting aspect gets a 7/10 from me, the fighting in itself is most of the time the same thing, you either shoot or slash through the enemies until you either fight a boss or get to a mission objective. The thing that makes the fightign better for me though is the variaty, you can basically be like a ninja and play to only do kills stealthy which 8 times out of 10 works perfectly fine, of course you still have to do bosses normaly. You could also go for a quickhack kind of style and make it your objective to never even enter the area your target is in. TL;DR the combat is pretty much the same unless you change your way of playing, but you have a lot of options on how you fight.  The missions get a 8,5/10 from me. If you just stick to the main mission then ofc you will see a certain pattern being repeated here and there, but if you actually look around and do side missions either from certain fixers or just random gigs you find, you will most of the time be rewarded with either good loot for your current level or sometimes even a iconic weapon or piece of equipment. The good thing about cyberpunk side missions is that most missions are kind of unique and some even offer different outcomes to other missions, ofc there will be some that are nearly identical to other ones, but cyberpunk is one of the first games where i actually played the side quests because they were something new everytime. Sure doing them one after another is annoying and kind of boring, but sprinkling some side quests here and there has a nice touch. TL;DR the game has nice missions which make it even more enjoyable as long as you dont just ruch the main mission  Now one of the most important things, the difficulty, i can only speak out of the perspective of someone who played the game only on the second hardest difficulty. The Difficulty id say gets is between a 4/10 and a 9/10. The Difficulty first of increases/decreases depending on how you want to play. You want to play melee only, well then get yourself at least one thing you can use for ranged enemies otherwise you will die more then you need. Now ofc the game increases/decreases in difficulty if you chose a lower/higher difficulty lol, but your playstyle changes the difficulty very drastically. While some builds just fly through enemies one by one from a very early point, others have to wait ages until they get a weapon that is actually useable, but i will say more to that later. One thing is for sure, if you just started dont, and i mean DONT play on Very Hard if you want to actually experience the game in a way where you will have fond memories of this game. The Difference between hard and very hard is like playing basketball against a 14 year old boy and playing against 3 genetically modified versions of Shaquille O'Neal while you have a vibrator up your ass making your legs shake. If you enjoy being the victim 9 times out of 10 then go ahead. Another thing is that some missions have bad way of explaining things, sometimes youll be trapped for 10 minutes because you didnt read a certain things right but that happens rather rarely. TL;DR The difficulty is not that much of a problem unless you play on very hard(dont)  Now onto the last thing before the big TL;DR, the loot/equipment The Straight up loot you get i would give a solid 8/10, i never had any problems with crafting and if i did you could always do a NCPD scanner or a side quest and you would get enough materials you could use, ammo was also never a real "threat" as you can loot more then enough ammo boxes or just craft them in your inventory for very cheap. TL;DR no problem ammo and material wise  Now onto the gear, for me the gear gets a 6/10 A lot of weapons a useable with some even better then end game weapons. Looting them is also pretty easy as every enemy drops the gun they are using when they die, the only problem and why i would only give it a 6/10 are the iconic weapons. The iconic weapons are like seeing a legendary item in fortnite, either it is the one and only legendary scar one of the best if not the best weapons in game or its a chug jug, in non gaming terms iconic weapons are just a hit or a miss with them being more often a miss. Some weapons like the breakthrough a legendary sniper that can pierce walls like they werent there at all and has a high headshot dmg allowing you to kill a enemies without even entering a building or even through entire levels of buildings is one of the better ones and then there is the "DEATH AND TAXES" a pistol that sounds like it will steal not only the money from low-middle class families but also KILL ANYTHING actually takes your hp for each shot you do and at low hp poisons enemies which maybe has some niche use but if you are using the Biomonitor which auto heals at low hp your will loose all of your hp item charges before you even get the unique effect of poison, and in a game where hp is everything losing it for dps that isnt that high is not really good. Like i said hit or miss. The worst part about this ICONIC weapon system is that some "classes"/builds feel like they are getting more then others, like the smart weapons for example, there are some that are incredible and not even hard to get, the problem you ask? You have maybe 3-4 that are acutally useable and that is not very much compared to other classes, especially if you have to do certain missions which you dont have access to in the first act and are more in the mid game areas. TL;DR Normal weapons are nice but the iconic weapons are like 65% trash and only those 35% are good/better then normal weapons with mods   TL;DR and this time its the last one.  This game is incredible, Graphic wise but also the missions and the combat can be pretty nice. The main story is well done and the DLC is probably my favourite in all of gaming. The weapons are unique with most iconics being kind of useless but still cool, the skill tree is nice and gives niche play styles also some options to become even better, the loot is at some times even too much and game runs smoothly even when not on the highest settings. The last few things i have to say is, dont just run down the main mission without doing at least some side mission, whether it is killing a couple of goons here and there or actually doing mission from panam or padre for example. This game is beautiful and if you just fly through it you will not only miss rewards that are good but also the experience this game has to offer.  And try mods lol they make the already good game even better.  Overall a solid 9/10 for me (with the dlc)

Main Game 5/5 Phantom Liberty 5/5 Achievements 5/5 Achievement Completion: 57/57 (100%)  Cyberpunk 2077 is one of the strangest gaming experiences I've had.  I bought the game at launch and, like many people, experienced some of the issues that surrounded the release. Despite that, I still gave it a fair chance and put around 11 hours into it before moving on. Some time later I came back and tried again, putting another 10 or so hours into a new save, but for whatever reason the game still wasn't clicking with me.  Then recently I decided to give it one more chance.  This time something changed.  Not only did the game finally click, but I couldn't stop playing it. I became so invested that after finishing the game I immediately started a second playthrough and completed the entire thing again while working towards 100% achievements.  Once you get a grasp of the mechanics, skill trees and general systems, everything starts to fall into place. The game does a lot and can feel overwhelming at first, but once it clicks it becomes incredibly rewarding.  The main story is outstanding.  The characters, writing, setting and atmosphere are some of the best I've experienced in gaming. Night City feels alive in a way very few open worlds manage to achieve. There is always something happening, whether it's a serious story moment, a side quest, random humour, or simply exploring the city itself.  The game also offers a huge amount of freedom in how you approach combat and progression. Different builds can completely change how the game feels, making multiple playthroughs genuinely worthwhile rather than simply replaying the same experience.  As a fan of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners, I also loved the references and connections throughout the game. They never felt forced and added another layer of enjoyment to an already fantastic world.  Phantom Liberty deserves special praise.  The expansion is exceptional from start to finish. The new area is fantastic, the story is brilliant and the new characters are some of the best in the entire game. Solomon Reed, played by Idris Elba, and Song So Mi quickly became two of my favourite characters in Cyberpunk 2077. Their performances and the choices surrounding them create some of the strongest moments in the entire game.  If you enjoy Cyberpunk 2077, Phantom Liberty is not optional in my opinion. It is a must-buy expansion and one of the best DLCs I have played.  Achievement-wise, I found the list very respectful of the player's time. There are a few achievements that benefit from planning ahead, multiple playthroughs or smart save points, but I never felt forced into repetitive grinding. During my first playthrough I did experience a few issues with achievements not unlocking correctly, which ultimately contributed to my second run, but thankfully I enjoyed the game enough that this never felt like a chore.  After 223 hours and 100% achievement completion, Cyberpunk 2077 isn't just one of my favourite games, it's my game of the decade.  It took several attempts to finally click with me, but once it did, I couldn't put it down.  A brilliant RPG with unforgettable characters, an incredible setting and one of the best expansions in modern gaming.

Some of the endings hit harder than any game I've played in years.  What truly elevates Cyberpunk 2077, however, is its atmosphere. After 50+ hours, I genuinely think Cyberpunk 2077 is one of the best open-world RPGs I've ever played, and honestly, it might be my favorite story-driven game period.  What surprised me the most wasn't the graphics, even though they're absolutely insane. Night City is one of the few game worlds that actually feels alive. During the day, the city is packed with people going about their lives, and at night the neon lights make everything look straight out of a sci-fi movie. Sometimes I'd find myself driving around with no objective just because I wanted to take in the atmosphere. There are very few games where simply existing in the world is enjoyable, but Cyberpunk nails it.  The story is what really sold me, though. I expected a good story, but I didn't expect to become so invested in the characters. The game somehow makes you care about the people you meet, their struggles, and the choices you make throughout the journey. There were multiple moments where I sat staring at my screen after a mission ended just thinking about what happened. The writing feels mature, emotional, and surprisingly human for a game set in a futuristic dystopia.  What I love most is that Cyberpunk isn't afraid to teach difficult lessons. Throughout the game, you're constantly reminded that life isn't fair, that power isn't always enough, and that sometimes there simply isn't a perfect ending waiting for you. Night City doesn't bend to your will just because you're the protagonist. In fact, one of the biggest themes of the game is realizing how small you can be compared to the forces controlling the world around you.  The Peralez storyline is probably the best example of this. By that point, V can become an absolute monster capable of taking down entire gangs, elite soldiers, and some of the most dangerous people in Night City. Yet when you uncover what's happening to Jefferson and Elizabeth Peralez, you're suddenly faced with something far beyond guns, cyberware, or brute force. You start pulling on a thread that leads to a conspiracy so massive and unsettling that you realize you're completely out of your depth. Then there's Mr. Blue Eyes, a character who appears briefly yet somehow manages to leave one of the biggest impressions in the entire game. The mystery surrounding him and what he represents creates this feeling that there are powers operating in the shadows that even legends like V can't truly understand. It was one of the few moments in gaming where I genuinely felt powerless, and that's exactly why it was so memorable.  The game constantly delivers moments like that. It explores identity, mortality, ambition, friendship, sacrifice, and what it really means to leave a mark on the world. It asks questions that don't always have easy answers, and that's what makes the story stick with you long after you've finished playing.  The side quests deserve a special mention because they don't feel like filler. In a lot of open-world games, side content feels like a checklist. In Cyberpunk, some side quests are so well-written that they feel like main story missions. Many of them introduce memorable characters and stories that stuck with me long after I completed them. Some of the most emotional moments I experienced weren't even part of the main story.  The lore is also incredible. The deeper you dig into Night City, the more fascinating it becomes. The corporations, gangs, politics, technology, and history all blend together to create a world that feels believable despite how futuristic it is. You can spend hours learning about the world without ever touching the main story, and you'll still find yourself discovering new details.  The freedom you have is another huge plus. Whether you're talking your way through situations, hacking everything in sight, sneaking around enemies, or charging in guns blazing, the game lets you create your own version of V. The cyberware system is one of my favorite progression systems in any RPG because every upgrade genuinely changes how you approach the game.  Now, the game isn't perfect. I've had more crashes than I would've liked, and I've run into bugs that occasionally break immersion. Sometimes NPCs behave strangely, and there are moments where the game still shows some technical roughness. But honestly, those issues never outweighed everything the game does right.  Cyberpunk 2077 is one of those rare games that completely pulls you in. The combination of incredible visuals, unforgettable characters, emotional storytelling, deep lore, meaningful choices, amazing music, and thought-provoking themes made it incredibly hard to put down. There were times when I wasn't just playing the game—I felt like I was living in Night City.  For all its flaws, Cyberpunk 2077 gave me something very few games ever have: a world I couldn't stop thinking about even when I wasn't playing. The fact that a game can entertain you is impressive. The fact that it can make you reflect on life, power, identity, and the things beyond your control is something special.  10/10. Night City got me, choom.

I'll just go out and say it - this might be one of the best games ever, and definitely one of the best I have ever played.  Cyberpunk 2077 simply pulls you in like very few other games could. Night city feels incredibly immersive, in large thanks to Mike Pondsmith's RPG series upon which it is based, but also thanks to the masterful game design and plot. CDprojekt took a page from the great Half-Life series as there are no cutscenes in a classical sense throughout the game. You almost never see the world outside V's eyes, and that just lets you inhabit their body on a level I can confidently say is unbeatable. You don't [i] play as [/i] V, you [i] are [/i] V. Even though a great majority of dialogue options don't have particularly far reaching consequences, they offer just enough variety to truly express yourself and give V your own spin.  But immersion means nothing if the story you immerse yourself into is as bland as real life, which this is categorically not. The plot hooks are numerous and engaging with an ensemble of characters so fleshed out you begin to question game from reality. Johnny especially is such a charismatic and strong persona many would get up and follow him to Arasaka tower if it existed today. He is probably Keanu Reeve's best performance. Romance character quests are also captivating: some better, some worse, some gutwrenching and some heartwarming, but that's just how life is. Don't expect too much from your date after their personal plotline is finished, though. You get a couple fun text interactions and that's about it.  But what about gameplay? The gunplay? Pristine. The options? Numerous. Do you want to sneak around like a ninja: deadly and silent? Sure, spec into reflexes, swap some chrome and be invisible. Do you want to go in guns blazing, faster than bullets and indestructible? Of course, grab a sandy and armor up like hell. Is standing back as your enemies drop like flies from the viruses you inject into their minds more your speed? Become a netrunner. There is so so many strategies, builds, fun little quirks one can explore that no two experiences can ever be the same. It's all so incredibly satisfying but at the same time full of expression that you just have to experience it to understand.  This is where we come to the few gripes I have about the game. Number one is the bugs. If [i]this[/i] is the fixed version of the game then day one must have been pandemonium. Cars dropping from the sky, sliding through the floor, npc's getting stuck, objectives not finishing, graphical glitches and at one time a flat out crash are just some of the wonders I personally experienced. Also car handling on PC is ... bad. I imagine some of it might be better on a game pad, but most of the cars in the game are flat out impossible to control with a keyboard. They seem to drift out more at lower speeds somehow, to the point making a 90 degree turn without crashing borders on impossible (maybe a bit exaggerated but does not feel great). Bikes are slightly better but still not perfect. These mistakes are however, in the grand scheme of things, pretty insignificant.  Overall a must play.

I believe i originally preordered this game way back in 2018, before it was delayed multiple times. By the time it came out, i wasn't even too broken up over the rough state the game was in. After years of waiting, the money i had spent on it hardly felt like it had ever existed. I played the game for 10 hours and then dropped it.  Fast Forward to 2026 and i get the urge to come give it another shot. I remembered enjoying the bit of the story I did get to experience, and i knew that the gameplay and bugginess of the game had been improved to various extents.  Having now binged nearly all of the content in the base game over the course of two weeks, i can confidently say that i am satisfied with my purchase of this game eight years ago.  While occasionally rough around the edges, i did thoroughly enjoy the combat and character progression of the game. Running mostly a blade build let me enjoy an up close, frenetic combat style that i imagine to be wholly different but equally as enjoyable as to what might be experienced from focusing more on quickhacks or on smart weapons. I found myself doing nearly all of the side jobs the game had to offer (save for the gigs, but i occasionally still did those if i stumbled into them), and was well satisfied with more of them than i would have expected. This is really all thanks to the character writing in this game.   By far, the standout feature of Cyberpunk is its writing. Dialogue between characters feels natural and animations in important moments are incredibly well done. I found myself really invested in the relationships between many of the main cast, and especially the relationships that V has with Johnny, Panam and Judy.  I won't speak on the endings too much, but i think they are all very well written. Something tells me that people were not happy with some of them when the game came out, but maybe i'm just being harsh on the average gamer in 2020.  I will say, the performance in the open world can sometimes be lacking, although i will admit that i run the game on ultra settings with a 2k monitor and average above 60 fps. I will especially mention that I never had any performance hiccups during important story scenes, I never once found myself taken out of a moment because of lag. The game also has occasional small bugs, like a cop walking around inside the sidewalk or a civilian loudly and repeatedly running their car into a wall 20 feet away from a conversation you're having. Nothing serious.  Honestly, my biggest complaint with the game is the content surrounding the romantic relationships in the game, or the lack of it. [spoiler] I can only speak on the relationship with Judy, but i imagine the others are quite the same. There's a whole big mission (and honestly a decent amount of setup in the background throughout the game) of this potential relationship blossoming, and once it finally does, the only thing that comes of it is occasional text conversations that eventually dry up, and a repeatable date mission in which you have access to a few small events and a set of dialogue that never changes and is largely the same as what you would get when you called Judy before you were even in a relationship. [/spoiler] I think it speaks greatly to this game's strengths that this is my biggest issue with it.  I know this game has largely positive reviews today, but i imagine there are still a lot of people who view the game in the light it was (often justly) received in at launch (although there were certainly unrealistic expectations surrounding the game at the time as well). I hope any of those people who may have dropped the game like i did come give it another shot some time, it's really worth it.  I think I'd give this game a 9/10. I'm very happy I came back to it. Really looking forward to the DLC next time it goes on sale :)

The DLC is great, the characters are great, and the small details of the world are excellent, leaving very few stones unturned when it comes to making the city feel like reality. Night City as a whole presents as a not-so-far off vision of the world in fifty to a hundred years if corporations triumph over government regulation entirely and become rulers in their own right. The average person in Night City lives uninsulated from violence, environmental ruin, and poverty, problems which have been exacerbated by the dominance of the billionaire class in America today.  Technical:  (spec: i9-14900 (non-K part), 4080 super FE on 566.36, 64gb ddr5, samsung 990 pro)  From my recollection, the game ran essentially flawlessly until about the 50 hour mark, where either some game data or cache issues began to show themselves, or I simply began to interact with elements of the game that somehow hadn't been as thoroughly debugged (although that doesn't make much sense). Sometimes this glitch reoccurred almost immediately and was typically worsened by opening the menu, making me wonder if it is caused by some sort of memory leak or something else that could progress as the game runs. Few games in history have undergone a redemption arc quite like Cyberpunk 2077. While its initial launch was famously rocky, CD Projekt RED’s unwavering commitment to their vision—culminating in the massive 2.0 update and the brilliant Phantom Liberty expansion—has officially transformed this game into a certified masterpiece.  Night City is the undisputed star of the show. It is a towering, neon-soaked vertical labyrinth that feels genuinely alive, dangerous, and intoxicating. Walking through the crowded streets of Watson or driving through the desolate Badlands offers an unparalleled level of environmental immersion. The world-building is incredibly dense, capturing the corporate-dominated, gritty essence of classic cyberpunk lore.  It is impossible to talk about the renaissance of this game without mentioning Cyberpunk: Edgerunners, the phenomenal Studio Trigger anime series. Edgerunners didn't just capture the hearts of fans; it perfectly mirrored the game's high-stakes, tragic, and adrenaline-fueled atmosphere.  The anime injected a massive wave of fresh energy into the game, making the exploration of Night City feel even more personal. Visiting locations featured in the show, listening to "I Really Want to Stay at Your House" on the in-game radio, or equipping David Martinez’s iconic jacket adds a profound layer of emotional depth for anyone who loved the series.  With the overhauled cyberware systems, revamped skill trees, and chaotic vehicle combat introduced in recent updates, the gameplay finally matches the narrative's ambition. Combat is fast, brutal, and highly customizable. Whether you want to be a stealthy Netrunner hacking enemies from afar or a sandevistan-powered solo slicing through corporate guards with a katana, the playstyles are incredibly rewarding.  At its core, the story of V and Johnny Silverhand is a deeply moving tale about legacy, identity, and survival against all odds.  Cyberpunk 2077 is no longer just a game about promises; it is a triumphant delivery of an unforgettable sci-fi RPG. If you were waiting for the right time to lose yourself in Night City—especially if you are a fan of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners—there has never been a better time to chrome up and dive in.
