i'm conflicted on whether i just barely recommend this game or just barely advise against it. i might change my overall rating, but for now, i can't recommend it, particularly when i've had so many people tout it as the greatest game ever made.  i'll start with the things i enjoy;   a great story with meaningful decision making.  excellent voice acting and casting.   a wide variety of playstyles.  beautiful graphics.   proper atmos support that scales with a home theater very well, plus a generally decent audio mix (for a video game).  and now the things i don't like;   poor balance with difficulty scaling where enemies just get insane amounts of health while you start dying in a couple hits and don't get enough resources like ammo or upgrade materials to keep up. elden ring is a prime example of how all games should balance difficulty. make it as hard as you want, but do not use difficulty sliders. know your audience and balance accordingly. breath of the wild and tears of the kingdom are great examples of the opposite end of the difficulty spectrum, making the game very approachable to beginners and children while still being challenging. difficulty sliders are simultaneously one of the laziest forms of game design and a nightmare to program. no one wants them; just properly balance your game. this has been long proven with time, going back to some of the earliest games like mario bros, which single-digit children could beat, or a grown adult could rage at. that is perfect game balance. a difficulty slider requires devs to finely tune like 5 versions of their game instead of 1, and almost no one puts in the time to do this because it sucks and costs a ton of money. i will never comprehend how so many video games still get this wrong today.  the combat is fairly uninteresting as well. while i enjoy the talent trees, item varieties, upgrade materials and general out-of-combat RPG elements, the combat itself is pretty shallow. not that bad, just boring and not much room for skill growth.   poor optimization as you get into higher framerates 100fps+. changing even the heaviest settings barely changes your framerate. the difference between medium-high 4k and ultra 4k + ray tracing is like 30fps average. though if you are just aiming for 60fps this game is optimized surprisingly well given the scale of the world and how good most things look.  third party CDPR launcher every time you start the game, paired with nags to log into your CDPR account for a single-player game. blegh.   way too much unskippable crap every time you launch the game. like two minutes between game launching and gameplay, and only about 5 of those seconds are spent actually loading into the world.  the UI and general UX when using a controller is bad. so many elements just force you to use the joystick cursor, such as the horrid menus that won't properly scroll through your items, settings etc with the d-pad. the joystick mouse SUCKS. just build proper controller support. this isn't a competitive shooter where MKB matters enough to warrant neglecting controllers this much.   the quest tracking is frustrating and inconsistent. sometimes i'll be on a main quest, then someone will call me and start another main quest, and that will override my current quest tracking. if you're not paying attention to the quest marker moving, it can have you trek like 15 minutes across the map for a completely different quest. other times the exact same scenario will happen and it WON'T override my quest tracking even though i'm only doing main quests in both scenarios. i haven't been able to figure it out but the inconsistency drives me nuts. it shouldn't be touching my quest tracker at all until i complete my current quest chain or otherwise clear my currently tracked quest.   while i love the decision making style of storytelling, the logic behind some of it borders on nonsensical. SPOILERS, but i played blind and i wanted to get a good johnny ending, and as i am about to invade Arasaka tower, he warns me that he doesn't want me helping Corpos, which makes sense. the other option is to kill yourself, of which he also disapproves, so naturally i went with invading Arasaka tower so i could kill Adam Smasher which i figured would matter more to him, and also because killing yourself is a pretty lame ending, but nah he just brutalizes you for selling out to the Corpos, never mentions a word about you killing Adam Smasher and basically says you're dead to him. i spent the entire story trying to veer things towards a good ending with Johnny but one vague decision killed that entire plotline and gave me the bad ending. i wouldn't have minded it much if it was obvious which one he preferred, but he literally objected to both and told me earlier in the game to promise that i'd kill Adam Smasher. it was such a lame way to end my favorite aspect of the story.  and speaking of the ending, i can't tell you how much i despise rollback endings. there is nothing more insulting than beating a game then just reverting to your save from two hours ago and wiping all your loot from the final zone. Zelda games do that as well and it never stops pissing me off, but at least they have the decency to only roll you back from the final boss instead of a giant quest involving tons of loot. just implement new game+ so you can have a persistent world, and if players make mistakes on a playthrough and miss items or endings they can just run it back with NG+. rollback endings are just a lazy way to avoid having to implement a changing world, which admittedly is a ton of work, but again let's look to Elden Ring for an example of how tremendously well this works if you spend the time to flesh it out.  honestly i could say more, good and bad, but i will conclude by saying that this game certainly has a lot to enjoy, i just don't care for much of this games design philosophy.

This was an unforgettable experience.  Truth be told, my first playthrough of this game back during the pandemic felt like a slog. I got maybe a quarter through the game and abandoned it. Second and third playthroughs were better but I could never finish it. I came back to it in April of this, a little after my birthday after rewatching Edgerunners. Until now, I'm not sure what happened, but I got hooked instantly.   [b] The Good: [/b]  1. Immersion. The dialogue, characters (specifically during the opening sequence), world, the corporations are believable enough to exist in the real world which helps with them being so believably distinct. They have slang, history, tech, and gear that are just believable enough to have my brain go 'yeah, that makes sense' every time someone speaks or talks about techno-babble. 2. Strong Opening. Every lifepath is strong, and the subsequent 'tutorial' phase with Jackie really helps with keeping you engaged. There are several options in these quests for roleplay and getting to know what kind of V you're going for. 3. V. V is well-written, consistent, and amazingly voice-acted (regardless of which gender you select). I won't lie and say there aren't some dialogue options where I think they might be too emotional because there are, but these are so far and few between in side missions that you just tend to forget about them after another hour of hearing them speak. They have believable goals and actions that help immerse you in the character. 4. Music. I genuinely just had to place this here. Cyberpunk would not be Cyberpunk without its music. Whether they be original songs you only hear on the radio or songs integral to the plot (specifically with Johnny), they all sound great and all fit the world. 5. Car Design. I love the sound and designs of ALL of the cars and bikes. Seriously. They're either intentionally goofy or just look cool as hell. 6. Phantom Liberty. I can't go into depth on this point, just know that if you're interested in buying this game then the DLC holds some of the best quests, side missions, unlockable gear, and characters in the whole game. It would be a shame not to play it.  [b] The Bad: [/b] 1. Bugs. Game still has bugs, some were more internal with the game wiping all autosaves and needing me to load in a manual save a few hours prior. Some were minor, like NPCs floating, repeating dialogue (which would correct itself eventually), repeating animations, etc. And some were game-breaking, some involving main quests found in the DLC which I can't explain better without spoiling a good chunk of a main story mission. 2. Driving. Some of the cars feel like you're driving with wheels made out of butter while some cars feel like you're driving a rock. Do yourself a favor and download a mod that enhances the driving experience. 3. Johnny's Friendship. No spoilers: there is a meter that tells you how close you are to a certain character and it matters very little. Spoilers: [spoiler] I absolutely DESPISE how you have to choose the "correct" dialogue options arbitrarily just to get a secret ending and how Johnny describes their relationship with V as "tumultuous" in some side quests (specifically with Kerry's) even when your friendship meter is the highest it could be. WHAT WAS THE POINT OF ADDING A METER IF YOU AREN'T EVEN GOING TO USE IT???? [/spoiler]

I first got this game back when it came out, put about 10 or so hours into it and couldn't finish it due to the bugs and my save corrupting. From what I played at the time, I thought the story was something interesting but was held back because of all the issues at the time. I uninstalled it and didn't look at it again for a long while.  I recently redownloaded this game, I've started to really love these types of games (big Deus Ex fan) and I figured it would be a good time to start again. After putting in about 40 hours, this is my review -  Gameplay - 8/10 Everything felt incredibly smooth, your stats and talents are able to be upgraded at a solid pace and goes with the game well so you're not making yourself overpowered within the first act. The upgrades you can make to your cyberware and quickhacks felt meaningful and you could definitely feel the power increase when you added in those upgrades or waited to long to upgrade. The only negative is the driving was very slippery and didn't feel very fluid. I'm on KBM so when making micro adjustments on the car or bike, it definitely moved more than I would expect it to and made those small micro-adjustments during chases or vehicle combat to avoid obstacles a bit of a pain. Bikes are definitely better than cars and you can feel it as soon as you get on a bike.  Combat - 9/10 Gunplay feels so fun and I really enjoy the fight against the AI. ADS and aiming was smooth, hip firing was relatively clean when you were in close range, and the upgrades to the scopes made ADSing much better as the game went on. The iron sights to the guns felt a little rough, but nothing that a little practice couldn't get you through. The modifications you could get to your guns were, just as I mentioned above, impactful enough to make you feel like you were actually progressing and getting stronger, as well as the option to just upgrade the one gun you were using rather than having to pick and choose between the hundreds of guns you end up getting throughout the game. Melee combat was really clean and the dashing felt very fun, doing a melee-based playthrough definitely seems like it could be a blast with all the unique upgrades and talents you can acquire  Story - 10/10 The games story is, by far, one of the best game stories in many of these cyberpunk RPG-style games. You meet some really incredible characters in the story and you can very easily get attached to them and their stories. Each of the side character storylines were well thought out and felt fun and unique, even Johnny's. The main story, while not very unique at it's core, gives a really fun take on cyberspace and pushing through to the other side of the net. Johnny's construct coming out at random points to either help or deceive you was a nice way to further change your decisions, wondering whether or not he's helping you or working towards his own motives. The endings you can get seem really fun and unique, I kept telling myself with the decisions I was making "Oh man I hope this happens with X/Y/Z, it would be a perfect ending" and by the end of the game, I got exactly the ending I was hoping for and it was definitely emotional.  Technical (graphics, quality of play, etc) - 8/10 I have a pretty decent higher mid-range PC and most of the time I had absolutely no problems with the game on mid-high settings. The environment is done up beautifully, the weather is very well done (rains way to damn much in Night City), the backgrounds and landscapes look beautiful, and they really nailed the dreary and gross feel of big city back-alleys. I did have some frame drops and lag randomly, and also when there was a LOT of entities on the screen or in the area (looking at you, parade mission!) but it smoothed out after a few minutes and never gave me much more of an issue.   Overall - 9/10 Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 is an absolutely fun and enticing game with a story that will really suck you in and have you coming back for more. I binged all 40 hours in the course of three weeks and honestly couldn't be happier with it. There's so much replayability and so many unique ways to be able to go through not only the main storyline, but the side character storylines and misc storylines that you could easily put 300-400+ hours in and have different outcomes each time. I would 100% recommend this game to others and I would say this is one of those games that you just have to play at least once in your life if you're someone who loves the story and character-building the most

You know if you had told me that the game I played on December 20th, 2020 would end up becoming one of my favorite games of all time, I would've burst a kidney. The very same game filled to the brim with game-breaking bugs, horrible optimization and pushed out the door knowing damn well it would never live up to to initial trailers. A game built on lies and false hope, yet the next RPG from the studio that brought us The Witcher 3. We had no reason not to trust CDPR and now their reputation hurts to this day. It took me almost 3 years and a whole new console to end up giving it a fair shot. 3 full playthroughs and a hit anime later, I can confidently say that Cyberpunk 2077 is nothing short of a masterpiece. A flawed one, yet a masterpiece all the same.  In all fairness, the story, characters and lore have always been there, just masked by all the muck surrounding it. In my opinion, Cyberpunk has the most interesting and fleshed out worldbuilding in all of gaming. From the exhilarating main story to some shard on a dead body in a ditch 15 miles outside the city. Every single gig, NCPD scanner, cyberpsycho sighting and quest flesh out the world in a way I have yet to really see in any other title. This is without even mentioning the exceptional Phantom Liberty expansion or Edgerunners anime which warrant their own reviews in all honesty. Other than CDPR's own Blood and Wine, I can't think of any other DLC that comes anywhere close to it. Trust me when I say you want to get the Ultimate Edition of Cyberpunk and experience everything from start to finish. The universe has a TON of potential and countless more stories to tell in it's sequel and (hopefully) further expansions. Overall, the biggest compliment I can give a game's world is watching lore videos of it on YouTube in my free time and Cyberpunk falls into that category.   Do I even need to mention the visuals? This game is still the internet's benchmark for good reason. It's (now) very scalable and optimized across a vast range of configurations. Whether you want to play at 1080p low or 4k with path tracing, the required hardware is really reasonable and provides a buffet for the eyes as you walk the streets of Night City. NVIDIA still uses Cyberpunk as their playground for all of their new technologies to this day which is a testament to it's quality and future-facing development. Because of this, I'm honestly really disappointed that CDPR is ditching their proprietary tried and true RED engine for Unreal, but hopefully if anyone can tame the beast that is UE5, it's them. As far as I'm concerned Cyberpunk still offers the best looking and immersive city environment in gaming.  Ever since update 2.0, the gameplay has also been massively improved and offers up a handful of super fun and engaging playstyles through various weapons, skills and cyberware options. Pre-2.0, the game felt lackluster and disjointed in its gameplay systems due to a lack of weapon combinations and cohesion in the skill trees. Well, no more. Even after 3 playthroughs I still haven't fully engaged with each build as there are quite a few. My favorite to this day is without a doubt the "Sandevistan Blade dancer". Slicing up groups of enemies while time is slowed to a crawl and as limbs fly around you is genuinely some of the most fun I've had in a game. This is even better as the various faction songs blast in the background or just listening to your radioport. Cyberpunk has a fantastic soundtrack and is sure to leave you adding at least a few songs to your playlist, which is another thing Phantom Liberty does even better by the way. Errr - yes ?  First acknowledgement - there are no more than a half dozen to a dozen companies on the face of the planet capable of designing a game of this complexity.  And two - all the mad, bad, s...tuff that was originally wrong with the game at launch.  All gone.  We're now running at quality product across the board.  So why the equivocation ?  1) Twenty five hours in I really don't know what I'm doing.  It's not the basics.  I can drive vehicles, travel without vehicles, shoot people, occasionally use melee weapons, loot bodies, find items.  My problem is that I really don't know what I'm doing in game.  I'm trying to be a street samurai.  Cool, polite, reliable.  But then I get spotted sneaking into a building and the entire mission becomes a bloodbath.  One way through the storyline I effectively get an option to do the big thing.  But should I do it with these people.  Is there a better choice ? I have no idea how ammo works.  2)  There are really bad design choices.  You have special powers that you need to activate the red screen where you really can't see what the f is going on.  Just killing everyone that's in your way is an amazingly viable tactic.  I have no idea where my standing is with all the myriad groups in the city.  A very early mission is collect a free gun.  Does the dealer hand it over to you at first conversation ?  NO !  You have to go through his entire inventory to find the free one.  Ditto with some free implants.  This was a good design choice, why ?  At that stage I don't have enough cash to buy anything.  3) I'm not living it and I'm not loving it.  I love CRPG's.  The original Baldur's Gate trilogy.  Mass Effect Trilogy.  Skyrim.  All completed successfully, all great.  This ?  Meh.  I really want to enjoy the game but 25 hours in I just don't feel that attached to the world or my character.  I'm recommending the game because I'm gambling that it's me who is wrong, me who is missing the big picture.  That other people will say "Galli - you called Cyberpunk wrong".  But I have a genuine fear that the concept is great, the technical problems resolved, but the game's systems don't work clearly enough, and there are serious issues with the way the story and the characters line up. 🌟 [b][url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/45575657]Follow Ainsel Reviews - Curator for the weird & lovely[/url][/b] 🌟  Most people will tell you Cyberpunk 2077 is about corporations, cyberware, crime, violence, or technology. I don't think it is. I think Cyberpunk 2077 is about humanity desperately trying to survive in a world that has already decided what a human being is worth.  Night City is a place built on dreams and consumption. Everyone is selling something. A product. A service. A body. An identity. A future. Above all else, Night City sells a promise: Become a legend. Be remembered. Matter.  At first, that promise feels exciting. You chase jobs, money, reputation, implants. You watch V climb toward the same dream that consumed countless others before them.  Then the game quietly starts asking questions. What is a soul? What makes a person real? What remains when memories can be copied, personalities can be transferred, and consciousness itself becomes data?  Johnny Silverhand enters the story as an unwanted ghost. A terrorist. A rockerboy. A self-proclaimed revolutionary.  Yet the longer he stays, the harder it becomes to separate him from the person he is slowly replacing. And that's where Cyberpunk hit me harder than I ever expected.  The game isn't afraid of death. It's afraid of identity. The real horror isn't that V might die. The real horror is realizing that the line between two people can slowly disappear until nobody can say where one ends and the other begins.  Who are we? Our memories? Our bodies? Our choices? The people who remember us?  Cyberpunk never gives a comfortable answer. Instead, it fills its world with people searching for one. Jackie dreams of becoming somebody. Judy searches for honesty in a city built on exploitation. Panam fights for family in a world obsessed with individual success. Viktor keeps helping people despite having every reason to stop. Misty sees meaning where others see chaos. Even many of the game's villains feel less like monsters and more like warnings about what happens when ambition consumes everything else.  That's why I've never been convinced that the true legends of Night City are the famous ones. Not Johnny. Not Smasher. Not the names people whisper in bars.  The people I remember most are the ones who remain human despite living in a world that constantly rewards the opposite. The ones who choose loyalty. Compassion. Connection. The ones who refuse to become machines long before any chrome enters their bodies.  And beyond all of that philosophy sits a genuinely fantastic game.  Night City remains one of the most breathtaking worlds I've explored. Every district feels distinct, every street seems to tell its own story, and simply wandering through the city can feel like a journey in itself. The gameplay offers enough freedom to support wildly different playstyles. Whether you prefer stealth, hacking, blades, precision gunplay, or complete chaos, Cyberpunk gives you the tools to create your own version of V.  The game also deserves recognition for one of the most passionate modding communities in modern gaming. Years after release, players continue to improve, expand, customize, and reinvent the experience. Night City doesn't merely exist because CD Projekt Red built it. It continues to thrive because countless players refused to let it stop evolving.  When the credits rolled, I wasn't thinking about builds, weapons, levels, or even endings. I was thinking about truth. About identity. About the strange human desire to leave something behind.  Night City teaches its people that becoming a legend is the highest goal imaginable. Cyberpunk 2077 spends hundreds of hours questioning whether remaining human might be the greater achievement. And honestly? I'm still not sure which answer scares me more.

The gameplay is fun enough, there's some cool fashion, and if you like the aesthetic of the dystopian near future there's some interesting environmental design. But if you're here for cyber punk I got bad news for you, they forgot all the punk. This is cyber punk written by people who have clearly never engaged with the concept of punk past ripped clothing, studded belts, and angry tones. Their anti-corporate and anti-establishment sentiments are nearly exclusively shown through gangs and goons who just wanna destroy stuff. Other than that there's Johnny, who's depicted as every narcissistic angry dude at your local hardcore scene; the Mox, who are actually a great depiction of rough community oriented punks, but the most we see of them is from Judy (who do give credit is I think the best written character); And lastly the Nomads, who do I think the best job of depicting anti-establishment community first punk ideology but unfortunately don't engage with night city very much.   There are a few more characters with compelling and interesting arcs but it all feels somewhat hollow and hopeless. I stopped playing the game not from boredom but just from feeling like there was no point. Not every game needs to have a  happy ending where the good guys win but in the world this game was released into and the following years it feels more like an oppressively pessimistic view of our own world rather than a genuine cyber punk game. The heart of cyber punk is the notion that even in the most oppressive times those of us at the lowest end of society can find community, stand for something, and enact change in a setting that serves as a warning for the things our current world is capable of. It feels like CD Project Red is only willing to engage with the surface level of that, they saw mohawks and body mods and didn't look any deeper than that, and it feels disappointing.

It's been a while since I last booted up Cyberpunk 2077. In fact, while writing this review, I checked my achievements to see when I last played and realized it was June 2025. Almost exactly a year ago.  And honestly? That realization shocked me.  Because Cyberpunk has stayed with me so strongly that I would've sworn it had only been three or four months. I think that alone says more about this game than any score ever could.  Today, I consider Cyberpunk 2077 my favorite game of all time, alongside Persona 5 Royal. After those two, there's a pretty significant gap.  What's funny is that I already played Cyberpunk at launch. Like everyone else, I heard all the stories about the disastrous release. And yet, my own experience was surprisingly smooth. I remember a few visual glitches and getting stuck somewhere due to a bug exactly once. Other than that, I had a good time. I felt like I got my money's worth, but that was about it. I finished the main story, moved on, and didn't think much more of it.  Years later, I decided to give the game another chance. By then, everyone was talking about the updates, the fixes, and how much the game had improved.  Thank God I did.  Night City is unlike any other open world I've ever experienced. Especially the city center. The atmosphere is incredible. It's one of the best aspects of the game, and that's saying something because almost everything here is first class.  Of course, you have to let yourself get immersed. But Cyberpunk makes that incredibly easy. From the very beginning, I connected with V and tried to put myself in her shoes whenever possible. Female V's voice acting deserves enormous praise here. She absolutely nailed the role.  One of the game's greatest strengths is its dialogue system. No, the choices don't always create massive branching consequences. But they do something equally important: they make you feel like you're shaping who V is. How she reacts. How she feels. What kind of person she wants to become. If you allow yourself to engage with that, the illusion becomes reality.  And then there's Johnny.  The relationship between V and Johnny Silverhand is easily one of the greatest achievements of the entire game. Sure, Keanu Reeves gives Johnny an unfair advantage from the start. Most people are predisposed to like him. But over time, Johnny becomes far more than "the Keanu Reeves character."  By the end, he's your best friend.  At least if you make certain choices and experience the conversations that truly define his character.  And that's what makes the ending hurt.  Because eventually, one way or another, those roads come to an end.  Even now, a year later, I still find myself thinking about this game. About the conversations. About the relationships. About the choices.  And of course, about the endings.  I'm usually the type of player who desperately wants a happy ending for the characters I've grown attached to. Cyberpunk doesn't really give you that.  "No happy endings in Night City."  There are better endings and worse endings. There are endings that offer hope and endings that don't. But there is no perfect ending where everyone rides off into the sunset.  Normally, that would bother me.  Here, I respect it.  Because the game commits to its themes all the way to the finish line.  I could spend paragraphs talking about the soundtrack, the gameplay, the art direction, the quest design, and countless other things. But that's not really what this review is about.  I just felt like writing down my thoughts.  Maybe this is a weird review. Maybe it's incomplete.  But somehow that feels fitting for my relationship with V and Night City.  So thank you, CD PROJEKT RED, and everyone who worked on this game.  Thank you for the experience.  I hope Cyberpunk 2 won't make us wait too long.  And one final thing:  As much as I absolutely despise The Tower ending—and I genuinely believe it's the worst ending in the entire game—  "G'night, Valerie. Today was a good day."

Having seen the trailers and this being a new IP, I was excited, though knew from the start that I won't play on day one as I generally never do (for both monetary and bug reasons). Turns out this could not have been a better idea, given the absolute shambles the game was in on launch.  After all of the bugs were sorted and the DLC was released, I finally decided to sink my teeth into the game, and when I say that, I mean it, as I have put in 230 hours into the game, finishing every main story mission as well as every side gig / side mission. Given the amount of time I've spent, you would think that I was a big fan of the game, but sadly, Cyberpunk is no Witcher and the game ultimately disappointed me. Without getting too into the weeds, the world just didn't pull me in, which mostly resulted from (in my opinion) poor writing, plot inconsistencies, characters that are not likeable and are either shoehorned in or are clearly missing something (presumably due to content being cut) and of course, the bugs. Don't get me wrong, there are definitely parts where the game shines and some missions that were really impactful and well written, however all this was in a sea of inconsistencies and issues, which ultimately made me disinterested. I started and stopped playing this game multiple times, but just kept pushing myself to go through everything and "experience" the game fully, but at the end I feel like most of it was a waste of time.  All in all, Cyberpunk is not a terrible game, but it is definitely very flawed. While it is definitely a cultural moment in gaming history, it's remembered more for how it launched than for what it actually is. And that's the problem: strip away the redemption narrative and you're left with a good-looking game built on a shaky foundation. The highs are real, but they're rare, and they never added up to the experience I'd hoped for. I'm glad I finally played it, if only to form my own opinion - but I don't see myself going back, and I'd struggle to tell anyone they need to.  P.S. If you do end up playing it, the Phantom Liberty DLC is MANDATORY! In my opinion it was the best part of the game and if the rest of the game was more like it, this review would have a different tone.

When Cyberpunk 2077 first came out in 2020, it didn’t spark much enthusiasm in me. Although I watched the hype surrounding the game, I didn't get a chance to play it until recently. First and foremost, I was pushed away by the state of the game prior to the patches and the DLC. However, after 5 years, I gave the game a chance and played through it along with the expansion. Starting this game, I had no idea what it all looked like, though I knew what I was aiming for—survival.  Answering DeShawn's question, I wanted a quiet life, and that is what I achieved. Night City wasn't that kind of place for me, unlike for many people; I didn't long to become a legend and die young just to have a drink named after me at the bar. I played this game with the awareness that the main character is the city, not me, nor anyone else. In a world ruled by corporations, where the individual can achieve nothing and governments are merely an extension of corporations—or behave like corporations themselves—your only way out is to leave. And even if you have to give up your soul for that freedom, up until the very end, I felt that this was what I wanted and what mattered to me.  Night City is a sort of modern interpretation of "bread and circuses," where young mercenaries destroy their lives and health just to become an item on a bar menu, feeling like they are becoming gods, believing until the end that they have risen above the city and ruled it for a brief moment. But that isn't true; from start to finish, you are just a little figurine in a corporate snow globe. I chose the path of freedom, and it cost me everything.  Johnny Silverhand, though he initially seemed like a narcissistic sociopath type, turned out to be a guy deeply hurt by life, trying to resist a sense of meaninglessness while feeling the breath of death pushing him toward destructive behaviors. He wasn't honest with himself or anyone else; he was always trying to claw something away from life, only to undergo a complete metamorphosis by my side in the end. At first, I wanted to get rid of him, but later I felt only pain and regret that he had to leave. I also felt an overwhelming sense of guilt and regret giving So Mi up to the FIA, even though I knew that, just like me, she only wanted to survive and escape from it all. But I had to look out for myself, even if I wished I hadn't...  I sacrificed everything for survival, but looking back at it all now, I feel that I did everything in my power to start over, and that's what counts. Johnny got a second chance, and I let him live a second life, if only for a moment, but this time he left as a changed man, full of empathy and free of anger, after being trapped for 50 years in a state between life and death. I was sorry to abandon Panam after we became almost like soulmates. But I helped her stay with her family, hoping they would help her and make things easier for her. Well, I know I won't play anything this unique again until the release of the next Cyberpunk, but it was worth it. Sometimes I didn’t feel like booting up my PC for a few days, but I always felt the need to finish this game, and here I am.

After more than 100 hours in Cyberpunk, I can tell you it has made up for its sins. The game still has the occasional flying car or quicksand pavement, but nevertheless, much less buggy than nearly every AAA launch in 2026. Night City is one of the most immersive game cities ever, with each district having a unique art style and feel to it. Exploring it without UI is one of the best experiences you can have in an open world. The main storyline is not bad, but also not good. It doesn't really grip you until the end, and has you doing cookie cutter missions to get to it. However, the thousands (literally!) of side quests make up for it. Each has lore involved and are practically endless, with a huge variety of quests. Gunplay feels amazing but melee is even better. Enhanced with cyberware and one of the best skill trees in games. One nitpick I have though is the inventory system, it doesn't really work too well, just there to put your items in your weapon wheel. Characters are also a great part, with optional questlines being much better than the main game (River's was my personal favorite).   Phantom Liberty takes everything Cyberpunk 2077 does well and pushes it even further. Dogtown is a darker, more dangerous setting that perfectly complements the expansion’s spy-thriller tone, and the new story delivers some of the best writing and choices in the entire game. Idris Elba’s Solomon Reed is an incredible addition, bringing tension and moral complexity to every scene he’s in. The expansion also improves the core gameplay with better enemy encounters, redesigned skill systems, and meaningful cyberware upgrades that make combat feel faster and more tactical. Most importantly, Phantom Liberty captures the feeling that every decision has consequences, often forcing you to choose between terrible outcomes rather than obvious good or bad endings. For longtime players, it doesn’t just feel like extra content—it feels like the complete realization of what Cyberpunk 2077 was always meant to be.

Awesome game, a bit misunderstood and overhated at launch.  Graphics are incredible overall, especially after all the updates. Night City is one of the most detailed and immersive open worlds ever made, full of life, neon lights, crowded streets and beautiful environments. Character models and facial animations are excellent, and the combat animations feel fluid and satisfying. Some NPC behaviors can still feel a bit awkward at times, but the overall presentation is top tier.  Sound design is amazing. Weapons sound powerful, cars feel aggressive, the city ambience is immersive, and the voice acting is top tier across the board. The music is absolutely phenomenal, perfectly matching every moment, whether you're cruising through the city at night, fighting through chaos, or experiencing emotional story moments.  Gameplay is great and highly engaging. Let's start with the combat, because many people still think Cyberpunk is just "GTA with RPG elements", but it offers so much more than that. There are many different playstyles to choose from: stealth hacking, aggressive gunplay, melee combat, katanas, throwing knives, cyberware-focused builds, snipers, shotguns, netrunning, and more. Every build feels different and has strengths and weaknesses depending on your approach and preparation. Combat is fast, fluid and rewarding, especially once your build starts coming together. The movement also feels great, especially with double jumps, dashes and cyberware upgrades that make you feel increasingly powerful. The progression system is great, allowing you to specialize heavily into your preferred playstyle. Skill trees offer meaningful upgrades that genuinely change how you approach combat and exploration. Cyberware customization is one of the best parts of the game, letting you turn your character into an unstoppable machine, stealth hacker, samurai or whatever style you prefer. Looting and equipment are also very satisfying. Finding iconic weapons, upgrading cyberware and experimenting with builds keeps the gameplay fresh for dozens of hours. Exploration is another huge strength. Night City feels alive and dense, with hidden events, side gigs, random encounters and environmental storytelling everywhere. Even just driving around the city at night can be immersive on its own. The side content is surprisingly strong too. Many side quests are written with the same quality as the main story, often presenting difficult choices, morally gray situations and memorable characters. Some side quests end up being more emotionally impactful than entire main campaigns in other games. Another great mechanic is how your choices and relationships affect quest outcomes, dialogue and endings. Some opportunities, conversations and endings are only available depending on how you played and who you connected with throughout the game. These are only some of the great mechanics the game offers, the rest are for you to discover.  The enemies are varied and fun to fight. Different gangs use different weapons, tactics and cyberware, forcing you to adapt your approach. Boss fights and cyberpsychos can also be very memorable, especially when your build is tested properly.  The story is excellent, emotional and extremely well written. The characters are memorable, believable and full of personality. V and Johnny Silverhand have fantastic chemistry throughout the game, and many side characters leave a strong impression too. The role playing aspects are very well done, with meaningful dialogue choices, different character backgrounds and multiple endings depending on your decisions. The game constantly presents morally complex situations where there is rarely a completely right or wrong answer. Also some of the endings are brutal, so be prepared to a rollercoaster of emotions.  In short, awesome game, a bit misunderstood because of its disastrous launch. After years of updates and improvements, the game became what people originally hoped it would be. Many people still judge it based on old impressions without giving it another chance. If you enjoy immersive RPGs, great storytelling, strong world building and flexible character progression, this game is absolutely worth experiencing.

[h2]A Masterpiece That Broke My Ultimate Gaming Rule[/h2]  As a lifelong gamer, I have one ironclad rule: [b]I never play a game twice.[/b] Once the credits roll, I move on. But [i]Cyberpunk 2077[/i] didn't just break that rule; it shattered it.  Having absolutely loved CD Projekt RED’s previous work on [i]The Witcher[/i] series, I had high expectations for Night City. While Geralt of Rivia will always have a special place in my heart, the dystopian world of Cyberpunk offered a completely different kind of magic. The storytelling depth I loved in [i]The Witcher[/i] is fully present here, but with a gritty, neon-soaked edge.  I loved this world so much that I did the unthinkable and booted up a second playthrough to experience it from two entirely different perspectives:  1. [b]Playthrough 1:[/b] Male V, living on the fringes as a rugged [b]Nomad[/b]. 2. [b]Playthrough 2:[/b] Female V, navigating the ruthless, high-stakes world of a [b]Corpo[/b].  Experiencing Night City through both voice actors and life paths felt like playing two distinct chapters of an epic saga.  [h3]The Base Game: Welcome to Night City[/h3]  The base game is an absolute triumph of world-building, narrative, and atmosphere. The gunplay, netrunning, and driving feel incredibly satisfying, and the emotional weight of V’s journey with Johnny Silverhand stays with you long after you turn off the laptop.  That being said, it isn't completely flawless. Even after all the massive updates and overhauls, you will still occasionally run into minor bugs or visual glitches in certain portions of the game. They don't ruin the experience, but they do slightly nudge you out of the immersion.  * [b]Base Game Rating:[/b] [b]9/10[/b] [i](1 point deducted solely for the lingering bugs).[/i]  [h3]The DLC: Phantom Liberty[/h3]  If the base game is a masterpiece, the [i]Phantom Liberty[/i] DLC is perfection. This spy-thriller expansion takes everything that made the original game great and refines it to an absolute razor-sharp edge. Dogtown is a brilliantly dense, atmospheric warzone, and the stakes feel incredibly personal and intense. The storytelling, choices, and characters (looking at you, Solomon Reed or SongBird) represent CD Projekt RED at the absolute peak of their powers. No notes. No caveats.  * [b]DLC Rating:[/b] [b]10/10[/b] [i](An absolute flawless victory).[/i]  [h3]The Verdict & What's Next[/h3]  Combined, [i]Cyberpunk 2077[/i] and [i]Phantom Liberty[/i] form one of the greatest gaming experiences of the modern era. It took me from a skeptic who never replays games to someone who has memorized the streets of Night City.  Now, the long wait begins. My cyberware is itching for more, and I am officially on the edge of my seat waiting for the next chapter in this universe: [b]Project Orion[/b]. If CDPR can carry the momentum from [i]Phantom Liberty[/i] into the sequel, we are in for something truly legendary.  [b]See you in the major leagues, chooms.[/b]

Cons: The Driving - Steering a supercar still occasionally feels like steering a shopping cart on a slip-and-slide, but at least the vehicles look incredibly cool right before you wrap them around a streetlamp.  Spending three hours meticulously sculpting your character's face, jawline, and perfectly winged eyeliner, only to remember the game is entirely in first-person and you will literally only see yourself when you accidentally open the photo mode or look in a bathroom mirror. All the people here who bought this wireless tungsten cube to admire its surreal heft have precisely the wrong mindset. I, in my exalted wisdom and unbridled ambition, bought this cube to become fully accustomed to the intensity of its density, to make its weight bearable and in fact normal to me, so that all the world around me may fade into a fluffy arena of gravitational inconsequence. And it has worked, to profound success. I have carried the tungsten with me, have grown attached to the downward pull of its small form, its desire to be one with the floor. This force has become so normal to me that lifting any other object now feels like lifting cotton candy, or a fluffy pillow. Big burly manly men who pump iron now seem to me as little children who raise mere aluminum.  I can hardly remember the days before I became a man of tungsten. How distant those days seem now, how burdened by the apparent heaviness of everyday objects. I laugh at the philistines who still operate in a world devoid of tungsten, their shoulders thin and unempowered by the experience of bearing tungsten. Ha, what fools, blissful in their ignorance, anesthetized by their lack of meaningful struggle, devoid of passion.  Nietzsche once said that a man who has a why can bear almost any how. But a man who has a tungsten cube can bear any object less dense, and all this talk of why and how becomes unnecessary.  Schopenhauer once said that every man takes the limits of his own field of vision for the limits of the world. Tungsten expands the limits of a man’s field of vision by showing him an example of increased density, in comparison to which the everyday objects to which he was formerly accustomed gain a light and airy quality. Who can lament the tragedy of life, when surrounded by such lightweight objects? Who can cry in a world of styrofoam and cushions?  Have you yet understood? This is no ordinary metal. In this metal is the alchemical potential to transform your world, by transforming your expectations. Those who have not yet held the cube in their hands and mouths will not understand, for they still live in a world of normal density, like Plato’s cave dwellers. Those who have opened their mind to the density of tungsten will shift their expectations of weight and density accordingly.  To give this cube a rating of anything less than five stars would be to condemn life itself. Who am I, as a mere mortal, to judge the most compact of all affordable materials? No. I say gratefully to whichever grand being may have created this universe: good job on the tungsten. It sure is dense.  I sit here with my tungsten cube, transcendent above death itself. For insofar as this tungsten cube will last forever, I am in the presence of immortality.

Despite it's great many flaws upon release way back in the great year that was 2020, Cyberpunk 2077 slowly built itself up from its ashes to become one of the best modern open world RPGs on the market.  Night City is a world you can't help but get captivated by, whether it be due to the neon lights and lively atmosphere or the many memorable characters you meet within it's alleys.  The themes of hope amidst insurmountable odds is its world in reflected well in it's story, making you feel strong before reminding you of your inevitable march towards oblivion.  It's one and only DLC, Phantom Liberty, embodies all these aspects while keeping to an motif more akin to an '80s spy thriller. Once you feel you have everyone figured out, another rug is pulled out from under you. That's an amazing and absolutely unforgettable game.  Cyberpunk 2077 is all about the process. You can spend a few hours in Night City and not even notice how much time has passed. You WANT to explore. Maybe it's just me, but I genuinely wanted to look into every district, discover every possible thing, and just live in that city for a while. Night City feels believable — and at some point, you stop feeling like a player and start feeling like a person living there.  This game has an insane amount of content. There’s always something to do. Gigs, side jobs, random encounters, characters, hidden stories — at times it feels endless. And honestly, trying to finish everything in one playthrough is almost impossible.  But then something interesting happens. When you finally start running out of things to do, the city begins to feel strangely empty. Almost confusing. Like, “come on… this is Night City, there should always be something happening.” And somehow, that feeling fits the game perfectly.  Of course, the game isn’t perfect. The biggest issue for me was the bugs. There are still plenty of them — sometimes small, sometimes really noticeable. Occasionally they can completely break the immersion and make you laugh at a serious moment. Maybe I’m just too used to Rockstar-level polish, but I definitely felt that Cyberpunk could’ve been more refined in terms of quality of the open-world details and overall gameplay interactions, not just "a beautiful picture".  And of course — the ending. The characters are written incredibly well, so whichever path you take, it hits hard. For me, this was a story about change. Everyone has their own V, their own journey, and their own version of Night City.  I definitely recommend this game to anyone who hasn't played it yet.  And for everyone who already finished their journey in Night City — a tight embrace 🫂  P.S. — whoever was responsible for the soundtrack deserves their hands kissed. Some tracks hit harder than entire missions.

I played Cyberpunk 2077 on day one. Yeah, the bugs were there. NPCs losing their minds, cars spawning from another universe, the usual apocalypse. Fair enough. But even back then, underneath the chaos, the game was already something special.  Night City felt alive in a way most open world games never manage. Not just visually. Emotionally. Every street, every conversation, every broken character had weight. And the storytelling... fu**ing incredible.  I played Corpo, Street Kid, and Nomad, and somehow each path genuinely felt different. Same city, different scars. That’s rare.  What Cyberpunk does better than most games is atmosphere. Not just aesthetics. Atmosphere. The world feels obsessed with detail, packed with quiet moments, existential dread, corporate madness, and people desperately trying to survive their own emptiness. Basically the future.  Then Phantom Liberty came out and somehow pushed everything even further. The writing, the tension, the choices. Absolutely unreal.  At this point, Cyberpunk 2077 isn’t just a great RPG. It’s a cyberpunk masterpiece. One of the few games that actually stays with you long after the credits roll.  And honestly, reducing this game to “that buggy launch” is like judging Blade Runner because somebody spilled coffee in the cinema.

Cyberpunk 2077 is the definition of ‘they fixed the game and nobody moved on fast enough to admit it.’  I’m on my fifth playthrough now, and somehow Cyberpunk 2077 still feels more alive than most new open world games coming out today. Night City isn’t just a map, it feels like a real place with exhausted people, fake dreams, dirty money, and nonstop chaos hiding behind neon lights.  What surprised me the most after replaying it so many times is how emotional the game actually is. Under all the chrome, guns, and explosions, Cyberpunk is really about loneliness, identity, survival, and trying to matter before the world forgets you. Few games make side characters feel this human. Panam, Judy, Johnny, Viktor they genuinely feel like people you knew for a while instead of quest dispensers.  And honestly? The atmosphere is unmatched. Driving through Night City at 2 AM with the radio on while rain hits the windshield is still one of the hardest vibes gaming has ever created. No game captures “beautiful but broken” like this one.  People talked nonstop about the bad launch, but after five runs, I can confidently say the comeback deserves just as much attention. The amount of detail, storytelling, soundtrack, world building, and freedom in combat is insane now. Whether you play stealth, netrunner, samurai build, or complete cyberpsycho, the gameplay actually lets you feel unique.  The craziest part is that Cyberpunk doesn’t try to make you feel like a hero. It constantly reminds you that in Night City, almost everyone loses something. And that’s exactly why the story hits harder than most RPGs.  Five playthroughs later and I still catch small details I missed before. That’s rare. Most games get boring after one ending. Cyberpunk somehow gets more personal the longer you stay in Night City.  “Wrong city. Wrong people.” Still one of the coldest lines in gaming.

Man... this game is very controversial.  First and foremost, it earned its bad reputation because of the technical state it launched in, and honestly, even after all these years, I still feel like many parts of the game remain unfinished: a cardboard-like city with awkwardly behaving NPCs, Night City feeling huge but dead, janky object physics that still cause bugs, and inconsistencies between some story branches, as if not every possible scenario was properly finished.  And that’s kind of sad, because you can clearly feel that this game had the potential to become one of the greatest games in history. But because it was rushed out and, even years later, never fully polished to the end, Cyberpunk was never destined to take its place at the top of Olympus.  BUT – it still has to be said: Cyberpunk is a very good game.  Let’s start with the obvious: the game offers absolutely gorgeous graphics, some of the best I have ever seen in video games. From a purely visual standpoint, Night City looks stunning. The cyberpunk setting is also implemented really well here. Sure, this kind of futuristic, neon-soaked dystopia is not for everyone, but personally I’ve always liked cyberpunk and future-oriented settings, and I’m pretty sure fans of this kind of atmosphere will appreciate it as well.  But it’s not just about the graphics. The RPG side of the game actually feels pretty solid: it lets you create the character you want and constantly puts you in situations where you have to make decisions – many of them being difficult moral choices that directly affect the story and the world around you.  Story-wise, I’d say the main questline feels rather short, to be honest. On the one hand, this can be partly explained by the core narrative premise of the game. On the other hand, that same premise somehow still allows you to run around doing a ton of side quests, which kind of contradicts the urgency of the main story.  That said, the side missions are very well written and fit quite organically into the main part of the game (some of them affect the ending as well). Cyberpunk’s story is built like a proper blockbuster: it keeps you engaged, rarely gets boring, and often puts the protagonist in moral dilemmas where there is no obvious easy choice. It also helps that the game is full of well-written, fleshed-out characters, many of whom feel memorable and genuinely interesting.  There is also quite a lot of pure farming content, if you’re into that kind of thing. Personally, I think it gets boring pretty quickly, and luckily you can level up just fine without grinding everything on the map.  As for the gameplay, thanks to the extensive skill progression system, cyberware, and weapons, it is very diverse. Personally, I didn’t want to turn the game into yet another regular shooter – although if that’s what you want, there are more than enough firearms here for every taste. What I liked is that the game allows you to play with much less standard builds: netrunner, melee weapons - high mobility, and so on. Basically, everyone can find a playstyle that suits them. On top of that, most story locations are designed in a way that lets you approach them differently, and different progression paths actually help with that. From a gameplay perspective, the game is interesting enough – probably even for more than one playthrough.  Overall, I’d say Cyberpunk ended up being an excellent game that fell short of becoming the masterpiece it could have been, even though the potential was clearly there. Still, despite its flaws, it remains a highly enjoyable experience and one that absolutely deserves the attention of every gamer.  Must play.

Your choices do not matter. Cyberpunk 2077 has a story that it wants to tell, and you are not a part of it.   I came to Cyberpunk 2077 after years. I suppose I expected something between Skyrim and GTA. And that is there. Let's compare it to Skyrim for now. In Skyrim, faction quests matter, alter your character, and affect the world around you. In Cyberpunk 2077, they really do not. From the beginning of Cyberpunk, I was asked to choose a background: Nomad, Streetkid, Corpo (corporate). I had never heard this before the game as I came in spoiler free. I chose Corpo and at first, I was delighted. A cool story of intrigue and corporate espionage....for about the first 10 minutes of the game. It then blends it all together, throws it all out, and rolls every character into the same "merc starting from the bottom" story line.    These backstories could have been cool factions like in the old MMO "The Secret World." Nomads could tell stories of honor and tradition in the Cyberpunk 2077 world. Streetkids could get invited to underground street races and be involved in gang wars. Corpos could navigate power in the corporate world. But it was not to be. These backstories were probably intended as factions like the faction quests in Skyrim, but were probably cut. All you get is dialogue options based on your backstory and that is it. The game oozes cut content everywhere. It oozes this because of one Johnny Silverhand.  Yes, I had heard of Johnny Silverhand played by Keanu Reaves before I played this game, and frankly I believe his implementation in the main quest is what holds this game back. Keanu does great work, honestly, with tons of voice lines. He is a character in this world and he put in a lot of work. He clearly respects this game as a story telling medium. However, I cannot help but think the inclusion of his celebrity is what derailed the development of this game from what it could have been.  Is Cyberpunk 2077 a good game? Sure. I give it a solid B-. In the end, the combat is fun. I relax and play the game at my own pace, but my choices do not matter. Oh sure. The character and combat customization of a Skyrm/GTA mix in a cyberpunk world is there, and that is fun. But the way your character plays is just a part of the experience. Your agency in a game like this has to effect the world around you. Night City feels living and immersive. I often see game critics try and defend the degree to which the story in this game is ultimately static. "V cannot save Night City" is a common defense I hear of this game. So let's fix that. "V does not have any effect on Night City." There we go. Fixed it. Because your choices in Cyberpunk 2077 do not matter.

Cyberpunk 2077 is an impressive game even years after its initial release. It sounds like an oxymoron, but Night City is brutally, savagely beautiful.  ------------- What I liked: -------------  Gameplay Variety: The game gives you a lot of freedom in how you want to play. You can go full cyborg Yakuza/Samurai with a katana or Mantis Blades, feel like a Terminator smashing people with Gorilla Arms after running out of ammo on your heavy machine gun, or take a stealthier approach with optical camo if you’re the kind of masochist who enjoys going for “Suit Only, Silent Assassin” in Hitman.  These are all valid options, and while I’m personally not big on stealth, I can only appreciate the amount of choice the game gives you.  The Characters: Oh my god.  Without spoiling the story, the final boss of the main story has serious charisma. Sure, he’s evil. Sure, his lore is absolutely terrifying. But a good indicator of strong character design is when you totally detest a villain, yet still find them epic. It’s like Sauron: absolutely awesome and powerful, and you’d hate it if he ever crossed your path, but damn, you can appreciate how powerful he is.  There are also characters like Panam… The others don’t matter.  Except Jackie. Love and miss you, brother.  ------------------- What I didn’t like: -------------------  I dislike when a game presents itself as a full RPG without fully immersing the player in that role. Cyberpunk 2077 feels more like an FPS with a rich story and RPG elements than a true RPG. You wouldn’t call GTA an RPG just because you make decisions in some missions, so I’m not sure why this gets placed in the same category as something like Fallout: New Vegas.  Is the story great? Absolutely. But while you initially choose a background for your character, the game ultimately pushes you away from it pretty quickly. For example, you can pick a corporate background and then get kicked out of the corporation within five minutes. What, no Arasaka counter-intel missions for V? It felt wasted, if not pointless.  That said, the unique dialogue options are definitely cool, and I do recommend the Corpo beginning. It makes the Devil ending make a lot more sense.  Also... it saddens me to say this, because I love this developer studio, but CD Projekt Red really needs to show its modding community some TLC. Every update breaks core mods, and I’m not going to lie: they should be hiring some of the people making those mods. They’re holding up a whole community, and yet CDPR doesn’t seem to give them the time of day. It feels like a step backwards and somehow makes Bethesda look like saints, which is saying something.  -------------- Performance: --------------  Please don’t look at my current specs and assume I’m going to glaze my own setup. I first played Cyberpunk 2077 on a PC with a Ryzen 5 2600, a GTX 1070, and 16GB of RAM, and it still looked and performed great with standard rasterisation.  Ray tracing and path tracing are genuinely nice upgrades, but if you’re sitting there with specs similar to what I originally had, or slightly better, don’t worry. You do not need a 5090 to enjoy this game. It runs well on a variety of hardware and also plays nicely on a gaming laptop.  That said, I won’t lie: I do not recommend it on the Steam Deck. It needs work out of the box, and even then, it just doesn’t feel properly optimised.  ---------------- Final thoughts: ----------------  Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 is absolutely something you want in your Steam library. Even if you only want to drive around Night City listening to the radio, this game is a perfect example of immersion. You really do feel like you’re in a lived-in world. Thanks to CDPR for the BREATHTAKING experience, but I expect nothing less from the people who brought us The Witcher 3.  Rating: 9/10 Recommendation: Highly Recommended

There's a lot of different types of weapons although if you're min-maxxing, you're pretty limited in terms of what the "best" weapon is for a given playstyle. I wouldn't say it's overly difficult - even at higher difficulty levels, the enemies aren't smarter or playing with different abilities, they just hit harder and have more health. I really do wish they would let you respec your attributes more than once - there's even a tip about "exploring different playstyles" by choosing different perks but the perks are directly linked to your attributes (and you can't max all attributes out), so you're limited within one playthrough as to how much you can move the perks around.

I think the idea a lot of people still hold about Cyberpunk date back to its disastrous first release with its game breaking bugs. I would not have considered picking this game up if it weren't for a friend of mine vouching for it!   As someone that has now played through most of the base game on the steam deck, I have still run across a couple bugs ranging from falling out of the map, floating weapons and npcs, to issues with CDPR's launch system, but none that impede my engagement aside from an immersion break. It is a far cry from the game breaking bugs first reported, and from other recent reviews, people either have a bug free experience (like my friend) or are unlucky like myself.  This is all to say, these bugs do not at all overshadow the sheer world building and wanderlust of the game itself. On the steam deck, it runs better than a couple other AAA games I've put through the system. With optimisation you can get an easy 50 fps in dense crowds.   Overall, I think the crowning achievement of Cyberpunk is its diverse combat system. I would say it isn't a very difficult game in terms of combat at all, but it has a high plasticity in terms of builds and seamless combat systems. This is alongside the stat/perk tree, which they have integrated very successfully in function. Nothing feels as though it is to waste.   I would also say that the story is quite engaging, especially in its various discussions on the interaction between humanity and technological advancements, the parameters of what it means to be sentient, and the limit to which we are still able to maintain a sense of self while uprooting biological parts for metal and code. As with any game however, I find there are some minor short comings in other aspects of storytelling (pertaining to cliches, predictability, and secondary character focus), but there are many quests that have very in depth nuance akin to Witcher 3. (Though I believe out of these two very strong instalments from CDPR, Witcher 3 is a stronger contender story wise.)  TLDR: good game. I think I've spent too many hours in photomode, though...

This is first time i write a serious review, so yeah... 👀 The game run on average 30-45 FPS on a potato laptop with Medium to High settings (Low Crowd Density), i'll say it's good performance wise if you are gaming on the budget like me.   as for the game itself, i think i will give it 8/10, PROS: - It's fun to run around as Netrunner in Night City, but after several hours i kinda feel that the game is kinda too easy, maybe my decision making a Netrunner V is have a big role on it too.  - The world itself feels big and lively (even at low crowd settings),   - The story is good enough to keep me playing, especially Phantom Liberty DLC part, i think the Relic mechanic it introduce is really fun, and Tower Ending (without Spoiler) might be the best ending of all time in my opinion. I would say though, after you watch some in-game news on tv, you probably will be like me and think "wow, the world building in this game is kinda fun and chaotic".  - CDPR also have make mod support for the games, making it kinda easy to add mods, especially for stuff like tiny immersion fixes, you know, the unnecessary detail like making all in game ads fully animated or pettable cat (yes you can adopt cat and iguana in this game, weirdly enough, you can only pat the iguana, still, they are both cute though).  - also, the music are awesome, if you have watched Edgerunner on Netflix, you might already have taste a little bit of those juicy bangers. but let me tell you, most of the songs in this games are really good. Recently, i even start to make a habbit of listening to some of the songs while doing chores, especially Chippin In, Pon Pon Sh*t (Jhonny Silverhand version, it's easter egg, not in Radio) and Never Fade Away, they really make me forgot how exhausting doing daily laundry was. (FYI, most of the songs from anime are in Body Heat Radio btw, including that song).  - Easter eggs, lots of easter eggs, really fun. I kinda don't want to talk too much about this because it was really fun if you notice something you don't know, but just you know, there are a lot of eater egg in this game. (just so you know, Murkman is the best detective)  CONS: -Even though most of annoying bug from first released was already been patched and fixed, there are still some minor bug or glitches in the game, Some like driving drift, texture pop-in (not as bad as first released) and that one time Jackie walk through lockers during the first mission are might tied to FPS and you machine, but stuff like auto drive feature driver recklesly or showing negative million numbers (it was without mod btw) and monowire doesn't glow at all sometimes are still small stuff that need fixes in my opinion. (also, i know Fream gen is bad since it will give you low latency, but so far, i can't use frame gen at all. It will crash on me when i open map, even when using the settings for RTX 30s and 20s, so i don't know what kind of stuff that will happened if you able to use it on RTX 20s or 30s).  - lack of consequences might be one factor that make the story can feel a bit monotone and less exciting for me. Like, don't get me wrong, some dialogue choice does lock you out from good reward, like when i miss my chance to get Jackie guns for free, but like what i just said, "for free", mean you don't really missing out much when you make a wrong choices, if you own the DLC you can just buy your best friend's gun from the vendor in Dogtown. pretty neat since it was your best friend's gun, you know something that supposed to be sentimental for his family and people close by :). And not only that, if you fail to save someone who will give you car if you save them, you can also just,,, buy the car. Cyberpunk 2077 is, in my opinion, one of the most overrated games released in recent years. While the visuals, atmosphere, and overall world design are undeniably impressive, the actual gameplay experience falls far short of the praise the game receives.  The mechanics feel clunky and unpolished. Combat, especially the shooting, lacks weight and responsiveness, and even basic movement around the world can feel awkward at times. For a game that focuses so heavily on immersion, the gameplay often ends up breaking it instead.  The story is also not as strong as many people claim. Much of the progression consists of being sent from one objective to another without enough depth to make the experience consistently engaging. The game repeatedly emphasizes that the protagonist is dying and running out of time, yet at the same time encourages the player to spend countless hours doing unrelated side activities.  Cyberpunk 2077 feels like a game carried heavily by its presentation rather than its gameplay or storytelling. The visuals are excellent, but a visually impressive world alone is not enough to make the overall experience truly great.

I'm used to RPGs giving me a lot of options on how I want the story to progress so I was a bit disappointed. Cyberpunk reminds me more of games like Far Cry than typical RPGs and I guess I expected a different experience. I feel like it's more of a shooter than an RPG.  - Cutscenes and some quests can be very tiring and feel slow because in most of them you just listen to a character talk and follow them around or sit in a car with them.  - The game tries to create a sense of urgency but in reality there's no time limit and you can complete as many side quests as you want without affecting anything. Even missions that start with a character calling you and saying they'd like to meet you at a certain time today have no time limit and you can delay them for as long as you want.  - The romance is okay but a lot of things get repetitive and feel a bit mechanical. I romanced Judy and every time she visited my apartment, she said the exact same thing, no new dialogue appeared and nothing interesting happened. She was just there and that's it.  - I'm not a huge fan of Johnny Silverhand. I like the idea of his character but I feel like his potential wasn't fully realized and his relationship with V could have been more interesting. It was a bit strange to me how he suddenly went from being hostile towards V to being nice. Also, Keanu Reeves' performance in this role felt flat and emotionless at times.  - I dread to think how bad this game was when it first came out because even after all these years it's still very buggy. Disappearing NPCs, items getting stuck in NPCs' hands, messy AI that causes enemies to randomly pause during fights and allow you to kill them easily, enemies seeing you through walls, NPCs bugging so you're unable to talk to them when you want to start/finish a quest, NPCs talking with their mouth closed, identical NPCs spawning in the same place, cars crashing into each other and exploding when you're not looking at the road (sometimes it looked like one car spawned on top of another and exploded), V picking up the phone, saying she can't talk right now and then immediately calling the person back, and many, many more.  - I've seen a lot of people complaining about the game's poor performance, but in my case it wasn't that bad and mostly ran smoothly even though my computer isn't high-end. It randomly crashed twice and that's it. Perhaps I just got lucky.  Overall, I'd say it's a pretty fun game but it does have a lot of flaws and I definitely recommend buying it at a discount. Maybe if I didn't have such high expectations because so many people consider this game to be one of the best, I wouldn't be so critical.
