Firstly, I will talk about spoilers.  I have played through this game twice, once when the update after the Edgerunners anime released and once this past few weeks with the DLC. This review will almost completely be a negative one because the more I played this game the more I hated it. It might come as a surprise because I do recommend this game, I think it's a great game but it is a game I truly did not enjoy. The two praises I will give to this game are these: 1. The story is really well [b] written. [/b] 2. The gameplay is fairly fun.  I think that most people who are looking for a basic but fun RPG in a cyberpunk setting will enjoy this game so I do very much recommend it.  Now with that said, why do [b] I [/b] dislike this game? Simple, this game is terrible from a TTRPG perspective. Cyberpunk is a TTRPG, this game is supposed to be a video game companion to Cyberpunk the TTRPG. And yet, it is simply a game in the cyberpunk genre. All it has to offer you is anything any other RPG in the cyberpunk genre can, it simply has names of the Cyberpunk TTRPG and nothing else.  First issue? Player choice.  There are few choices you can make in this game, fewer choices that matter. The way you unlock 2 endings is simply by doing the side quests and not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ up, the way you unlock the third is with just 3 dialogue choices that don't change much. The DLC did improve this, the way you get to the ending the DLC unlocks is still basic but more involved and I do like that. But considering 4 out of the 5 endings to the main story have prerequisites that are extremely basic and have very little to do with your actual choices sucks. There is another level to this too however, your builds never matter in narrative. By the end of the game, I had 20 INT and the only thing I can do with that is just getting some throwaway lines in some missions. I can't be a proper Netrunner outside of combat because that's not the role CDPR wants V to play. And this isn't just an issue with INT, through the 2 playthroughs I've gotten 3 stats to the max, and it's all the same.  I will reiterate, Cyberpunk is a TTRPG where the way your character is built can change so much and yet the video game that is based on Cyberpunk is unable to capture the same essence? At that point would this game have been any different if it was say Bladerunner, Akira etc. Sure there would be some aesthetic differences and the names would be different but there's no part of a TTRPG here.  Repetitiveness. This gets into spoilers specifically so avert your eyes if you're reading this for some reason.  Every time V gets close to finding a solution with the relic, we get told that no it won't work and everything is worse actually! Yay, yippie, hurah. Now the issue I have here is not that everything sucks and things are horrible, this is Cyberpunk that's to be expected. The issue I have is that it happening that many times is just frustrating. Going around in circles is not fun, especially not when it happens so many times.  Length.  This game relies on its side stories to carry how short the main story feels. I don't have any problem with shorter games, I don't think more playtime equates to a good game. But what I have a problem with is that the main story straight up feels incomplete. When I got to the final quest I was genuinely confused and thought that surely there's more to do afterwards. Though well considering the development cycle of this game, it might genuinely just have been incomplete. Now the side stories, first I'm gonna talk about the important multi quest romancable character side stories. I think they're all written really well. I really liked them all. One issue, they share the problem of the main story. You do one gig and then poof, that's all folks. They have you yearning for more, and not in a particularly good way I'd say. And now the unimportant small side stories. They're fun enough, they're not meant to be anything massive, just interesting and fun quests and they do manage that.  Waiting. Know what would've cut my playthrough by like at least a quarter? If I didn't have to wait for characters to slowly walk to mission objectives. At some point it starts feeling maddening you know? I shouldn't have to wait for a character to get to an elevator, then wait in the elevator and then wait for them to walk into a room.  Skill Checks. Wanna know what's not fun? Being punished for leveling up. Did you know that before 2.0 the skill checks used to be static and depend on the area you're in. Now, they change with your level. You could be in the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ area in town and it will still scale with your level. This was genuinely the single worst part of the game in 2.0 for me.    In essence, it feels like this game is playing Cyberpunk the TTRPG with a spiteful controlling gm. Every lead you find? Empty and ♥♥♥♥ keeps getting worse. Narrative choice? Who needs that, I have the best ideas so you should just do this. You know, after I finished my second playthrough I was thinking and I remembered a bit from (Baldur's Gate 3 spoiler ahead) [spoiler] Baldur's Gate 3's ending. There's a bit there when you can attempt to take control of the elder brain with a bunch of checks increasing in difficulty. The final one is a difficulty 99 and there's no way to pass it other than rolling a 20 on the die. And your reward for passing that check? The reward for you doing a godly feat to take control of the elder brain? It is a bit of damage in the final boss battle. [/spoiler] This entire game to me felt like that bit. I was given the illusion of agency, but when I tried to push to see if I truly had it I found that it simply wasn't there. I truly think CDPR were the wrong people for this game. They have made a great game set in a cyberpunk world, but they made a terrible game set in the Cyberpunk world.   Anyways, all of this rambling was kinda to get my feelings out after I finished the game for the second time. I now hope to never look at this game again because I can confidently say I hate it and the experience of going through it is something I hope to not relive again. If CDPR release another cyberpunk game, I may give it a look but I hope to close the book of my life that is this game for good.  And yet the review is still a recommendation for a simple reason. This game is not made for me, nor was it made with me in mind. CDPR made a great game for the people who like ARPGs. Maybe had I gone into this game, knowing nothing of the Cyberpunk TTRPG or TTRPGs in general I also would have enjoyed it, but alas that is not my reality. As it stands, this is a truly amazing game that I would recommend to anyone that isn't like me and doesn't care much about the TTRPG genre, or just plain enjoy ARPGs. And yet it is also a game I loathe.

Cyberpunk 2077 might have the greatest gaming comeback.  When the game launched, it was basically a bug simulator with some emotional damage included for free. Players were crashing more than their in-game cars, and CD Projekt Red got cooked by the entire internet.  But instead of giving up and disappearing into the shadows like a stealth build, the developers kept grinding. Update after update, they fixed bugs, improved gameplay systems, reworked mechanics, and finally delivered the experience people were originally hyped for. Then came Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty, which honestly felt like the developers saying: “Alright, let us cook one more time.”  And somehow… they actually did.  Now Night City feels alive, polished, and insanely immersive. You can genuinely tell the devs cared about the game and refused to let it die. That kind of dedication is rare nowadays.  Cyberpunk 2077 went from being the internet’s favorite joke to one of the best RPG experiences of the last years and honestly, that redemption arc deserves respect.  Thank you CDPR, and never stop fighting.

Cyberpunk 2077 isn’t just a game, and Cyberpunk: Edgerunners isn’t just an anime. On the surface, both present a hyper-stylized futuristic dystopia dripping in chrome, visceral violence, and the oppressive shadow of megacorporations. But if you strip away the sci-fi aesthetic, you are left with a mirror reflecting something painfully familiar: our own reality.  Today, we watch people burn themselves out at the altar of hustle culture, constantly chasing status, wealth, and systemic validation. In Night City, that desperate climb is literal, measured in dangerous cyberware, synthetic implants, and chrome. In the real world, the destruction happens in quieter, less neon-lit ways, but it hollows people out just the same. You see it clearly in the protagonists. David Martinez didn’t just want power; he wanted to prove his worth to a world that treated him like trash. Meanwhile, V didn’t want to conquer the world; they just wanted to survive a system that was stacked against them from day one. It begs the question: how many of us are living our own versions of that exact same struggle right now?  The ultimate thesis of the Cyberpunk universe is a warning that when ambition goes blind, it ceases to motivate and begins to consume. Characters stop living for themselves and start chasing a ghost, desperate to fill an emptiness that no amount of chrome or eddies ever will. That is the secret ingredient that makes this universe so profoundly special. Behind the blinding neon, the chaotic action, and the aggressively unhinged, NSFW energy of Night City, lies a raw, bleeding heart. It is a masterclass in exploring humanity, trauma, loneliness, and the astronomical price of trying to "win" in a fundamentally broken world.  There are no happy endings in Night City. It is a rule the franchise refuses to break. Just like in real life, closures are rarely neat, and endings are rarely perfect. Yet, despite knowing the house always wins, the people of this world still choose to love, still dare to dream, and still fight like hell anyway. Maybe that is the real message of Cyberpunk. It is not about surviving the city; it is about holding onto your humanity while it tries to tear you apart. It is a masterpiece of existential dread disguised as high-octane sci-fi—one that makes you want to overthrow a corporation, cry over a radio song, and realize that while half the city desperately needs a therapist, the other half just needs to log off and touch some grass.

Cyberpunk 2077 is an open-world RPG that has improved a lot since its original launch. The game takes place in Night City, a huge futuristic city filled with crime, corruption, technology, and different groups fighting for power. The world is one of the strongest parts of the game because it feels detailed, dark, and full of personality.  One of the best parts of Cyberpunk 2077 is the story. Playing as V, you get pulled into a dangerous situation involving Johnny Silverhand, and the game gives you a lot of choices in how you handle missions, conversations, and combat. The characters are memorable, the side missions are strong, and the story can feel emotional and intense at times.  The gameplay is also very fun because there are many ways to play. You can use guns, stealth, hacking, melee weapons, cyberware upgrades, or a mix of everything. The upgrades and skill trees make your character feel more powerful over time, and customizing your build adds a lot of replay value. Driving around Night City, taking on gigs, and upgrading your gear makes the game easy to sink hours into.  However, Cyberpunk 2077 is not perfect. Some bugs can still happen, and the open world can sometimes feel more visually impressive than fully interactive. The game also takes time to get into because there are many systems, menus, and upgrades to learn. Still, compared to how it launched, the game feels much more polished and complete now.  Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 is a great RPG with an amazing setting, strong story, fun combat, and a lot of customization. It is especially worth playing if you like futuristic open worlds, deep character builds, and story-driven games.  Rating: 9/10

My background with cyberpunk 2077: I have played through the game 3 times now, starting since update 1.5, and most recently after 2.2. I am experienced with shooters and would recommend those who are play on the "very hard" difficulty. My first playthrough was a body/tech shotgun build (4.5/5, slightly overpowered), my 2nd was primarilly a combat netrunner (3.5/5, DEFINITELY overpowered), and my 3rd was a cool/reflexes glass canon with throwing knives and stealth (5/5, very challenging but rewarding). To say I was obsessed with this game for a while is an understatement. The TL;DR here is I strongly recommend CP2077, and would give it my highest recommendation to mostly anyone.  The Good: combat - excellent. different enemies fight differently, and the variety is refreshing. Vehicle combat feels good too, although vehicle durability leaves something to be desired. weapons - ALL weapons feel relatively good. ARs and smart weapons feel moderately underpowered. Shotguns and late-game quickhacks can feel overpowered. Most any weapon you pick up will be servicable. I strongly recommend you do not settile into the same 3. open world - EXTREMELY IMMERSIVE, due mostly to a COMPLETE LACK OF LOADING SCREENS (exceptions; initial load-in, fast travel, and metro system). Vibrant and detailed world with a vast intricate map, distinct districts with their own style, gangs, aesthetic, etc. Sometimes assets are reused but this is infrequent enough that it does not ruin immersion. Night City feels like the main character of the game. Very easy to fall in love with the place. Animation - NPC mannerisms in dialogue are quite lifelike, or at least not bethesda-stiff. At no point did I feel like gestures or speech were wooden or inhuman. Perk/build system - With update 2.0, perks were completely reworked so that some abilities now synergise well with others, leading to a "build" system. A well-thought-out build inspires confidence through competence. Music - Gangs have themes, corps have themes, characters have themes. They're all fire, and react dynamically to combat. The music that was made for the game that plays on the radio stations is also great. Please note that if you disable copyrighted music, some stations (Impulse and Royal Blue for sure) will be silent during times when copyrighted music would play.  The Neutral: lack of NG+ - frustrating for a seasoned player wanting to return to play more, but I understand this would likely be difficult to balance heavy subject matter - this is a mature game, and some quests can be rather dark at times (themes of rape, human trafficking, suicide, etc). Attribute point re-specc-ing is limited to one time per playthrough. Plan accordingly. Stealth - Fair and balanced IF you take the "gag order" perk. I'd call this perk necessary, even if you aren't maining a stealth playthrough.  Nitpicks/ The Bad (VERY minor spoilers for act 1): Information overload at the start - CP2077 has SO MUCH TO DO, that to get the player properly acclimated, they are bombarded with information at the start of the game. This pushes the player to just tune out and ignore phone calls. Some unskippable calls at the start, notably Regina and Mr. Hands calling you, feel out of place and rushed. lack of utility in player homes - There are multiple player homes throughout the city, of differing levels of luxury. These function as closets, storage lockers, and places for romantic partners to hang out through repeatable mini-missions. Although immersive, the storage locker can be accessed from any owned vehicle, and clothing/outfits can be customized directly while at a clothing vendor. Waypoint auto-update - when receiving a new quest through proximity, phone call, etc., it is automatically marked as active. This can be frustrating if you pick a quest and are interrupted by an occurance that updates the waypoint you selected. Rarely, the writing - I'm not forgiving "amazeballs". Some NPCs function more as a utility, rather than a person, even though the writing starts off making you believe that you have a pre-existing relationship with these people (see Wilson, Coach Fred, Mama Welles, Padre if you do streetkid start, etc).  my recommendations to maximize your enjoyment and immersion: Turn off subtitles, you miss so much happening in the world if you spend all of your time reading. Turn off enemy markers, they make the game feel too easy and arcade-y. Learn to recognize enemies from their style and behavior. You can always scan an enemy to confirm their identity. The max level being 60 lets you can get 3 attribute points to max level, so specialize, don't generalize. I recommend reading through the perk trees, especially the highest level perks, to see what sounds appealing, and heavily invest your attribute points into those attributes. A jack-of-all-trades approach will leave your character feeling mediocre at everything. turn off hud elements to mark chests, etc (2nd+ playthrough only) Disassemble weapons once you start collecting ones that are tier 4 & 5 instead of selling them. You'll need the components for upgrades to your weapons/cyberware more than the money.

Yet another mixed bag, but an interesting experience nonetheless. Some disclaimers first: I do not own the Phantom Liberty DLC, so keep in mind that my review will not touch on any of it. And I am aware that this game has been discussed to death already, so I'll make this as subjective as possible, and focus on my personal experience.  This game is the first to give me the Deus Ex feel since the original Deus Ex was released 26 years ago. Some people will eviscerate me for uttering this but Dishonored sure tried, and failed, being mostly carried by Viktor Antonov's brilliant art and design, may he rest in peace. But Cyberpunk 2077 really gave me that "you can tackle a task any way you see fit" that I relish so much (the closest being Dark Souls because building around STR, DEX, FTH and INT all feel really different from each other). I LOVED the hacking, whether it was computers, machines, or people's brain implants. I loved that the stealth was almost always optional, only bringing you more money or a better reputation in some cases. I loved that you could disobey your missions, for example convincing someone to leave town instead of killing them, and it still counts as a win. I felt more freedom than in GTA even. I even tried to Mirror's Edge it from roof to roof as often as I could just to see if it was viable... and it was very doable at least half of the time, it even helped in certain missions. That was great.   This game follows a pattern that I've seen in so many open world games especially since 2017: the main quest is dogwater, sidequests are where all the fun's at. Interestingly, Cyberpunk 2077's three best quests had the exact same plot: some AI is starting to sound too human, and people do not like that (Delamain, Skippy, Brendan). Here's one piece of advice: do NOT give the talking gun to Reggie. Worst mistake of my life.  The music was great, but could it have been any different with Marcin Przybyłowicz at the helm of the audio department?  The graphics... OK, this is where things get complicated. They are all over the place. On one hand you've got stylish art direction, and fantastic attention to detail (I remember zooming in on characters in Photo Mode and admiring how unique their belt buckles looked)... on the other hand, this game has the worst vLOD issues I've seen since Dark Souls 3 and you can constantly see models gaining and losing polygons right under your nose, which is very distracting and immersion-breaking; and on top of that the clipping is so bad that it sometimes made me feel I was playing a Nintendo 64 bargain bin game. Annoying. I guess that's a very aggressive way to optimise? I was getting around 90 FPS in 4k high settings with no DLSS and RTX off (and honestly this game has the best looking RT I have ever seen but it did tank the framerate to a cinematic mid-twenties, no thanks). There were also some weird cut corners, like all children looking like adult heads on shrunk bodies for example, or a flashback sequence taking place more than 50 years in the past where the city looks exactly the same and people dress the same as in 2077 (and use the same slang too). What the ♥♥♥♥?    The game, as you know, has a Bethesdaesque amount of bugs. I saw almost constantly cars randomly falling from the sky, people half buried into the pavement, or enemy blood unexpectedly changing colour... many such cases. I've seen games with more bugs obviously... but not with a budget like that one. The writing was also all over the place but I think that was by design. Nice characters suddenly acting like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and vice-versa solidifies the feeling of a morally gray society where you can't trust appearances and nothing is reliable. Although I felt like some aspects were oversimplified. Helping cops does not make your street cred go down? Come the ♥♥♥♥ on!   All over the place is what I'd call most of this game. The writing was globally good but there were strange incoherencies and inconsistencies, as if the writers didn't agree on a lot of things. Sometimes it felt like they were trying to make the characters appear more complex... sometimes it seemed very random and nonsensical.  There's a million errands to run so obviously they become repetitive, but also if you simply walk around and explore you'll never run out of XP, money and loot. This plethora is probably punishing for people who want to 100% the game and get all achievements, as always I'm glad I'm not one of them anymore. Also if you decide to help the cops here and there, half of the time they thank you and the other half they start shooting you and call reinforcements despite the fact you just did their job for them. That could be intentional though.  But in all honesty, what I liked the most about this game is the fashion. I spent a lot of time admiring people's style, and much more time even going to absolutely every clothing outlet, trying to curate the biggest and coolest possible wardrobe. I really locked in when it was time to create new outfits. It's what kept me excited about the game half of the time.  Oh and the combat? It's okay. The majority of weapons felt useless to me, 99% of the time I used shotguns, grenades and offensive hacking, sometimes revolvers. It was a bit chaotic, but it was fine. Using people's implants against them was definitely the best part.  I don't know if I should recommend this game or not because it's definitely an acquired taste. It's one of those games that have a lot of everything, and your brain needs to be wired for that. I personally love that but I can totally see how it can be a turn-off. There's lots of dialogue and lots of reading to do. There's also lots of gunfights, and it's during the same missions. Lots of ♥♥♥♥ to learn if you wanna really appreciate the game, but also lots of action. The pace constantly goes from slow to fast to slow to fast... it never stops being a rollercoaster. Think you can handle it? Then absolutely go for it, this game is not mind-blowing but still a pretty good time.

Cyberpunk 2077 ended up becoming one of my favorite RPGs once everything finally came together. The launch problems were rough, but underneath all that was an incredible world, great characters, and one of the most immersive cities I’ve experienced in gaming.  Night City is honestly the real main character. The city feels alive in a way very few open-world games manage to achieve. Every district has its own atmosphere, style, music, and chaos. One minute I’m walking through neon-lit streets surrounded by ads screaming at me from every direction, and the next I’m in some dark alley dealing with cyberpsychos, gangs, or people making terrible life decisions.  What really hooked me was the storytelling and characters. Almost every major character felt memorable, and a lot of the side quests honestly felt better written than main stories in other RPGs. The game constantly throws morally messy situations at you where there isn’t really a perfect outcome, which fits the whole cyberpunk setting perfectly.  The combat also became way more fun than I expected once I started unlocking better cyberware and abilities. You can play like a stealth hacker, a katana maniac, a walking tank, or a complete cyberpsycho sprinting through enemies at Mach 5 with mantis blades. By the late game I genuinely felt less like a human and more like a heavily armed software problem.  I also loved how immersive the world feels outside of combat. Driving through the city at night while the soundtrack blasts in the background just has a vibe that’s hard to explain unless you’ve played it. The atmosphere carries so much of the experience.  And then there’s Phantom Liberty, which honestly elevated the game even more for me. The expansion adds some of the best missions, characters, and spy-thriller moments in the entire game. Dogtown feels dangerous, corrupt, and completely different from the rest of Night City in the best possible way.  That said, the game still isn’t perfect. NPC behavior can still feel weird sometimes, driving physics can be questionable depending on the vehicle, and occasionally the game reminds you that the engine is holding together through pure determination and chrome-plated duct tape.  But for me, Cyberpunk 2077 became one of those games where I stopped fast traveling because I genuinely enjoyed existing in the world. Between the atmosphere, music, characters, combat, and storytelling, it’s one of the few RPGs that fully pulled me into its setting and kept me there for hundreds of hours.

Cyberpunk 2077 had a rocky release due to the premature release, but it eventually redeemed itself with the release of Phantom Liberty along with several quality of life improvements. Now, it would be safe to say that Cyberpunk 2077 is in a playable state, although not perfect by any means. It is still possible run into some bugs, and the AI still needs adjustments, especially for the pedestrians. They simply jump in front of the car, causing NCPD to tail you unnecessarily.  However, they’re not too big of a problem to take you out of the experience. Night City looks astonishing, the combat feels great, and the story pulls you in just fine. Can’t forget about the amazing soundtrack as well. All in-game soundtrack and the radio stations are simply bangers that they got me hooked the day I started playing it.  As I’ve mentioned before, the game used to be a wreck, therefore; I purposely waited for them to sort out the kinks before playing, and I don’t regret that decision. It was marketed as an open world RPG initially and I believe it still qualifies as one despite many claim it isn’t. There’s an in-depth character customization, and many skill trees to choose from as well as implants that can personalize your experience according to your tastes and needs.  Depending on which skill tree you chose to upgrade, the gameplay changes drastically. They can even be combined with others to create a hybrid build. Furthermore, Phantom Liberty adds the additional Relic Tree to flesh out the already existing builds. There are simply too many possibilities that it would be unfair to say that there isn’t enough to lead a unique experience.  The story is where the game shines best, as many have already stated before. However, the main missions are mostly focused on world-building, thus they lack enough combat to make you properly appreciate what the game truly offers. Nevertheless, Cyberpunk 2077 isn’t a game that should be breezed through. One should tackle side quests too if they want to unlock the other endings and see the bond between V and other characters.  Johnny Silverhand’s story also gets fleshed out and told mostly through side quests. Many also claim that Keanu Reeves’ involvement ruined what could’ve been a great game otherwise, but I’m inclined to disagree with that take. While it is true that his involvement happened quite late in development and led to many rewrites in the script, I’d say it turned out great.  The only aspect that left me a bit disappointed was the fact that V’s background doesn’t impact that story as much as I had hoped. The only truly different part, depending on your background, is the introduction mission and how you ended up in Night City and met Jackie Welles. All in all, Cyberpunk 2077 is a must-play. You could also watch Edgerunners to get a better grasp on the universe it is based on.  [h1]TL;DR[/h1] Despite having a rocky headstart, Cyberpunk 2077 managed to pull itself together with Phantom Liberty as well as other patches. It offers a great storyline, strong combat, and a heavily customizable experience. The soundtrack is also noteworthy, and the universe it was built upon feels real in all aspects!

当2077年的霓虹灯光穿透夜之城的阴雨，义体的金属冷光与人类的温热呼吸交织，CD Projekt RED用一场关于生存与救赎的叙事，将赛博朋克的内核刻进了每一段剧情肌理。这款承载无数期待的开放世界RPG，虽曾因优化争议步履蹒跚，却凭借极具张力的剧情叙述、鲜活立体的人物群像，以及对“科技与人性”的深刻叩问，成为赛博朋克文化的经典载体，历经数次更新迭代，终不负“杰出剧情游戏”的盛名。 剧情的起点，是玩家对主角V的塑造——流浪者、街头小子、公司员工，三种出身不仅决定了开局的叙事视角，更铺垫了V截然不同的性格底色与人际关系。流浪者的自由不羁、街头小子的市井圆滑、公司员工的精于算计，让每个玩家都能找到属于自己的代入感，而这种代入感，在第一人称视角的加持下被推向极致。CDPR放弃了传统第三人称的上帝视角，转而让玩家以V的双眼凝视夜之城，感受义眼扫描时的科技质感，聆听对话时的情绪波动，这种沉浸式设计，让每一次抉择都变得格外沉重。 故事的核心脉络，围绕一枚能实现永生的Relic原型芯片展开。V在一次盗窃行动中意外将芯片植入脑中，从此与数字幽灵强尼·银手绑定共生——这个曾为营救女友突袭荒坂大厦、在核爆中失踪的传奇摇滚巨星，带着对企业巨头的刻骨仇恨，与V共享一具躯体，也共享一段注定走向终点的命运。两人从最初的针锋相对、互相排斥，到后来的彼此理解、生死相依，这段羁绊成为剧情最动人的底色。强尼的桀骜不驯与内心柔软，V的野心勃勃与坚守底线，在一次次对话与抉择中逐渐丰满，他们既是彼此的枷锁，也是彼此的救赎。 夜之城从来不是单纯的背景板，而是剧情的重要参与者。这座被企业资本浇筑的超级都市，既有霓虹闪烁的繁华表象，也有底层挣扎的黑暗真相——荒坂、军用科技等巨头掌控一切，帮派割据、义体滥用、贫富悬殊成为常态，赛博精神病患者的疯狂嘶吼，诉说着科技对人性的异化。游戏通过无数支线剧情，将这座城市的肌理层层剥开：巫毒帮的黑客诡影、莫克斯帮的坚守反抗、清道夫的冷酷无情，每个势力都有自己的生存逻辑；而德拉曼的自我救赎、约书亚的信仰挣扎、朱迪与帕南的深情羁绊，更让夜之城的每一个角落都充满了人性的温度。 非线性叙事与多结局设计，让剧情拥有了无限可能。玩家的每一个选择，无论是对话中的立场倾向，还是任务中的行动方式，都将影响剧情的走向。是选择与荒坂妥协换取生机，还是与强尼并肩摧毁企业霸权；是坚守人性底线，还是沉迷义体改造沦为冰冷的机器，每一种选择都对应着不同的结局，没有绝对的对错，只有立场的差异。这种设计，不仅增强了剧情的可玩性，更让玩家在抉择中思考：当科技可以改造肉体、储存意识，当永生成为可能，人类的本质究竟是什么？ 或许有人诟病其初期的优化问题，但这丝毫无法掩盖剧情叙述的光芒。CDPR用细腻的台词、精良的过场动画，将“赛博朋克”的核心命题诠释得淋漓尽致——科技是救赎也是诅咒，资本是权力也是枷锁，而人性的坚守，才是黑暗中唯一的光。V与强尼的最终告别，夜之城的霓虹依旧闪烁，那些关于野心、背叛、深情与牺牲的故事，却在玩家心中留下了难以磨灭的印记。 《赛博朋克2077》的剧情，从来不是一场简单的冒险，而是一次对人性与未来的深刻叩问。它用破碎却真挚的叙事，告诉我们：即使身处霓虹乱世，即使肉身早已被科技改造，只要守住内心的温度，便不算沦为赛博时代的傀儡。这不仅是一款游戏的剧情，更是一段关于爱与救赎、坚守与反抗的精神独白，历经时光沉淀，愈发彰显其不朽的价值。

What impressed me the most is that each playthrough felt genuinely different. Not just because of the combat styles, but because of the choices, relationships, quest outcomes, and endings that completely changed how I experienced the story.  The first thing that makes Cyberpunk special is that your choices actually matter.  A lot of games promise meaningful decisions, but very few deliver. Cyberpunk does. The story evolves naturally based on your actions, and perhaps more importantly, the consequences make sense. You never get the feeling that the game is changing things just to prove that choices matter. Instead, characters react in believable ways, relationships develop differently, and the world feels responsive to who you decide to become.  What makes this even better is that every major ending feels justified. Whether you agree with a particular outcome or not, each path feels like a natural conclusion to the choices that led you there. By the time I reached the ending, I wasn't thinking about which ending was "best." I was thinking about which ending was right for the version of V I had created.  The story itself is phenomenal.  I spent roughly 60-80 hours completing everything I could find: the main story, side quests, gigs, exploration, and character storylines. When I finished, I wasn't ready to leave Night City. In fact, I started another playthrough and experienced the story again together with my wife because I wanted someone else to experience it too.  That's how good the writing is.  The side quests deserve special praise because they are some of the best I've ever seen in gaming. Most open-world games eventually fall into the trap of "go there, collect this, bring it back." Cyberpunk rarely does. Almost every side quest has its own story, memorable characters, difficult decisions, or unexpected twists.  Some quests stayed in my head long after I completed them. The crucifixion storyline (or Peralez) alone is more thought-provoking than entire campaigns in some other games. The game constantly presents situations that are morally complicated, uncomfortable, or emotionally challenging. Even simple gigs that start as "go eliminate this target" often turn into something far more interesting once you learn who the person is and why they're in that situation.  Many times I walked into a mission expecting a simple objective and ended up spending twenty minutes debating whether I should even pull the trigger.  That's what makes Night City feel alive.  Then there's the gameplay.  Cyberpunk gives you an incredible amount of freedom in how you approach the game. You can become a stealth-focused assassin, a walking tank, a cyber ninja slicing through enemies with katanas, a netrunner destroying entire groups without firing a shot, or something completely different. Every build opens new possibilities and changes how encounters play out.  The progression system constantly rewards experimentation. New cyberware, weapons, abilities, and playstyles keep the gameplay fresh for dozens of hours. Few RPGs manage to combine story depth and gameplay variety this well.  The result is a game where both the narrative and the gameplay are equally strong.  The biggest problem Cyberpunk created for me is that it raised my standards too high. After finishing it, I found myself comparing every other RPG to it. Other games might have a good main story, but their side quests rarely reach the same level of quality. They might have decent combat, but lack meaningful choices. They might offer choices, but fail to make them feel important.  Cyberpunk is one of the few games where the main story, side content, characters, world-building, role-playing, and gameplay all work together to create something special.  For me, it's not just a great RPG.  It's one of the best games ever made.

I played this game on and off for 4 YEARS before seeing my first ending. It's that kind of game. There is just soooo much to do, and even when you aren't actually doing much of anything, it's plenty fun to just exist in this world.   Without exaggeration, these people have crafted perhaps [i]the[/i] most immersive digital world to date. Aside from NPC interaction, everything genuinely feels like you are interacting with a living, breathing environment influenced by your actions. The level of detail and depth is easily my favorite thing about this game, and I often find myself falling back into the rabbit hole of videos discussing niche little elements of the world's history, geography, and iconography. Every element of this world's presentation is meticulously crafted to reflect its history, to the point where it's impossible [i]not[/i] to also occasionally feel the crushing weight of despair burdening every other inhabitant of Night City. The swaths of advertisements covering every wall, in particular, always piqued my interest. There is so much to be said about how eerily close to home this specific depiction of the cyberpunk dystopia feels.  One element of this game that I personally took issue with was its characters. While there were certainly standouts like Johny and Misty, the rest felt either severely underdeveloped or incoherent, resulting in a generally forgettable cast for me. Adam Smasher, especially, felt like he was set up as this huge presence throughout the game, but even by the end, I felt like I barely knew who he was or what he wanted. I'm not entirely sure what it was about my experience, but none of the love interest characters felt like much more than plot devices for me, with Panam in particular becoming such a conflicted mess of inconsistent motivations by the end that she ended up being the worst part of the ending experience for me. From what I hear, Judy's route seems like it would've been a bit more fleshed out and less annoying, but like wtf was Panam on at the end there?? (If you need characters, best just watch Edgerunners)  Which brings me to the ending—probably the weakest part of the story for me. In my view, this game shines most in its side missions. Heck, the only reason it took so long for me to get to the end is because I just really enjoyed driving around and solving problems for random people. Especially because a lot of those missions [i]rewarded[/i] you for being tactical (i.e., using stealth). For me, those were easily my most memorable experiences. While the main story can be exciting at times, especially at the beginning, it can get to feel sort of at odds with the type of game this is. The main thing that threw me off about the ending was how disconnected the story I was being told felt from the actual gameplay I was experiencing. By the time you get there, V is so ridiculously overpowered that tactics [i]do not[/i] matter in the slightest, so the enemy the game has been building up since the start, and still takes very seriously, just feels like a really sturdy punching bag you have to just slowly hack away at. This, combined with how ridiculous everything Panam was saying and doing, made for a very confusing, immersion-breaking experience.   That said, Night City has a way of lodging itself deep inside your mind, to the point where a certain part of you may never truly be able to leave. If you can accept that, I think this game is very much worth your time.

It's been a while since I've played this game, but I figured I'd finally leave a review for it since one's been pending for a while.  This game was honestly always a good game. It may have had a rough start due to bugs and performance issues, but the core storyline and gameplay, as well as the more interesting questlines you can follow, were always there. Then with all the QoL changes and the complete overhaul they did to the perk system, it became much more refined and enjoyable to play since you now had a variety of builds and perks you could experiment with.   I think one of my favorite things about the game was the story and characters. Every character has an interesting and expressive personality, including your own as expressed through the voice acting (I personally prefer Male V's voice direction). Everyone feels fleshed out and like they actually have a growing relationship to you the more you interact with them. The main story itself feels very personal and high stakes, though some of that is admittedly ruined by the open world nature of the game since you can just dally along however long you want. As the meme goes, "Anything but meeting Hanako at Embers" lol. Even so, I think it manages to portray a nice drama about the meaningfulness of life, self-determination, and even hope in a world that seems determined to grind you down.  The environment is effective in portraying just how degenerate and trashy (literally, even) Night City really is, which helps in creating this sense of "contamination" and a desire to separate yourself and rise above it.   Also, the music. The music in this game kicks ass, and I still listen to some of my favorite tracks on my Spotify every so often.  I'd say my only real complaint with the game is the lack of being able to clearly show yourself as cybernetically enhanced, such as by having clearly mechanical limbs or metallic embellishments like a Kano-style red eye. I was also never too fond of any of the romance options, but it was nice that I never felt forced to pursue any of them from what I can remember.

This game is wide as an ocean, shallow as a puddle. It's good, but people keep overrating this game. The endings fit the settings theme and it's very cinematic. The shooting is mediocre, character creation is not really that engaging, the "choices" you make don't really matter all that much, on both a micro and macro level, and EVERY single mechanic is very surface level. Jack of all traits, master of none.  It's also just a god awful RPG. Like to the point that it being described as that feels like false advertising. There's literally no "roleplaying" in this game beyond picking dialogue options. The backgrounds hardly matter beyond how you meet your character's first friend. Shooting is boring, driving is awful, the cybernetics aren't that interesting of a system. (Deus Ex and even 'Cruelty Squad' do it better! Which is embarrassing for a game that was in development for this long.)  I've tried my best to care for the characters, but I kind of just don't. You hardly get to know each other, and you don't really "work" with another beyond the individual missions. Your "friends" are not plot relevant at all, beyond Panam for Act 1 and the finale. The "ending" of the game is probably what 'saves' this game at all, as it resonates so thematically with the nihilistic world that it almost convinces you the story was actually good, and not boring meaningless filler for 80% of it.   You are so absurdly powerful in this game - both mechanically and storywise that it kind of makes all mission "planning" a bit boring and annoying. Why even do all of this if I can just kill everything that moves? Phantom Liberty is a little bit better about this but it's still not really enough.  The themes and story is so annoyingly nihilistic, and to make it worse it comes from a pretty decently sized studio with a huge budget behind it. Oh, I'm sure a corporation would be HAPPY to promote a game where capitalism is some magical all consuming force that enslaves the planet and cannot be stopped by literally any means possible. Solutions? To capitalism? Well the writer doesn't want you to think about that, they just want you to bask in how miserable everyone is! It's individualist slop that I can't tell is out of ignorance or out of malice for the world.  The anime just saved this game's ass insanely badly. It's THE "hype moments and aura" game. If you like that, play this game. If you want an actually good story with good gameplay??  Hope that maybe the sequel will be actually good.

You used to be able to re-work your attributes for in game currency, but now you can only do that once.  The game then only allows you to re-work your talents, but your attributes are fixed. Right off the bat, go experience the game.. just go and play and experience the miriad of stories and characters it hides inside this marvelously crafted world. You may not have the emotional connect with the side quests as you might expect from a Witcher 3 fanatic but that's okay. In this world where the line blurs between humanity and machines and where emotion is a data chip, it is expected that you take the deaths in a monotonous tone and it doesn't affect us much, no matter how much depth the characters might have. But given that, there are also stories that hits you and you will not see it coming. To do that level of immersion in this hopeless city, in itself, is a great achievement.  Now coming to the world building. The world is a living breathing city. Each corner and alleys have something to tell. Each district has a unique style. Each have their faction and a history. And the people you meet there, well they add more to the world. And they entangle well with the missions where you have the choice to go which route you wanna go. I once tried climbing an impossible sky scraper just to avoid paying 50 eddies and guess what, I was greeted with the only scissor lift mechanism in the entire game. And to think they have an option to enter the building via the garden at the top floor is an icing on the cake. Brilliant game design, that I felt so satisfied with each different way I try to enter a building for the missions. I could give a 10 outta 10 just for that. Then later I switched to a melee build with blunt weapons and the finishers that come with this tree are my personal best in the game.  Just to finish it off. Cyberpunk boiled down to bones is an upgraded version of GTA, full stop. For quests, instead of doing yoga or goofing off at a port doing nothing for hours like in GTA, you will have the most insane side quests AND get paid for it. Just to give a glimpse into what that could mean - you pick up an AI pistol off a dead guy in a shady alley and it makes you kill 50 people with it while it talks to you, you drive a creepy clown to a specific burrito vending machine (found everywhere in the city btw) only for him to kill the people standing in front of it for no reason, you eat Chinese food from a stand with a Japanese man and he calls it ♥♥♥♥ to the chef’s face, you use a light machine gun to mow down a homeless camp while they charge you, you have a street fight with a guy and take away his car in front of his pregnant girlfriend (dw tho, it makes sense and he ends up better off), the list just goes on.   How is the game though? Overall it runs amazing and have had no major issues. One crash an hour in or something when I blew up 8 cars at the same time by accident (dropped a grenade when I went to change weapons into a car pile up). Never had an issue again. The city is beautiful, the quests are awesome, the game takes way over 100 hours to complete, the city and surrounding badlands is huge map wise (yes, you get fast travel points everywhere), the cars are fun, the clothing is awesome, the choices during conversations will require a few playthroughs (just bought the game for my main account so haven't finished the nomad one yet), the physics make sense, and the save button is the most used thing you will ever use (very very useful for going back if you screw up a convo or fight). For the story, it is a must play.   Anything wrong with it? Yeah, nothing major but "stuff happens" sometimes. You could be on a hill trying to spawn in your car after a quest and it may explode on another car (nothing happens it's just annoying because you need to respawn it - ps it is NOT common), a quest could get stuck if you go into a cutscene and you weren't standing in the place they told you to be in (just reload last save, takes 4 seconds), people speaking can sometimes overlap (NPC 1 finishing their sentence and NPC 2 starts talking on the last word or something), loot can get stuck on bodies that you can't dispose of or loot, that kind of stuff. Most importantly, does it impact the gameplay? 100% no, it just "happens" and you reload and move on.   Why the pos recommendation? The story and character development is worth it, full stop. Once you start, you can't put the game down because you want to complete the 270+ missions they have available. There is a LOT to do lol.   ^ With all the above said, any negatives? Yeah, this game is way too into LGBT stuff. One character that you do street races with added in randomly that they were trans for 0 reason (you can't tell at all btw, knowing the fact added nothing to the gameplay) and then they suddenly had a personality shift to get revenge on their partner's killer mid race despite the dude dying fair and square. Made 0 sense and was forced. You could also talk about this girl that has the EXACT same romance lines as if you were a woman (because she's apparently gay) and you don't find that out until the last quest where she leaves the city. The lines were double dipped and the devs were lazy there 100%. As a straight male, she just shuts you down out of left field. Last major character was this cop you did quests with. The game gives you an option to start a gay relationship with the guy, keep him as a friend, or leave entirely all in the same conversation prompt. Does the game force you to be gay or bi or whatever? Def NOT, but you will have the "option" to if you wanted it. Wish there was a feature to turn on a "straight male" mode to avoid it altogether but I guess they want night city to truly feel degenerate and without morals. "No happy endings" right? It does not impact your gameplay, it just makes it slightly annoying to see. I am totally hyperfocusing on this despite it not even being 1% of the game because it could have been perfect with an option to let you avoid all that stuff.   Right, enough said about that. Cyberpunk is worth every dollar and you should dive right into night city choom. Thanks for reading and God bless.

We are all aware of this game's horrible launch state, but with 2.0, the Phantom Liberty DLC and subsequent updates, I believe CDPR has turned that launch disaster into what it was always meant to be, that being one of the greatest games in recent memory. Something I'd happily call this generation's New Vegas.  Pros: - Incredible worldbuilding through lifepaths. I would recommend a new player starting with Nomad but Corpo is my favorite - Well-written and complex characters that feel like actual people with everyone hiding at least something under the surface, no matter how insignificant they may be to the story - Great story with a well-handled approach to many complex themes along with emotional hard-hitting moments (Especially Phantom Liberty) - Incredible amounts of replayability, that can be owed to rewarding, deliberate and varied buildcrafting (especially on higher difficulties), satisfying gameplay, multiple endings, and of course, mod support (I have way more hours on the GOG version dw) - Great soundtrack - Fashion potential is off the charts, especially with mods  Cons (if I really have to nitpick): - Some jank is still to be found if you look for it - The open world sometimes feels a bit lifeless, but you'll be too busy doing gigs to care Lol - The first ten levels or so are pretty slow to do, especially on harder difficulties (despite which I can still absolutely recommend them regardless) - Some guns are straight up useless for 80% of players, which ends up diluting gunplay a lot more than it should  Despite some minor flaws, I'd still say this game has 100% earned its roses now.

[h1]Cyberpunk 2077: A game that everyone must try[/h1]  The graphics:  Nowadays a game like this is hard to find, it remains within a small select group of games that I and many others would consider near perfect. And here's the reasons why: Starting with the obvious, the graphics. Cyberpunk boasts some of the greatest looking visuals within gaming as a whole as it takes full usage of the neo-lit world. It truly immerses you into the position of V as you're put into this ginormous worst-case scenario world. It is also openly used as NVIDIAs golden goose for gaming visuals, as it's spoon fed the newest features such as higher frame gen and the exclusive path tracing which I am lucky enough to try. And it is nothing less than breath-taking.   The story:   CDPR is known for they deal with their stories, as primarily seen within how they adapted The Witcher. Similarly Cyberpunk 2077 is merely adding onto the Cyberpunk world created by Mike Pondsmith, and it does it more than enough justice. The story perfectly resonates with the main source material and is able to encapsulate you into it immediately. After the heist and with V's slowly deteriorating health it was able to make you feel true sympathy for both V and those around you. It makes you feel for characters and at times it really feels like you're sharing their misfortune. And with the decision-based story (albeit sometimes it doesn't make full use of it) it allows for you to carve your own path within Night City.   Overall no game is without its flaws. For instance, the NPC depth could have definitely been further worked upon as sometimes the walking animations can feel out of place and their reactions uncanny and unrealistic. Furthermore, the bugs. Now I remember the horror movie that was Cyberpunk on release, and they did indeed build upon this game from the ground up. But sometimes I do find myself encountering a few bugs that really feel like they shouldn't still exist within the game's current state.   Cyberpunk holds a special place within my heart as both the base game and DLC allow for CDPR to show the true extent to what they can do with games. I hope this review either convinces you to buy the game or at least makes you aware of Cyberpunk 2077's greatness.

Cyberpunk is a really good game. It is considered a reference on multiple fronts which combined result in a highly entertaining experience. If you get the chance, buy it and play it.   Cyberpunk is an ambitious project in terms of scope and technical capabilities. Despite its rough start, it's undeniable this is one of the most good looking game there was when it came out, and the dimension of the project is not something that many studios would dare to tackle for an entirely new IP. I'm happy they did and we should give them credit that they took it to the end, to ensure its mostly failed launch was just a light stain on their track record.  This game was designed with realism in mind and it will pull everything out of your graphics card to make it happen. At the same time, it is still somehow flexible to be able to run on something as restricted as a steam deck. It's impressive. If you have the necessary hardware, your eyes will feast. It's a game from 2020 but still used as a tech demo reference in 2026. That's saying something.   I feel the Cyberpunk can be best described as a linear game built on top of a massive (open?) world. Yes, you can take quests in mostly assorted order but you do feel they're all leading to the same outcome. Your decisions don't shape the world, you're just following the pre-destined path, but this path is highly entertaining.   To be fair to the devs, open world games are tough. It's hard to get them right. Most just end up being too sprawling with little substance (looking at your Starfield) and struggle with pacing. In Cyberpunk, the devs decided to use this massive maps to sprinkle curated experiences all over the places: the quests, the gigs, the NYCP arrests, etc... All in all, making sure in every region, that there was at least something interesting happening there once.  It's not a game where the world on its own has the built-in dynamics to entertain you by itself, but CD PROJECT RED left plenty to do everywhere. I personally loved the gigs, secondary to the plot, because it provides that kind of experience you get with Hitman: "here's a constrained location and goal, there are multiple ways to fulfill the goal, go and have fun". The NYCP arrests were a bit more trash tier casual events for me. I didn't really connect with them and I failed to see their appeal.   The world building and design this project did is amazing and they just deserve praise.  The weapon systems are interesting; the way gameplay changes based on the implants you decide to install on your character is peak. The implant and skill system is solid and built to ensure that only your imagination is the limit in deciding how you want to play this game: in your face bruiser, long range assassin, sneaky cyber-runner, a combination of the previous, etc. There are more combinations than the time you'll have to play them.    Phantom Liberty is DLC done right. The DLC has its own review page but this doesn't subtract from the value it added to the experience, although you can't help but to feel that they are detached. The way it intertwines with the main story is superficial. To be fair, it would technically very hard to have it any other way.  Regarding music and soundtrack: I remember spending hours driving to the radios in GTA 3 and Vice City. That was no longer the case in Cyberpunk. I mostly kept the radio quiet and can't really pinpoint why. Maybe I just got old, the samples I got from the radio didn't really connect on the first listens and then I just ended up turning off the radio. Or maybe it's a sign that in general I didn't feel them appealing enough, despite the random sampling. I know there are at least 2 or 3 banger tracks, that I felt welt placed, some of them during key dialogs that really helped to shape the mood. In the places it really mattered, the score was there and provided the necessary lift. However the passive listening experience (radio) was not the best. Maybe it's just the reality of Night City of being very self-imposing with its piercing ads and obnoxious jingles.    There was nothing I really disliked in this game. Only things that I would not mind the see changed into the next iteration of Cyberpunk 2077, if that ever ends up being a thing:   1. V's personality was extremely bland. I picked a corpo path and the way V spoke just sounded often like a low education gangster. This dissonance between personality and background killed immersion. 2. I would like to see the design philosophy behinds the gigs more present even in the main quest. Right now everything is absolutely scripted. One way in, one way out. I feel "The Last Of Us" showed us there's is flexibility for having both. If you have level designers on your team that can develop maps like the gigs, I'm sure these can still flow into your main quest. 3. I felt sad the gigs never really tied properly with the world lore. The story is baked-in and its not reactive to decisions you took in some of these gigs.    It's a great game. Be ready to commit some time to it :)

To me, Cyberpunk is a modern iteration of some of the overall themes and tone of the original Fallout. Cyberpunk is a game about you against the world a true uphill battle where there is no possible way of winning. The world is built around you losing, and you know that. V knows that. But we keep fighting; we have to.  While Fallout 1 leans into a pulp vibe and focuses more on racial themes and the failed foundations of social Darwinism, Cyberpunk focuses on the crushing aspects of late-stage capitalism, where the sky is filled with ads and the only way to make a living is by getting yourself killed. The system is built to destroy you, to isolate you so what is your answer? How do you keep yourself alive? You build connections, you live your life, and you fall in love.

Easily the best AAA game I played in the last ten years, and probably one of the best action RPG and open-world game too.  Didn't finish the main story yet, nor played the DLC, though the story and narration is solid. The choices feel interesting and impactful.   The city really feel alive, dangerous, and overall represent well the ultra capitalist corporation-dominated dystopia its supposed to be. The universe is interesting with a lot of detail and fluff being present in the game.  Encountered very few bugs during my playthrough for now.  Playing a stealth build with some support netrunning is really fun, feel like HITMAN but with a giant open-world and plenty of interesting zone to explore different approach. For instance some areas of the cities offer a great environnement for outdoor long-range snipper shots, while other are more compact and enclosed, perfect for infiltration. I like how the game use its setup to offer levels with verticality, and a really good amount of plausible physics, move and tools to make the most out of them.  On the negative side, the progression curve is a little weird, in particular in Very hard difficulty but not only. Basically, it's really hard at the beginning, but suddently after the 20 first levels everything feel quite easy and less challenging. The voice acting and dialogue are quite inequal, the protagonist for instance has sometime quite unsufferable edgelord lines which does not really feel in-character or fitting the condition they are facing. They are sometimes way too phlegmatic for the stuff happening around them. Otherwise the most important NPC are way better, with strong identity, struggles, goals, development during the story and various way of dealing with what's happening. You can easily feel attached (or repulsed) to them.  Overall the tone remain quite edgy, sometimes boomer-esque, but that fit the Cyberpunk universe, which is so maximalist it becomes really goofy at some times, lightyears away from the very serious and eerie neo-noir aesthetic of Blade Runner or the first Deus Ex and its never ending socio-political schemes and conspirations. That is not a problem at all, just don't expect any profound political or metaphysical meditation from this game because it will not deliver that. Though, I think the setup (and the game !) is really good at exploring the unheimlich/unhomely aspect of cybernetics due to how common it is in the universe and the first-person perspective.

Cyberpunk 2077 isn’t just a game. And Edgerunners isn’t just an anime.  Both present a futuristic world full of chrome, violence, and massive corporations… but at its core, it reflects something very real: real life.  Today, people often burn themselves out chasing ambition, money, status, or validation. In Night City, it happens through cyberware and implants. In real life, it happens in quieter, less neon-lit ways—but it still destroys people just the same.  David Martinez wanted to prove his worth to the world. V just wanted to survive in a system that was already stacked against them. And honestly, how many people today are living versions of that same struggle?  Cyberpunk constantly reminds us that when ambition goes blind, it stops motivating and starts consuming you instead. People stop living for themselves and start chasing something that may never fill the emptiness.  And that’s what makes this universe so special: behind the neon lights, intense action, and the absolutely unhinged amount of chaos (and yes, NSFW energy) in Night City, there are real lessons about humanity, loneliness, love, trauma, and the price of trying to “win” in a broken world.  There are no perfect endings in Night City. Just like there are rarely perfect endings in real life.  But people still love, still dream, and still fight anyway.  And maybe that’s the real message of Cyberpunk.  (Also, half the city definitely needs therapy… and the other half needs to log off for a bit.)

Cyberpunk 2077 Review:-  After playing for around 16 hours, I can honestly say this game surprised me in a very good way.  When I started GTA 5, I mostly treated it like an open-world sandbox. I enjoyed driving, causing chaos, and exploring, but I was never deeply invested in the story. Cyberpunk 2077 feels completely different to me.  In Cyberpunk, I am not just treating it as an open-world game — I am treating it as an open-world story-based choice matters game. The storyline is genuinely great and emotional. Some moments actually hit hard emotionally, and the characters feel memorable.  What I love the most is that my choices actually matter. I feel like the story changes depending on what I choose, and that makes me think before making decisions. It makes me more attached to the world and characters.  The gameplay is also really fun: ✔ Cool cars and bikes to drive ✔ Great action (not too hard, not too easy — balanced difficulty) ✔ Amazing world design ✔ Freedom to do many things  But the biggest difference compared to GTA or many other open-world games for me is hacking.  I absolutely love that I can use intelligence and strategy instead of just shooting enemies. Hacking enemies, using quickhacks, scanning, and planning attacks makes combat feel unique and smart.  Honestly, after 16 hours, I understand why people love this game so much. It feels immersive, emotional, and gives me freedom while still making me care about the story.  Highly recommended if you love story-driven games where your choices matter.

A good game, but a game that falls short on most of its original promises.   [h3] Gameplay [/h3]  I’m pretty sure the original vision of the devs for the gameplay was to land somewhere between an action RPG and an immersive sim. Which could have been a cool concept if it worked out, unfortunately it really didn’t.   For the immersive sim side of things it’s all super simplistic. Sure most of the time there are a couple of approaches to handle things. However “couple” is usually just two or three - either you go guns blazing, do stealth or pass a skill check. Skill checks are almost completely irrelevant, the game isn’t super hard even on hard so I’ve always had enough points to dump into some skill tree to unlock the route If I wanted to. And even if I hadn’t, there always was an alternative route quite clearly highlighted. I’ve never felt some consequences of my gameplay related choices and in every scenario it was visible how the devs wanted to accommodate every play style. As for stealth, its mechanics are rather rudimentary, NPCs are easy prey for the player and in general it doesn’t feel that good. Even the Phantom Liberty DLCs, which could have been stealth heavy, didn't make it fun.  As for combat it’s OK-ish. After the initial shock that headshots don’t do insta kills and absolutely ♥♥♥♥ iron sights that are close to unusable before upgrades I’ve quite enjoyed the flow. Between hacking, tossing grandes and a lot of running and gunning it was quite fun. However, even with some interesting augmentations it all got quite stale after some 30 hours. There really aren’t much of a difference between enemies, or at least they don’t matter when you are shooting at them so every encounter started to feel quite the same. And also by then I’ve mostly settled on my build and experimentation really wasn't possible - since perks affect chances of crit hits, aim accuracy and everything, whole weapon classes become unusable by mid game since they had to be neglected in the skill tree. Also as enemies scale to your level you A) don’t feel that much power, maybe expect against the most basic of gangsters and B) enemies are bulletsponges throughout the whole game. Lot of the encounters towards the game weren’t fun but just annoying.   As for the role playing side, first there is the character customizations. There are 5 main skill trees all of them filled with many perks that usually are just some stat increase, granted not simple stat increases, but + 5 % crit rate for pistols is still just a stat increase. Cyberware works in a similar aspect so there obviously are ways to stack some stacks to create some ridiculous builds. However, chances are most common players would need to copy such builds from some guides which is boring. I felt that in games like idk Witcher 3 the skill system was much more legible, had much more impact and different builds were immediately distinguishable. The second part of role playing would be players' choices, of which there are many, and most amount to nothing. Sure there are a couple of endings, some characters can die, but it’s nothing compared to previous CDPR experiences.  [h3] Worldbuilding [/h3]  The amount of detail in this game is ridiculous. Be it city streets, suburbia, badlands or insides of random apartment buildings, diners, hotels everything has been crafted with immense level of care. Combined with things like TV broadcasts, the Night City can be really immersive and feel alive. Even the factions that occupy the space are well written and their behaviour makes some level of sense. Granted, a lot of the work was done for CDPR as they were working with already established IP, but still they’ve managed to bring it to life really well.   My only gripe in respect to worldbuilding is that CDPR really should have hired some technical advisors. Granted most players don’t have a degree in electronics engineering, but as a guy who has, some of things look really stupid. Sci-Fi smart guns, implants and things like this are ok. I can suspend my disbelief for it. But for things like idk parabolic antenna the physics is set and won’t change.  [h3] Story and Quests [/h3]  The story in general is a mess. Clearly ruined by rushed development and it will never be fixed. And the problems start almost immediately, when after a too short route specific start you are presented with an epic montage of budding with Jackie, a montage that would be fun to play, but not just a mp4 for the player to build attachment to him, before he is unceremoniously killed.  It’s no surprise that things didn’t get much better after that. Like it’s not terrible and especially a lot of the side routes work quite well, but it could have been so much more.   On the topic of side routes, a lot of them are really great. But the problem is they don’t plate that well with the main story. Especially when it comes to Johnny, his character was really erratic with how he acted in different side routes, not to mention the DLC. One time V and Johnny had a profound understanding for each other, only to start the next mission where suddenly every understanding was thrown out of the windows and just animosity remained. Johnny as a character doesn’t work at all because of this.    However, in respect to Johnny/V the story would have never worked without some time limit mechanic. If nothing else the devs should have made it a toggle when creating a new game, or at least make it so you cannot complete every sidequests - with the game having a couple radically  different main routes each with a couple of endings. Most of your decisions already don’t amount to much so I would gladly take a more linear experience in exchange for the main story conflict to actually play a role in the story.  I’ve found sidequests to be really lacking. There are like two somewhat good side quests you don’t get a call for. And even those you get a call for by your fixer there really aren’t that many. And for some great ones you can easily get locked out of them by picking wrong choices, which isn’t a bad thing. But most side quests or gigs still follow the basic formula of go there, kill enemies, maybe retrieve something and that’s about it. It’s a shame given how well the world is crafted.   [h3] Technical Aspects [/h3]  While I’ve had only a couple of crashes, I’ve encountered quite a large number of bugs during my 50 hours with the game. Only a couple required a reload - as they soflocked me, but way more “gamebreaking” were bugs in bosses behaviour. Three of the bosses in the main story got stuck in the air and let magazine after magazine be dumped into them. On one aspect this ruined their impact quite a bit - especially when it came to Adam Smasher. On the other hand given they were bullet sponge garbage that lasted twice as long as they should have I don’t really have a problem with it gameplay wise.  [h3] Conclusion [/h3]  Despite my critique for the first 30 hours the game was really good and Phantom Liberty was especially a standout. The game should have been in the oven for at least two more years and then maybe it could have been great. Cyberpunk we got is just kinda sad in this aspect. Still it’s worth playing just for the great setting, despite it being rather poorly utilized.

I spent more than 208 hours in the world of Cyberpunk 2077, and during that time I managed to earn the platinum trophy as well — I think that alone says a lot about how immersive and engaging this game is. Night City is incredibly detailed, alive, and atmospheric, always offering something new to discover, whether it’s a quest, a story, or an interesting character. The story and characters are outstanding, especially the depth of both the main storyline and the side quests. It’s rare to find a game where you genuinely care about the characters and where your choices actually feel meaningful. The progression system and the variety of builds kept the gameplay and combat fun even after hundreds of hours. The game has improved massively since launch, and today it delivers an amazing RPG experience. The graphics, soundtrack, and overall cyberpunk atmosphere are simply incredible. For me, getting the platinum trophy never felt like a chore — it felt like completing an unforgettable journey that I enjoyed every step of the way. I can highly recommend it to anyone who loves story-driven open-world games.

This game is a solid 9.0/10 for me. I was expecting an almost Hollywood-level sugar-coated narrative you would see in generic action flicks. To my surprise, it made me really sad that V lives in a world with choices and trade-offs that come to a bitter end, simulating reality in that regard really well. The surrounding characters are also very well written and never stick out one bit in the plot at all, all their personalities resonate well with what they deal with or what they will deal with as the plot goes on. I couldn't get past completing more than two endings because I would just get grief. This game really captured what it's like living in a big city where everyone is a blip in a large population. It also captured what people always say about good stories in games that I've never seen in the usual genres i play until the point i felt empathetic with how everything transpires.  The gameplay is good, especially for an RPG. It has the most action-packed combat depth compared to the limited selection of RPGs I have played. There is some jank that isn't game-breaking, although it still requires some TLC. No, thanks to it being a rush job, I'll hedge my bets that needing to be a console release made it very hard to optimize as well. I heard from multiple people that CD Projekt Red cared enough about their product to fix it instead of shilling it to a community of fans that become both nostalgic and jaded over time because they have to fix it themselves to then make it playable like classic fallout games.  The graphics are good, nothing out of this world, especially in the case of the rendered models of the characters, they pale in comparison to the world around them. Where it does ramp it up is how the developers really captured the claustrophobic layout of cities, with buildings forming small bazaars on street levels. The buildings themselves had a lot of signs, pipes and other small details caked on them for that extra pop giving u the stimulation from city settings u would picture irl, and the detritus all around the city adds to the world-building really well. I would say it's the best modern city layout I've seen in an open world game yet, with the added flair of a futuristic cyber punk aesthetic.

Cyberpunk 2077 is easily a 9/10 and is definitely in my top 5 favorite games.  The game has come a looong way since launch, speaking as someone who SOMEHOW played through the initial release on PS5. There's still plenty of.. quarks but not nearly as many game breaking bugs as before. More likely than not, it's actually one of my mods that breaks the game now.  The world is big but not massive. Everything is very densely packed together for the most part, and I think that works for the benefit of the game. There's a very solid variety of cars, and even some cyberware that makes traversal a lot of fun.  The story is really good, basically from start to finish. There's absolutely some areas that could've been fleshed out more but overall I think it's fine. The "Choose Your Path" and Jackie downfalls have been spoken about enough and are what I feel weigh down the start of the game the most, but beyond that I think the main story holds up perfectly well. There's ample side missions to take part in, a lot of which have self contained stories, some short, some a bit longer. There's rarely anything that's as simple as "go to point A, talk to NPC, go to Point B, kill some bad guys" that a lot of Open World RPG's/FPS games tend to lean on.  There's plenty of opportunity to make interesting builds if you pay attention to your weapons, cyberware, and skills. Although I tend to lean on mowing through people with A shotgun, Katana, and Rifle combo, playing around with the Netrunner and stealth side of the game is equally as fun and rewarding.  Visually, needless to say, the game looks great. I'm a glutton for pain so I choose to play with Path Tracing so my performance is.. questionable to say the least but without Path Tracing, whether on normal Ray Tracing or neither RT or PT, the game runs pretty well for modern standards (which is a low bar, but still). The game is very CPU dependent which is my primary bottleneck so results may vary.  Gunplay in the beginning feels kinda sluggish and sometimes unresponsive but within an hour, maybe 2, you can get enough skills/guns to vastly improve the feeling of combat. At surface level, combat is nothing crazy but if you mix in the Netrunner and various other abilities, you can add a lot of depth to the combat and how you approach missions.  And finally, Panam is the only romance option that's worth it and I will die on this hill.  There's so much to say about this game but most of my complaints are minor issues that can easily be looked past and likely won't ruin your overall experience. I highly recommend this game and look forward to the sequel.

Hated this game at launch. Now I can't stop thinking about Night City. Bought it day one in 2020, crashed every 20 minutes, refunded it, swore I'd never go back. Four years later I came back. Easily one of the best gaming decisions I've made. Night City feels alive in a way no open world has for me. Not because it's massive but because it's dense. Every alley, rooftop, and abandoned room has something to say. Once I wandered into a random apartment with no quest marker, no objective, and found a heartbreaking story told entirely through text messages on a laptop someone left behind. No game has given me a moment like that before. The characters are something else. V and Johnny Silverhand's dynamic has a depth I genuinely didn't expect going in. The side quests aren't filler either, some of them are more memorable than the main campaigns of other RPGs I've played. Phantom Liberty is legitimately great. No regrets. Honest criticism: crowd AI still feels thin. NPCs don't react dynamically enough when things go sideways around them. The city looks alive but the interactions beneath the surface are still shallow. And a lot of choices feel weighty in the moment but don't actually ripple outward into the world. For the sequel I'd love to see CDPR build something truly reactive, not just at major story beats but in the small everyday texture of living in that city. That's the version of Night City I want next.

I was pretty sure I'd hate it forever but after coming back to it last year and beating it twice it's both one of the best fps games ever made and one of the best open world games ever made. The world feels densely packed like Sleeping Dogs while having the scope of something like Red Dead or Ghosts of Tsushima. The universe is absurdly well thought out and brought to life so vividly its hard to believe this is the mess I played years ago. Side quests are divided into jobs and gigs and while the gigs feel like a relic of late 2000s/early 2010s open world games the side jobs are almost all phenomenal and have a cinematic feel that many main stories in other games don't have. Gunplay and melee combat are snappy and satisfying, hacking is a blast and elevates fights in such a fun way, the driving isn't great but it's good enough I can play with a mouse and keyboard without wanting to grab a controller and through my PC through a wall. It's made better by the fact that there's some really fun vehicles, especially for people who are fans of the movies this is influenced by (yes of course I want to park the Akira bike next to the Blade Runner noodle shop). CD Projekt Red deserves all the grief they got for this game at launch but I've loved the story, characters, world, and gameplay that Cyberpunk has become now that it's. You know. A finished game.
