God I could write a novel on my mixed feelings on this one - approaching 6 years of 2077 here, good lorde.  Few games had me as hyped as Cyberpunk 2077. From its 2015 reveal to the delayed 2020 launch, I was completely locked in, in 2015 I basically discovered the cyberpunk genre through the world Mike Pondsmith created. It felt like the perfect middle ground between overdone fantasy and surface-level sci-fi.  This was the only game I have ever preordered. I played it at launch on PC and, despite bugs like T-posing, broken AI, and weird visual glitches, I still enjoyed my first run. A lot of the bigger issues felt fixable, and I was more excited for what the game could become. Things like deeper RPG systems, meaningful AI, gang dynamics, and customization all felt like they were coming later.  That is where the disappointment really sets in. Even now in 2026, after patches and Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty, it never became the RPG it was presented as. If you were (like me) expecting something closer to The Witcher but in a cyberpunk setting, this is not that.  And yet I have played through it six+ times.  Because what is here is still incredible. Night City is one of the most detailed and immersive worlds ever made. Just driving around, watching the skyline, and existing in that space is unmatched. It honestly feels like the scale and ambition of the world came at the cost of the systems meant to support it.  Amazing world, unforgettable vibe, but a missed RPG opportunity, and they clearly knew it from how they focused on all its positives in Phantom Liberty.

I did really enjoy this game, and it is worth the investment (on sale) if you are an RPG lover like myself. HOWEVER, as CD Projekt Red unfortunately also made my favorite game of all time (The Witcher 3) I will say a few things fell short that I know these devs were capable of executing better. Firstly I think perks railroad your gameplay instead of complimenting it. In the Witcher 3 I could utilize a strong sign, some potion perks, weapon perks etc. in tandem with each other. Cyberpunk it becomes more like.....another percentage increase in headshot damage, a little more stealth damage and I have to invest a decent amount of progression to get truly impactful perks. While it isn't bad per se, I think it makes it hard to have a more diverse experience and disincentivizes swapping between playstyles on the fly in favor of min-maxing more specific things. Romance is also lackluster, in a world this large and vibrant and active I shouldn't have only one romance option per orientation. If you are like me and you 100% stuff then late game gets pretty stale as you max your street cred and level pretty well before the end of the game even with the 10 extra levels from DLC which is always unfortunate. Side content (gigs, scanners, jobs) is decent and they did a good job of making even NCPD scanner missions feel important by connecting them through text logs in each district. And yeah, Phantom Liberty was nice with the way it perfectly interweaves into the narrative, not truly feeling like an "add-on." Its a lovely sci-fi sandbox and it is worth playing through in any capacity, but man it could've been even better.

341 hours. 4 full playthroughs. 57/57 achievements. Base game + Phantom Liberty completed.  At some point this stopped being “playing a game” and started looking more like me paying rent in Night City.  I originally told myself I’d do one playthrough, see the story, maybe mess around with a few builds, and move on like a normal person.  Instead, 341 hours later, I’ve done 4 playthroughs, unlocked every achievement, and somehow kept finding reasons to come back. Different builds, different choices, different endings... and yes, convincing myself “this time I’m making different decisions” only to get emotionally attached to the same characters all over again.  Night City is one of the most immersive worlds I’ve ever experienced. The atmosphere, soundtrack, side quests, characters, and the insane amount of detail make it dangerously easy to lose track of time. “I’ll play for an hour” is one of the biggest lies I told myself during these 341 hours.  And then Phantom Liberty showed up and somehow made everything even better. The writing, missions, characters, and overall tension were incredible. It doesn’t feel like DLC—it feels mandatory.  Combat stayed fresh the entire time, whether I was sneaking around like a professional merc... or accidentally turning every mission into a small-scale war crime.  After 4 playthroughs, 341 hours, and 57/57 achievements, I can honestly say Cyberpunk 2077 went from “a game I wanted to try” to one of my all-time favorite gaming experiences.  10/10. Would ignore my sleep schedule for Night City again.

[RU] Cyberpunk 2077 — игра не «на века». Сомневаюсь, что через десяток лет кто-то сильно захочет в неё вернуться, но в то же время чувствуется, что авторы вложили в неё всего себя, и игрок получит массу положительных впечатлений. Другими словами, возникает ощущение, что игра сделана для игроков, от игроков — это сразу выделяется, и в ней приятно провести время. Сама по себе игра несложная: никогда и нигде не ставят настоящее испытание, но при этом предоставляют множество различных способов решения возникших ситуаций. На фоне всего контента основная сюжетная линия, на мой взгляд, относительно короткая, однако здесь полно второстепенных заданий, наполненных продолжительностью, качеством и деталями. За этими историями интересно наблюдать: персонажи харизматичны, сюжеты продолжительные и детализированные, а также зачастую оставляют вопросы, о которых можно подумать. Причём эти вопросы касаются не только игры, но и в целом ситуации в мире, людей, неоднозначности решений и их последствий. Временами встречаются баги, но я не наткнулся ни на один софтлок, и в большинстве случаев они даже слегка забавляют. Однозначно рекомендую ознакомиться тем, кто хочет провести время в качественном RPG и лишний раз поразмышлять над вопросами, которые в ней возникают. Однако я не думаю, что через 10+ лет после выхода её будут называть культовой.  [EN] Cyberpunk 2077 isn't a game "for the ages." I doubt many people will want to return to it in a decade, but at the same time, you can feel that the developers poured their hearts and souls into it, and players will get plenty of positive impressions. In other words, it feels like a game made by players, for players — that stands out right away, and it's genuinely enjoyable to spend time in. The game itself isn't overly difficult: it never throws real challenges at you, but it offers a ton of different ways to tackle emerging situations. Against all the content, the main storyline seems relatively short in my opinion, but there are loads of side quests packed with length, quality, and detail. It's fascinating to follow these stories: the characters are charismatic, the plots are drawn-out and richly detailed, and they often leave you with questions to ponder. Moreover, these questions go beyond the game — touching on the state of the world, people, the ambiguity of choices, and their consequences. Bugs pop up from time to time, but I didn't run into any softlocks, and in most cases, they're even mildly amusing. I definitely recommend it to anyone who wants to dive into a quality RPG and mull over the questions it raises. That said, I don't think it'll be called a cult classic 10+ years after release.

I'm glad I waited for so long to give this game a try because at this point it feels like a complete game and one great RPG to dive into. I've played all the previous CDPR games and you can feel the the through line that get's them to this point and some of the lessons they must have learned with adapting the Witcher. They have a fantastic ability for your character to be a living and breathing personality before you even start making choices that would sway them. V isn't as characterized as Geralt was, but they are a veteran of the world they are thrown into and it shows by the options you are given.   Gameplay wise, they are focusing on a shooter/RPG hybrid where you have plenty of abilities to mix and match to make it the way you want to play. For myself, I did a stealth hacker and not sure if by default that is one of the more powerful ways to play the game, but wow you really start to wipe the floor soon. Beyond some set pieces, I realized early on that you can level very quickly and that sets you well above most enemies you will encounter. You will probably need to turn up the difficulty a bit to have that dangerous feeling they are intending their to be in the world. Cause by the end I'm hitting overdrive and forcing enemies to kill themselves before wiping out the remainder of enemies with a smart gun. f  As far as the story goes, its fantastic, but it has almost no build up unless you take the time to dive into the side missions. I would not rush the main story here as I think you will find that it is a pretty unsatisfactory trip without all the details you find in the side missions. The choices wouldn't have the weight they do without V having established the identity that he did. Though there are some filler quests in there so it might be best to play it by ear as well so you don't just get lost in the more boring quests.   Finally, Phantom Liberty is probably the best part of this game and I hope that the story it tries to tell and it's themes are something you see again. It's gritty, serious, and full of conversations with hidden depth. If you buy this game, don't miss this DLC with it.

As a big fan of the Witcher 3, I went into Cyberpunk 2077 with high expectations, but I can definitely say that those expectations were met. The combat system is also very flexible with many different weapon types and cyberware options for all sorts of different builds, and the game features a nice variety of enemies you can test your skills on. I also thought the soundtrack and radio songs were great, and appreciated the excellent voice acting in the quests. My only complaint about the game is that although most of the bugs were fixed since its initial release, I still encountered a few crashes and weird glitches throughout the gameplay, some of which were pretty funny. Overall, I'd give this game a 9.5/10, definitely an incredible and memorable experience!

This game has come around in a way that's hard to quantify.  While it was utterly broken on launch, over the intervening years it's become one of the best RPGs ever made, and handily meets the high bar left by CDPR's previous masterpiece, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt.  Even more impressive than the base game is the quality of the expansion, Phantom Liberty.  More than just adding content, it expands the already unmatched world of Night City, adds new characters, conversations, etc. but most of all, it's just got that sauce where you know you're engaging with something special.  That lift in quality has spilled over into the rest of the game, and now it not only feels feature-complete, but even a bit transcendent.  When you play this game, you don't feel like you're watching virtual puppets.  Those first-person conversations are so immersive, the biggest flaw is that you can't choose to respond however you please.  The gameplay experience is straight out of Deus Ex.  It's an immersive sim with deeper RPG elements than most games of the genre, and with more satisfying moment-to-moment combat than most as well.  The animations and sound design are stellar, and the visuals are simply among the best to ever be seen in a video game.  One aspect that deserves special praise is the music, which ends up conjuring the same transportive vibe as something like Grand Theft Auto, except instead of transporting you to Los Angeles in 2013, it transports you to a fictional futuristic city.  They do this by inviting tons of real-world artists to make music as in-world musicians, a creative challenge that leads to a suite of music that feels like you stepped into a Spotify playlist from an alternate timeline.  The effect is undeniable: the moment you're in a car driving through the city and you hear I Really Want to Stay at Your House, it feels like returning to a city you've been away from for a while.  I think that's the strangest great thing about this game: it could have easily been purely shock factor and spectacle, porn-adjacent slop with no artistic value.  And ironically the game dabbles in this regularly, but there's always a feeling of intent behind it.  The awkward, piercing moans of an orgasmic energy drink advertisement say more about the depravity of Night City than any monologue could.  In fact, with gore and nudity being so inescapable, it means that the moments of the game that really shine are those moments of deep, abiding humanity.  When a character opens up to you about her past, and lets you explore her home, you have a moment of realization that I've experienced numerous times in real life, "Oh thank God, I've found someone real in this place."  For a fictional video game to make me feel that way about characters made of polygons and pixels is perhaps the highest praise I could possibly give.

OK. Cyberpunk 2077 was a tough one for me. I started this game years ago, when it was still a buggy mess. I couldn't get into it. And not only because of the bugs. I couldn't get into the story. There was too much happening, too many characters introduced, too much cyber-lingo I didn't understand, until I was phasing out during the conversations. I gave up after the first 15-20 hours.  Came back to the game after Phantom Liberty, and decided to start a new character. It was a bit better, less bugs, and I had a better grasp of the world, story and characters. But it was still a bit much. I got lost with how much the game was throwing at me. I forgot who each person was, Got calls or messages from people I was supposed to know, but didn't remember, and couldn't give a s*** about. And I realized I wasn't enjoying the most important part of the experience: the world, the characters, the story. I was enjoying the combat, but going through the game just checking every icon on the map, not caring about anything or anyone. I stopped, and uninstalled.  After two years without thinking about it, I stumbled upon the great Edgerunners show. And it pulled me back into this world. I decided to do things right this time. Installed the game, and modded it to improve the experience as much as possible with the "Welcome to Night City" mod list. Started a new game, and went in with my mind set on really paying attention to the stories, not just completing tasks. And the game finally clicked for me.  This was a hard game to get into, specially since I am more of a casual player nowadays, being a dad and having two jobs. It took me 9 to 10 months to finish it, because I can't just do the main missions. I like seeing as much as possible, completing every fixer gig and side mission. The only things I didn't fully complete were the crimes, assaults, criminal activities and races.  Well, after so many hours, I was on the final stretch, and I couldn't stop. Stayed awake all night. I needed to see how it ended. And I am so glad I did it. It was rewarding, exhausting (in a good way). There are so many little things that make the world so authentic. Little call backs to previous events, characters I crossed paths with that show up, and recall what happened previously. It's fair to say, doing all those missions was worth it.  I really enjoyed some of the side content, and some deep, strong and uncomfortable topics the game touches on. I liked the moral ambiguities that are depicted. (Almost) nothing is ever black or white, and you're faced with some nerve racking decisions to make, many times not fully knowing the consequences of your actions. These are the things that stayed with me the most.  The ending was bitter sweet, but so fitting to this world. And I'm happy with the one I got. V's story ended on a sad but hopeful note, and open enough to interpretation that leaves room for me to imagine what comes next. Also, the people I cared about (mostly) got their stories wrapped up in a satisfying way, and I'm so happy I got to know them.   Although I'm NOT PLAYING THIS GAME EVER AGAIN, or any other open world RPG in the near future, I couldn't be happier of having decided to come back and giving Cyberpunk this last chance. It finally did it for me.  Can I recommend this game? YES. ABSOLUTELY YES. Specially with a few mods to improve the experience. It's not for everyone. It's very hard to get into, it demands too much of your time and energy, it has too many characters, too many stories, and they don't always work in sync with one another. It can get messy and confusing. The gameplay systems can also be a bit overwhelming, specially if you're not familiar with RPG mechanics.  But Night City is a place I'll never forget, and its people and stories will be in my mind for many, many years.

A flawed masterpiece...  Pros: - Graphics are gorgeous. Played without raytracing (didn't feel it added enough to warrant the drop in FPS), mix of high to very high otherwise, 4k around 100 fps throughout the whole game with one exception near the end where fps tanked in one scene (but it fixed itself before combat started). - The gameplay is great with many ways to play. Gunplay is good, but melee feels very satisfying as well with different options. Netrunning is also a very valid option, turning you into a god towards the end if you want, and more fun than you might expect. - Stories are interesting. The main one is pretty good, but especially many of the side quests. CDPR clearly is still very good at making things interesting. There are also some 'go here, shoot him, collect that' quests, but many are truly good stories. - Acting is very good overall, and it was fun having Keanu around (not to say his character is especially likable, but he has depth and development).  Cons: - BUGS! Oh my god, I can't even imagine how bad it must have been at launch since people say they fixed it up so bad. It's not like it's unplayable, but I've had many issues. Cars spawning upside down falling from the sky, camera stops following you while driving, getting hit in the street by invisible cars, getting ragdolled for no reason, motorcycle suddenly teleporting somewhere else the moment you get on... it goes on. I've not encountered many gamebreaking bugs, only had to load an old save once or twice (aside from quick save and quick load to fix things like the camera when driving), but it's still annoying. - Driving is really mediocre. Speed is faked, you apparently only drive about half the speed it says (someone did the math), and it doesn't feel fast at all. At one point I tested, I was passing other cars going 240 km/h and it felt like there was maybe a 30 km/h difference between us. Slowed down, they were going 70... Cars also have pretty bad handling. The traffic also has an issue where in the distance it will show fake cars... then when you get closer they disappear and when you get closer still, other cars (less) will spawn in. It's very jarring and not handled well at all. - The endings suuuuuuuuuck... I've seen a couple now, not all of them, but from looking online it doesn't seem like it gets much better. For some reason, CDPR seems to REALLY want to make sure you end on a low note. No happy ever after for V... The problem with this is, it makes everything feel futile. And that might not matter the first time, but this is a game made to be played many times.  - The worst was (minor SPOILER) when I'm making all my decissions just to get back to my in game girlfriend, as we said we would get away and leave the city together once my problem was fixed... only to get a voicemail during the credits that she's left already and wishes me a nice life... WTAF?! I felt so cheated and it made no sense at all. It just felt like CDPR saying FU to my face. Well FU2. - There are also annoying design decissions like how after every quest, the game automatically switches you to the main quest again. But the main quest is actually not that long and if you push too far in it, you get locked out of the rest of the game (and towards one of the unhappy endings). Also when you get a call about some other quest, the game switches you to that quest and you have to manually switch to what you were doing if you don't agree. There is a setting to have fixers not call you but only text, but I don't want to deny myself content just to fix this stupid design. - Quests also lack proper descriptions. In your journal you only see Johnny's ramblings. That in itself is pretty cool, but with how many side quests there are, often I will not remember why I have a certain quest and Johnny does not really tell me. So then a cool story might still devolve into a fetch quest again because you have no idea what's going on. - Cops are mostly still irrelevant... They are VERY easy to run from, they give up chasing you real fast. But, the one time I decided to try fighting them, already being a netrunning god, I died within a minute because the game escallates insanely fast. I was out in the desert, and infinite cops just spawned around me, until maxtaq showed up and just flatlined me (right through several cheat deaths, didn't stand a chance at all). This means there is zero reason to fight them, and zero reason to fear them when you don't actively engage them. So they're irrelevant, bad design.  All in all... yeah, it's still a great game and anyone that likes this type of game should at least give it a chance. I just think it's such a shame that they made certain decissions that actively make it worse than it could and should have been.

After the recent mega update, and really sitting down with this game for the first time...I can say this is one of the best single player games I've ever played, and one of the best games period. It's basically a first person GTA 6 before GTA 6 set in a real world inspired futuristic capitalist dystopia. That level of story and world building. With MUCH better combat and RPG mechanics, it's not even comparable.  The lore/setting and world building are incredible. It's set in a sort of dark semi-near future Tokyo/China inspired city state called Night City with crazy verticality, which is owned and controlled by several huge corporations and has apparently separated from what used to be the USA.  It's often funny and scary at the same time. The commercials on various TVs you'll walk by remind me of "interdimensional cable" from Rick and Morty. They really hit home that corporations have taken over the world in 2077, but also have depictions of violence and sexualization that are taken to comical extremes. If you play it in front of your wife or GF she'll be like "WTF" at many points so play it after she goes to bed.  The number of ways you can build your character is awesome.  You can have: -small pp -less small pp -no pp -crazy movement sliding teleporting double jumping assassin builds -big pp melee builds (blunt, blades, and fists...and even blades from your fists lol) -small pp sniper stealth builds -close range throwing weapon ninja stealth builds -hacker tree where you basically use slowmo V.A.T.S to place different negative effects on enemies -driving is legit better than GTA 5, and many dedicated racing games. Really unexpected how good the physics are. I leave a controller plugged in and hot swap. Driving with wasd in any game makes me want to slap a baby.  I recommend playing on hard, it makes you actually need to use strategy and think about smart upgrades to survive.  Some of the boss battles were tough and rage inducing when you get 2 tapped lol. But it's worth it. You can do it.   What's great about the difficulty settings in this game is that hard/very hard doesn't mean enemies become bullet sponges like the majority of other games (*cough* Borderlands) when they're lazy with it. At harder difficulties, the enemies are smarter and will flank and push you out of cover, shoot you though walls with tech weapons, quickhack you etc. Another thing is that guns all have unique bullet veolocity, tiers, upgrades etc. What is also something I've never seen in a game and most noticeable when your movement is upgraded is that you can dodge enemy shots by sliding, crouching, strafing, jumping, whatever. But not like, RNG in the game allowed you to not get hit based on whether you're behind cover or not. In slow-mo especially, you'll actually see the enemies shoot where you were or where they think you're going to go. There's even a tool tip that points this out.  It's awesome. Did not expect the combat to be so deep and rewarding of creativity.  There are 100 ways to tackle each fight/enemy. Full hacker build is like ez mode and feels like cheating (but still fun) if a person wanted to do that, even. Or you can turn yourself into a literal cyborg and chop people's legs off with 20 foot long metal wires that come out of your arms, shoot missiles out of your hands, or install "Gorilla Arms" and run around making your enemies' heads explode with robotic super punches. And that's just the "arms" slot. There are like 10 different body slots...   11/10 game. One of the undisputable GOATS, and crazy with how supremely mid it was at launch.

Cyberpunk 2077 is honestly one of those rare games that feels bigger than just a game — it’s an experience, and revisiting it on PC after already putting around 70 hours into it on PlayStation has only made that more clear.  I already loved my time with it before, but playing it on PC feels like seeing Night City the way it was truly meant to be experienced. The jump in visuals, smoother performance, higher frame rates, and overall immersion completely transform the game. It’s not just an upgrade — it genuinely feels like rediscovering the entire world again.  Night City itself is one of the most impressive settings ever created in gaming. The scale, atmosphere, verticality, and detail are on another level. Every district feels distinct, alive, and layered with its own identity. Whether you’re walking through neon-lit streets, cruising through crowded highways, or just taking in the city at night, there’s a constant sense that you’re inside something special.  What makes Cyberpunk 2077 truly stand out though is how much substance there is beneath the style. The story is gripping, emotional, and deeply personal, with characters that actually stay with you. V’s journey, combined with Johnny Silverhand’s presence, creates a narrative that feels both intimate and massive at the same time. It’s one of those stories that sticks in your head long after you stop playing.  Gameplay-wise, the freedom is incredible. Whether you lean into hacking, stealth, brute force, or a hybrid build, the game gives you so many ways to approach combat and progression. On PC especially, everything feels sharper and more responsive, making the gameplay loop even more satisfying.  And visually — this game is absolutely generational. Cyberpunk 2077 on capable hardware is one of the best-looking games ever made. The lighting, density, reflections, and environmental detail can genuinely feel next-gen in ways that few titles manage.  After experiencing both PlayStation and PC, I can confidently say Cyberpunk 2077 is a must-play title. It’s a game that pushed boundaries, evolved massively, and now stands as one of the defining experiences of its generation. This isn’t just a comeback story — it’s a modern masterpiece that every gamer should experience at least once.

Cyberpunk 2077 + Phantom Liberty An Honest Review From Someone Who Almost Quit  I nearly bounced off this game twice and I'm glad I didn't.  The honest scores Main game: 7/10.  Phantom Liberty: 10/10.  The world and side characters: 10/10.  The RPG systems once they click: 8/10.  If you want a single number, call it an 8 - 8.5 but that's not the whole story.  It is not the best game ever made. It is absolutely essential if you have a capable PC and the patience to let it breathe.   Slow down The game will tell you everything is urgent. It is not. I hit the main story point of no return in around 18 hours without feeling like I was rushing. The narrative momentum pulls you forward and the writing frames everything as life or death. Stop and turn around.  The enjoyment starts when you invest in the world rather than sprinting through it. Do the NYPD scanner huscles and gigs. Talk to the people. Spend your money on cyberware at the ripperdoc rather than hoarding it or on cars and apartments. You probably don't need to buy guns and you mostly end up with iconic weapons anyhow. Upgrade your build deliberately. The game only opens up when your character has shape and you have context for the world you're moving through.  If you hit the point of no return feeling underpowered and confused, you went too fast. The game will never tell you.  The side characters and their stories are frequently better than the main quest. Some of the best writing in the game is tucked into missions that look like filler on the map.   Pick a lane and go all in Do not spread your attribute points across multiple trees. Pick a build direction early: stealth, netrunner, blades, tech weapons and commit. The game does not tell you this and it will punish you badly in the early hours if you don't. The viable endgame builds are fewer than the skill trees suggest, though each plays differently once it coheres. That click moment, when combat finally feels like yours, is worth getting to and it's awesome.  On normal difficulty the game stops being challenging well before the halfway point, and I say that as someone who isn't a hardcore gamer. For me, the regular enemies feel like nothing much but the bosses are often dull and spongey. This is much worse on harder difficulties where the regular enemies feel about right but the bosses are nauseatingly boring. The gun handling feels good and the skill trees are much improved since launch, but a lot of the praise you'll read for both assumes a difficulty calibration that isn't there. If you want a test, play on hard from the start but be prepared for the early hours to be rough before your build sticks.  The world Night City is one of the most extraordinary environments ever built in a video game. The density, the verticality, the neon and rain and rot underneath the corporate gloss. There is nothing quite like it. However, it sometimes feels like a crowd scene in a film rather than a place that exists without you. But this was with the crowd setting a bit lower which I had to do with my PC. Your milage will vary here and we'll get to that soon. The NPCs wander but they don't quite convince outside of scripted moments.  Dogtown in Phantom Liberty is smaller, more curated, and fixes all of this. Every person there feels like they belong in that exact spot.  The open world underneath the beautiful surface is largely checkbox busywork. Scanners, gigs, and assorted map icons follow the same compulsive loop you'd find in any Ubisoft title, just dressed in better writing and a more interesting setting. You can mostly ignore it. But it's there and I enjoyed the ticking the boxes towards the end and quite liked getting all the acheivements. But I am a lapsed Ubi addict.  The music The soundtrack has a reputation for being exceptional and largely gets a pass in reviews. The reality is more uneven. Three or four radio stations are really great. Pacific Dreams is the obvious standout and earns every word of praise it gets. But several stations feel included for demographic coverage rather than tone, and a game that otherwise obsesses over atmosphere occasionally jumps into something weird mid-drive and pulls you straight out of it. Not a dealbreaker and the sountrack is great, but it's not this perfect thing people say it is.   A note on VRAM My 4070 Super has 12GB of VRAM and that is borderline enough for this game with path tracing on. If you push it too hard you won't get crashes necessarily, but you will get texture pop-in and stutters that make the game feel broken when it isn't. You need to monitor this actively.  Download MSI Afterburner and run the overlay while adjusting settings. Watch VRAM usage in real time. This is how I worked out that DLSS Quality was pushing me over budget while DLSS Balanced brought it under control, and that reducing shadow quality clawed back additional headroom. Those multiple shadow settings were key and you'll need to spend hours with settings. Those two changes together made the difference between a stuttery mess and a stable, beautiful game. I spent roughly ten hours getting settings right. Budget your time. If you have 8GB you will struggle significantly. 12GB is workable but requires careful management and 16GB will give you proper breathing room.  You need a real PC Steam Deck verified means it runs but it does not mean it does the game justice. Half the point of Cyberpunk 2077 is standing in a rain-soaked street watching neon reflect off everything. That experience requires proper hardware. I cannot believe this game shipped on PS4. That decision forced compromises you can still feel throughout the base game and is surely one of the reasons that Phantom Liberty is so much better.  The sweet spot on my 4070 Super was 1440p with path tracing on and DLSS Balanced. 4K sounds better but you sacrifice too much ray tracing fidelity for the resolution. Path tracing is breathtaking for a game where the entire aesthetic is built on light and reflection. It is worth the settings investment to get there.  Phantom Liberty — I say finish the main story first Do the main story first, then go to Phantom Liberty. I played it mid-late game, I was maybe 40 hours or so in and spent more than 20 hours in Dogtown meeting extraordinary new characters, then returned to the main game feeling completely disoriented. People I'd forgotten, momentum lost, a massive tonal shift back to a story I'd half left behind.  Phantom Liberty is a different and better game within the game. A well-paced spy thriller with outstanding writing, a paranoid atmosphere, and some of the best character work in any game I've played in years. It is essential. But treat it as a second act rather than an interruption. It's almost like another game. The two endings are worth playing seperately. Reload and do it again. Proper good stuff and I thought far better than the endings of the base game.  Overall... the onboarding is crap. The power curve collapses way too fast. The three lifepath options vanish after the prologue despite being sold as defining choices that shape your experience. These problems were never patched out and they got overshadowed by the redemption story.  Should you play it? Yes, if you have the hardware and the patience. No, if you want to sprint through it or you're on modest specs.  This is the Crysis moment of this generation. A game built ahead of the hardware that can fully run it. Path tracing on a capable PC is what it was always supposed to be. Phantom Liberty is what the whole game was always supposed to be.  I'll come back to Night City in ten years on whatever hardware exists then and think whoooaaa. I'm confident of that.

So I've had the game for a bit and played through the launch which has had enough said about it and the updates have been good overall.  Positives its a pretty good game and the narrative is fun to play through once in a while.  Some of the builds can get pretty fun.  I want to see what they do with the sequel.  Negatives-  The scaling... you actively become weaker as you level up as enemies outscale abilities. This just feels pretty ick as cyberware armor can get hilariously strong around lvl 20-30 (borderline invincible in some cases) but post that falls off like nobodies business and the gains from unlocking other aspects of the skill tree don't measure up to a very specific deliberately lower level scale character. Also suffers from enemies getting more spongy rather than smarter/more varied in ability which again means that keeping a character in a level sweetspot makes you feel stronger overall than as a maxed out/close to end game V.  Missed opportunities- the game feels like a lot of this. Gangs treat you the same whether you've been massacring them or playing non-lethal/non-aggressive towards them. This feels like missed opportunity to actually interact with the city. Furthermore there are 3 options to pick from on who supports you at the end... this feels off as there are several side characters you have moments you just want to scream at the screen to lend V a hand as they basically move heaven and earth for the sake of these side characters.  Missing content? This gets a question mark because some of it feels like a bit of deliberate mystery vs there is something missing but particularly with the Peralez section there are quite a few dangling plot threads that feels off. From Peter, to Mr. Blue Eyes, to Night Corps to potential AI interference it just drops off the map. Again that one could be a deliberate V needs to learn to leave things alone moments but it still feels off. Bartmoss is another where it feels like even if its not real might be something to check out rather than a throwaway easter egg.  Won't say who but some of the fixer's feel woefully underutilized in comparison to others. Even from a purely mission count standpoint it feels a bit like they were supposed to get some additions like Mr. Hands did in Phantom Liberty but just didn't.   Stealth gameplay- clearly got targeted over time as the updates went on. Very much a case of the toolbox might have been overtuned at the start but the game clearly has a "correct" way to go about stealth now rather than just silencers/netrunning. Some of the decisions I'd say were good but very much a case of this is the way the game is intended to be played not how people were doing it.  V also really could have used a personal antagonist and while yes the setting has the system itself as antagonistic fundamentally his vendetta's are Johnny's by proxy and trying to stay alive. While its very on brand for the corporate machine to not notice an insignificant cog its also possible to have some kind of personal connections a la Adam/Johnny which V is really just lacking.... dunno could have kept the impersonal nature overall as the overarching V vs the corporate culture but still had a bit more connection to one of its cogs.   Internal inconsistency.... there are things in the narrative that don't really add up to me. A case example being Regina's fascination with cyberpsychosis despite it being a kind of resolved thing... hell V has the opportunity to meet a reformed cyberpsycho embedded in a sidequest and the phenomenon isn't exactly unknown in the setting both causes and treatments and the game actually has an in universe example of a treated individual so.... ehhh. But there is a bit more floating that doesn't make sense.  As for the DLC.... the interaction between the NUSA and V is kind of a head scratcher. Ostensibly by the time they meet he's done something that they've quite literally fought world wars trying to do and were gearing up for another and they know about this... and its kind of an oh well no big deal you are still a hodunk merc lowlife.... it just feels more than a bit off if you stop to look at it for a moment. This kind of highlights another issue where the game feels very vertical slice of the setting and drops in a lot of little details that include the wider setting as hints and nuggets but functionally operates like it doesn't matter. Again referring to the Bartmoss thing is brushed over so quickly that it really doesn't give credit to what just happened. The man literally responsible for the state of the world and is acknowledged as such 50 years later and broadcast information about him is still referred to was just found to have been active for years after everyone thought he was dead and... what no one bats an eyelash at what might have been going on?  Anyways with all that said I'm still going to recommend the game for a play through or two and a return every once and a while for the things that make it worth playing. Just be aware its not flawless by any stretch and I hope that the next one follows in the witcher franchises footsteps and continues to improve from game to game.

My personal gripes for disliking the game are as follows: The way it is designed means you can do any kind of run or build an all around character and let me tell you the content and world building is to die for. But it begins to fall flat when there is not much variety in weapons due to them just being scaled into tiers of 1-5. This was a great RPG to play but there is no pacing with the side quests and a lot of the purchases you make can be avoided and you can just focus on getting Cybernetic augments and that becomes the game as become and evolved lifeform. You can ignore hacking, you can ignore melee combat you can ignore being a stealth build. Which is fine and proper but once you find a gameplay style that works for you the entire game stops feeling fun and its just a "go here and do this, kill x amount of people, get paid."  Still one hell of a story, one I admire but you see the flaws. V's story is one where there are no good endings only what you willing to sacrifice to go big or die in an unmarked grave. Once you put speed bumps on the story I find you can easily break this the perk systems so your playstyle moves from FPS to mass murdering simulation. Good if you want that but I honestly wish I knew more going into the Cyberpunk universe. Its a very old RPG and the California setting really did not to it must justice if you ask me.  I adored the characters and the journey. Hell I almost 200 hours into it. But its so good it misses out in other areas and many of the character customization features are designed for looks not for real immersion. Sure its got quality but to me its just another grind fest where you can ignore all the side quests and till have a fine time. That is a red flag for me. I have always been a fan of CD Projekt Red but trying to do a dystopian rogue AI landscape works except there are no monsters and the ruins of civilization for a corporate supremacy becomes a boring environment quickly. I felt drained and disappointed after completing the main missions in both Vanilla and Phantom Liberty because nothing improves in the world its just you signing off permanetly what is a well written world where technology replaces a good degree of mythology but so much is missing.  I would have loved to see real mutants or hybrids which do exist lore wise in the game but again, so much time and money was spent on making a high fi retro vibe for all designs and culture you see inside of 2077 it removes everything else. You remain a boring human with boring yet flashy character designs or customizations to your body but they really do nothing. You are in a vice grip of conflict that coexists such interesting character story arc's that once you realize not many of them end well the experience becomes draining but a ride worth taking once. Repeated playthroughs with making different choices offer some thrill and then its gone. Violently, you are left looking for the next thrill, firefight or something you didn't discover. Like the desert of the Mohave, this place dries you up fast.   You are in for a wild ride but don't expect any rewards long term. Feels good to become a badass and literally become the center of attention but how that plays into exploring anything beyond that? Its a hollow shell like those drained oil fields or trash heaps, and the world becomes very boring. I give them a 9/10 but personally the more I play and beat the game over and over again, the more I dislike 2077 with a heavy heart. I would have liked to see a game modeled after the original source material this RPG was molded by decades ago. But alas, my purist pursuits of old world RPGs and their iconic names means this game could never have lived long to my expectations.   Still I was fine paying 60$ for it, the quality and content is there but once you milk it all.....don't expect it to give anything back with interest. I am happy to say now I know what the hype is about. CD Projekt Red can make a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ killer story which remains emotionally charged and damaging. I just wish there was more options and variety. I don't hate this game but I expected more when it came to roleplaying. This plays like "Doomplaying" given how your main character is running out of time regardless of what happens.

I won't forget in the state this game was at release, even if I didn't purchase it then and purchased it after a few years, I still found a bug where at the prologue Ripperdoc Viktor drive, if you entered the car from the passenger's seat, the car would be stuck. At that time I just laughed it off and never played it again until after some time.  So at the light that I remember the buggy state, I can say for sure CD Projekt made their best effort to redeem themselves, a literal No Man's Sky scenario. After the bugs were polished and some content added, I fell in love with the game.  I was already a bit of a cyberpunk nerd, but this game ended up selling me the whole genre. The main selling point: The ambience. Night City is the definition of a high tech cyberpunk city, multiculturalism (specially oriental), neon, oriental influence, and lots of crime and poverty.  The story is also a good chunk of the package, having three routes to play with different branches and lifestyles (Nomad, Street Kid, Corpo) was truly brilliant, it allowed you to see the game from different perspectives and add replayability to the game.   Sadly, I wish it was more like Skyrim. It has the pseudo RPG vibes, but it lacks long-lasting replayability, as for now you only have the official content as a reason to replay the game, and I wish the game was more modding friendly to allow for the community to take the lead and keep the game alive. I'm aware CD made some advances in that scenario, yet still I'm eager to see a "Cyberpunk Skyrim" regarding amount of mod content.  Also I know the whole aspect of cyberpunk is to show corpos in a bad light, I just wish there was a more human path. I think that's why I like Goro so much, he's the most human part of Arasaka and corpos in general.  Anyways, final rate 8.5/10, still needs more replayability content, but a good redeemed game nonetheless

Cyberpunk 2077 is a breathtaking experience, visually, mechanically, and narratively. This is my second time 100% completing the game (first on Xbox, now post-Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty), and it still manages to pull me in in a way very few games can.  The jank and existential threat to your sanity that came with launch? Long gone. What remains is a genuinely polished, deeply immersive masterpiece that leaves you wanting more and maybe questioning your life choices along the way.  The base game alone delivers a thrilling story, packed with hours of side content, gigs, and jobs to keep any merc busy. The characters are compelling, and Night City feels truly alive… even if it’s mostly chrome, neon, and bad decisions. Since the 2.0 update, the game feels like an entirely new experience compared to my original playthrough, smoother, deeper, and far more engaging.  And then there’s Phantom Liberty, which is not just the icing on the cake, but the icing, the cherry, and the entire bakery. It’s that good. The expansion constantly shifts your focus, subverts expectations, and keeps you in a state of tension where you’re never quite sure who you can trust. Who’s really your choom? Honestly… probably no one.  The writing is exceptional. It takes the already strong character work from the base game and pushes it even further, diving into themes of loyalty, control, and survival. By the end, the idea of a “good” ending feels almost irrelevant, because in Night City, there really aren’t any. Not for V, and not for the people they care about.  I won’t spoil anything, but this game sticks with you. The sounds, the atmosphere, the skyline, it all lingers long after you log off.  And yeah… you are breathtaking.

This is a game with cybernetic implants yet there's so little ability to meaningfully change or augment your character. The story itself seems decent enough, there's good voice acting and facial animations, but the game refuses to break first person which can make the storytelling feel stiff and limited by this decision. I find it hard to immerse when protagonist V just feels like a camera & voicebox watching people talk rather than a living part of the world.  Combat is very bland & repetitive and there is just so much of it to get through. Driving is the absolute basic level of serviceable. This is a crowd-pleasing 'RPG' for those that just want to mindlessly kill things and experience a drawn out story, but for me it all just feels so empty and soulless despite trying to like it.

Before anything, I am saying this now: I will be spoiling the endings. And probably more of the story. I am also saying this: I played the game with some mods, and on the latest version, 2.31, with PL installed.  I didn't know what to expect out of Cyberpunk. Maybe an open-world game with RPG systems and semi-futuristic guns with a bunch of chrome tech too. Skyrim but in Night City, or something. This was my first CD Projekt RED game, and now I know full well why they are as legendary as they are.  The guns feel great, vanilla, DLC, or custom. The skill trees are unique, you can build the stats you want and find many ways to progress. By the end you're maxed out on everything if you know what you're doing, but you aren't punished for full-sending something.  Wanna go full netrunner with offensive quickhacks? Make like Dishonored and be a ghost that no one ever saw? Go in guns blazing with ARs and shotties and melee with some Berserk in your back pocket? Lure 'em all out with distractions and pick 'em off with silencers and snipers? Mix of all of it? Something else? Night City gives you that freedom if you grab it.  Until the end.  See, there's a handful of endings for the game. Everyone's gonna lean towards one of two. Temperance, where you let Johnny live a new life, and one he doesn't take for granted, because you, V, left an imprint on him. Or the Sun, where V puts it all on the line and achieves the goal he promised he and his best friend Jackie would get: Becoming a legend of the Afterlife.  Now depending on your choices, two other options open for you. You can sell your soul out to Arasaka, and help a samurai avenge his master, like a Devil would. Or you can choose to run away, escape Night City, and hit the open road with a clan of Nomads that treat you like family.  All of these are mutually exclusive to each other. What they aren't is mutually exclusive to everything else within Night City. Want to help the ones you meet? Take on gigs from every fixer from the oil fields to Pacifica? Win a few street races, a few bare knuckle brawls? See some saucy braindances? You can do all that and more. And that makes Night City feel alive. Like the beating heart it is.  And that's not even mentioning the little world within it. Dogtown, the storyline of Phantom Liberty. In essence, that story only gives V one ending and you have a 50/50 chance of even having it. Instead, you give someone else their four endings. You decide what happens to one Songbird. Do you send her to the stars? Send her home? Or do you choose to side with the NUSA and hand her over, denying her final request? Or do you honor that request and give her peace? Your choices decide what the Tower is.  This circles back to the endings. Of the five total (not counting the secret endings), none of them end well for V. Temperance? V is gone, lost into Cyberspace to give Johnny the body that selected him as it's owner. The Sun? Risking it all for a gig that could save your life. You're on a 6 month timer and it's counting down fast. The Star? Same gig. Riding out to Arizona and prayin' that those outside Night City have what you need. The Devil? Well, that one's your choice. Siding with Arasaka til the end, you're given a contract. Do you take the word of Takamura, and trust that when the time comes, there's a body waiting for you, but have no idea when or where? Or do you say to hell with it, and end your last 6 months of life on your terms? I know what I'd choose.  And then there's the Tower. The one ending that doesn't put V on a time limit.. but at what cost? If you make the right calls during Phantom Liberty, you have the choice to put your faith in NUSA to save your life. And they do.. but they leave you a mortal man. Not one capable of using cyberware or high tech guns or any fancy stuff. Just an ordinary choom on the streets of Night City. You survive, free to live YOUR life.. but was it worth it? Only you can pick that.  Of course, i'd be remiss not to mention your other option. You and Johnny can choose to end it all on your terms. Swallow a bullet and put an end to your story. Or, you and Johnny can go it alone. Strut in the front door of Arasaka Tower guns blazing. And this ties back to a question someone asks you in the game real early.  Live a long but quiet life? Or a short life that ends in a blaze of glory?  THAT is the beauty of Cyberpunk 2077. At the end of the day, it comes down to that question, that choice. And what you do with it and what you do to get to it.  What I picked, what I did, won't be what someone else did. And that's the point.  Every V carves their own path in life. As they should.  Play this game. You owe it to yourself to experience this story. You owe it to yourself to make it YOURS.  And heck, mod the game. I know I did. I was running around as a biosculpted exotic, with an early 60s Mustang at my call, and some extra firepower in my hands. And of course, with a car like that I had some proper music too. Blastin' some 2000s alt-rock and more. All what I would call preem.  This game is worth experiencing, chooms. Just remember... don't fear the reaper.

I got rather addicted to the gameplay loop I would find myself in. Once you find your preferred playstyle, it unlocks all the great things in this game. The gunplay and stealth were well balanced. The movement is rather smooth.  The story is compelling as are many side quests. I would also say, the vehicle handling is amazing. Most every vehicle you can get feels different in their own way. Turning was not always easy, but felt great. I could see a lot of potential if CD Project decided to go back to this kind of game, Id be incredibly interested right up front.  Going through the Phantom Liberty dlc, I found that more compelling (and possibly the ending) than the core game.  For some critique: It never really felt as deep with its systems as Witcher 3, but that is an unfair comparison. Totally different types of games. I complimented the gameplay earlier, but I fell into "my way of gameplay" early on. And from reading descriptions of augmentations one can purchase for their upgrades, I never felt compelled to branch out and try new things.   The world of Night City does feel huge, but in a container. I never felt small. But that may be in a way that you are limited to ground traversal at all times.  The voice acting is up and down, and will admit to playing male V, and found the voice acting grating. The accent continuously through me off. Since I was playing with Phantom Liberty, the quality and accents of certain characters change often.   A worthy get for a game. I got mine on sale. Id recommend  that if you want the complete game.

Cyberpunk 2077 delivers a rich and flexible RPG experience set in the breathtaking Night City. Rather than relying solely on its main story, it shines through its side missions, which are often just as meaningful and impactful. The central storyline is relatively short but engaging, driven by the relationship between V and Johnny Silverhand, whose presence adds tension and personality despite a somewhat stiff performance.  The game opens slowly, taking several hours to fully unfold, but once it does, it offers an impressive level of freedom. Night City is dense, visually striking, and filled with diverse locations, making exploration consistently rewarding. The structure emphasizes player choice early on, giving access to numerous missions that branch in different directions. While this can feel overwhelming and slightly disorganized, it also allows for highly personalized playthroughs.  Player decisions significantly affect both immediate outcomes and long-term story developments. Missions range from emotional to absurd, often blending tones seamlessly. Importantly, side quests are not just filler; they can unlock new endings and reshape the narrative in meaningful ways. The more time you invest, the more rewarding the experience becomes.  Character progression is flexible, allowing players to adapt their playstyle without heavy penalties. Combat evolves as you unlock new abilities, weapons, and cyberware, offering multiple approaches from stealth and hacking to aggressive gunplay. While not deeply complex mechanically, the variety keeps encounters engaging.  However, technical issues remain a major drawback. Bugs, animation glitches, and occasional performance drops can disrupt immersion, even on high-end PCs. While patches have improved stability, the experience is still not fully polished.  Verdict Cyberpunk 2077 is an ambitious and deeply engaging RPG that excels in player choice, storytelling, and world design. Despite its technical flaws, it offers a memorable and highly customizable journey through one of the most detailed open worlds in recent years.

Petit préambule : je rédige cette critique après deux runs complets (DLC compris) effectués début 2026.  Cyberpunk 2077 a fait couler beaucoup d'encre et suscité beaucoup d'attente suite à sa présentation à l'E3 et la diffusion de multiples trailers alléchants. Lorsqu'il est sorti, de nombreux bugs et des finitions bâclées ont fait les choux gras de la presse et enflammé les réseaux sociaux. Pourquoi me sens-je obligé de faire ce rappel des évènements passés ? Tout simplement car on peut constater qu'en 2026, après de nombreux patchs et une v2 salutaire, Cyberpunk 2077 me paraît être pleinement à la hauteur des promesses faites à son annonce.   D'abord, ce qui saute aux yeux, littéralement, c'est la beauté et la cohérence graphique du jeu. Il n'y a pas un recoin du jeu ou l'on ne sente pas le boulot et l'amour des artistes de CD Projekt. La moindre affiche, le plus petit bout de ruelle, le couloir d'immeuble le plus banal témoignent tous d'un sens du détail admirable.  La partie graphique est également magnifiée par une surcouche technique bien musclée qui à grand renfort de ray tracing (ou path tracing) produit des ambiances lumineuses et colorées qui renforcent l'atmosphère des lieux.   Ensuite, on est frappé par l'habillage sonore extrêmement touffu du jeu. Les longues promenades pédestres que l'on fait en jeu permettent de se sentir plongé dans cet univers grâce à de multiples couches de sons: des conversations, des jingles de pub, la circulation aérienne et automobile, des fusillades... Tout cela renforce l'immersion.  Quant à l'ambiance musicale, elle est particulièrement soignée. Les nombreuses pistes musicales dispensées par les multiples radios thématiques sont toutes excellentes et raccord avec l'univers du jeu. La bande originale n'est pas en reste avec de nombreux morceaux illustrant efficacement les différentes phases du jeu.   Le scénario nous met dans les chaussures d'un mercenaire débutant qui va au fil de ses aventures acquérir un statut légendaire jusqu'à un dénouement final qui ne manquera pas de vous surprendre ( plusieurs fins sont possibles, mais il n'y a pas de happy end à Night City). Toutes les missions, des principales aux secondaires, bénéficient d'un niveau d'écriture très élevé : il y a toujours des situations intéressantes, des personnages intrigants, des pans de lore à découvrir. Les dialogues sont particulièrement vivants et n'interrompent jamais le flow du jeu. Les choix du joueur ont des impacts appréciables sur le déroulé des échanges verbaux. Mention spéciale aux choix de dialogues liés aux compétences ou background du personnage principal qui apportent vraiment une variété bienvenue lors de multiples runs.  Enfin le gameplay est vraiment satisfaisant. Les fusillades sont toujours excellentes, avec de nombreuses combinaisons possibles entre les armes, leurs modificateurs et les compétences du personnage. Les capacités de hacking permettent vraiment d'enrichir l'approche tactique: utilisation des caméras de surveillance, explosion à distance d'éléments du décor, suicide des ennemis, affection contagieuse, cécité, surdité... La boîte à outils du joueur est très garnie et il n'appartient qu'à lui de se constituer son petit panier sur mesure d'armes, d' améliorations cybernétiques et de hackings. Différents builds sont ainsi possibles, du ninja adepte des armes blanches au gros bourrin spécialiste des explosifs et du shotgun en passant par le hacker adepte des armes aux munitions téléguidées. Il n'y a pas un build qui n'apporte pas son lot de surprises bienvenues ce qui apporte une rejouabilité bienvenue.   Vous l'aurez compris, Cyberpunk 2077 est un  jeu fantastique. Ce n'est pas les quelques bugs (jamais bloquants) ou les plantages (évitez le fast travel) persistant encore aujourd'hui qui vont vous empêcher d'apprécier ce qui est aujourd'hui à mes yeux l'un des plus grands monuments du jeu vidéo AAA moderne.

"The Greatest Comeback in Gaming History"  It is 2026, and I can finally say that Cyberpunk 2077 is the game we were promised back in 2020—and then some. If you were holding off because of the launch drama, the "Redemption Arc" is officially complete. This is now a mandatory experience for anyone who loves RPGs or immersive sims.  Night City & Atmosphere The city itself is the main character. It is the most dense, visually stunning, and atmospheric open world ever built. Now that the technical issues are ironed out and PS5 Pro/high-end PC support has peaked, walking through the neon-soaked streets of Japantown or the lawless slums of Dogtown is breathtaking. It finally feels "alive."  Build Variety & Combat (The RPG Core) The 2.0 and 2.1 overhauls changed everything. Combat isn't just about shooting; it's about Synergy:  The Cyberdeck/Netrunner Build: You can clear entire rooms without firing a shot by jumping from camera to camera, uploading quickhacks.  The "Sandevistan" Ninja: Using slow-mo tech to deflect bullets with a katana feels incredible.  The Synergy: Just like a good TD game, you can mix and match. Combine poison-tipped knives with hacks that spread on death, or use high-explosive arms with perks that make you immune to your own blasts. The skill trees are finally deep enough to reward creative playstyles.  Phantom Liberty & Story The Phantom Liberty expansion is the gold standard for DLC. It adds a spy-thriller vibe with Idris Elba that is arguably better than the main quest. The writing is mature, the choices actually feel heavy, and the emotional payoff is brutal in the best way possible.  Performance Note Unlike the early days, the game is now remarkably stable. It's no longer a "resource hog" for no reason; the optimization is top-tier. Even on mid-range hardware, you can get a smooth, beautiful experience.  Pros:  Impeccable Storytelling: Top-tier voice acting and cinematic direction.  True Build Freedom: Every perk feels like it adds a new way to play.  Visual Masterpiece: Still the benchmark for "Next Gen" graphics in 2026.  Cons:  Initial Grind: The first few hours have a lot of dialogue and setup (though the payoff is worth it).  Driving: While improved, the vehicle physics can still feel a bit "floaty" compared to dedicated racing games.  Final Verdict Night City eventually wins, but the journey to the top is the best 100+ hours you can spend in a digital world. Don't skip this one.

I finally put real time into Cyberpunk 2077, and honestly—it’s a completely different game compared to launch.  The biggest thing that stands out is how immersive Night City feels. The world is packed with detail, and just driving or walking around makes it feel alive. Between the lighting, sound design, and overall atmosphere, it’s one of the best-looking open-world games out right now.  Gameplay-wise, there’s a ton of freedom. You can go full gunner, stealth, hacking, or mix everything together. The combat feels smooth now, and the skill trees actually let you build your character how you want. Gunplay has weight to it, and cyberware upgrades make a big difference.  Story is where the game really shines. The main story pulls you in, and the side missions aren’t just filler—they’re actually worth doing. Some of them hit just as hard as the main storyline.  Performance has improved a lot too. It’s way more stable now, and most of the bugs that killed the game at launch are gone. It finally feels like the game that was originally promised.  That said, it’s not perfect. NPCs can still feel a little lifeless at times, and some systems don’t go as deep as you’d expect for a game this big. But overall, those issues don’t ruin the experience.  Final Verdict: Cyberpunk 2077 went from a disaster at launch to one of the best RPGs you can play right now. If you skipped it before, it’s absolutely worth picking up.  Rating: 8.5/10

I have my Steam library on a very fast Samsung external SSD (USB 3.2, 10 Gb/s) because Apple charges ridiculous prices for more disk space, so I'm not sure if this helps or hurts.  So how does it run and how does it compare to the PS5? I run it frame locked at 60 fps because I don't see the need to run any higher and it's rock solid at that rate. If I unlock the frame rate, the benchmark gives me 71 fps average, so not much difference. Ray tracing doesn't seem to add much to the graphics, but that could be because my eyes are shot. Turning ray tracing on sends the frame rate in the benchmark all over the place from a high of 112 to a low of 41 with a 61 fps average.  Compared to my experience with the game on PS5, the game loads slightly faster and the draw distance is much better. Pop-in was very noticeable on PS5 and though it's not completely gone, it's much better. The game is also very stable on MacOS. I think I've had maybe 4 or 5 crashes over 300 hours, but a couple of those were probably caused when the SSD intermittently disconnected. As for thermals, let me put it this way: I haven't burned my thighs. The laptop gets warm, but never uncomfortably hot and fan noise is barely noticeable. I normally run off of the AC adapter, but sometimes the MagSafe connector falls off and I don't notice. Unplugged, it'll be about 1-2 hours before I see a battery low warning or the frame rate goes to hell.  So if you have a Mac and wonder whether it can play this? Well, I can't say how well it runs on lower end Macs, but it helps to have one of the higher-end CPU's and lots of RAM. If you short on SSD, get a fast external and problem solved.

Cyberpunk 2077 is a very good game with a lot of personality and an incredible atmosphere. Night City is genuinely one of the most impressive open worlds ever made, both visually and artistically. Even on older hardware, the game runs surprisingly well after all the updates and optimization work.  The story is strong, the main characters are well written, and the game allows for decent roleplay and replayability similar to The Witcher 3, your V can feel quite personal depending on your choices and attitude.  Gameplay-wise, the game has great potential, although some systems can feel clunky and overcomplicated, especially progression and stats management. Boss fights are probably one of the weakest parts of the game: several of them feel poorly balanced or frustrating rather than genuinely challenging.  The difficulty balancing also has a Skyrim-like problem. If you start on a high difficulty, the early game can feel unnecessarily punishing, but if you stay on Normal later on, your character eventually becomes overpowered and destroys almost everything too easily.  One thing that deserves more praise is the driving. After the patches, driving in Cyberpunk became genuinely enjoyable, and honestly, some vehicles feel better to control than in certain games that are entirely focused on driving mechanics.  Overall, despite some frustrating design choices, Cyberpunk 2077 became a beautiful, memorable, and technically impressive RPG that is absolutely worth playing.

It was what happened afterward.  Instead of abandoning the game and moving on, CD Projekt Red stayed. They listened. They worked. Back then, I only knew CD Projekt Red as the studio behind The Witcher 3—a game that I considered nearly impossible to surpass. The same feeling I had when I first played GTA: San Andreas. The same feeling I had while journeying through The Witcher and its DLCs. Even without reading the books, Geralt became one of the most iconic protagonists in gaming history.  Whatever comes next, I trust CD Projekt Red. Because they've earned that trust.  To every writer, artist, animator, designer, composer, programmer, and developer who helped create these worlds—  Thank you.  Thank you for the sleepless nights.  Thank you for the laughter.  Thank you for the heartbreak.  Thank you for the memories.  And thank you for proving that when passion meets talent, video games become art.  Whenever I buy a CD Projekt Red game, I know I'm not just buying a game.  I'm buying a world.  A cinematic experience.  A journey.  And a memory that I will carry with me until I grow old. One of the best games ever made, for a lot of reasons.  1. The Story  - Masterfully done, never a dull moment when it comes to the plot of this game. The twists and turns will have you hooked and desperate to play that next story mission.   2. The World  - I believe this game accurately depicts a version of Mike Pondsmith's Cyberpunk. While a few small details are perhaps missing, cyberpunk fans will love this game.  - THERE IS SO MUCH DETAIL. Everytime you play this game again you find something new, and it really shows just how much work the devs put in when building the world.   - You never run out of stuff to do. Even when you complete all the side quests and side content for this game, you can still find things tucked away in the nooks and crannies for you to explore.   3. The Combat  - THRE IS INFINITE BUILD POTENTIAL IN THIS GAME. Whether you min max. or play a generalist, pretty much any build you can think  of will be viable, and it always makes me want to go back and start over completely to try something new. You wanna play a tank that absorbs bullets and smashes gonks? You can do that. You wanna play a stealthy hacker that kills majority of enemies before combat even starts? You can do that. You want to be a total badass with a pistol and crazy  movement? You can do that. You want to be a tank, hacker, and total badass? You. Can. Do. That.   - The actual combat and gunplay in this game is soooooo unique. There's so many differentt ways to play. You can utilize cover and hit and run tactics with a stealthy build. You can bring a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ SWORD to a gunfight and utilzie crazy movement mechanics and hack away at gonks. You can do none of that, stare at people, and fry their brains before they can even unholster their weapon. Wanna be a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cyber ninja with swords, throwing knives, and flys from enemy to enemy? DO IT. You wanna casually walk down enemies with a shotgun and (litterally) rip and tear through enemies like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ doom guy?? DO IT.   - All in all, never a dull moment in this game when it comes to shooting people, or cutting them open...  4. The Progression System  - As stated before, this game has INFINTE BUILD POTENTIAL, and my favorite progression system of all time. Leveling up in this game feels sooooooooo goooood. A single perk can change the entire way you play, and once you start getting a lot of perks, you can start killing a lot of gonks, with the master level perks turning you into a total cyberpunk. - The attribute system is perfect. Opening certain areas or doing certian things in dialogue sometimes requires a certain amount of attribute points, litterally affecting your personality in game, which is CRAZY.   5. The Side Content  - All of the gigs are unique and are well put together. All of them have some story element that is interesting and sometimes funny, and a lot of times ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up, which is the cyberpunk way. I never feel bored when doing the side quests, ESPECIALLY in the Phantom Liberty Expansion, where everything is turned up to the max.   This game had a terrible launch, and it's a realy shame, because this game could've had the potential to surpass super big games like GTA. This game has improved so, so so much. I would reccomend the game to everyone, worth every single dollar 10 times over.

[i] “Let us go then, you and I, When the evening is spread out against the sky…” [/i]  CDPR managed to create a world that’s perhaps one of, if not the most immersive world I’ve ever experienced in video games. Night City genuinely feels lived-in, and it’s full of places to explore, characters to meet, and things to do.  The story narrative is gripping and hits on a unique, personal level. Your relationship with V and how you manage to endure and survive with them is a dramatic projection of our lives and how we find ourselves in situations that force us to question our own identities and what we stand for. That along with the more dark, mature themes, such as corporate colonialism and the fall of society - which I find rarely explored in video games especially with this level of depth.  As for gameplay mechanics, you’re in complete control over choosing your playstyle and building your own perk tree - RPG textbook. There’s a wide variety of weapons, cyberware, quickhacks, clothing items and even vehicles that will fit your style and help you progress through the game.  Though, some people are still claiming it’s clunky and unplayable, even after all these fixes. I’d absolutely suggest not listening to them. In fact, don’t go out with them. Might as well consider cutting ties with them.  Sure, a game with this sheer magnitude and scope is prone to have a few flaws or even a bumpy launch, but that doesn’t take away from the overall experience it has to offer.  Bottom line is, there’s something for everyone in Cyberpunk 2077. It will take you down a path full of wonders. You’ll find yourself in a strange place faced with questions. [i] Where do we go now? [/i] is a reflection in your rear-view mirror and the answer lies in the next stop.  The best thing I can tell you is to experience it yourself and become fully immersed in its world. Even after beating it a couple dozen times and unlocking that sweet 100%, I'm still cruising around the city blasting [b] Samurai [/b] over the radio and finding things I’ve never seen before.  [i] NEVER FADE AWAY [/i]

Absolute Cinema!  Cyberpunk 2077 is a neon drenched body in a Capitalistic Dystopian world. The way V (one of the best written protagonist) tries to be a legend in a city that only cares about blood, money and sex is nothing sort of an epic in itself. Now they are complex characters that you feel like, you wish to know about, Yet their questlines are small, interactions are quick and as soon as their stories completes. It makes progression feel significantly better as your cyberware really does build up, and the game WILL kick your butt until you reach that stage. Become a Netrunner that kills before anyone else sees you, or a Desperado from Metal Gear Rising with some heavy & sharp Mantis Blades.  For example, I set out for a "Gorilla Arms" build and at first I had to draw out Cyberpsychos from their den so I could run them over with my car. PERSONALLY however I found this game hits a point where many elements I prize in a game: discovery, leveling up, upgrading, enemies hit a plateau, somewhere about 50% through the game. You start to see a limit to the guns/builds, a repetition in the enemy engagements, a been there done that to the quests, so on and so forth. I come from traditional Borderlands/Fallout/Skyrim esque open world plays where it felt like there were no matter how many times or long you've played, the game can find a way to surprise you. Not CP2077. I also found the emotional hook of the game quite shallow. I wasn't particularly invested in any characters' plight, least of all my own. The romancable characters were okay, rather one-note, and with limited interactions so if you wanted the immersion of V leaning on them for relief or escapism, you don't very far. By the final 90% of the game I found myself quick-tabbing through all the dialogue of the game in general.  As far as actual game function goes, seems as of 2026 the majority of the bugs are gone. Ironically in the first 5 minutes of cinematic some chars were T-posing, but other than that, everything seemed to work the way it was supposed to. Only 2-3 times over 80+ hours of play did I have to reload a game since an NPC wasn't moving to the next checkpoint.   I'm glad I played it through to see what all the hubaloo was about. Would not replay and give me a year or two and I probably won't remember much about it.
