[h1]One of the best stories I've ever lived through[/h1]  For once, no decision felt 100% right. The narrative speaks to you personally and it reflects your own ambitions and ideals as a person. Felt good finally seeing the game polished enought to enjoy it properly, even though there are minor flaws, the gameplay is amazing and worthy of an RPG, no combat felt dull independently of the build choice. The worldbuilding is beyond belief, few games made me feel that immersed. Hard to have a story-driven singleplayer game to keep me actively obsessed for 300+ hours.    SPOILERS AHEAD (my takes)   [spoiler] It was extremly interesting having my own take/perspective of the situation being respected the entire time. I felt like a man living with borrowed time (from Jackie) and trying to make the most of it. The actualization of late stage capitalism was amazing to witness as well, I just can't express how much I liked the parallel stories and how they turned out in different runs. My last one as Male Corpo V was the one that satisfied me the most. Accepting that there are things we cannot change and trying to make the best of it was an interesting experience. Having Judy not suffer the Clouds massacre and leaving (becoming actually happy in the end), even if it meant leaving it all to the Tyger Claws. Having to kill Reed (loyal soldier, would've died like that sooner or later) to give a second chance to Songbird even after her betrail (I couldn't help but to feel sorry for her, an animal trying to survive, just like us). Alena having her "spy retirement" to Monte Carlo (nice post card). Giving Johnny his revival of his old days of glory (Samurai perfomance, Rogue romance), becoming friends with the very own thing that is killing you. Panam romance (the Jackie toast on the campfire was what made me change to Male V and replay the whole game just to get with her). The small gig stories and side missions made the game feel so alive and complete. Narratively, The Star ending was my favourite. In life, we struggle to find a sense of belonging, personally, I've found it in people I love and choose as family. Conections make it all worth it, independently of where you are.  Maybe there are happy endings in Night City.[/spoiler]

So far I've been really enjoying this game.   [h3] Story and setting [/h3]  I've been positively surprised by the quality of the story and setting. I thought it might just feel like a mindless Nvidia GPU ad, but I feel like it has heart. I love the inspiration it's taking and showing from works such as those of William Gibson, Ghost in the Shell, Akira, the Matrix and Mad Max. As a fan of the cyberpunk genre this game really doesn't disappoint. You see familiar things everywhere and it really makes my heart sing. There are easter eggs related to other franchises, [spoiler] such as Portal [/spoiler], as well. You have futuristic vehicles, computer-controlled robot spiders, people entering "the net" or even being digitized. Futuristic weapons, AI and robot people. Japanese tradition mixed with future tech. Everything you'd expect from a cyberpunk epic. It's very nice.  I love Night City, it feels like a place set in the future. It's a sprawling city, where technology is always present. You see flying vehicles glide across the sky and holographic ads everywhere. The mega corporations dominate the scene with their huge buildings, not to mention how they dominate politically. So you feel the tension and dynamics between the crime-ridden streets, the police department, military, street gangs and corporate affiliates.  I love the characters. You have the super sweet Jackie Welles who invades your heart and all the love you see within his family. You meet street criminals, desert nomads, corporate people, netrunners, etc. All with their own personalities and desires. So I'd say the story feels immersive. I love how people make you a part of their lives, asking for help when they need it, inviting you to funerals when someone died, asking to talk when they're feeling down. It's fun to see what people have going on and to be a part of it. You're also often given dialogue options and it does give you a sense of agency although it's unclear to me how big of a difference the choices make.   [h3] Graphics and performance [/h3]   I run the game with the RT medium setting at 1440p with FSR 2 set to Quality. But with RT shadows turned off. FPS vary depending on scene, most of the time laying around 50-60 fps. Sometimes it's over 60 too. While riding a vehicle it's typically 40-50 fps. I'm sad that I can't have RT reflections on, I feel like it would make a big difference visually, but it pulls my fps down to the 30s. :'( Maybe some day I'll upgrade my gpu and experience that. Personally I'm pleased with the performance, but I'm not very sensitive to fps. I can be really bothered by poor 1% frames but I feel like in this game the framerate is pretty steady at all times. Even if it drops a bit lower, at least it's steady instead of having sudden drops or jitter or anything like that.   Graphically it looks great too. Sometimes I feel the uncanny valley of something looking photo-realistic, but typically you can tell it's a game. The lighting looks really good in my opinion. You can also tell the artists went all out putting lights and volumetric fog everywhere to add to the ambiance. I think it works. Bars and clubs feel atmospheric in their own futuristic way.   [h3] Sound design and music [/h3]  Speaking of atmosphere, the sound design is phenomenal. Right as the game is loading you hear these futuristic, digital-sounding noises that really set the tone. Then in the main menu you get a similarly futuristic atmospheric track and you already feel like you're being transported to another time, where people have robotic enhancements and have brain computer interfaces that they use to connect to the internet. Or at least I feel that way. The sonic atmosphere on the streets of night city feel like you're really in a futuristic town. You hear the people and cars, music from nearby restaurants, ads constantly blaring and the sound of flying cars buzzing somewhere above you. I love the music in the game. It's super nice to ride to the next mission while watching the scenery and listening to the radio in your car or bike. I also love the music during fights, it's high-adrenaline, pumping future music that really gets your heart pumping.   [h3] Gameplay and mechanics [/h3]  For me this game had a bit of a learning curve. It has you go through a bit of a tutorial in the beginning and to be honest the gameplay felt pretty intimidating for me. I did not understand how to be stealthy and get around or neutralize targets without being seen. So for quite a while I'd just get spotted, even in stealth missions, and end up in a big firefight. For quite a while I'd put off playing this because I felt intimidated and like I wasn't good enough. The game doesn't hold your hand just as much as some other games do. There can be more than one approach to finishing your objective and the game doesn't fail you for being spotted.  But over time I started to figure it out. It often does guide you through its design, even though I didn't notice it at first. Now I'm glad it doesn't hold your hand and gives you freedom to deal with things how you want. I also had to swallow my pride and accept using the quicksave and -load function. It's just a lot more fun that way. It frickin sucks to be spotted and blast your way through a stealth mission and feel like you messed up. Sometimes that happens because I expected something to work differently than it does in the game. For example in one mission you're looking for stached money in a casino. Even going near the door leading to the second floor suddenly triggers an all out gunfight from the guards. How was I supposed to know that would happen? But when you do manage to sneak around unnoticed and take care of guards silently, it's very satisfying. It's also actually not too difficult which feels nice. Sometimes MGS felt too difficult for me personally, this feels more like something I can handle.  I also felt intimidated by the abundance of menus. You have skills and perks, equipment you can wear, crafting, enhancements and consumables. It can feel overwhelming. But it's fun to learn new perks and see how it gives you new abilities to use when sneaking and fighting.  Anyway, I haven't finished the story yet and I don't know how far along I am. But so far I've been thoroughly enjoying it and am playing a bit every day. I love the variety in the missions you get and how you can at least seemingly decide how to relate to missions and different people. Too bad the story will end at some point, but I am looking forward to how it all ends. Wonder if it has multiple endings... Guess we'll see. :)

Cyberpunk 2077 is a game that borders on greatness but ultimately fails to achieve it. Nevertheless, I truly believe that everyone should experience this game at least once in their life. A truly unique experience that only CD Project Red could have produced  [Performance and Optimization]  In its initial release, Cyberpunk was lambasted for its poor performance and optimization, as well as being riddled with bugs. In the current year however, Cyberpunk 2077 is a feast for the eyes and runs phenomenally. Additionally, in my current 47 hours of gameplay, I have only observed a single bug. This complete turnaround speaks to the dedication of CD Project Red towards their fanbase and they should be commended for taking the criticism and actively working to make the game better.  [Story and Environment] Cyberpunk is often touted as an action role-playing game set in an expansive open world. While this can serve as an apt description for the game, in practice. this description falls apart. The main story and many of the side jobs  attached to primary characters for the most part, are extremely well done, with amazing writing, voice acting and animations that bring everything together in a neat package. Problems with the story arise whereby the player is presented with a multitude of choices and methods to complete given missions. However, there are no consequences for any player actions and to this extent, your choices ultimately don't matter.   Night city is an expansive, visual spectacle but there is practically nothing to do in the city. If you go into this game expecting to have random NPC missions, dialogue and activities such as in Fallout or Elder Scrolls you would be greatly disappointed. NPCs on the streets are basically non-interactable with the majority having only single lines of dialogue. Missions are given via phone call, so all the game's important characters will just contact you to do missions as long as you attain the relevant level and street cred. As such, outside of finding collectibles and completing missions for steam achievements, there is ZERO incentive to explore Night City.   [Gameplay and Systems] Gameplay is extremely fun with a variety of upgrades, weapons and vehicles that all feel great to use and experiment with. The game's systems are a bit complex at the start, but as you continue through the story and the open world, they are integrated seamlessly.  The game's cyberware upgrades in the beginning are substantial but as you go further up the tree, they become mostly minor stat upgrades with no substantial effect on gameplay.

Cyberpunk changed the way I think about games. Firstly, the storytelling is astounding; you have the power to decide dialogues (I would like to highlight this). Each decision you make is based on your behavior, such as story path (Nomad, Street Kid, Corpo) and attributes (Body, Reflexes, Cool, Intelligence, Technical Ability, and Relic).  Despite the freedom, there is no massive impact on the narrative; however, you can know more about the characters or quests just by asking. Each life path has a different beginning and choices of dialogue. It means that a "Street Kid" could be more of a hustler due to knowledge of local gangs, fixers, and slang. A "Nomad" is the outsider; you are a traveler who lives in the Badlands with your clan, the Bakkers or Aldecaldos. In addition, you are an expert in repairing machinery, fixing cars, and securing resources—kind of a smuggler. As a "Corpo," you are in charge of a huge company that controls the majority of society's sectors. Consequently, your choices result in tiny gifts or different quest lines.  Furthermore, Night City has a bunch of things to do, such as gigs, police scanners, side quests, secrets, car races, and so on. Likewise, the city is gorgeous; each corner is extremely well-designed. Each neighborhood is well-developed, from the richest to the poorest, and their NPCs' outfits too. In addition, we notice gang fights, car pursuits, and spots dominated by them. It's always a pleasure riding to the North, South, or Badlands to appreciate the colors, either during the day or night, within opposing seasons.  Nevertheless, facing gang spots provides you with substantial resource gains to spend on whatever you want—for instance, clothes, weapons, cars, or apartments. Moreover, the core attributes are split into Body (fortitude), Reflex (agility/dash), Intelligence (hacking), Technical (explosives), and Cool (stealth). You are in charge of your playstyle.  In summary, CD Projekt Red built a game with originality and identity. A quick tip: if you want to get 100% achievements, the time will probably be around 100h+.

To be honest the only thing I have against the game itself is the performance of the game on common hardware at its time of release. After years of patches the game has been purged of most of the bugs but the performance was never really brought to the level that makes it truly accessible.   In regards to the gameplay and the story, well it works I guess but the years of marketing presented a product that has turned out to be less of an RPG and more of a Far Cry style open world shooter. In demos we were presented with a story that would be defined by non linear progression and player autonomy that would rival and ultimately supersede previous RPGs such as Fallout: New Vegas. Instead what we ended up with was an on rails system more like Fallout: 3, where your given illusions of freedom that ultimately course correct you back to the destined path. One of the main themes of the game is the idea of fate, a lack of control over the world, and the daunting seemingly unstoppable institutions and mechanisms that your powerless to do anything against but instead of the main story addressing those themes in any meaningful way the story just focusses on what I can only describe as  Vs "shenanigans", a series of quests that might as well be side quest's as they all turn out to be inconsequential and barely related to the main story. The DLC is the shining example of this where for some reason V is asked to save the president of the United States by infiltrating a city controlled by a paramilitary organization. Upon learning that you HAVE to save the president upon starting the questline for some arbitrary reason or else she kills you I decided the best and most reasonable course of action was to just run away from this strange call for help from a person I've never heard of and go back to doing laundry for Takemura or something like that. This is really the only type of dilemma you see in this games quests, either you do something or you don't and everyone dies, or literally nothing happens and the story continues like nothing happened. The president dying literally has no impact on the games ending or world as with most other major quests in this game, not because they wouldn't have an impact to some degree but because CD project red just it just too lazy to present those consequences in subtle or meaningful ways, just like Bethesda I guess.   Anyways besides that Refused did a good job portraying Samurai, Keanu Reeves did a great job voice acting Johnny Silver hand, and if your looking for a Far Cry style shooter then here you go. Cyberpunk 2077 feels like a true masterpiece. Every action you take and every ending you reach never gives V a truly happy conclusion. No matter what you choose, there’s always a sacrifice—power, soul, or even the people around you. That’s what makes the experience so impactful. CD Projekt Red created a world where I didn’t just play the story—I felt it and got completely immersed in it. Every decision carries weight, and every ending stays with you. Truly a masterpiece.

I went into this not really knowing what to expect, but by the end I can say I’d recommend it, especially if you’re into near-future sci-fi with light RPG elements.  What stuck with me most wasn’t the combat or even the world at first. It was the characters, and how much of them is only revealed through the endings. There isn’t a clean, perfect resolution waiting for you. Every ending I reached left me feeling at least a little conflicted, and that feels intentional. The game leans into themes of sacrifice and justice, even more so in the DLC, and the different conclusions do a great job of reframing what you thought you knew about people. Seeing those different sides is where a lot of the replayability comes from.  The characters themselves have more depth than they initially let on. Motivations aren’t spelled out, and your understanding of people shifts the more time you spend with them. That was especially true for some of the DLC characters. I found my opinions changing as I saw more of their perspective.  Johnny Silverhand is probably the best example of this. He starts off feeling one-dimensional, almost like a stereotype, but that impression doesn’t hold. The more you learn about his past, and especially if you take the time to engage with optional conversations, you start to see the regrets and reasoning behind who he is. He became a much more empathetic character than I expected.  The world itself feels immersive, and a big part of that comes from those hidden motivations. It feels like people have their own agendas, whether you fully understand them or not.  Gameplay-wise, I liked how flexible things felt. You can approach situations however you want, whether that’s stealth, direct combat, or using quickhacks alongside either. I started off playing it safe, sneaking around with a silenced pistol and relying on quickhacks. Over time, I shifted into a more aggressive style, running in with mantis blades. That change didn’t just feel mechanical. It felt like a natural progression for my character. Going from someone unknown to someone with a reputation, maybe even infamous, fit well with the world.  If I had to point out a downside, driving can feel inconsistent. I had trouble judging corners at times, though that might just be on me.  Overall, I’d recommend it. It’s not perfect, but if you enjoy strong character writing and morally complex choices, there’s a lot here to appreciate.  Achievements achieved at time of review: 57/57

Секс, кибер-люди и рок-н-ролл. Игра очень сильная в плане сюжета и затянула с головой на несколько дней. Было прикольно и интересно проходить её на разные концовки. В первый раз я только изучал этот мир, поэтому пришел к финалу за корпоратов. Думал, что на этом всё, но потом решил пойти на другую концовку и уничтожить «Арасаку».  Во время второго прохождения стало еще веселее: игра ощущалась гораздо динамичнее, я начал активно выполнять другие миссии и закрыл ветки Панам, Джуди и Джонни. При повторном прохождении было сложнее выбирать варианты ответов в диалогах, так как понимание, что они реально влияют на отношение персонажей к тебе. Единственный раз, когда я пошел наперекор это квест с гонками от Клэр. Я решил поехать к финишу вместо того, чтобы убивать типочка который убил ее "мужа". Честно говоря, изначально, увидев флаг на её машине, вообще не особо хотел с ней ездить. После моего выбора она перестала со мной общаться, но мне было на это пофиг.  По геймплею: тут всё решают пушки и импланты (двойной прыжок и киберимплант на замедление времени  это мастхэв). Евродоллары фармятся элементарно — просто собираешь оружие и продаешь в почтоматах. Ближе к концу, когда ты уже сильно прокачан, деньги копятся сами собой, потому что с врагов падает куча легендарок, которые стоят очень дорого.  В итоге я вышел на концовку с Панам, и оно того стоило. Единственное, чего хотелось бы чтобы Сол и другие ребята из Альдекальдо остались живы, а то к финалу мы приходим всего вчетвером. После этого мы остаемся без Джонни и покидаем Найт-Сити. Очень понравились видеосообщения в титрах: Джуди, Виктор, Мама Уэллс, Мисти и Митч искренне рады тому, что ты выбрался из этого города.  Моя оценка — 9/10. Есть легкое ощущение, что игре всё же чего-то немного не хватает, но эмоции она дарит отличные. И возможно в будущем пройду на остальные концовки и приобрету DLC.

This is simply the best story focused RPG of the last decade or more. The story, characters and universe is just superb, and the city is an amazing place to explore. The gameplay is fun and varied, to the point where you can build and roleplay vastly different characters.  And speaking of different characters, it is wonderful to replay, as doing things different will open up loads of hidden reactions and changes to things. Every part of the game is interwoven with everything else, so even thousands of hours in, you will still find new details or connections you never realised before. Like often you will realise that seemingly separate events like a bigger side mission, a smaller side mission, one or more open-world events, and various hidden little notes all spread out over the entire map and across hundreds of hours are actually connected through events or characters. There are also a bunch of different endings that you can choose from based on how you want to roleplay your character.  Definitely recommend everyone interested in great story-telling give this game a chance.

This is hands-down the best game I have ever played. Steam only shows around 100+ hours for me, but that's just part of the story—trust me, I've sunk way more time into it. I played hundreds of hours on GOG (easily 300+ across multiple playthroughs), plus a solid chunk on PS5 as well. Night City has become my second home, and I keep coming back to it even years later.  Before diving into the actual review, I want to address the elephant in the room: I was one of those players who jumped in at launch back in 2020. The game had issues—there was even one game-breaking bug that forced me to restart a section—but I could already see the incredible potential buried underneath. Fast-forward to today, and Cyberpunk 2077 has completely redeemed itself. Thanks to years of massive updates (especially the game-changing 2.0 overhaul and beyond), the Phantom Liberty expansion, and ongoing polish, it now delivers on nearly every promise CD Projekt RED made. It's no longer the buggy mess some remember—it's a polished, immersive masterpiece that feels alive in ways few games ever achieve.  One of the things that keeps pulling me back is how many favorite moments this game has given me. The storytelling is exceptional across the board. The main campaign is a gripping, emotional rollercoaster about identity, mortality, and survival in a brutal dystopia—your relationship with Johnny Silverhand (brilliantly voiced by Keanu Reeves) alone is one of the most compelling dynamics I've experienced in gaming. The side quests and gigs aren't filler; many of them rival the quality of the main story, with heartbreaking twists, moral dilemmas, and unexpected depth. And then there's Phantom Liberty—the DLC feels like a premium spy-thriller packed into Night City, introducing Dogtown as a brand-new, gritty district full of intrigue, new characters, and high-stakes choices. Every playthrough reveals new layers, and the multiple endings still hit hard.  The world and atmosphere are simply unmatched. Night City is a neon-drenched beast—crowded, chaotic, and overflowing with personality. The streets pulse with life: holographic ads screaming for attention, flying cars zooming overhead, street vendors hawking cyberware, and random encounters that make the city feel dangerous and unpredictable. Sure, NPCs don't have hyper-detailed 24-hour routines like in Red Dead Redemption 2, but honestly, I never missed that. Why would I want to tail a random stranger just to watch them grab a coffee or go home? The density of interesting individuals you can interact with more than makes up for it—fixers, mercenaries, netrunners, and everyday citizens all have their own stories if you take the time to listen.  Visually, Cyberpunk 2077 still stands at the top of the mountain in 2026. The graphics are breathtaking, especially with Path Tracing enabled (if your hardware can handle it). The way light bounces realistically off wet streets, chrome implants, and rain-slicked surfaces creates an unparalleled sense of immersion. Reflections, shadows, and global illumination look so natural that it often feels like you're watching a high-budget sci-fi movie rather than playing a game. Even without max settings, the art direction, character models, and environmental detail hold up incredibly well. Driving through the city at night with the radio blasting is pure atmosphere porn.  The characters—both major and minor—are fantastically written. V feels like your character, but the supporting cast steals the show. Panam, Judy, Kerry, River, Takemura, and so many others feel like real people with their own motivations, flaws, and arcs. You'll want to help them, romance them, or just hang out and talk. The voice acting and facial animations are top-tier, making every conversation feel meaningful. Building relationships (platonic or romantic) adds huge replay value, as different lifepaths and choices lead to wildly different interactions.  Gameplay-wise, the experience is pretty much flawless once you embrace what the game is: a deep first-person RPG, not a pure shooter. Yes, the gunplay is satisfying and highly customizable— you can go full netrunner, stealthy blade assassin, tanky shotgun psycho, or anything in between thanks to the excellent skill trees and cyberware system. The 2.0 updates massively improved combat, police AI, vehicle handling, and progression, making builds feel impactful and fun. Exploration rewards curiosity, with hidden gigs, cyberpsycho sightings, and endless loot. That said, if you're expecting something like Call of Duty with RPG elements tacked on, you might need a slight mindset shift— this is a role-playing game first, where your choices, attributes, and playstyle shape everything.  In the end, Cyberpunk 2077 isn't perfect (no game is), but its strengths far outweigh any minor nitpicks. The music, sound design, and overall vibe are addictive. I've lost count of how many times I've just driven around aimlessly, taking in the sights and listening to the radio. If you gave the game a chance at launch and bounced off, or if you're new to it in 2026—do yourself a favor and dive in now, ideally with the Ultimate Edition that includes Phantom Liberty. This is the version of Night City we were always promised.  Story/Narrative — 10/10 Graphics — 10/10 Gameplay — 9.5/10 Atmosphere — 10/10 Sound Design — 10/10  Overall — 9.9/10  Also, Sasha Grey is a radio host. :D

A very strange beast of a game that will have been received very differently based on exactly when you got around to experiencing it, and to this day still serving as a cautionary tale for why no one should ever pre-order anything with how disastrous the game was on-release after nearly a decade of anticipation, *and* coming off the dramatic success of 'The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt'.   The mismanagement was hellish enough behind the scenes for CDPR staff to bounce off the project at multiple points and to go form their own studios - such as Rebel Wolves, working on 'Blood of Dawnwalker' - and the released product so unfinished and janky that it required multiple soft re-launches (ala the 1.6 and 2.0 updates respectively) to bring the game closer to the promised state alluded to in the barrage of incredibly atmospheric and hype-accelerance that was the suberbly-made marketing, trailers that *still* serve to masterfully convey the tone and aesthetic of the ttrpg's setting.  The years of messy development and contentious reception behind it, what's here after the additions of the 'Phantom Liberty' DLC and the broad changes of the 2.0 patch have smoothed-over and consolidated systems is a solid, massive, action-RPG (that unfortunately emphasized more 'action' than 'RPG' elements after many updates simplified and overhauled the nature of the weapon, armor, and perk systems) that, if nothing else, nails the atmosphere of its setting and the blood-and-chrome aesthetic of the ttrpg it's based on (and was even dragged into the Edgrunners anime more or less without any change to its visual language or OST). Even on-release, environments of Night City's urban dystopia and the surrounding desert landscapes were hyper-detailed, complicated to navigate, and readily screenshot-able, with an above-and-beyond soundtrack that remains probably the best-made component of the game and an easy resource for use in soundscaping a game of  the ttrpg.  If you're looking for RPG 'crunch' rather than vibes, the story is unfortunately more or less linear in the same way CDPR's 'The Witcher' games are, and the gameplay won't have much to sell you on mechanically, though there remains distinction and build-variety among the options of gunplay, melee, and netrunning. If you don't mind the concession of moreso 'being along for a ride' rather than something closer to playing a direct adaptation of the Cyberpunk: RED tabletop ruleset, then Cyberpunk 2077 is a masterclass in delivering on the tone and worldbuilding of the property it's based on; this finally 'finished' version showing the promise of what a less-erratically-developed sequel in the portions of the setting 'Phantom Liberty' hints at could look like.

Starting off with barely being able to win a fistfight, to quite literally having gorilla arms attached to your character that lets you beat an entire gang hideout with your fists. Or, maybe you're more interested in a stealth profile with sniper rifles and hacking into anyone with cyberware in the game.   There are just so many ways that you can enjoy this title from a gameplay perspective and even a graphical standpoint. It's one of the most beautiful games you can play on modern PC's, with probably the best usage of Ray Tracing in any current video game that makes 3000-4000+ series of Nvidia cards reach their actual potential. Photo mode was a welcome addition to capturing some of the best vistas or atmospheres that you can find in the lively Nightcity.   Without getting into any spoilers, my only disappointment with the game that never was addressed was the lack of influence your background actually gives your character throughout the game. Sure, you'll be prompted with some dialogue that your background allows you to answer differently or find a way around skillchecks, but in terms of consistent missions or things that allow you to "roleplay" your V to potential simply are non existent. Act One of the game should've been more focused on your actual background and should've been longer overall so players could experience the importance of their background.   Despite that flaw, I cannot find many others with the game at this point. You play it and get lost for hours at a time from how much nightcity sucks you in. Everytime you finish a mission or a bounty, you'll tell yourself "just one more" and before you know it, it's midnight. The impressive audio rivals games like GTA V and some modern FPS with quality that goes above and beyond.   I would recommend this game to anyone at full price, especially on sale, and find yourself an RPG that lives up to the standard set by games like Skyrim over a decade ago. The post-game support (even adding an expansion) shows the TLC that the devs had for reaching their vision for the game. I'm happy to say they redeemed themselves and Cyberpunk from it's horrendous launch.

Of course I enjoyed CP2077, but I almost want to give it a negative rating to emphasize why I think it's merely a "really good" game as opposed to an "incredible" one.  The storyline was a highlight (compelling and with choices that mattered), but there is very little mechanically in the game that hasn't been done before: GTA4/5 defined the standard for open worlds decades ago, and any mainline RPG has similar depth for character choices, skill trees, progression etc. So, does CP2077 differentiate with an immersive world that is truly novel? For me, not really.  The map is expansive with some incredible artwork, but can feel samey within any given district. The characters, while memorable, are ultimately formulaic. The voice acting was surprisingly lacking in places (male V sounds like he's reading out instructions for a dishwasher). Towards the latter stages of the game, the combat starts to feel mundane due to a lack of enemy diversity.  Despite playing with the latest patch (April 2026), the game is still super buggy: floating world items, stuttering animations, glitching quests, CTDs (all of which are perhaps to be expected for a game of this scale, but still no less annoying).  I enjoyed my play-through, but don't see a reason to replay any time soon!

Writing of the main plot is extremely shallow and leans more into interpersonal drama instead of using the greater elements of the world to push the story along, but this second part is subjective. Most "RPG mechanics" and systems wind up unimpactful due to power creep, and the ability for more unique playstyle is absent (i.e. most tech weapons are handguns, so you are forced into specing into "cool" stats if you are also specing into "technical" stats). Cyberpunk 2077 tries to do too many things and live up to hype and player count, and they then wind up as mid, AAA slop and another ARPG that does not live up to the genre. Not a bad game, some major flaws objectively, and many subjective flaws if you share my preferences. Would have been better as a linear world with more fleshed out narrative (more than interpersonal drama) and more fleshed out systems and mechanics (especially since it is the cyberpunk genre).

Overview: Cyberpunk 2077 is an ambitious open-world RPG set in a futuristic city (Night City). It delivers an incredibly immersive experience with strong storytelling and visuals—but it has also been criticized for technical issues and some underdeveloped gameplay systems.   Pros  1. Immersive Open World Night City is widely praised as one of the most detailed and atmospheric game worlds ever created. Dense environments, strong world-building, and tons of side activities make it feel alive.  2. Stunning Graphics Incredible visuals, especially on high-end PCs with ray tracing. Lighting, reflections, and character detail are top-tier.   3. Strong Story & Characters Excellent writing and memorable characters enhance the narrative. Side quests are often as engaging as the main story.   4. Flexible Gameplay & Builds Multiple playstyles (stealth, hacking, combat) give players freedom. Deep RPG systems allow for character customization.   5. Voice Acting & Presentation High-quality voice acting and cinematic storytelling elevate immersion.    Cons  1. Bugs & Technical Issues (especially at launch) Frequent glitches, crashes, and performance problems were heavily criticized. While many fixes have been released, reputation damage still lingers.  2. Some Gameplay Systems Feel Incomplete Melee combat and certain mechanics feel underdeveloped or “half-baked.”  Balancing issues between different playstyles.  3. Main Story Length The main campaign is shorter than expected for an RPG of this scale.    4. Limited Impact of Choices Dialogue and choices don’t always significantly affect the world or story outcomes.    5. NPC & World Interaction Limitations Some players feel NPCs lack depth or realism compared to the environment.   Final Verdict Rating: 9/10 If you want a deep, story-driven RPG with amazing visuals, this is a great pick. If you care most about polished gameplay systems and perfect performance, it may still feel inconsistent in places.   Bottom line: Cyberpunk 2077 is a flawed but highly enjoyable game—one that delivers unforgettable moments, even if it doesn’t fully live up to its original hype. Highly replayable.

Cyberpunk 2077 is easily the best game I have ever felt. It is a pure masterpiece that will stick with me forever. The developers clearly poured their entire lives into this and the result is an insane emotional gauntlet. This isn't just a game you play for the action you play it for a story so intense that you’ll find yourself staring at the screen for several minutes paralyzed trying to decide what to do next because ngl the choices are really hard to choose.  The beauty of this world is staggering. I’ve lost count of how many times I just stopped driving or stood on a balcony staring at the buildings and the lighting just to soak in the atmosphere. Every single character has their own deep story and unique design. Tbh most games out there straight up lack this kind of perfect balance. And by balance I mean the story and the world-building and the fighting styles all coming together not just one thing. You can switch from ghosting everyone in stealth to going full-on combat mode whenever you want and the game handles both perfectly.  Phantom Liberty pack: Listen you MUST buy the DLC. It is the absolute gem of the experience. You’re basically missing the soul of the game if you don’t have it. From the second you finish the Voodoo Boys mission and get that first mysterious call the stakes hit a level I didn't think was possible. Best DLC ever made no cap.  dlc pack:[SPOILERS] The journey from the Voodoo Boys to the surgery is a masterclass in tension. The betrayal part is what actually breaks you fr. Whether you turn on Songbird or Reed it feels like a physical weight on your chest. You aren't just picking a path you are betraying someone who trusted you and the guilt is real. Not to mention that second massive choice later on—deciding whether to still send Songbird to the moon or give her up after the insane shock that she played you the whole time. The genius of the writing is that the consequences don't always hit you immediately. Sometimes you discover the true cost of your choices hours later.  The Endings: The endings aren't just win or lose screens. They are deep philosophical questions. There is a huge debate where many say the best ending is sacrificing yourself for Johnny. I kind of agree imo but it’s a heavy price. You can also choose to live out your 6 months with hope, which as a Nomad means everything since clan comes first. But for me the surgery ending is easily the most depressing. You get exactly what you wanted—to survive—but lose everything that made you V. Going from a legendary merc to getting tossed down stairs by random thugs is a brutal reality check. It proves every miracle has a price, leaving you with a hollow bittersweet feeling forever. There is no perfect ending here. Pro tip save the game before the point of no return so you can experience all these crazy conclusions.  Overall Rating: 10/10

Ok, where do I even begin... This game is an absolute masterpiece. - Story 10/10 (RIP everyone) - Gameplay 9/10 (only hand to hand combat is clunky, the rest is fantastic) - Graphics 10/10 - Music 10/10 - Voice Acting / Motion Capture 10/10 - DLC 10/10 (I'd recommend buying the DLC since the beginning)  I'm doing this review at almost 160 hours, this includes main story + DLC + all the side quests in the game + all the endings (excluding "(Don't Fear) The Reaper", more on this later). You do not need to spend that amount of time to complete the game, you can probably 100% in 120 if you don't do side quests and if you actually only use a single play-style (more on this soon). Key points to remember:  - Male V vs Female V, there is a lot of discussion here. I chose male V, it felt like it worked better with Johnny, romance with Panam is great and it makes more sense to me for Aldecaldos ending (The Star).  - Whenever playing you don't need a guide for anything imo, BUT, please CHECK A GUIDE for "Chippin' In", the dialog decisions will lock you out of the ending "(Don't Fear) The Reaper". This happened to me, and given that I did that at around 40 hours, I wasn't gonna restart the game when I was already in 100+. I'll have to use mods if I want to play that that ending without replaying the whole game.  - Another tip would be when you find the weapon Skippy it will ask you to choose between "Stone Cold Killer Mode" or "Puppy Loving Pacifist Mode", choose the puppy-loving mode, this will get you the best rewards long term.  - There are many other decisions I could suggest my opinion, but honestly, play the game and make mistakes.  - You can't max out all specs and attributes in the game (not without mods), so make sure you pick according with your play style. I screw up the first time around and I had to use my "Reset Attributes" (there is only 1) to accommodate what I wanted for the rest of the game.  - Max level in the game is level 50, unless you get the DLC, which allows you to go up to level 60. This also comes with more attribute and perk points, so buy the DLC before you reach level 50.  - Play the endings whenever you want, right after the ending, it basically brings you back before to the point of no return, and you can continue playing any other missions you want, so might be worth just experimenting and having fun.  - You don't need to upgrade your Cyberware all the time, it goes from Tier 1 to Tier 5+ (or 5++ with DLC), I'd say to upgrade once mid game around level 30, and then just wait until you are around level 50 to get everything at Tier 5+ and be absolutely broken.  - Quickhacks (Netrunner build) are broken if you max them out, so it's everything else. But I found that the best option for most endings is going with the Sadevistan build, it's just a great help to avoid damage and to inflict it too. Berserk build is my least favorite option, it's cool, just not as cool.  - Depending on the DLC choices you make and the ending you choose, you might be able to get certain weapon. Best loot overall are in the "King of Pentacles" ending, but imo, the most best ending is "King of Wands".  Only thing missing for me is NG+ where I can keep all my loot and just level up until I am the most overpowered character ever with every attribute and perk (even though it already feels like that without maxing out everything!)  PS: Worst main ending is by far "The Devil", and for the DLC I'd say "King of Swords"  PS2: I was able to use commands to be able to play the secret ending "(Don't Fear) The Reaper", and I gotta say, if you are choosing Temperance or The Sun as your favorite endings, this path is better, imo. Also, more challenging since your max health drops as time passes, which is awesome.

Cyberpunk 2077 has turned out to be one of the most immersive and rewarding games I’ve played on Steam. Going in, I had heard mixed opinions, but my personal experience has been overwhelmingly positive—and honestly, it exceeded my expectations.  The first thing that stands out is the world itself. Night City feels alive in a way few open-world games manage to achieve. From the neon-lit streets to the dense urban design, every district has its own personality. Simply walking or driving around can be an experience on its own, with constant details, side activities, and random encounters making the world feel dynamic.  The story is another highlight. It’s engaging, emotional, and filled with meaningful choices that actually feel impactful. The characters are well-written and memorable, and the narrative does a great job of pulling you into its futuristic setting. It’s not just about action—there’s depth, moral ambiguity, and plenty of moments that stick with you even after you log off.  Gameplay-wise, the flexibility is impressive. Whether you prefer stealth, hacking, or going in guns blazing, the game gives you the freedom to shape your own playstyle. The skill system and upgrades allow for a lot of experimentation, which keeps things fresh over time.  Visually, the game looks stunning, especially on a well-optimized setup. Lighting, reflections, and overall atmosphere contribute heavily to the immersion. I’ve played quite a few RPGs in my time—some on Steam, some on Xbox, and others on older PC setups. After putting what I’d consider a solid amount of time into this game, I can confidently say it’s more than deserving of all the praise it gets.  The story and characters you encounter are incredibly strong, but the real magic happens when you fully lean into the world—immersing yourself in the side quests along the way. Do that, and you’ll find a narrative that’s not only engaging, but almost effortless to get lost in. Before you know it, you’re deeply invested—maybe even dangerously attached—to the people you meet. The icing on the cake is just how much depth the game continues to gain through its updates.  From a gameplay perspective, it’s easy to fall back into old habits with your usual playstyle, but there’s a surprising amount of depth in how you can approach nearly every quest. Outcomes can vary in subtle ways or shift dramatically depending on your choices, which keeps things feeling fresh and meaningful.  Visually, the game looks great—and with mods, it can look even better. Personally, I ran into very few issues—maybe one or two—and they were quickly resolved with a simple restart or minor setting adjustment.  Overall, it’s just a great game that somehow manages to get even better once you finish it and dive into Phantom Liberty.

Cyberpunk 2077 is not really about becoming the best mercenary in Night City.  It is about personhood under siege.  It is science fiction, but only by degree. People are already flattened into profiles, performances, labour value, social image, sexual currency, and marketable identity. Cyberpunk 2077 just pushes that process until it becomes impossible to ignore.  Its cruelest idea is simple: you are born hoping to become someone real, and the world immediately starts negotiating what parts of you it can own.  Johnny Silverhand is what makes that idea personal. He is rage, regret, defiance, and the voice that refuses to let compromise feel normal. The part of you that would rather burn than disappear quietly into something obedient and useful.  The journey is about trying to stay a person in a world that wants a product.  And even then, it still leaves room for one stubborn answer:  No.

This game pisses me off. This [i]should[/i] be a masterpiece, if not for one egregious flaw. The combat is terrible, specifically the enemy AI. I'm just going to instantly end any fight I get into and the rewards are meaningless crafting supplies I already have 10,000 of and have never needed to use ever.  Everything else about this game is amazing. The soundtrack, the city, the visuals, the driving (the only game to make me avoid using fast travel because driving around is really just that fun), all of it is great, except for the archaic Gamebryo-ass NPC AI. There are so many cool quickhacks and weapons you can use and none of it matters because you just gun down everyone instantly. I ended up skipping the DLC because I was so bored of the same combat over and over and over.   All of that being said, there is still plenty of enjoyment to get out of this game, it just disappoints me that they screwed up such a fundamental aspect of gameplay so badly that it kind of ruined the game for me. Yet, all these years later, I’m still running into various glitches that are definitely not "gameplay features" or "implant malfunctions."  - [b]visual glitches[/b]: blinking shadows, dissolving cars, Path Tracing issues with strobing lights, and jittering textures. - [b]soft-locks[/b]: several bugs in different quests that force you to restart from the last checkpoint.  I really wish there was an option to save while in elevators or during scripted scenes, but alas.  By the way, this isn’t an RPG in the classical sense. I mean, it’s a bad sign when the dialogue system in Fallout 4 is fundamentally better (which is hilarious in itself). This is a [i] "new school" RPG[/i], where the role-playing element is mostly limited to picking your skill tree.  That said, the game does have a decent and, at times, high-octane story (even if it is mostly "on rails" and follows a character who consistently makes stupid decisions). It also boasts a great soundtrack (I’m talking about the original score, not the radio stations) and, of course, Keanu Reeves.

Tried playing this again for the first time in over two years. Couldn't recall why I hadn't played more than the first couple of story beats. Figured it was probably due to a mix of busy with work and busy playing other games.  So I go on Nexus, setup a collection of mods, and proceed to get into the game. Or so I thought. Right after the first conversation with Jackie, I realized what the stumbling block was that prompted me to spend time on other games. When not in a vehicle, you're stuck in first person. No options for Third Person. So I grit my teeth and go search for a mod that provides Third Person view, should be something out there yea?> ... Well, there is. Kind of. There's a set of mods on Nexus that do exactly that. Both buggy as all hell. Animations don't play right, sometimes crash to desktop, often character will be bald when first loading into a scene or room, as the game isn't accustomed to having to load your hair, the list goes on. And you DO need both of those mods. One provides the ... "Framework" we'll call it, for having Third Person, the other tries to fix the various animation issues created by playing a game meant to be only in First Person - in Third Person. I don't blame those modders though for not gift wrapping me a perfect fix for this. They're creating that stuff on their own time, and presumably doing the best they can. But it's been over 5 years. CDPR could certainly have corrected this failing.  And hey, it's ok if you don't see it as a failing. You can choose to be wrong and disagree with me on this. No hurt feelings. Cept for the fact that players accepting this kind of nonsense just means more of it is likely down the line.  There in lies the problem. It's an RPG, I do not get the all encompasses desire some jackals have for First Person. It works for shooters though. I guess. For some people. But more than that, I detest game devs that eliminate choice for players. Being able to choose my own keybinds is important, but being able to toggle between First Person & Third Person should be a given. Being able to pan out away from my character, should be a given. It certainly is in many RPG games over the years. For Cyberpunk I don't know if this was a hardline choice from the folks at CDPR to force players to experience their game a certain way, or just ineptitude.   CDPR does a lot of great stuff, and props to them for dragging this game out of the buggy mess that it was at release. But refusal to implement a Third Person option in their RPG turns what might otherwise be enjoyable hours of gaming into a sloppy mess I'd rather not waste time with.  So, great game, yadda yadda, and I do recommend it, with the caveat that you should avoid it if you don't enjoy first person perspective. For $60, gamers deserve better.  [Edit]  Soon as I post my review, the games trailer starts playing, and I'm struck by the ironic idiocy that they show "Your" character's face, in trailers, in game you actually design your look. Why? You won't be showing up in any mirrors. In fact if you pick up a body to move it, and walk past a reflective surface, the dead body will be floating as you don't have a proper model cause why would you need one? No need to display you in mirrors etc. BUT you took the time to give your character a face at creation. Perhaps you get to glimpse yourself in cut scenes or when you get in/out of a vehicle, who cares? That's a fraction of the time you play and honestly if I'm not pausing to look at a my character I certainly don't care what the plethora of NPCs think about it. I'd say well played CDPR, but that'd just be silly.

Oh my GOD I love cyberpunk 2077 so much.   The world is amazing and full of depth, every nook and cranny is full of life in some way and the setting is unlike anything I've seen before.   I know CDPR usually has good writing but even so these characters can be amazing. Everyone has their own level of depth and feels like a real person. The plot is phenomenal; my favorite kind of story is one that can genuinely make you feel something, and this game does that. Just the vibe (so to speak) at times is palpable-feelings of helplessness, of being lost, of feeling like everything is out of control or that you're just another bug under the greater world's shoe. Emotions stick with you for a long time-the ones cyberpunk's storyline made me experience have.   I absolutely love the combat-it kicks ass. There are so many unique weapon types with perks and cyberware that make gameplay a whole buffet of choices for how you want to approach any given situation. Play behind cover with medium-long range weapons? Strategically utilize quickhacks to debuff or damage enemies? Stealth through it with camo and silent weapons? Speed blitz through an entire scavenger outpost with a sword? There's a little something for everyone.  What I don't see nearly enough appreciation for is the soundtrack. Combat tracks are amazing and give so much tension and flare to everything; the radio is full of stations and the number of unlikable tracks fitting on one hand.  Cyberpunk is my favorite RPG-open world or not-of all time, and I would go as far as to say it's in my top 5, maybe even top 3 favorite games of all time. Whether it will be for you I can't say, but it would be a disservice to yourself not to try it.

What started as a controversial launch has turned into a seriously immersive and polished experience, especially after all the updates and improvements.  The world of Night City is easily the highlight it's dense, alive, and visually stunning. Every district feels unique, and there’s always something happening, whether it’s random encounters or side gigs that actually have depth. The storytelling is another strong point. The main story is engaging, but what surprised me most were the side quests they don’t feel like filler and often hit just as hard emotionally.  Gameplay-wise, the combat and character builds are very flexible. You can go full stealth, hacking, guns blazing, or a mix of everything. It gives you freedom to play how you want, which keeps things fresh even after many hours. The RPG elements are solid, and progression feels rewarding.  Of course, it’s not perfect. There are still occasional bugs and some AI quirks, but nothing game breaking in my experience. Compared to its launch state, it’s a huge improvement.  Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 is now a must play if you enjoy open world RPGs with strong storytelling and player choice. Definitely worth it.

I went into Cyberpunk pretty excited, but the beginning honestly threw me off more than I expected. Right away you’re hit with a ton of characters calling you... a lot of dialogue and its not always clear whos who or why it matters yet. It felt overwhelming and confusing early on. Looking back I think I played it the wrong way at first because I rushed the main story. This really isnt a game youre supposed to blow through. Its way better when you slow down and explore. The main story didnt fully land for me either. Theres a lot of talking and dialogue choices but not much action if you just go mission to mission and a lot of the responses didn’t feel like what I actually wanted to say. Things only really started to click for me near the end of the Takemura and Hanako storyline, which felt like weird pacing since I was just starting to understand the mechanics when the game was basically over. On top of that, I was pretty disappointed that after finishing the final mission it just loads you back before the ending.  Once I started digging into side content, my opinion improved a lot. The side gigs and NCPD activities are honestly where the game shines for me. There are a ton of them and you can approach each one in completely different ways depending on your build. The gameplay really opens up once you invest in skills, especially mobility. I found myself running and scaling buildings instead of driving most of the time. Driving does feel clunky at first but you do get used to it. The hacking system is one of the best parts of the game and really sells the futuristic feel. It opens up a ton of creative ways to approach encounters. Throwing knives especially surprised me with how strong they are, and once I leaned into that it made you feel like a ninja. One of my favorite moments was setting up a full stealth chain where I hacked into cameras to ping enemies, used distractions like generators and a ferris wheel to turn them around, then moved across rooftops landing throwing knife headshots one by one. Even the chaos side of things is fun, like getting max wanted level and hacking enemies to turn on each other.  The world itself is one of the best parts of the game. You can just be walking around and see cops arresting people or fighting gangs and it actually feels alive. The map and tracking system is really clean and easy to use, especially being able to mark multiple objectives and follow different routes. The only downside is that it keeps defaulting back to the main story after you finish the game. I wish there was a simple way to turn that off or fully deselect it, because it will keep tracking the final mission with the yellow route. There were a few times I wasn’t paying attention and thought I was heading toward a side activity, only to end up back at the point where you meet Hanako at Embers. Once you go in, you’re locked into the ending again, which gets pretty frustrating... Weapon variety is great and honestly reminded me of Borderlands but better, with a wide range from common to legendary and solid customization options. Performance wise it ran really well for me on an i9 9900k and 2080 Ti at 1440p on high settings with no ray tracing, averaging around 115–150 fps. There were still some bugs especially in the main story where a few bosses glitched out and got stuck but I didnt run into nearly as many issues in side content. Overall the game has a really immersive world and strong gameplay systems but the main story pacing and heavy focus on dull dialogue held it back for me. If you take your time with it instead of rushing like I did the first time, chances are you are going to love it.

I say this to say: for all the complex user interface decisions, it's not a complicated game mechanically.  The next most-immediate part of the experience is the story. Maybe more specifically the lore. I felt like I was drowning for the prologue. To the game's credit, this isn't really an important part of the game. I think the peak was in the desert with Panam and her crew where there was a fairly straight forward story with some personals takes. I'm on the literal last mission -- where it tells you "this is the point of no return" -- and I have no idea what is happening in this story.  What drove me to review this game — after 50 hours and slowly going through it for more than a year — was the unbelievably insulting side quest design. This extends to Phantom Liberty too. Every side quest — and I really mean EVERY SINGLE SIDE QUEST — is not designed to be played, it is designed to be watched. This game has more than 10-20 hours of standing there while someone talks at you. It is unbelievable how boring this game can be.  I have been agonizing finishing this game. There was a part of me that enjoyed it enough to buy the expansion and make it through 50 hours worth of content. Cyberpunk 2077: A dystopian future masterpiece  I really can't understate how phenomenal an experience this game is, and having just finished my 2nd playthrough this time with the Phantom Liberty DLC (which was incredible), I have a whole new appreciation for the storytelling and universe of Cyberpunk.  The first time around, I was a Street Kid V who leaned more towards a balanced persona with my dialogue options, whereas this time I played a much colder Corpo V. Same story, totally different perspectives. It's amazing just how much depth and gravity your choices end up making throughout your journey, I'll definitely be picking this back up to try a 3rd run as Nomad V. Unlike how quickly I move on from other games, I actually need some time off to process the choices I made, and the outcome I got as a self-serving Corpo Merc who accomplished his ultimate goal of surviving, but lost pretty much everything in the process. Cyberpunk 2077 is a game that pulls you into the story like nothing else, and if anything exists as a spiritual successor to the like of Fallout New Vegas.  From a gameplay perspective, I've experimented with different builds, weapons, and cyberware, and never felt bored no matter which areas I specialized in. I think it's fair to say some skill trees got more love and attention than others, but the ability to blend them together into something new will keep you curious and invested for quite a while. This game really gives you the freedom to step into your own persona as portrayed by V, and depending on which direction you go, you'll get very different results.  From a lore perspective, this game is so realistic it makes me feel uncomfortable at times, thinking about what could await humanity in the future with Rogue AIs, cyberspace, the integration of cybernetics into the human body, and the inevitable corporatization of society. It's almost as if nations and countries don't even really matter anymore, just the corps that fight for control over them. It makes you feel incredibly small when you take in the totality of things going on within the cyberpunk timeline.  Your companion throughout the game Johnny Silverhand is a layer cake of selfish and noble personality traits that end up manifesting in very thought provoking ways. He's someone that you'd instinctively dislike, yet you come to understand him and his motivations on a much deeper level, and realize that nothing is ever that simple. What you choose to make of the time you get spend with him is what makes his presence so unforgettable. He can be your best friend, or your worst enemy, depending on your point of view. Keanu Reeves may be criticized for always just playing another version of himself in movies, but I felt he really did stand out as Johnny Silverhand, and gave an incredible performance. Not to glaze a celebrity, but had it not been for Keanu, I don't think I would have grown to like Johnny at all, and that deserves recognition.  As for criticisms, I don't have many. Yes there were a few small things that I felt could have been executed better, like some of the relationships of the friends you meet along the way. I would have liked to have more time getting to know Jackie, as it felt like I got a case of whiplash from that montage of doing gigs with him. A longer prologue exploring the early days of the different types of V would have made for a smoother transition to the life he gets pulled into after the events of Konpeki Plaza. Also iterating a bit further with some of the friend/love interests would  have been interesting, as some of them felt a bit short or half-baked. Not bad, just not totally satisfying at times. I felt the clothing options in this game could have been better, but luckily there are mods to address that, which I only really used 1 to do. The vehicles and driving also aren't great at times depending on your ride, but it does get better after some time behind the wheel. I appreciate how difficult driving in first person is, and if you actually try, it adds another layer of immersion to the game. The weapons are really cool, and there is a pretty good variety, but more customization options would have been welcome, like different mods or paint jobs, cyberware etc. Depending on your playstyle and preferences, you'll have plenty to work with. The game did have a rough start due to bugs in it's early days (which I wasn't around for), and I think some of those small bugs do still exist within the engine. Strange behavior or random occurrences from NPCs and vehicles glitching out, mostly harmless and sometimes funny, but also immersion breaking. The frequency of glitches I noticed wasn't nearly enough to frustrate me or ruin the experience.  Overall, I would give this game a solid 9.5 out of 10 with Phantom Liberty. A damn-near flawless masterpiece with very little to complain about, and so, so much more to offer than the vast majority of other titles being released these days. The base game alone was incredible, but with the DLC is just kicks it up a notch to a truly phenomenal experience. If you haven't played this game, you're missing out, choom.

I waited to write this review to let time pass, observe mechanical updates, and distance myself from real-world events I experienced during my first playthrough. My conclusions remain unchanged. I played on release via Stadia (logging around 600 hours, bug-free) and later transitioned to Steam with the expansion.   If you are looking for a highly structured, immersive world where you can exist as a single character, this game delivers. But beneath the surface, it is a heavy, uncompromising examination of autonomy, mental health, and the ethical cost of survival.  ## Fair content warning: ##  This review contains spoilers and discusses severe mental health issues and suicide.  ## THE WORLD AND THE ATMOSPHERE  As someone who grew up in the 80s, the retro-future aesthetic resonates well with me. The environmental design — ranging from corporate skyscrapers to neon-lit, trash-filled alleys — balances surface splendour with the tragedy of an unforgiving dystopia. The soundscape is very good, and the OST remains in my regular rotation. I particularly liked the diegetic inclusion of music through radios, speakers, etc. It feels natural.   The developers successfully created a graphically believable universe with its own distinct clothing, colloquialisms, and professions.  On the downside, I wish they had done something like the procedural, emergent roleplay of games like *Daggerfall*. The city is dense, but the NPCs lack complex schedules or interactions. Most of the world is setting, and there are few things (or people!) you can interact with. It was a satisfying (but frustrating) realization to find out you could actually confess yourself in the absolution vending machines.  There is also a distinct tension  — and this is a crucial issue  — between exploring the world and the main quest. The narrative insists V is dying rapidly, urging you to rush. It makes absolute sense, but doing so deprives you of exploring the setting. But if you suspend the dissonance this urgency creates, the lore and visual storytelling are highly detailed.  ## GAMEPLAY AND MECHANICS  The gunplay and movement mechanics are satisfying, offering varied approaches: fast-paced reflexes, time-dilating cyberware, or real-time quickhacks. The combat functions well, accommodating everything from stealth to direct assault.  However, the RPG elements lack structural consequence. The reputation system is shallow: working for one gang should logically anger others, and aiding the police should make you a target in the underworld. This all could lead tor restricting access to certain resources or quests based on alliances, and would foster replayability.  Similarly, the game allows complete character respecs. I value games where you can make your own choices, but choices must have some degree of consequence, and this applies also to character creation and development. A system where choices have permanence — where mastering hacking precludes being a swordmaster, for instance — would ground the experience.   The game also omits cyberpsychosis as a gameplay mechanic for the player. Lore dictates that heavy bodily modification risks mental breakdown, yet the game imposes no such penalty on V. This is ironic because cyberpsychosis is hardly forgotten in these modern iterations of the setting: the entire Edgerunners series runs on it. It is also (in the TTRPG) a very important mechanic to limit the possibilitites of expanding your own character or respeccing it.  These issues I am critiquing are not a problem for Cyberpunk 2077 only — this plague is an AAA development philosophy hesitant to lock players out of content, but in doing so, robs them of actual consequence to their actions.  ## NARRATIVE, MENTAL HEALTH, AND ENDINGS  Yet, apart from my appreciation of its lore and aesthetics, where the game holds the most value for me is in its somber handling of psychological trauma and survival. I have seen other players too credit this game's themes with helping them process dark times in their own lives, and looking at the quests, one can imagine why.   The game repeatedly forces engagement with autonomy and personhood: The Delamain Arc requires permanent choices regarding a fractured AI's perception of reality. Brendan is vending machine treated as corporate property — he insists he is not sentient, yet acts as if he is, raising practical questions about the definition of personhood. Lizzy Wizzy is clearly suffering from cyberpsychosis, but also facing the horror of having her mind tampered with by a partner. Barry's story is an approach to depression from a darkly humorous angle, but delivers a grim look at how mental health struggles are ignored by peers.  Cyberpsycho sightings themselves, on which I haven't seen much comment, are excuses for boss fights, ok. But if you look through them, they are tragedies. The one titled 'Family Matters' hit very hard, with one woman struggling to help her sister, and ultimately losing her husband and even her life to it.  People often cite that the main narrative is 'V is dying', but that isn't accurate: the body can survive. V is facing her mind being rewritten by the Relic, and that is a much more horrible reality. I think the game does a good job at presenting this, both subtly and explicitly: V's dialogue options and actions (like smoking) begin to mirror Johnny Silverhand, and Johnny's own arc shifts as he realizes this, moving from hostility to empathy. You are fading away, and the game acknowledges the terror of that process.  ## CONTENT WARNING: SUICIDE DISCUSSION  During my first playthrough, I was dealing with the immediate aftermath of a suicide attempt by someone close to me. I interrupted the attempt, but witnessing their intense pain left me grappling with whether I did them a disservice. I prioritize personal autonomy, and intervening felt like an intrusion on their ultimate choice, even if it stemmed from a compromised mental state.  Processing the game through that lens influenced how I saw the final choices. Players often view the endings as a way to «win» but, to me, they were a calculation of whom I was willing to sacrifice. Asking the Nomads for help gets many of them killed to buy you time. Siding with Rogue gets her killed. Siding with Arasaka surrenders both your mind and Johny's to them. The secret «solo» ending requires the mass murder of corporate guards who are ultimately just working people.  Under this light, the suicide ending seems the cleanest, most ethical option. It respects the autonomy and safety of everyone else. You prioritize your friends' lives above your survival, deciding not to drag them into your self-destruction. Johnny respects the choice. Your friends will call in the credits, grieving and cursing you, but the structural fact remains: you did not force anyone else to pay the price for your life.  ## CONCLUSION  I acknowledge my experience with this game comes from a very specific, difficult place in my life, which colored my perception. Mechanically, it has flaws and missed opportunities for deeper RPG consequences. However, it captures the genre's aesthetic accurately and delivers a solid narrative. If you are willing to engage with its themes of autonomy, mental health, and the systemic cost of survival, I think it offers a dense, worthwhile experience.

7/10, A flawed work of art that deserves recognition…After completing all life paths and getting all achievements, this is by far one of the most hauntingly beautiful games I’ve ever played. In a game that seems to have more loot than Skyrim. There's no pressure to pick up everything that falls on the ground (though you may miss some iconic loot if you’re not careful). It’s a game that takes itself a bit too seriously at times and shares the same kind of bleak atmosphere that GTA 4 has but with a lot more neon and much better graphics. A lot of characters like Johnny and Takemura are surprisingly funny at times as neither can seem to comprehend the size of their own egos. Whilst the game pushes a strong narrative that Corpos are the worst thing to ever exist, there also seems to be a somewhat subtle narrative that the AI in this world could potentially be worse and far more catastrophic than its human creators. Unfortunately, it never digs deep enough to give you a much bigger perspective of what this could mean besides some hints from characters like So mi, Alt and Mr blue eyes. Outside of that there is also references to the dangers of the ocean which seem to be controlled by AI. Its possible that CDPR could just be laying the groundwork for the sequel with Mr Blue Eyes potentially being an antagonist in the next game, though nothing seems to be confirmed yet at the time of this review.  Gameplay This is where the game starts losing points, for an FPS it feels very safe. Much in the same way that Bethesda sacrificed depth for accessibility to those new to the genre in the world of Skyrim. CDPR has done this with a first-person shooter, having played the likes of Wolfenstein and the Metro games, the FPS aspect is unbearably easy for me, even on higher difficulties. The game gives you more money and guns than you know what to do with, I had over a 100k eddies by the time I did the Arasaka heist with Jackie (This was on my first playthrough). Despite these issues, the overall atmosphere of the game was compelling enough to try different lifepaths and builds.   Customization Another reason why I’m only giving this a 7/10 is that It’s a game that seems to contradict itself at times. It surrounds you with a wide variety of npcs whilst limiting the player customization without mods. Some of the npcs barely look human due to how chromed out they are and it was surprising that I could not achieve the same sort of look for V. Car customization is also limited as you can only buy a certain amount colour designs for your car, the cap on this feature makes no sense.   The Phantom Liberty This is arguably the best DLC CDPR have ever produced and gives you an insight into what the base game could have felt like if it spent more time in the oven instead of rushing into a buggy release (which thankfully I skipped). The relic skill tree was a nice touch and it should have been in the base game really (similar to the unique perk tree from dragon age inquisition). Having said that the DLC is still worth it for its price, if you’re new to this DLC, the roads in dog town are terrible and I recommend getting yourself a bike for smoother navigation (I went for the custom bike in the base game which is easy to miss). Songbird is a tragic yet manipulative character and her complexity is what makes this DLC so interesting, Reed is basically just a NUSA Takemura. He is blinded by loyalty to something that doesn’t really care about him but his loyalty is somewhat admirable nonetheless, even if its misplaced. The gameplay isn’t that much different from the base game in terms of combat but the new chrome, perk tree and different weapons add some flavour along with the story. the black market and the contracts from Mr Hands are a nice touch and add a bit more moral ambiguity to the side quests compared to those in the base game.  Overall	 It’s a great RPG that’s worth playing, but if you want a less beginner friendly FPS and you don’t care much for the story and atmosphere of this game then it may not be for you. If you view this game as a work of art that can be interacted with and more importantly if you treat Johnny as more of a comedian that makes perfectly timed commentary on what you’re doing. You will find that this game has a lot to offer (I also recommend the Johnny and Rogue ending at least once as its just pure comedy). The Don’t Fear the reaper ending was surprisingly easy for those with more experience in FPS like me, even on higher difficulties, though I still highly recommended it. (This may not be the case if you go in with terrible weapons and chrome obviously.)  Despite some of its flaws, it really is worth it just for the atmosphere and experience alone.

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of those rare games that feels as much like an experience as it does a story. Set in the sprawling, neon-soaked Night City, it drops you into a world that’s chaotic, beautiful, and deeply immersive. From the moment you step into the shoes of V, the game pulls you into a narrative filled with ambition, identity, and the cost of chasing dreams in a broken system.  What really stands out is the world-building. Night City isn’t just a backdrop—it feels alive. Every district has its own personality, from the polished corporate towers to the gritty back alleys. The attention to detail is incredible, and it rewards exploration in a way few open-world games do.  The story is another highlight. With strong performances—especially from Keanu Reeves as Johnny Silverhand—the game delivers emotional weight alongside its action. Your choices matter, shaping not just the ending but how characters perceive you along the way.  Gameplay-wise, Cyberpunk 2077 offers a lot of freedom. Whether you prefer stealth, hacking, or going in guns blazing, the game supports multiple playstyles. The RPG elements, including skill trees and cybernetic upgrades, let you tailor V to your liking.  While the game had a rough launch, it has since been significantly improved with updates and expansions, making it far more stable and polished. Today, it stands as a testament to how much a game can evolve post-release.  Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 is a bold, visually stunning, and emotionally engaging game that’s absolutely worth playing—especially now.

Я качал всё равномерно, а значит прокачка шла долго, а навыки, которые я открывал первое время были либо бесполезным говном, либо абсолютно дефолтнымиперками.
