Стоит ли говорить, как я был удивлен, когда обнаружил что мой лутер-шутер превратился сначала в ULTRAKILL, а потом чуть ли не в DOOM Eternal. А когда я увидел видосы в тиктоке с геймплеем ниндзя, нетраннера, милишника — я натурально охуел. ОКАЗЫВАЕТСЯ, я играл в Киберпанк неправильно. Стоило скинуть все очки в одну ветку — и я сразу почувствовал вкус игры. Да, стоковая стрельба и мувмент невыразительные, боты тупорылые, как призраки из Пакмана. Но перетерпите первые пару часов, выберите ветку и качайте её, уверяю – геймплей удивит. Единственное, чего не хватало (хотя бы как суперредкого события), — киберпсихоза. Через лор и персонажей нам говорят: если напихивать себя хромом с ног до головы, то ты сойдёшь с ума. На мой взгляд, возможность превращения в киберпсиха было бы в духе киберпанка. Я понимаю, CDPR не до этого, но хотя бы минимальные изменения реплик или сбои биочипа не только в катсценах. Это добавило бы в погружении  ЗВУК И ВИЗУАЛ: Музыка разочаровала. Помимо заглавной темы, трейлер-темы и темы Джонни — ничего. Пресное радио, слабый звук оружия. Русская локализация — ужас. Позвать блогеров на озвучку… ебанный бобанный… Вместо актёров — нормисные блогеры, которые не понимают, что делать. Отсутствие интонации, неуместный или выдавленный мат, нет актёрского образования. Самое смешное: даже Кирк Сойер (Поперечный) звучит лучше, чем Ви. По визуалу буду краток. Графика, дизайн — наравне с RDR 2, а то и лучше. Не постесняюсь сказать, что Cyberpunk 2077 - одна из самых красивых игр в индустрии. Единственное, чего не хватило в визуале – это малое количество жести. Игра сразу была заявлена как 18+. И вроде кровь, кишки и голые сиськи на месте, но явно меньше, чем задумывалось. RoN (2023) показывает абсолютный ♥♥♥♥♥♥ на экране и поднимает спорные темы. За что его разрабам регулярно прилетает, чувствуется  что «полякам» не хочется таких же проблем. Однако я считаю, что если бы игра вышла с таким же количеством жести, как планировалось, то игре бы это пошло лишь в плюс.  ТЕХНИЧЕСКАЯ ЧАСТЬ: Честно говоря, могло быть и лучше. Критические баги залатали (встретил1–2 за всю игру), незначительные баги есть, но немного. Проблемы с хитбоксами и регистрациями. Раздражает враньё про оптимизацию. ИГРА ОЧЕНЬ ТРЕБОВАТЕЛЬНАЯ. Когда в Найт-Сити ночь и ты едешь в Japan Town за неончиком — при любом железе 25–30 кадров, оператива и проц в нули, а потом вылет. О вылетах: это раковая опухоль игры. Я люблю делать скрины в играх. Однако если вы смотрели мои скрины в CP 2077 — того, что мы подразумеваем под киберпанком, там нет. И не стоит думать, что я такая нетакуська и мне не нравилось происходящее на экране, наоборот, первые 5 часов я ходил с отпавшей челюстью. Дело в том, что игра вылетала, когда я хотел сфоткать небо, вывески или неон. Причём иногда выдавала ебанный синий экран. Ну это же уровень Таркова! Я думал, что проблема в драйверах они и правда были староватые, однако НИЧЕГО НЕ ПОМЕНЯЛОСЬ. Движок проклят. Ведьмаки тоже тяжело релизились, но это переплюнуло всё.  ИТОГ: Cyberpunk 2077 — очень противоречивая игра. С одной стороны, хороший геймплей, невероятная графика, спорный, но скорее хороший сюжет. С другой — отсутствие RPG-элементов, тонны вырезанного контента, отвратительное техническое состояние на релизе и спорное сейчас, на мой взгляд скучнейшее DLC. Cyberpunk должен был стать игрой мечты CD Projekt, но долгая разработка, амбициозность и самоуверенность не дали игре стать той, которой она заслуживает быть. Многие говорят, что CDPR учтут ошибки в сиквеле. Но выйдет ли он? Будущее киберпанка на плечах DLC к Ведьмаку 3 и Ведьмака 4. В Cyberpunk 2077 у CD Project был карт-бланш на свинство — фанаты готовы были принять любую ошибку. Примут ли сейчас? Сомневаюсь. Cyberpunk 2077 — это действительно хорошая игра, которая заставила меня поменять мнение о ней. Уверен, я ещё вернусь в неё и игра мне скорее понравилась. Однако то, какой она должна была стать, расстраивает намного больше, чем радует то, какой она вышла.  Cyberpunk 2077 — 7/10

I have a very tumultuous relationship with this game. Touted as one of the greatest rpgs of the modern day, as well as having a significant impact on the revitalization of the cyberpunk genre within mainstream pop culture, Cyberpunk 2077 felt inescapable. All that being said, CD Projekt Red’s The Witcher III failed to fully resonate with me, so I never bought into the hype for their shiny new game, nor did I experience the crushing disappointment of its damn near unplayable state at launch. Years removed from its horrific launch, with countless updates, a DLC, and a hearty recommendation from a dear friend, I finally gave it a try. After playing it for damn near 100 hours and fully completing every achievement, did it live up to the hype? If you want the TL;DR answer, I recommend the game well enough. If you want the long answer, keep reading.  First of all, it’s a lot. I think I failed to recognize the sheer scope of the game when I first started playing it. Like, they really did make a colossal dystopian metropolis for you to explore, with an entire ecosystem and flow to it that makes sense. From a purely artistic standpoint, the game is a resounding achievement. The art direction, music, and voice acting here are genuinely A1, and speak to an immense amount of passion and confidence in the developer’s vision. It’s no wonder the game captured so many people based on its visuals alone, as the game is capable of creating sequences you can’t help but look upon in awe. I only wish they placed more attention on the game’s RPG mechanics.  Have you ever played Fallout 4? “Fun game, terrible RPG” is the tagline many associate with it, as it abandoned much of the player agency native to the Fallout series in favor of a more limited, linear style of storytelling, with major choices being relegated to ♥♥♥♥ like “who do you want to blow up” at the end of the game. I actually quite like Fallout 4, but I think the criticisms against it as a narrative RPG are undeniable, save for the wonderful Far Harbor DLC. I think far and away the worst aspect of it is its insistence on offering you meaningless choices. You will see “Yes, Sarcastic (Yes), No (yes but later), More Info” for damn near every conversation in the game. I think it really speaks to how vapid the dialogue options are when the developers themselves don’t even tell you what you’re actually gonna say, instead choosing to condense the intent into three and a half laughable ways of saying yes.    Now, why am I bringing all this up for a review on Cyberpunk 2077? Well, I honestly see quite a lot of similarity between the two! More specifically, I am ASTOUNDED that people give Fallout 4 so much flak for its poor RPG mechanics when Cyberpunk 2077 fares even worse as a narrative RPG!  The game opens with a seemingly vital decision: your background. Are you a nomad living on the fringes of society? A gang member trying to get by in the seedy underbelly of Night City? Or a corpo, a part of the upper echelon of society, callously trampling on any and all beneath you? An interesting selection! I chose Nomad, and got a fun opening sequence of getting into Night City through a job to transport a real, living iguana. This set me down the path of forming a bond of friendship with the guy who hired me, acting as my leading narrative thread through Night City. Awesome! I wonder how drastically this would’ve changed if I chose corpo or gang member? Spoilers! Not at all, or at least, not in a way that actually matters. No matter what fun opening sequence you get, you will ALWAYS befriend Jackie, who will ALWAYS prompt the Arasaka heist, which will ALWAYS end the exact same way. Learning this opened my eyes to the true nature of Cyberpunk 2077: this is not an RPG; this is a futuristic Grand Theft Auto.  The game, like Fallout 4, is confused. Is it an open-ended game about impacting the world through your choices? Or is it a carefully-constructed roller coaster through a campaign the devs planned out piece by piece? It tries to be both, much to the detriment of each half. The developers have constructed a well-built, engaging campaign for you to play through, yet they also want the game to be a narrative RPG where your choices matter. There are many complicated aspects that go into this game being a weak RPG, in my opinion, but there are two fundamental ones that harm the experience most severely.   First problem: voiced protagonist. This was a problem in Fallout 4, and it’s a problem here. I play RPGs to imagine what decisions I’d make in fantastical, unrealistic situations, and, yes, roleplay in them. That goes out the window when a wholly new voice is attached to them. Multiple times, I’d pick a dialogue option I read to be more reasonable or calm, only for V to shout them out aggressively, completely altering the flow of the conversation in a way that was unintended by me, the player. Also, this single choice has a profoundly negative effect on replayability. If I want to replay the game trying to roleplay as a corpo-loving jackass, guess what? He’s gonna have the exact same voice as my nomad character. Not only does this game not allow you to make meaningful decisions, it doesn’t even give you the courtesy of having what little decisions you CAN make even superficially feel different.   This is further compounded by the second problem: not showing the full dialogue option. Again, just like in Fallout 4, Cyberpunk 2077 makes the baffling decision to not show the full dialogue option before you choose it. Numerous times, I’d pick an option I read one way, only for the FULL line to come off the complete opposite way, prompting a very annoyed reload. I have to imagine this was done to reduce the amount of reading players would have to do, but I want to read! I want to know the full context of what I’m gonna say in this game where, supposedly, what I say impacts the world! The truth is, a vast majority of what you say is flavor text, with actual decisions being relegated to the end of the game, once the developers know you’ve thoroughly enjoyed their roller coaster. You can choose how the ride ends, and you can do so in spectacular fashion, but everything up to that point is premeditated. It’s disappointing, and can lead to some genuinely infuriating narrative moments.  Take the Voodoo Boys mission, for example. Placide has made it abundantly clear that you, an outsider, are worth nothing to them beyond this single job that mutually benefits both parties, so it comes as no surprise that Voodoo Boys betray you. I chose to trust Placide during the mission, and when I was betrayed, I thought it was awesome! It made perfect sense for them to cut out this loose end tracing them back to the job, and I was excited to now go back to their hideout and have to fight them to get what I want! Except, that’s not what happens. You step outside the mall, where two of Placide’s goons are waiting for you. They call Placide, informing him you survived. I assumed I was too slow to kill them, and you could prevent them from calling Placide if you’re fast enough, but, no, they’re immortal! They even offer to DRIVE you to Placide, after which, you have a sheepish conversation where Placide goes “erm… what the scallop?” and then Brigitte shows up and continues like nothing happened. I ended up reloading the save and siding with the Netwatch guy, and you know what changed? NOTHING. Johnny makes fun of you for choosing this option, almost like the devs laughing at you for expecting player impact in their narrative RPG, the two guys Placide sent still drive you back, and then you have the SAME conversation with Placide, only now, he’s a little upset. Hell, you can even PUNCH Placide, only for Brigitte to interrupt the conversation the exact. same. way. Why even give me the option when it’s ultimately meaningless? Cyberpunk 2077 is one of those games where I would sometimes stop what I was doing just to look at Night City. Driving down the highway at night while it was raining, with all the neon reflecting off the road and path tracing turned on, genuinely made me think about how far video game graphics have come. I played with DLSS Quality and Frame Generation, and it looked incredible, even if my PC turned into an oven half the time lol.  The side missions were probably my favorite part. One minute I was getting pulled into a prisoner’s crucifixion braindance, and the next I was talking to Brendan, a friendly vending machine. Stuff like that is what made Night City stick with me instead of just feeling like a pretty backdrop.  It still has some glitches, but nothing that ruined my playthrough. The driving also took a little getting used to because some cars felt slippery and almost like they handled in GTA IV, kind of boaty. I was disappointed by the radio stations too since I only found one or two songs I really liked.  I get why CDPR committed to first person, but I still wish there were a third-person gameplay option outside of vehicles.  I had a great time with it, went back to 100% it, and Phantom Liberty is easily one of the best expansions I’ve played. Cyberpunk 2077 has its problems, but it still ended up being one of my top 10 single-player games.

Like a lot of people, I bought this game early on and put it down fairly quickly, deciding I'd come back to it after some patches fixed the myriad of bugs.  I actually ended up forgetting about it and moved on to other things, only coming back to it recently when I saw the drama surrounding the VR mod.  As an Oculus owner, I thought I should grab the mod before its gone and give it another try - as it turns out its been over 5 years since I had uninstalled the game awaiting a patch.  The game on its own in flat I'm sure would be great, but in VR, it is honestly a masterpiece or close to it.  Definitely the best VR experience I have had to date.  Experiencing life in Night City in VR is really something.  In VR, you can really appreciate the level of detail the developers put in to the world.  Sometimes to get to missions I would simply walk or take the metro, just so I could experience and explore the city fully.  Generally in a game like this, I would only drive.  In addition to the world detail you can take in through VR, the story and emotions within it hit harder to.  The game is well written, and the voice actors do an excellent job with their line delivery - but in VR, it enhanced even more.  In the dog eat dog world of Night City, there are some tough choices, and I found myself thinking about them long after after I put down the headset.  Looking the characters in the eyes while events you put in to motion start to unfold, also carries a lot more impact in VR as well.   All in all, I really enjoyed this game.  I hope the legal and community attention the VR mod got gets CDPR to have native VR support for the next game in this universe.    In order to play the game in VR on my rig, I used a variation (a bit lower) of the Hardware Unboxed optimized settings.  It is a resource hog, but even on lower settings it still looks great in VR.

I have played this game periodically since it was first released and I admit, it filled a gap in genres that I needed.   This game has such depth - the story line, the choices, the customizability. The graphics are beautiful. The NPCs are people you sincerely grow to care about.   And you can taste the fall of civilization in every image. The depravity, the hopelessness. The projects. People dying on the streets near crowds. The killers and the mad. It grabs you viscerally.  But the endings? I took a wrong turn one night in dialog and my character made a decision that erased all other futures. After400+s of hours on her, it was shocking. The credits started to roll and I burst out crying.   I haven't played since. That ending was so well done, with other characters giving emotional vignettes. I am still upset about it. That moment is stark across my mind, even over a year later. I suspect I could reverse the outcome if I tried, but the emotional scarring is deep.   This is one of maybe 5 titles I can say that hit that deep. The best thing I can say is that the game is still a masterpiece, even for all that I cannot play it anymore.

Considering its shaky, turbulent and, at times, broken start in late 2020, early 2021, you'd be well justified to write Cyberpunk off as all hype; a AAA game completely failing to live up to its potential. How things can radically change with the eb and flow of time. In this case, entirely for the better.  For someone who grew up with and was moulded by narratively driven behemoths, the likes of Metal Gear Solid, Mass Effect and Fallout, Cyberpunk is well and truly shoulder-to-shoulder with the absolute best. Everything from the world building to the aesthetics, the ambience to the choices, both pivotal or otherwise, all come together seamlessly to build a fully immersive RPG experience that may well linger with you long after you've completed the game.  So many of the characters are remarkably realistic; relatable, flawed, conflicted, haunted by their pasts and each having their own individual motives driving them to their fate... including you, V.  Cyberpunk isn't your typical surface-level RPG. It makes you painfully aware of the fact that every choice, both of yours as well as those around you, has a cost... not just within the world of Cyberpunk but in life as well. Some choices cost too much. Some will cost your freedom but some may set you free.  I can't stress enough that, although the base game on it's own is incredible, it is genuinely incomplete without Phantom Liberty. Still not sure? Watch the music video for Phantom Liberty by Dawid Podsiadło. It's so outstanding that it belongs in a Bond movie. No joke, it is truly breath-taking.  Finally, you will almost certainly feel bittersweet once the story is over. If, like me, you're something of a completionist with RPGs and you want to finish Cyberpunk 2077 in the best possible way, save "The Star" ending for last. Trust me.

Cyberpunk 2077 had one the roughest launches in recent memory. Unfinished, buggy, hated. Deservedly so. Today? It's an absolute powerhouse.  Edgerunners broke me and made me crave more of Night City. After swearing off the dumpster fire, I dove back in after a few years. It was absolutely worth it.  Night City is absurd, alive, and dripping with personality. The slang, the culture, the overwhelming feeling of dystopia - it all clicks and works flawlessly. It screams a perfect parallel to a world ran by unsatiated corporations, a world that could exist in an alternate reality.   The story was crafted with such care and attention to detail. Relationships hit hard. Motivations rest in morally grey areas and every character has justification that feel real. Your own choices have weight and the consequences hit like a freight train.  Johnny Silverhand is a dope mf and a standout. V and Johnny clash, argue, and evolve together. Sometimes you hate him, sometimes you respect him. That's the point. He's a poignant reminder of what this world is and what happens when you fight the corporations.  Combat is insanely crispy and chaotic. Apogee Sandevistan + Byakko with a sneaky throwing knife was unhinged and so much fun. Not to mention, the movement felt buttery. I found myself scaling every possible skyscraper and pushing the limits of what the game would allow. (Incase you're curious, Mega Buildings are the only skyscrapers with solid, climbable assets through and through)  The story of Phantom Liberty lives up to the standards already set by the main game. Dogtown is fine, but the story slaps. Every ending is justified and only further reveals the twisted and pervasive nature of Night City.  Cyberpunk went from a disappointing laughingstock to legend. $60 in 2026 is still worth every cent. Night City will grab you by the throat, drag your through hell, and refuse to let go.

Despite all the crap I am going to say about it- I simply love this game.  This game is throughout quite an immersive and fun experience, that is ocasionally ruined a little bit with the hicups caused by some tedious issues.   The story, while it explores tropes that are typical to this genre - it does it quite well. Colorful (maybe too much during daytime) yet dark, near altfuture, urban dystopia. Society indulged, obsessed and drained both with consumerism and sex. Uploading the very soul to the net. Exploring the topics of afterlife, leaving a mark in the world, identity and fighting with the system.   Characters are well written, they fit in perfectly and so does the dialogue. There is a lot of memorable quests and peeps, especially among the main cast. I love both Johnny's and V's characters, their relationship and how they interact with eachother. Kudos to English female V voice actress, her performance was amazing.  Graphically it is stunning. The lights, effects, sounds, atmosphere, weapons, buildings and especially car models - all of this builds up the world almost flawlessly. Night City does look and feel authentic. The music is spot on, both in the game's soundtrack and it's radio track selection - they literally did a 10/10 job here, especially with the Samurai bits.   But...  Sadly this whole immersive experience can be broken by the bugs that persisted in this game over the years.  You can spot civilians phasing through walls, multiple car models being stuck on top of or inside each other, enemies shooting you through some walls, animations/scripted events not playing correctly or at all. One of the more annoying bugs that I remember from when I first played the game ~5 years ago was "clown boots" - the game loops the sound of the crushing bottles as your footsteps when you first walk on them in specific area during the Evelyn questline and it doesn't stop unless you restart the game...   Luckily I didn't run into anything that was game breaking or soft locking my progress. The game also flatlined like two times for me. Yet it is still disappointing seeing that those old issues weren't fixed, despite devs supporting the game and pushing new updates over the years. Bugs are very rare, yet they are there. It also feels that the further you go from the start of the game, there is less of them.  AI could also be better as it is very basic. Civilian behaviour feels mostly like an "A" than an "I".  On top of everything the police is not a threat at all. You can lose a tail in mere seconds and it feels like they are not even interested in chasing you. Whats also a bit wild is that pedestrians tend to jump under your wheels for no reason, as if they were trying to avoid your vehicle... in the wrong direction.., even if you were not a threat to them to begin with.  And then, there is a Sinnerman quest - an absolute joke...  I would still strongly recommend getting this game. It's not without its flaws, but it is truly a great experience. It also does hold a replayability value with the build variety, some choices you make during the story and it has a mod support. Just keep in mind that you will eventually encounter bugs that will make the world of the game less believable to you.  Would bomb Saka tower again tho.

This is a tough one to rate. Trying this 5 years after release, with hardware that allows me to experience it in path traced glory on a 4K OLED monitor, I did initially enjoy the novelty of looking at those neons at night and the way light bounces off of of high resolution skin textures.   However, the game makes me feel awfully empty, and the world while big, is barren, with very little that can be done in it that isn't a subset of repetitive actions. Combined with the dystopian setting, and the game being pretty big, playing it feels.. lonely for the lack of a better term.   I'm a sucker for large open world games and great graphics, so on paper this was supposed to be a win. But I find myself just not enjoying playing with it, not enjoying interacting with the world in its extremely limited capacity, or the few unique characters that last beyond specific missions.  Despite 5 years passing since launch, I still fell through the ground for the game to crash hours into my playthrough. Despite those same 5 years passing, and there being some more cars, weapons, it feels like the content added is fairly mundate, adding inconsequential type of novelty. I was able to make the world a bit more interesting with mods, as 5 years allowed the community to produce quite a bit. And while the most ambitious can add some things to do, they can't address the fundamental issue of how uninterractable and barren the world feels.   The negative rating isn't a reflection of the bugs or technical prowess of the developers, which they have demonstrated. The game looks good and generally plays at a C+ reliability level. Totally acceptable if the game was actually fun. But most of it is doing the same few things slightly differently dozens of times. The big city serves little purpose beyond providing a distance you need to drive between places where you do those things. Interesting things happen just during finite missions, and then they end, and the world is unexciting again. If something happens, it's usually a one-time scripted event where you just watch it. There is a whole lot of filler to make the city appear like a city-ish, but you can't do anything with it. And it leads to an experience that isn't particularly fun, and it isn't as enjoyable as the other large open world games that either add interactivity, or at least introduce pleasant worlds to make up for it. I don't hate this game - I felt indifferent and slightly more negative with each hour spent in the game feeling like more and more of a waste of time on something that didn't feel fun, and I will likely not complete the story, as it feels like too much commitment to something that surprisingly doesn't spark joy.

The lighting, reflections, and overall detail make the world feel alive and immersive.  Gameplay feels just right. If you really want to level up and unlock the best upgrades, you’ll need to put in the time.  Combat? No major complaints. Gunplay feels good, skills are fun to use, and overall it’s satisfying.  Bugs still exist, but nothing too game-breaking (at least in my experience). [b]Note:[/b] Didn’t play much vanilla. I mostly used a visually upgraded + QoL-rich mod pack.  [h1]PROs:[/h1] ✅ Large and unique world ✅ Plenty of lore from various sources ✅ Great modding community ✅ Visuals can be amazing with modding ✅ Lots of small details and collectibles in the world ✅ Solid OST ✅ Lots of viable playstyles ✅ Plenty of fun easter eggs to find ✅ Driving system felt pretty good (even though I probably had mods improving it) ✅ Panam ;) [h1]CONs:[/h1] ❌ Still a lot of bugs even with mods that fix various issues ❌ Broken HDR (needs a mod to fix) ❌ Vanilla lacks a lot of QoL features ❌ Heavily relies on ray tracing for a lot of its beauty (world is filled with screens and reflective surfaces, especially indoor clubs and city centers) ❌ Maxed difficulty still feels pretty casual ❌ A lot of side missions became way too samey (go in, do the thing, go out) [h1]Comments:[/h1]  Another disclaimer: I didn’t even finish the main story, so my thoughts are based on a limited playthrough. Sadly, I lost interest pretty quickly because most sessions started feeling very forced. Long story short — this game just wasn’t for me. Cyberpunk worlds are usually packed with drugs, sex, low morals, heavy violence, ugly augmented people and chaos. (which I don't mind if done in a way I enjoy it) This game does an excellent job diving deep into that theme with insane amounts of detail, a huge world, and tons of lore. Still, I’d rather play Skyrim.  If you enjoy FPS/RPGs in a Cyberpunk setting, it delivers a great world with lots of build variety and many ways to approach objectives. There are endless stories and characters to discover.  However, even though many characters have deep background lore, I didn’t find most of them likeable. Almost every character I met I genuinely didn’t care about. Silverhand was entertaining at the start thanks to his crazy personality and Keanu’s voice, but he quickly became an annoying, deluded, self-righteous punk. His speeches turned moronic fast.  Visually the base game looks decent, but you need a bunch of mods (plus ray tracing in certain areas) to get that real “wow” eyegasm.  Combat felt oddly easy for the most part. My stealth + power sniper build didn’t help with that easy feeling — I could just snipe everyone through walls from outside the building when I didn’t feel like sneaking. In the end I was mostly doing checkbox hunting from point A to B and felt more exhausted than excited.  Driving around the city was genuinely nice though.  I gave this game a shot mainly because I really loved the Cyberpunk Edgerunners anime. In the end, the lore, the characters, and the overall feel wasn't simply my cup of tea. It’s definitely a good game (aside from the jank and bugs), it just wasn’t the right fit for me. Short comment: I started playing Cyberpunk 2077 at the end of 2025. The game is very enjoyable, however there is a lot of room for improvements. The dark world in the game is very tragic, but also a good warning for possible future.  I would honestly score the game as strong 9/10 (Modded) and 7/10 (without any mods). Huge thank you for CDPR for making ability to create mods, as they really help with minor inconveniences that Cyberpunk 2077 has.  My take on the game details: Gameplay: 10/10 Graphics: 9/10 Performance: 8/10 Mechanics: 7/10 Main game finish time: ~ 340h (All gigs, all ncpd, cyberpsychos, exploration, main story (Temperance) + PhantomLiberty DLC (King of Wands))  Mods I used: Skip intro, Lizzy Braindances, Enhanced Romances, change of color for arms cyberware - we can say all are cosmetic, not changing gameplay.   Detailed description(Contains spoilers):  Very interesting dark world scenario in possible near future. Multiple warnings and truths about possible dark scenarios with usage of AI, big corporations and people just trying to survive. It is still hard to believe that our MC dies no matter what, but the whole road to death of V is very interesting. The world is corrupted, twisted and basically all residents of Night City are evil, with maybe very few exceptions(like River, seems he was one of very few that actually were not bad).  When it comes to gameplay - it is really cool. Multiple interesting aspects, details, fun interactions. Multiple options for most of gigs. Fun action gameplay with a nice scenery to it.  Graphically the game is pretty nice, with only some drawbacks, but it is for sure one of highest standards.  When it comes to performance, the game has hiccups on my 12GB RTX2060 dual by Palit. Of course for enjoyment of gameplay I turned off unnecessary things like DLSS, raytracing and rendered native. Nonetheless with native rendering it was working fine with around 70fps, with AI frame generation using AMD FSR it reaches target that was interesting me of 120fps at most times, however as it is with frame gen - sometimes it creates artefacts. I wish the performance would be good enough to last at 100-120fps without AI frame generation, but nowadays engines it's quite hard to achieve.  Game mechanics are pretty interesting and very likeable, with some exceptions. I really hoped that clothes and "legendary" items would prevail, but now I can see that the system lacked a lot of options and Damage over time was not actually implemented as long-time damage over time I always seek in games. Level scaling for statistic check is quite terrible in my opinion and should never be implemented.   Overall I enjoyed the game, had a lot of fun with it and might come back to it to finish with other endings some time, try out new builds, enjoy graphics and sing pon pon ♥♥♥♥. This game surely is one of a kind and honestly I am glad I did not play it at launch time, as I would not enjoy it as much. A lot as I see has changed, most of it for good - maybe except for some pre 2.0 mechanics.   Tragic story in tragic city with tragic people and tragic outcomes, crime is everywhere, AI takes over the world behind the scenes, corporations treat people like crap, government treats people like crap, it is very relatable to Real Life 2026 and this game shows a good warning on what direction might all of this take.  That's all from me, see you around, chooms!

TLDR: Play if you want to experience the power fantasy of a professional mercenary fighting for their life in a bleak dystopia, with an amazing story that has some pacing issues  In this game you play as V, a mercenary who lives in a dystopian hellhole that is Night City, whose attempt at becoming a legend lands them in a whole lot of trouble. Your job is to fix that. The story is actually really well told, and you experience it entirely from the first person perspective and they put a lot of work into making it feel as immersive as possible. The writing of characters makes them sound like actual people, the factions feel believable and the slang actually feels natural instead of tacked on.  The world, as mentioned, is pretty damn bleak. Rampant capitalism has made most people miserable and everyone tries to find a way to cope. The game does actually do a great job at hammering that point home, sometimes a bit hamfisted, but often in pretty subtle ways. The first time I realized my apartment had a mandatory adscreen in the middle of the living area it started to feel a lot less like a home, and nobody will even comment on that. And of course violence, drug abuse and sexual exploitation is everywhere.   There is however the issue that this world is also very "set". You are not going to fix that (spoilers I guess), fine, but you are also going to have very little to no impact at all. Tons of side quests give you all sorts of decisions to make with interesting moral questions to ponder, but rarely does this have any affect but a slightly different quest reward or an angry voice call afterwards because things ended in tragedy - there are no happy endings in Night City - that it feels like a follow up was missing or you are playing an abandoned storyline. Outside of quests, if you start running people over you might trigger the police in a GTA style star system of escalations, but remain undetected for a minute and things turn back to normal. Similiarly, you can gun down a group of thugs belonging to a big gang and nobody ever will care about that, with the gang behaving just as before towards you. So this game is more about the powerfantasy of the moment to moment gameplay.  And my God is that well done. You can play all sorts of drastically different builds, like a hacker that infiltrates hideouts and triggers the grenades carried by every enemy, some shotgun wearing juggernaut that guns everything down, or a cyber ninja who parries bullets. The game lets you try everything out to find your perfect build, and if you know what you are doing your late game V is going to feel like a demigod of Night City.  Before you buy though, there is one big issue, bigger even than the non-responsive world. At the release of the game, that would have been the technical state, but nowadays CDPR managed to fix it that it runs mostly stable - still, save when possible. Now, the main issue is the pacing.  The game is structured to work with quest chains, where the main story paths, the excellent DLC story and important side stories (like the ones of Vs allies) get tons of quests, and each finished one triggers the start of the next. That works like every RPG ever. What is different that the beginning of the follow up quest often happens after a certain amount of time. So you will crash through a gang hideout, extract some data, send that to Vs friend, they will say that this will take some time to look through and they will message you once they have something. You can do something else in the meantime, and granted, you always have a full quest log, your phone constantly gets bombarded with new quests to take. The issue is if you found what you were doing really interesting and would like to continue that questline. So you wait 24 ingame hours. You wait another 24. You do another gig or five. You look up the wiki and read that the next quest step should trigger roughly 24 hours later, but at this point it has been an ingame week. This gets frustrating, because there seem to be triggers for quest updates, but they only update one quest per update, so you are at the mercy of RNGesus that you can continue the quest chain you found interesting. There also seems to be some priority with the main quest chains, which makes sense, but also means you only get to see some cool side content you would have liked to see earlier only after the main questlines have been exhausted until the point of no return. Which usually happens in the first third of my runs. A certain character is waiting a long time in the Embers, tell you that.  This issue with the quest progression triggers has no clear answer. You'll find all kinds of theories on what triggers progression online, from restarts, to specific elevators to take, to just standing still next to water for 5 minutes. The Mechanicus ain't got ♥♥♥♥ on the Cyberpunk community when it comes to esoteric tech solutions.  Still, if you can deal with the fact that some quest chains will just have an inconsistent pacing, you are rewarded with an amazing - if depressing - story, superb gameplay and overall a unique cyberpunk experience.

Honestly, I never review games. But given the amount of hours I've spent within Night City, I feel almost obligated. I played since launch, and personally I had no bugs throughout the entire playthrough, I finished the game, that was that. I thoroughly enjoyed my time and thought that would be the end of it. Well, I was wrong. It ended up being a complete masterpiece in my book.  Graphics wise, I have - by modern standards - a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ pc with a 1650 (I love you really). However, how a game this beautiful, diverse, vertical and detailed runs so well on medium settings is beyond me. It ran okay on launch and has since only gotten more stable.  The soundtrack in this game is insane. I'm not really referring to the songs on the radio, though I think they're pretty damn good too, but the ambient soundtrack is brilliant. If I ever put the Spotify playlist on, all of those songs have emotional nostalgic weight attached to them, because they play at such traumatic in-game events. Also I really enjoy the combat music, gets me super hyped.  On the topic of combat, I recall when the game released some reviewers not enjoying it. While I believe in 'to each their own' I couldn't really understand it. For me the gunfights are extremely satisfying, especially handguns, with most all weapons feeling really *punchy* when you fire. Melee has seen a massive improvement since launch and is as fun as the gunfights. However, I could never let go of my quickhack deck for a melee something more melee focused like a sandevistan, as I feel you're missing out on a massive aspect of the combat by not using them (quickhacks). Anyways, combat = awesome.  Story - what can I say. Story is phenomenal. Even in instances where the choices don't necessarily matter, you really think about what you want to say carefully. I honestly think the forced first person perspective really enhances this feeling of weight and immersion that you'd lose out on with the third-person so many are clamouring for (though I think it could be cool, first person really works well). By the end of the story, when making the final few decisions, I really sat with myself to consider what I thought was morally right, and as very few games have done that, it gets top marks in my book. Also the DLC credits roll had me feeling all types of complex feelings about it.   I think since launch the devs did some good work towards immersion. Initially there wasn't a lot you could necessarily do to engage with the world, but they've since added in some stuff like being able to go to the bar and have a drink (animated). Do I think there could be more? Absolutely. Mods fixed that for me, added loads of immersion spots, being able to lean, sit, smoke, drink anywhere. For this I simply can't rate it too highly, as if it were great already I wouldn't have sought mods to fix it.  I suppose I should go into more detail as I already mentioned it, but yes, mods are pretty great for this game. Don't get me wrong, it's not competing with a bethesda title for the types of game changing/overhauls mods, but Cyberpunk has some pretty great ones. A lot of the gameplay ones I used altered things very slightly, as I felt the gameplay was already great and I had no real desire to change anything about that, except for adding in survival aspects like eating, drinking, sleeping and nerve (which gives you tremors/ptsd). Plenty of gooner mods too (a lot actually), but I think you'll find whatever mod you would probably want (except the third person mod, that's still super janky).  The performances of all actors are all solid. The weakest performance for me is Keanu Reaves, but I've never thought he was a particularly good actor. However, he grows on you, and he for sure has some great moments and monologues. One thing I noticed on my second playthrough that I did not appreciate enough the first time I played was the body language. This is where I think third person would take away from the performances. With your little optical eyes, you can zoom in at will, and you start to notice during conversations with NPCs their body language is as good as the vocals. Honestly can't think of another game that's done it this well. Maybe RDR2? But the difference here is there's never a set cutscene. It's all first-person, all the way through, the interaction with a random NPC will be as cinematic as the most climatic moments, but it just works so well due to the performances (and the script I suppose).  Last comment is the fashion aspect. It's good. I enjoyed it. Especially when they removed the classic RPG "wear the things with the highest stats" so you end up looking ridiculous. Also it didn't make a lot of sense that in a universe with cyberwear, completely cybernetic bodies, that the real defining from gunfire is a hi-vis vest.   Really not sure what else to say. I like the shooting, I like the soundtrack, I like the story, I like the city, I like I can enhance the whole experience with minimal mods, and photomode (which I mentioning only now) is very well done.  10/10

But that's not what I want to talk about.  When I first started playing this game a couple months ago, my first impression, upon completing the game, was that it lacked in the story. Going in, I was expecting anti-consumerism and anti-capitalism/corporation themes, and they are indeed there, but not the fore front. I finished the game, complained about it to my girlfriend, then came back and played a few more times, getting a few more endings.  That's when I realized what the game is also trying to point out. Yeah, yeah, consumerism narrative or whatever, but I don't mean that, I mean V, your player.  Post prologue, V has everything ripped from them. Closest friend, they had trust taken and broken, they died and came back and now are stuck with a rockerboy terrorist in their head that's trying to take over their body.  The game has an artificial timer for this, but this is important to mention, the gameplay not forcing this timer is probably the most important to me. As you go through Night City, completing jobs, finding friends, partners, even developing your relations with Johnny, it all sets in, "you're on borrowed time, how will you spend it?"  One ending, which I can barely consider it an ending as it is very abrupt (with the player's choice), you see everyone you met, rubbed shoulders with or were acquainted. Depending on the romance option you chose, they could be furious or broken. Friends torn inside, wishing things were different.   Another ending, just, give in. Let the corporation win and what becomes of you? You abondoned everything you loved and had. In a sense, betrayal.  This is coming from a girl who came out of a really bad drug addiction and is just getting out of frequent suicide ideation. On surface level, this game asks, "what makes you human," but digging deeper, paying attention to your playthrough, you're asked, "if you're on limited time, you die next week, what do you do? Do you pretend things are fine? Prolong your life at the expense of others and the experiences around you, or do you leave everything behind, abandon it all; leaving behind scars, damaging the people you built community with?"  This game has many problems but its story isn't one of them. This game made me change my perception of what life is. From being nihilistic, hateful, I turned the spotlight and, sure some things didn't change but, my approach to life changed. There are a lot of things I could glaze this game for, a lot of themes I could beg and beg to become a reality. But the change that did happen, within me, I accept. This is a really, really great game. 20-50 hours per save gives you everything you need to experience this game in all aspects and I could not recommend it enough.

[h2]Look at my play time. I write this review with utmost confidence and personal experience. No BS included[/h2]  [h1] TL;DR - Just play it [/h1]  I played this game not long after its original release. Bugs, crashes and all. I still enjoyed it. The story was so different from anything I had played before, and the different builds I could use drew me in deeper. After diving deep into Cyberpunk 2077 and Phantom Liberty, I can confidently say this is one of best RPG experiences created. And with it's bad release, and fantastic comeback - that should be enough for you.   [h2] Story [/h2] The story is nothing short of phenomenal. What starts as a tale of survival, quickly evolves into a deeply personal journey filled with moral dilemmas, unforgettable characters, and choices that genuinely matter and change the outcome of the story. The narrative grabs you early and never lets go. It’s layered, mature, and constantly evolving based on your choices. Phantom Liberty elevates this even further with a spy-thriller twist that feels intense, unpredictable, and emotionally grounded. It injects a tense espionage storyline that perfectly complements the base game’s themes of identity and control. It throws you into a horror-type scenario that keeps your heart pumping towards the end, or throws you into emotional despair. Did you, or did you not make the correct decision? Johnny Silverhand starts off as an abrasive, self-centered arse. He is loud, reckless, and seemingly impossible to trust. He constantly clashes with you, challenges your decisions, and feels more like a curse than a companion. But as the story unfolds, layers begin to peel back. You see his regrets, his failures, and the ideals buried beneath all that anger. By the end, depending on your choices, Johnny can transform into something genuinely meaningful: a loyal ally, a voice of hard-earned wisdom, and even a friend. That evolution - from intolerable to unforgettable - is one of the most compelling character arcs in the game.  Night City itself is a masterpiece. It deserves its own spotlight. The world isn’t just big - it’s feels alive for the most part. Every district tells its own story through architecture, culture, and the people who inhabit it. Every alleyway, megabuilding, and neon-lit street corner feels handcrafted with lore and purpose. The world building is insanely detailed. From corporate power struggles to street-level desperation, making it feel like a real, breathing dystopia. Not to mention the views. I pressed F12 so many damn times in this city.   [h2] Graphics [/h2] Visually, the game is stunning. The neon-soaked skyline, dense crowds, and dynamic lighting create a level of atmosphere that few games can match. Reflective rain-soaked streets, to the glow of holographic ads cutting through the night. The game delivers a consistently cinematic experience. Whether you’re cruising through the city at night or exploring its darker corners, it’s consistently breathtaking.  [h2] Gameplay [/h2] Gameplay wise, the freedom is incredible. You can approach situations however you want - guns blazing, swords slashing, stealthy hacking, or something in between. The build variety is where the game truly shines: netrunners, cyber-enhanced melee monsters, precision snipers - each playstyle feels distinct and viable. Experimenting with different builds keeps the experience fresh even after dozens of hours. Don't forget about the mods, either. I sunk an extra 500+ hours with mods added alone.  [h2] Endings - where your decisions matter [/h2] And then there are the endings. There’s no single “right” conclusion - just consequences shaped by your decisions throughout the game. None of them feel like an afterthought. Each ending feels meaningful, emotional, reinforcing the themes of identity, choice, and sacrifice.  Cyberpunk 2077, especially with Phantom Liberty, has become the game it was always meant to be - and then some. It took some time for Projekt CD RED to live up to their promises for this game, but behold true beauty as of today. Definitely in my top 3 games of all time. I think so much discussion at release focused on what a steaming pile of trash this game's code was that it distracted from both the good and the bad. As I finally visit this game with a complete playthrough well over 5 years later, with I suppose a good chunk of the problems fixed, I can weigh in objectively having never played this game at release time.  First, this game is still horrifically buggy. People who say that the problems have been fixed are grading this on a curve versus the original release. Leaving the room where I flatlined the voodoo guy via the blackwall, I would, for example, be frozen in place while crouching and scope focused while stepping on a bit of conduit on the floor. That simple movement is still unsolved in some cases is glaring. I'm not going to go through all the bugs, just that this is still at a point that the problems are completely immersion breaking and required me to redo from saves many times.  Secondly, Keanu Reeves is a horrifically unsuited for his role here. It was a cheap and tawdry way to promote the game to cast him as Johnny. Keanu excels when he can play someone who is completely overcome by awe (The Matrix) or a stoned idiot (Bill and Ted). These are some of my favorite movies. I don't hate him as an actor. But let's face it, he should be typecasted into a very specific kind of role which is not Johnny. Keanu Reeves cannot play an emotionally stagnant revolutionary displaced decades into the future. This role is much too nuanced for him, and his voice bits come off as overread and contrived in the manner of a high school theater production. It's embarrassing. This comes off to me as cheap PR that compromises the work. Which is sad, because there are many characters here that are so well acted and could have created a timeless emotive experience that was beloved as Skyrim, but they are overshadowed by Johnny's piss-poor dialogue reading.  Anyways, the game is good enough. Play it.

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of the best games of all time. It’s genre-defining in both its aesthetic and its story. As an ARPG with a full capital A. it gives you an immense amount of playstyle freedom in its action. You can be a stealthy rogue hacking everything, or a ruthless tank taking hits like it’s breakfast cereal. Or everything in between. That’s where the gameplay really shines, the sheer amount of customization in how your character works. It’s an RPG that becomes an immersive sim in its depth.  This is tied together with one of the best stories in video games, especially for a game with a fully customizable main character. My V felt like a real extension of me, and I got so invested in the story because of the choices V gets put through. That's set alongside not just one of the best main characters in all of video games, but one of the best secondary leads too, Johnny Silverhand, played brilliantly by Keanu Reeves. But don't sleep on the rest of the cast either. close friends who genuinely feel like they care about V. To ambiguous fixers and morally grey but necessary allies.  The world itself is stunning. It’s one of the best-looking games out there. There is not a single shot of the skyline that looks bad. It does cost your PC some performance, it's not a light game to run, but it runs well enough, even with full path tracing. The raw graphics are made even better by the art style, which the game nails to a T. Cyberpunk's aesthetic has never looked this realized. Everything, from cars and clothes, to buildings and weapons, fits perfectly. As a total experience of walking through a cyberpunk world, nothing beats Cyberpunk 2077.  I really recommend this game. I know the launch game had heavy criticism, and a lot has changed since then. Updates have improved it massively, and the Phantom Liberty DLC is a must-play, adding an amazing side story. It's grown into a game that defines its genre, puts CDPR among the best game developers in the world, and creates a world I simply won't forget. A truly amazing game.

The Redemption of Night City (With Cavéats) I’ve been here since the beginning, and while Cyberpunk 2077 will be studied as a remarkable turnaround, we shouldn't forget that it launched two years too early. CD Projekt Red arguably got a "free pass" for a state they knew wasn't ready, but the current version of the game is finally something remarkable.  The Good The World: Night City is visually outstanding. It is easily one of the most detailed environments ever put in a game, and it’s easy to get lost in the atmosphere.  Build Variety: Spec-ing your character is a total joy. The game truly allows you to play how you want, making it incredibly approachable regardless of your preferred playstyle.  Masterful Side Quests: Some of the darker, gloomier side stories are the best parts of the game. They are masterfully written and stand as great stories in their own right.  Combat: Whether you're hacking or shooting, the combat loop is genuinely fun.  The Bad The Writing: While the characters are mostly great, the dialogue can often be "cringe." V feels somewhat bland as a protagonist, and the character creation system still feels like it lacks meaningful impact.  Navigation: As beautiful as the map is, it just isn’t fun to navigate. Its scale is impressive, but getting from point A to point B often feels like a chore.  The "Arasaka" Irony: There is a lot of deserved love for the game now, but let's not forget the corporate decisions behind the launch. In the end, CDPR acted a lot like the megacorps they satirize.  Verdict It’s not a solid 5/5, but the story and the sheer detail of the world keep me coming back. It is a must-play for the atmosphere alone, even if the "soul" of the protagonist and the dialogue occasionally miss the mark

This is a highly overrated game, essentially sci-fi GTA but worse.  I bought this game because I read reviews and comments that described it as an open world RPG; some people commented that it is "like a science fiction Skyrim." I spent 4 hours creating my character and going through the tutorial stage; after I got into the world and saw this game for what it really is it was already too late to get a refund (denied twice). So I played it some more to give it a chance.  This game is NOT an RPG. You are a pre-determined character that is just walking through a pre-set story on rails with a few possible different game endings. In one case I rescued an annoying monk from a gang who was going to give him cyberware against his wishes. I killed the gang to rescue him, and then he insults me saying I am worse than the gang members because I killed them. I immediately tried to kill him for insulting me like that, but the game wouldn't let me! I don't think this character is tied to a later quest, the game just refused to let me kill him because the game wants to force its morality onto you. The game is constantly pushing its moral message at you, your contacts always whine about you killing criminals and scum. Some cyber-freak could kill 20 people and then I go deal with him and he attacks me and I kill him. Then, my contact cries about it and harangues me. If this was an RPG, then I would be able to kill that stupid monk and I would just do missions for a different contact that appreciated my abilities. But this is not an RPG - you don't create your own identity, you don't make a character or even pick a name. You have hit points, you get to pick your appearance and you get to pick skills from a skill tree - that is not what it means to be a role playing game.  The world is boring and repetitive. It's just a sprawling city of closed doors with nothing behind them (well, you can't even open most doors or buildings), except a few areas that are defined for the mission objectives.

While the world build was gorgeous and took a toll on my pretty good GPU, this game heavily relies on it while ignoring a basic timeline for all of its quests. It feels more like a sandbox game where youre allowed to complete gigs however you want instead of experiencing the urge that the main quest desired to show, mainly the MC not having enough time to live. Another thing that i dont understand is while the DLC gives us an alternate ending, i really dislike it when I had to load an older save file just to complete the original last main story quest. I also find that the main story quests are shorter than the DLC quests which is a bit weird because im used to playing story based games where the DLC is just an extension of the story, not a separate ending. Another thing that disappointed me was the fight against Adam smasher, maybe it was just my settings or me being accidentally to strong, but Ive had way harder gigs at the beginning than the fight against the infamous big boss who looked AMAZING in the anime. Its an alright game but by far not worth it to name it your favourite game. I just wish there was more story and cool fight scenes and not just me trying to find something to do in the game before meeting Hanako at Embers. The DLC is definitely necessary if you want to enjoy this world more, because the original game alone is too little. I reccommend this game simply to just see it for yourself and enjoy the beautiful world, not because the story is big or immersive.

Cyberpunk 2077 is an ambitious and unforgettable journey into a futuristic world that pushes the boundaries of open-world storytelling. Despite having faced a rocky launch, the game has grown into something truly special thanks to constant updates, improvements, and expansions that transformed the experience into one of the most immersive RPGs of this generation.  From the very beginning, Cyberpunk 2077 impresses with its richly detailed setting: Night City. This vibrant megacity feels alive, unpredictable, and layered with stories waiting to be discovered on every corner. The world design is outstanding neon lights, towering skyscrapers, hidden back-alleys, bustling marketplaces, and diverse districts all contribute to an atmosphere that truly makes you feel like you’re living inside a cyberpunk dystopia.  The narrative is one of the game’s biggest strengths. The story is deep, emotional, and filled with intriguing characters. Every major decision you make has weight — whether it’s how you handle a mission, how you approach a conversation, or how you shape your own version of V. There are moments of humor, moments of heartbreak, and moments of sheer intensity that make the entire arc unforgettable. Characters like Jackie, Johnny Silverhand, and Panam are memorable, and their personal journeys enhance the game’s emotional impact.  Combat is dynamic, fluid, and highly customizable. Whether you prefer going in guns blazing, using stealth tactics, hacking enemies from the shadows, or crafting your own cyber-build, the game encourages different playstyles and rewards creativity. The cyberware system adds an extra layer of depth  upgrading your abilities and modding gear feels incredibly satisfying, and it gives players a real sense of progression and personalization.  Even years after release, Cyberpunk 2077 continues to impress with its visuals and performance on PC. With powerful hardware, the game looks striking  detailed character models, particle effects, lighting, reflections, and atmospheric weather all contribute to making Night City feel breathtaking and alive. Night City’s ambient soundscape and soundtrack only deepen immersion, making nighttime runs through the streets unforgettable.  Side content in Cyberpunk 2077 is also worth exploring. From small gigs to long-form quests, you’ll find a variety of stories that can surprise, entertain, and even challenge you  sometimes even more than the main storyline. There’s always something interesting around the corner, and many of the side missions feel like fully fleshed out mini-stories.  Cyberpunk 2077 is not just a game  it’s an experience. It blends narrative depth, freedom of choice, stunning world design, and intense gameplay into a package that’s bold, thought-provoking, and incredibly engaging. If you enjoy games that let you dive into a rich story, customize your playstyle, and explore a huge, detailed world at your own pace, this title delivers on all fronts. It’s a testament to how far immersive RPG design has come.

5+ years on from one of the most historically disastrous launches, Cyberpunk 2077 has become an experience that captivates and immerses the player in a world where nothing truly feels impossible. Not only is Night City itself one of the most fun game worlds I've ever explored, but the characters and gameplay possibilities therein give the game a sense of personality that keeps me wanting to come back and uncover every nook and cranny of it. I finished my first playthrough of CP2077 in a week and started a new one almost immediately - that alone should speak to how captivating the world here truly feels. This is not a game you play for only 30 minutes at a time.  The game world is so immersive, in fact, that while fast travel is an option, I'd sooner jump into a car and drive from point A to point B than use a fast travel point. And I can't say the same about a lot of other open-world games I've played.  Anyway, as far as the gameplay is concerned, it's heaps of fun overall. Being on my second playthrough at the time of writing this review, I've only barely scratched the surface as far as the build options at your disposal are concerned, and I'm looking forward to experimenting with many more different builds - I'm especially eager to try out a build that's less focused on direct combat. Now that isn't to say that the combat is bad - quite the opposite, in fact. It's all sorts of satisfying, especially once you settle into a set of perks and cyberware that synergize with your weapon(s) of choice. Prime example: blades + Berserk = *chef's kiss*.  Now the game does still have some intermittent issues - NPCs are proper idiots sometimes, models and textures have trouble loading, the game might crash outright - but in my experience, game-breaking bugs have been very few and far between all things considered. CDPR definitely did their best to improve the game post-launch, and improve it they did. It's arguably the redemption arc of the decade, and they have my utmost respect for it. In the relatively short time I've actually been playing it, CP2077 has already become one of my all-time favorites, and I expect it to be no surprise why that is the case.

Three years ago, this game was a disaster, but today, after the 2.0 update and the Phantom Liberty expansion, it is a completely different product with great mechanics and a GOAT atmosphere. If you quit because of bugs back in 2020, now is the perfect time to come back. The new skill trees finally allow for real specialization because every point you spend actually changes how you move or fight, rather than just adding a tiny damage bonus. This makes every battle satisfying, whether you use a katana or hacking. The new cyberware system also limits how much gear you can install, which forces you to plan carefully since every choice has real consequences for your stats. Night City is immersive with its neon lights, and the new Dogtown area is even better than the original districts because it is more detailed and packed with content, so it no longer feels empty. The story in Phantom Liberty feels like a political thriller with complex characters like Solomon Reed and Songbird, making every moral choice difficult and heavy. The improved AI and new police system make the city feel alive, as it now reacts to your actions in a logical and challenging way. On the other hand, driving is still not great because cars slide too much, which is frustrating during fast chases. Also, some side activities can feel repetitive after many hours. Despite these small flaws, the graphics look amazing with path tracing, and the deep story makes this one of the best action RPGs on the market, so it is definitely worth buying the full bundle.

There are few times in my life where I play a videogame that feels like it was made for me. Like some time traveller went back in time and made this game to show me something.   SPOILERS AHEAD [spoiler] The moment of epiphany came when I was doing the quest to find all of Delemain's vehicles. The 2nd part of the questline. Now I thought this was going to be some random completion quest, and at one point I even got so lost inside the air ducts of the facility I needed to look up a video to get me to the next room. When I got there, I was completely expecting to just kill the splinter personalities of Delemain and fix him, after all he'd been so good to me for the whole game. Saving my life, helping me get around, rewarding me for finding his splinter personalities; and that moment when I was driving into the slums and I heard GladOS on the phone I just burst out laughing because it, apart from the absurdity, brought back memories of Portal. Delemain's questline had been so memorable and I was so glad it was the first sidequest chain I did.   So when I went into the reactor room, Johnny stopped me right before I got to the console. "Stop you idiot, you're gonna end up killing living beings!" (not verbatum) I stopped for a moment to think, well sure they MIGHT be sentient, but if so then so is Delemain, who is dying right now. Johnny then acquainted the situation to being a cab driver asking me to kill his kids, which made me think about it. The splinter personalities were calling Delemain prime their father, and with how realistic Delemain was, I would've believed that he himself could be a sentient cyber-lifeform. This caused a mental conflict that I didnt expect from this random sidequest I chose out of the 12 other options. Johnny and I talked for abit and then left me with the option.  I couldn't pass the skill check to compress the personalities into Delemain's code, meaning my only options were to A: Reset Delemain and possibly kill 8 people, or shoot the core and... what? I didnt know what breaking the core would do. Might kill him? Might free them? Might kill them all? I had no idea. This confliction was overloading my irl brain and I started thinking erratically, worried I would make the wrong decision in the long run, till eventually I just shot it. I didnt think at all I just shot the damn thing.   Boom, the whole room goes dark. I am now hearing demonic screeching and roars from outside of the room. My first thought was "Oh ♥♥♥♥ what kind of demon did I just release on this world." So when I ran upstairs to see Delemain's children driving around saying that they were free, I was pleasantly surprised. I asked Johnny what he thought happened to Del, and he told me one of the car stayed. The music kicks in and I slowly walk down to the car, already mind blown by the ending timing, scene, and just aura of the whole moment.   I walk down to the car and get in to find Delemain inside, but not exactly, more like a new copy, completely reset. This moment brought me back to a youtube audiobook I listened to a LONG time ago, "What if The Enclave Survived in Fallout 76? - Episode 3 by The Omega Initiative". That story had a similar premise involving an AI dying but giving a smaller, reborn version of himself life as he dies. Not being reborn, but a whole other lifeform created. Now I had really only played Bethesda games so I was DEF not expecting this fckin sidequest to be this good, so when the car told me to "Drive V" right as the chorus of the background song started, my jaw was left agape. Completely brain melted levels of stunned. I had to literally step away from the computer and just take a breather for a minute cuz I had NEVER seen anything like this happen for an optional, easily missable SIDEQUEST.   I had to quickly go to work for a couple hours afterwards. When I got back I started thinking again about the story. Just how blown away I was. Skyrim, Fallout 3 and Fallout 4 never did anything like this. Then when I was in the shower, pondering the story meaning, as one does in the shower, as showers are known to give a +10 buff to intelligence and philosophy; I realized what the story meant. I have 22 hours in the game, I have only completed the Delemain quest, the Tarot card quest, and the Main tutorial up to meeting with Takemura. And yet in this moment I think I understood what the main character's story is. At least, this far in.   Cyberpunk's main character isn't V. It isn't Johnny. It's you. The player.  When V was shot, he died, even by the doctor's accounts. Johnny himself has already died. His soul left this realm decades ago. Instead, what happened was this being, this form, capable of life existed, at a point where no one really inhabited it. This being (the main character) held the memories, body, and emotions of V, while also accessed and interfaced with the memories and personality of Johnny. Quite literally, two dead guys in his head, not 1. V's body is dressed up with mechanical and cybernetic parts already, to the point he's practically more machine than man when it comes to the physical, so perhaps it could be like Delemain's situation.  Delemain was being bombarded by his splinter personalities, fighting for control and to be free of him. V is being bombarded by Johnny, fighting for control and to be free of him.  Doesn't seem that far different. So what I propose is thus, The main character is both V and Johnny, this new being born of the death of V and generated by the memories, personality, everything of both V and Johnny. The perspective of Johnny being the one invading the mind of the main character isnt accurate, Johnny IS the main character, the same was V is, the same way Delemain's GladOS car is still Delemain, the same way Excelsior(the newborn car) is still Delemain. The story isnt about Johnny slowly eating away at V's mind and taking control. It's about YOU, the player, this new being born into this world, living with the experiences of both V and Johnny. You are both of them. You are like Excelsior. Learning to live a life as both Johnny and V. The perception of Johnny taking control is just you adapting and understanding a different side of you, same as V.   I mean think about it, there's definitelly been times where you've meant to say something ingame and it came out WAY different than expected. A residual of V's memories, his way of speech, his personality. On the other hand, you have Johnny, slowly integrating, being understood, becoming more you the way someone growing up becomes themselves, not over forcing it, but over slowly growing and learning what you want to be. The story is about YOU, the player, given a life in the world, with the memories of V and Johnny, and the body of V, choosing what you will do. You have two tarot cards you can't get from the connected quest, I assume because they are later in the story. The Devil and Judgement. Misty explains that these cards are on your "path to discover" and are not required to complete her quest. In Cyberpunk 2077, the Judgment tarot card represents critical reflection, ultimate consequences, and finality. It symbolizes reaping what you've sown, acting as a reflection of the player's choices and the end of V's journey. The story is about YOU, and your decisions. It's about what YOU will do in this world. What life you want to make. What choices you want to make. Resetting Delemain, or shooting the core. [/spoiler]  I am amazed by this game. It's truly something else. I am so excited to get back to playing after finishing this review. 10/10 worth the money and time investment. Great game, instantly one of my favorites

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of those games that went from being a complete mess to something actually worth your time. I didn’t touch it at launch for obvious reasons, and honestly that was the right move. Playing it now, especially after the 2.0 update, it finally feels like the game they were trying to sell back then.  First thing, Night City carries the entire experience. The atmosphere, lighting, and overall vibe are insane. It’s one of the few games where just walking or driving around feels worth it. The world design is doing most of the heavy lifting here, which lines up with what a lot of people say: great presentation, everything else ranges from solid to just okay. ([reddit.com][1])  The story is actually strong. Characters like Johnny and the side questlines are where the game peaks. Some of the side missions are better than the main story, which isn’t something I expected. It’s immersive when it works, and it pulls you in way more than most open-world games.  Gameplay is where it’s mixed. Gunplay feels good now, builds are way better after the overhaul, and there’s actual freedom in how you play. But the AI is still questionable at times, and the open world can feel a bit shallow once you look past the visuals. That criticism hasn’t really gone away since release. ([Steam Community][2])  Performance-wise, it depends on your setup. If you’ve got a decent PC, it runs fine now. Bugs still exist, but nothing like before. Back then it was borderline unplayable for some people, now it’s just occasional weirdness. ([reddit.com][3])  Overall, this is basically a “what could’ve been” game that still ended up good anyway. If you ignore the original hype and just take it for what it is, it’s a really solid RPG with insane visuals and a memorable story. Not perfect, not revolutionary, but definitely worth playing in its current state.  Do expect it to be the greatest open world ever made.

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of my favorite games of all time, and in its current state I absolutely recommend it. I also want to be fair about it, because pretending the launch disaster never happened would be dishonest. It released in a horrible state, especially on older consoles, and it deserved criticism for that. But judging the game as it exists now, this thing is excellent.  What kept winning me over was the sheer feel of it. Night City still looks absurdly good. The lighting is ridiculous, the atmosphere carries almost every scene, and even years later this game still has moments where you just stop and stare at the environment. It is not just technically pretty, it has style, mood, and identity everywhere. Few games sell a place this well.  The other big strength is that the game is just fun to play when your build comes online. Cyberpunk absolutely nails the power fantasy. Once you get some real chrome installed and your build starts working the way you want, combat becomes a blast. Slow-mo, shotguns, LMGs, cyberware, explosions, chaos, all of it feels great. I spent a lot of this run doing side content simply because moving through the world and deleting enemies was enjoyable on its own.  Story-wise, I think it is very strong, especially in the character writing. The game has a lot more texture than people give it credit for. Even side gigs often have enough personality, weirdness, tragedy, or moral grime to make them memorable. Phantom Liberty in particular is outstanding. I think it is the best content in the game. It feels tighter, meaner, and more focused, with some great spy-thriller energy layered on top of the base game’s drama.  I do still have a few complaints. The game can still be janky. I ran into weird NPC behavior, some visual glitches, odd physics, and the occasional quest jolt. Nothing here ruined the experience for me, but the game still has rough edges. The driving is also inconsistent. Some cars feel amazing, some feel like boats with wheels. And the main story’s urgency can clash with the open-world design, because the narrative tells you your life is collapsing right now while the game also wants you to go do fifty side jobs and boxing matches.  Still, the good outweighs the bad by a mile. Cyberpunk 2077 now feels like the game people wanted it to be in the first place: gorgeous, stylish, mechanically fun, full of personality, and backed by genuinely strong story content. It is not flawless, but it is absolutely worth playing, and Phantom Liberty only makes that more true.
