Many years ago, I first stepped into Night City on my PS4 when Cyberpunk 2077 launched. Like many players at the time, my experience was… mixed. I ended up getting bored with the main story and dropped the game before even making it to the Arasaka Tower raid with Jackie.  Fast forward to the start of 2026, and I decided to return to Night City and give Cyberpunk 2077 another real chance. This time, I committed to finishing the journey. I played through the entire main story and even completed the Phantom Liberty DLC.  And after finally experiencing everything the game has to offer… I’m honestly blown away.  But at the same time, I’m also a little disappointed.  Main Story:  For this playthrough, I started as a Nomad instead of a Corpo like I did the first time around—and right away the beginning of the game felt much better. The intro felt more natural and grounded, and it pulled me into the world in a way that my first playthrough never quite did.  Once I made it past the Arasaka Tower raid—the exact point where I stopped playing years ago—the story really started to hook me. Things began escalating quickly, and the game introduced several important and memorable characters.  One of Cyberpunk 2077’s biggest strengths is easily its characters. The people you meet throughout the story genuinely feel real. The dialogue, the facial animations, the body language—everything works together to make interactions feel believable. Experiencing all of it through a first-person perspective adds another layer of immersion that very few games manage to pull off this well.  However, despite those strengths, the pacing of the story sometimes became a problem for me. There were stretches where things slowed down quite a bit, and during those moments I actually found myself dreading returning to the game. Still, I knew I wanted to push through and see the story to the end.  Around the 30-hour mark, something changed. The story started to grab me again—especially Johnny Silverhand’s storyline. His character became increasingly fascinating, and many of the side quests tied to him were some of the most interesting moments in the entire game.  Side stories involving Judy, River, and Johnny also surprised me. They pulled me deeper into the world of Cyberpunk and added emotional weight that the main story alone didn’t always deliver.  That said, I didn’t complete every side quest the game had to offer. Normally, in a game like this, I would try to do everything. But Cyberpunk has a massive amount of side content, and while some of it is fantastic, a lot of it felt like filler to me.  If I ever return to Cyberpunk 2077 again, I’ll probably take the time to explore more of those side missions. But during this playthrough, I wanted to stay focused on finishing the main story.  And when I finally reached the ending, I experienced one of the most surprising moments in the entire game.  The final cutscene before the credits—where I left Night City with the Aldecaldos and Panam in the tank—felt like a genuine “out-of-body” moment. For the entire game, you experience everything strictly through first-person perspective, including most cutscenes. So suddenly seeing your character in third person at the end was honestly shocking in the best way possible.  It was a powerful moment, and it made the ending feel very personal.  At the same time though, the ending also felt a little… incomplete.  Not in a bad way necessarily, but in a way that left me feeling like there was still more story left to tell. More adventures that could still happen in this world.  And that’s exactly why I immediately jumped into the Phantom Liberty DLC after finishing the main game.  Because honestly… I found myself wanting more.  Phantom Liberty DLC:  The Phantom Liberty DLC Kicks off with a BANG and hooked me way quicker than the main story ever did. It ties directly into the main story as well, giving the story new and important plot points and expanding upon the "lore" and knowledge we already know about.   The characters Solomon Reed, President Myer and Songbird are already interesting characters and at the start of the DLC, don't need much development or explanation. Dogtown is another important character of it's own, adding a more run down element of Night City. But Dogtown isn't just run down either, it has some hidden Gem's like the rest of Night City that are truly just beautiful!  I have not completed the Phantom Liberty DLC in full yet as it is time to make some room for Crimson Desert - but I will be back to finish it soon! I will edit this once I complete it!  Final Comments:  Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 has many highs, and a few lows (mainly story pacing) but the game is honestly a must play for anyone who enjoys a good story, and a great RPG. I must also say CD Project Red, you're team killed it with fixing all the bugs and turning the world of Cyberpunk 2077 into something amazing.  Rating: 8.6/10 | Great

TLDR: This is a great game but a weak RPG. Cyberpunk’s incredible narrative, enhanced by its DLC, is undoubtedly worth playing, or at least trying.  There’s a lot to say about this game’s launch and subsequent redemption, but from someone who played it through multiple endings before 2.0, most of the best parts of the game were always there, if not just more accessible now. The story is great, tense and complex with interesting characters that pulls you along all the while you as V build your rep by taking on fun, if not short, gigs throughout Night City. There’s some tastes of meaningful choice in the main story (and moreso in the DLC) but outside of that there’s little room for you to actually express yourself in this world, especially with how predetermined some aspects of your character are. Even basic features of expression like clothing, looks, and vehicles are seriously limited by a lot of modern RPG standards. More than that, one playthrough of the game’s main narratives will lead you through most of the game’s side content, with about 5 non-repeatable hours of “postgame content” (exclusively in the DLC). Sure, there’s always the other endings, but after that what are you left with? With how full Night City is I’m shocked by how dead the moment to moment exploration is. Night City is crowded, but hardly alive. It may be heretical to say, but outside of CD Projekt’s incredible curated content the transitory gameplay could be swapped with Starfield’s exploration. Its still well worth the money, ESPECIALLY recommended on sale, and mods can fill some of that empty space I’m dissatisfied with, but every so often I’ll stare wistfully at its icon before jumping in just to look at a cleared map and log out.

[h2]Main-Game[/h2]  [h2]Intro[/h2]  After the disaster that was the launch, I finally decided to play Cyberpunk 2077 and let me tell you, the game made a comeback. With new positive reviews, and recommendations I decided to give it a go. Which let me tell you, it was well worth the wait, and the reason for waiting was because I knew the game was gonna take a long time to finish. But now that I'm done, let me tell you what I think.   [h2] Freedom [/h2]  One of the best parts of the game is most definitely the freedom, most RPG games nowadays only give you like three solid choices when it comes to dialogue, or sometimes only two way's that you can go about things, or just two major choices. But in Cyberpunk all that's removed, instead what you get is a variety of things to choose from, I'm talking about 4 different lines of dialogue on almost every interaction, 9 endings, multiple ways of doing missions and with the manual save being an option you can also re-load a save and see how your choices turns out.  [h2] Builds [/h2]  In some RPG games once you commit to a build then that's it. There's no going back or if there is, you have to reach a certain level or get X or Y amount of items in order to "respec" or "re-build" your character....However in this game, you can literally pick and choose your build and play around with what you got. Whenever you want, meaning if you get bored of a build or if you feel like your investment was crap. Then just "undo" your skill investment and put it into something else or if you want to just try something new then you are free to do so whenever you want at any time.   [h2]Writing/Characters[/h2]  When it comes to characters or writing in this game, it honestly fits in so well. You actually care for the character's and what they want to achieve, the writing isn't cringe-worthy or predictable. There's dynamic, chemistry, growth, and character. All these elements and things that make the writing and character develop in such a way that feel's like real life or a movie. Plus there are lore-dumps everywhere meaning if you ever want to know more about Cyberpunk, then you can read everything you have collected in your pause menu.   [h2]Gripe[/h2] The only complaint I have about this game is honestly the lack of color, customization, and vehicles. For clothes Idc how much copium you have to inhale, but there isn't a lot of choices to pick and choose from with the odd colors, and the ugly shoes/pants. However Cyberpunk defenders will just look at this and say "But there is, you just have to look for it." But they are flatly wrong, my character was supposed to have a green theme, and the amount of bright neon green I could find was worrisome not to mention the fact that some combinations make the males look like clowns. For the customization, same thing. The game gives you apartments, and car's, but you are extremely limited on what you can design. You can change some pictures in your apartment's, but you can't reorganize furniture or add different things and change the headlights on a car....but somehow you can't add different types of engines, window tint's, rims, exhaust pipes or basic decal, even though there's already cool NPC vehicles that have some of these things. Funny enough though, there's an entire studio picture-mode set with lot's of gimmick's and way's to take pictures. Last but not least, the driving in this game is so f****** s*** that they need to re-work the physics behind driving and instead need to remove races if the driving was this bad. Because last time I checked from playing Gran Turismo, Need For Speed, Driving Sims, and just real life driving experience....cars don't slip and slide on asphalt, dirt, sand or cement like they are on ice. Especially the way they do in Cyberpunk. And again for those who want to defend the driving in this game, you are full of s***, never driven a car or you are just straight-up coping.   [h3]Good[/h3]  - Character Development - Writing - Freedom - Build(s) Flexibility  - Multiple Endings - Radio Station ;)  [h3]Bad[/h3]  - Vehicles  - Bothersome Glitches   [h3]Story Overall: 8.5/10[/h3] [h3]Game Overall: 9/10[/h3]  [h2] Phantom Liberty [/h2]  When it comes to the DLC for cyberpunk, at this point just get it. The entire DLC makes the entire game look like a downgrade, that's how good it really is. Plus the ending cutscenes literally look like something out of a movie, with visuals being extremely cool.   [h3]Good[/h3]  - Major Upgrade From The First  [h3]Bad[/h3]  - None    [h3]Story Overall: 9.5/10[/h3] [h3]Game Overall: 9/10[/h3]

While it's not without its glitches, Cyberpunk 2077 remains a rich source of fast-paced combat, highly immersive world-building, and splendid sci-fi scenery. It’s all the more impressive when viewed through the lens of a VR mod. Even with all of that modded VR performance jank, Cyberpunk has frankly unbeatable atmosphere. I found myself RP-walking through the markets, stopping to overhear strangers’ conversations and take in the cityscape. In a genre where “open” usually means miles of barren wilderness, Night City is a definitive deviation that feels dense, alive, and brimming with possibilities.  Cyberpunk has got to have one of the strongest prologues I can think of. It excellently brings you into the world, teaches you about the culture of Night City, and sets up a motive for the rest of the expansive game. Although, the time-sensitive nature of the main conflict does rather fail to match the amount of time that the game lets you faff about. This is an unoriginal critique and honestly kind of an unavoidable side effect of this being a video game, but it really stood out to a player who wanted to see as much of the world as possible.  Even though the quality of side quests did vary, the majority of them really stood out. There are some truly unforgettable stories to play through here. They offered so much insight into this fleshed-out world. Every significant character you meet through these stories has a place in this dystopian world, and the actions you perform for/with them consistently lead in intriguing directions. Player choice isn’t a big part of Cyberpunk, but there’s enough of it to give you a good sense of agency that further draws you into the setting.   Combat throughout the game was a huge highlight. All your futuristic firearms and cybernetic abilities feel great to use. Your cyberpunk guns all click, slide, and go boom satisfyingly. Your superhuman mods let you perform various feats of badassery. Even stealth, the bane of pacing and scourge of open-world games, provides you with plenty of options for going unnoticed or getting the jump on encounters. There are loads of playstyles/weapons/powers to experiment with. The skill trees always had something that was catching my eye. Finding the various stylish “iconic” weapons always enticed me and had me reanalyzing my build. As you accumulate more violent options, you do become pretty overpowered, which slightly undermines the tactical decision-making of combat. Still, it’s a great sci-fi power fantasy that parallels the unstoppable reputation you gain as an up-and-coming legend.  There’s a lot to enjoy about Cyberpunk 2077 now that it's long-since grown out of its infamously mucky release. Very few parts of the game are worth avoiding. However, if I could overhaul one thing, it would be the driving. It's not hideous, just sensitive and slippery as hell. Operating any vehicle using a keyboard is not recommended. Even the AutoDrive feature has pretty serious limits. Fast traveling can get you most places, but I found the few high-speed vehicle segments to be the least controllable moments.  Open-world games are becoming a more tiresome affair for me in recent years, yet Cyberpunk managed to fully capture my attention. If you’re like me and can only stomach, like, two open-world games a year, you should make Cyberpunk a priority on that list. You won’t regret it, especially if you’ve got the hardware to run it in VR. [i](Oh, and grab the DLC if you find yourself enjoying the game. That story isn’t worth missing either.)[/i]

A short disclaimer first: I never tried to play this back when it first released so I approached it without the same bad taste in the mouth a lot of people had after the launch fiasco. What I got is a pretty solid game that still has some rough edges but it mostly works and it's been fun to play and experience.  [h2]Gameplay[/h2] It's one of those games I'd describe as "GTA-likes", in that you navigate a sandboxy open world, often with vehicles, and do various violent and otherwise shady activities around it. There are some RPG mechanics, to a slightly greater extent than usual in the genre - you get several stats and skill trees to unlock stuff in to tailor the experience to how you want to play the game. The effective differences in how missions play out based on your playstyle are often mostly cosmetic, but sometimes it can pay off to go the stealthy route for example.  The gunplay is reasonably satisfying and you're frequently given ways to use the environment to your advantage or get an edge by using skills, I found it pretty fun. I kinda wish the loot system was dialled down a little though. You're constantly getting new weapons, usually with only minor differences in stats and I don't like having to pause the game every couple minutes to analyse if the new gun is 0.9% better than my current one. I'd rather have scarce upgrades that actually mean something.  [h2]Audiovisuals[/h2] The game looks nice, and I appreciate how customisable the graphics are so you really don't need a cutting edge computer to play it. I just wish there were more character creation options, but alas.  The music is pretty good and includes a couple of tracks made specifically for the game - and I mean "normal" songs that play on the radio, not the usual ambient or orchestral stuff usually written for OSTs. There's no one radio station where I like every single song, so that's a bit sad but not unusual, I'm a picky bastard.  [h2]Story & plot[/h2] The main plot thread is shockingly short, as in I unlocked the final mission around the time I thought "okay, we're probably like halfway into Act 2 by now, right?". That said, there's a TON of optional content and a lot of it actually ties into the main story and influences how it all ends. So you [i]can[/i] rush through the game in just a couple hours, but getting the full experience is a different story and I definitely recommend it.  There are several endings and it's one of those games where (some of) your choices actually have a lasting impact. It's rarely clear who you can/should trust and it often feels like there really is no good solution to a given problem and even after you've made a decision it's not always obvious if it was a good one. I like games that aren't afraid to do that.  Several NPCs have long rich quest lines that help you get to know them, tie into the central plot at least in some way (or at least play a world-building role) and you can even romance them. The choice of who you can and cannot romance is dependent on your sex (or perhaps your pronouns, I haven't tried mismatching the two), that actually feels real as opposed to the increasingly common "lol everyone is bi because we don't want to disappoint anyone" approach.  That last point is indicative of a broader tendency, in that the world rarely (if ever) feels like it's actively pandering to me, the player. I like that, it feels more real.  [hr][/hr]  So yeah, I consider this a pretty good game overall. Definitely recommended if you like GTA style games and/or cyberpunk aesthetics and/or interesting stories with believable characters. The DLC is worth it too.

I started playing Cyberpunk 2077 expecting a stylish futuristic RPG with a good story and lots of action. And while it definitely delivers on those things, what surprised me the most was how much the game makes you think about your choices. In many games, decisions feel simple. You usually know which option is the “good” one and which one is the “bad” one. In Cyberpunk 2077 it rarely works like that. A lot of the time you read the dialogue options and honestly don’t know what the best decision is. You sit there thinking about the situation, the characters involved, and what might happen next. Sometimes every option feels risky in its own way. What makes it even more interesting is that the consequences don’t always show up immediately. You might make a decision and then continue playing for hours before realizing that something later in the story happened because of that earlier choice. When that happens, it really makes you reflect on what you did. There were moments when I spent several minutes just staring at the dialogue options, thinking so much that my head almost started to hurt. The world itself is also one of the strongest parts of the game. Night City feels alive, full of different districts, characters, and small details that make the environment believable. The atmosphere, the neon lights, the music, and the overall cyberpunk aesthetic make exploring the city really enjoyable. Sometimes just walking or driving around the city can be fun on its own. The characters are another highlight. Many of them feel well written and realistic, with their own personalities, problems, and motivations. Because of that, the choices you make in conversations feel even more important. You start caring about what happens to these characters, which makes the story much more engaging. The gameplay itself is also quite flexible. You can approach situations in different ways depending on your playstyle. Some players prefer stealth, others go for direct combat, and the game allows you to experiment with different builds and abilities. Of course, the game isn’t perfect. Sometimes there can still be small bugs, and a few mechanics could feel a bit more polished. But overall, the experience is still very strong, especially because of the story, the atmosphere, and the meaningful choices. For me personally, Cyberpunk 2077 is a game that really stands out because it constantly makes you think about your decisions and their consequences. It’s not just about completing missions, it’s about being part of the story and shaping how it unfolds.  [h3] My rating: 10/10 [/h3]

I love this game with every cell of my body. Not just because I love the cyberpunk genre, but because of its story and characters. I always end up coming back to replay it and I never get tired, even knowing everything that happens. This game was there for me during the worst moments of my life and helped me immensely by making me forget my problems, even if only temporarily. The friendship that V and Johnny form as the story progresses is beautiful to see. A rockstar surrounded by people he considered 'friends' and fans who couldn't even stand to be in the same room as him yet V was there, putting up with his madness and nonsense 24/7, always listening and talking to him like a true friend. V could have taken the pills to get rid of Johnny temporarily at any time but chose to keep him there, which makes their bond feel truly genuine. The story is obviously one of the highlights. Seeing V go from just a random mercenary wanting the good life in Night City to a person desperate to survive having to help others to try and save themselves. Even if 'helping someone just to save yourself' sounds selfish, V doesn't just save them; they build real bonds. The gameplay is also super fun, letting you experiment with many different builds. If you want to go 'guns blazing,' you can; if you want to play as a hacker, being a terrifying Netrunner to the NPCs, go right ahead. The game offers a great diversity of builds without forcing you into a single playstyle. The side quests and quests, in general, are also excellent. To me, the best side quests are the ones featuring Johnny’s commentary because it adds an 'extra spice' to them, and the main quests are simply incredible. The endings are also amazing, especially 'Temperance' and 'The Star.' SPOILERS***>>** Personally, the 'Temperance' ending is and always will be my favorite. V sacrificing themselves at the end and going beyond the Blackwall with Alt Cunningham so Johnny can have a second chance at life giving him the opportunity to make different choices is exactly what I feel V would do after everything they went through together. You can clearly see Johnny actively making the most of this second chance. It’s a 'sad' ending, so to speak, but I still find it beautiful: Johnny visiting V’s grave one last time, leaving the bullet necklace, and leaving Night City by bus to finally move on, thanking V for the second chance. Now, 'The Star' ending features V becoming part of the Aldecaldos nomad family, whom they helped so much during the campaign. When they said they would help V no matter what, they weren't kidding. Raiding Arasaka Tower with the nomads feels like a suicide mission, yet they don't give up, choosing to go to the end with V even if it costs them their lives which is exactly what happens. After the chaos of the raid and returning to their body, V and the Aldecaldos decide to leave Night City to search for a cure. This ending gives a bit more hope that the protagonist might survive after everything, but it's left open-ended. Many consider this the best ending of Cyberpunk 2077, and I don't blame them; it makes total sense to choose it. Anyway, I'm just rambling about how much I love this game! :P

First and foremost, Cyberpunk 2077 is one of the best games I've played when it comes to worldbuilding and immersion. Every aspect of the game - from advertisements on billboards, to npc dialogue, to fancy street crossing indicators - work together to create a truly cohesive, fleshed out universe.  The main storyline is great, with a few alternate paths depending on the decisions you make, although it can be pretty short if you ignore all the sidequests. Speaking of sidequests: some can be a little repetitive (I personally don't mind the "kill everyone and grab an item" quests since combat is pretty fun, but I could see it get boring for some people), however there are also a number of very unique ones which provide a more detailed dive into different aspects of night city.  Combat might seem basic at first, but as you unlock more perks and cyberware options, you'll discover a variety of different playstyles which you can mix and match depending on your preferences. Upgrading your preferred playstyle is also a lot more than just seeing numbers go up, many perks and cyberware add completely new capabilities over the course of your run, so that by late game you might have half a dozen or more abilities to keep track of (or you can spec into simpler playstyles that don't require you to actively manage them).  Visually, Cyberpunk lives up to it's reputation of being one of the best looking games made to this day. Not every model is perfect, and there have been a few times when a bad one stands out, but overall the combination of both size and fidelity is very impressive.  The soundtrack is excellent. Cyberpunk features a huge variety of music from different genres with both the main composer, and tons of third party artists. The in game radio has over 100 songs total. I'm not sure I can put it on the same pedestal as doom or halo, but you could make an argument for it.

You can catch the game + DLC on sale for $40, but it's (probably) worth every enny even full price.

Having played through this game at least 6 times, I'd say I've seen what this game has to offer, and it is good. For a game that really screwed up it's launch, it has come a long way, especially after Cyberpunk 2.0 and Phantom Liberty. While it may have had a rough start, even under all the bugs and performance issues, there was still a great game under the grime. Not every game can say the same.  This is a great open world game with some really fun quests, and great gameplay. The gameplay was good but flawed before 2.0, but after the 2.0 update, the gameplay has been refined into a fine wine. It is fun being a cyber ninja chopping everyone in sight to pieces, being a netrunner wizard melting the brains of everyone on the battlefield with but a glance, Or being an assassin blowing the brains out of everyone you come across. The RPG mechanics backing up your playstyle are amazing, and the cyberware is awesome. You can become the ultimate killing machine and it is sublime.   Story wise, the main quest in this game is amazing, like honestly, the story of V while a tragic one, is a great one. I've seen every ending, and they are all really cool to reach. The "companion" characters and the other major side content are also really great. In the base game, the gigs from fixers are okay, a lot of them are pretty basic shooting galleries. But in Phantom Liberty, the gigs are amazing, they have full stories with interesting characters and interesting and hard choices to make. But also exploring night city is just a blast. There might be a fast travel system, but honestly I almost never use it because driving around night city, dodging traffic at 150mph is super fun, especially with the fine tuning they have done to vehicles, also there are a stupid amount of awesome looking cars, and while you can buy cars, you get plenty of cool ones doing side quests too for free.  My two main complaints for this game are. My first major gripe is that the life paths are very underwhelming, especially in the base game, aside from one extra quest and some special lines of dialog here and there, it really doesn't matter. In fairness, CDPR recognized that as a flaw, and in Phantom Liberty you do actually get a few special options based on what lifepath you have in quests.  My second main complaint is the lack of interactivity and simulation of interactions with the gangs, or more specifically reputation systems with the various factions. Except for a few specific circumstances, your actions don't really have an effect on the gangs of night city, even though you've mowed down hundreds, if not thousands, of them by the end of the game. I would say that expands to more world interactivity in general, and life sim elements that I wish the game had more of, or deeper interactions. There are a handful of mods that move to address this, but they can only go so far without new voice lines, especially for example, romance interactions with the 4 companion characters. So for the sequel, I hope CDPR adds a lot more world interactivity, and life sim elements. Not to the point of say survival, but just to help you feel really immersed in the world. In other words, I want more stuff in the game that isn't just "go and kill everyone here". I suppose it made sense for V as a mercenary, but still.

Cyberpunk 2077 with Phantom Liberty isn’t just a game, it’s a first‑person midlife crisis with ray tracing and way too many cool jackets.  Night City is the only place where you can be a broke merc, a glitchy rockstar, and an unlicensed therapist for traumatized NPCs all in the same side quest. You log in to “do one quick gig” and somehow end up knee‑deep in corpo conspiracies, brain surgery, and philosophical arguments with the voice in your head.  Builds range from anime katana monster to cyber‑wizard hacker to “I put points everywhere and now people just evaporate when I look at them funny.” Every fight is either a flawless John Wick montage or you screaming, over‑healing, and throwing grenades at your own feet.  Phantom Liberty is basically Season 2 of the story: darker, sharper, and with just the right amount of Idris Elba judging your life choices. Dogtown feels like a compressed warzone where every quest starts simple and ends with you staring at the screen, wondering if you accidentally picked the bad ending again.  Cyberpunk 2077 now is the game where you boot it up to change your outfit, then realize it’s 3 AM, you’ve finished another ending, and your screenshot folder has doubled in size.

Cyberpunk is truly a once in a lifetime game. I didn't play it when it first came out, so I experienced the game as it is now. And ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ it blew me away.  It's an absolutely gorgeous game, and the city feels alive. There are people everywhere, not just walking around but seemingly actually living their lives. I drive to every destination I have because I enjoy just existing within the city so much.  The story is amazing, the NPCs are memorable and deep, and even the side missions are amazing. They go from silly things like a man whose peepee is burning to genuine and unsettling injustices done against others that make you sit and think about how terrible people can be. It balances humor and dark themes effortlessly. I love this world so much. I avoided ending the game for maybe 30 hours or so just because I didn't want it to end, only to find out that the game is kind and allows you to keep playing even if you end it. The choices you face, especially at the end, feel heavy and hard. Even the happiest of endings feels bittersweet, and that's okay because the story is so good that it makes sense. It tackles its darkest themes with grace but without holding back.   I also love that V really has a personality - you're controlling her, yes, and you do make decisions, but you're playing AS her. She's a deep character full of flaws and grit and hope and emotion. I love the NPCs who become her friends in the game too.   I also just enjoyed the gameplay. Hacking is fun, sniping is fun, running and gunning is fun, throwing knives is FUN (my favorite playstyle personally). As you level up you slowly feel more powerful, but not so much so that you'd never struggle. Driving is fun with the right vehicles (the handling on some is rough, but once you find the right ones you're cruising). The amount of character customization is amazing too.  But at the core of it, Cyberpunk is just one of a kind. There's nothing like it. No other open-world game comes close to the depth of its world, the importance of its themes, its writing, its art. I've played so many single player games and none made me feel the way that Cyberpunk has. I would do anything to play this game again for the first time - I cannot recommend it enough.

--- Personal Thoughts ---  An incredibly enjoyable open-world RPG looter-shooter experience; The base game provides a palpable power fantasy, and does so by making it exceedingly easy to create an extremely powerful character from messing around with the build & cyberware system. As such, don't expect a challenge. Even on some of the harder difficulties, I wager most people will be able to get through the game with relative ease. By far the strongest part of the game is the environment & story itself. Night City is a vivid, striking cyberpunk dystopia riddled with bright neon literally everywhere.   The constant firefights happening as you drive through the city, the various gigs you can get, even the random calls you can get from important NPC's that start entire questlines helps sell that this is a city where things are actively moving and happening. The only real criticism with regards to that is a certain time-limited aspect of the narrative that clashes with what is, ostensibly, an unlimited amount of time to engage in the endless amount of side quests throughout the game.   --- Additional Thoughts on Phantom Liberty ---  Easily one of the most impressive DLC's for a game I've seen so far. It's a step up in terms of voice acting, difficulty balancing, and narrative. The DLC area is incredibly interesting, the characters are complex and compelling, and there are some scenarios in the game that genuinely had my adrenaline pumping. It was never truly unforgiving, but the step up in overall difficulty definitely helped sell a lot of the narrative beats within the DLC (something that the main game, unfortunately, suffers a little from).   --- Overall Thoughts on the Game ---  *Very* good game. I'd probably put it as it exists right now at around an 8.5/10. Highly recommended if you're into looter shooters with RPG mechanics. Good story and strong environment design. Pick up the main game and DLC if you can afford it, and *definitely* pick it up on a good sale.

If you’ve ever wondered what it would be like to live inside a neon-soaked fever dream where everyone has a cybernetic arm, a questionable moral compass, and at least three unresolved emotional issues, Cyberpunk 2077 is the game for you.  Set in the chaotic playground of Night City, the game drops you into a world where corporations run everything, the streets are full of chrome-plated chaos, and somehow the most dangerous thing you’ll encounter is still your own bad decision making. You play as V, a mercenary trying to climb the city’s ladder of power, fame, and very expensive jackets.  Night City itself is the real star. It’s ridiculously detailed — a place where you can admire glowing skyscrapers, overhear bizarre conversations, and accidentally run over a pedestrian while trying to answer a phone call from Keanu Reeves living in your brain.  Speaking of Keanu, Johnny Silverhand might be the only video game character capable of insulting you, encouraging you, and questioning your life choices all at the same time.  The gameplay gives you freedom to approach missions however you want: stealthy hacker, guns-blazing maniac, or the person who spends 20 minutes sneaking around only to panic and throw a grenade at the wrong moment. Recently, when it was on sale, I bought it again on Steam with zero expectations, and I am positively surprised by how much they have changed. The 2.0 update clearly turned this game around. The game is not only far more polished right now, it is also much more compelling in terms of story. Cyberpunk 2077  7 / 10 (good, I recommend it for players that like action games with RPG elements).  The Positive: * Excellent voice acting; * Very good characters; * Very good graphics and art direction; * Very beautiful Night City; * Good main story and good story for the most important side quests; * Good overall lore of earth and humankind in this alternative dark future; * Good performance and stability; * Good soundtrack and sound in effects and ambience; * Good character customization for ‘’builds’’ and gameplay style (but mainly for fighting); * Good character customization for body and clothes (but almost useless since we mainly play as FPS); * The way V interacts in 1st person with the characters is well done, very immersive and cool for us players. It’s done in a ‘’cinematic’’ way when we are in control or not; * Very good decision to let the players achieve different endings without having to reset the game entirely.  The Neutral: * Mediocre gameplay at fighting and exploring. Mediocre action and ‘’adventure’’; * Considerable part of the minor side quests are repetitive and uninspired; * Mediocre police mechanics; * Mediocre population mechanics; * The main quest is too short. I liked it much more than the side quests, but it ended when I wanted more of it; * Night City is beautiful and huge, but it lacks depth in its routine and main services/infrastructure.  The Negative: *  The game would be better if it had an alternative solid 3rd person mode, especially because it’s a cyberpunk game with good options for visual customization, just aesthetic or linked to body improvements… It’s a shame a locked 1st person mode to a very customizable V in a dark future where customization is a huge part of human culture. That’s not enough the motorcycle 3rd person camera; * The RPG mechanical elements linked to V’s roleplaying and choices-consequences are weak; * V’s origins are poorly linked to V’s journey; * I couldn’t feel Night City as a real living metropolis;  * CDPR lies and many broken promises about game features, easily noted even playing at March/2026.  CONCLUSION: * Cyberpunk 2077 is a good game, worth my time and money.

If you get this, it's for the aesthetic and not for the content.

The main motivation of the protagonist is to run from death so desperately, but they're a mercenary, and it just feels silly that they can kill a thousand people and get shot constantly but then later have panic attacks about their impending death.  This is in stark contrast to the developer's previous masterpiece The Witcher 3, where the protagonist is motivated to save someone he loves and is not afraid to kill everyone on her trail and die in order to do so. That simple concept makes the game more fun, but in Cyberpunk they're simply a gun for hire who wants to be a legend but is their time is running out. That doesn't resonate with me at all.  That is not to say that there are not moments of pretty powerful story-telling. Some quests/subplots are beautifully and poetically crafted and hit pretty hard emotionally, but the main story never did that for me because I just could not care about my character.  For the positives, I think most everything else is very well-done. The gameplay is extremely unique, varied, and fun, and everything/everywhere is visually stunning. Those alone make this an excellent game that I will always recommend—very fun gameplay that doesn't get old, and it's beautiful to look at, but for me the story is just a little lackluster. But it looks like most people don't share my opinion, so hopefully you may find something about the story that resonates with you.  Last thing— Phantom Liberty DLC: fun little expansion but still the same unlikable character and weak story.

A pretty decent game, I've waited to play it for a VERY long time, not having had the hardware or motivation to game for several years.  It has its charms, certainly, I bet I would've adored it 10-14 years ago when I was still a teenager throwing every hour I had leftover into gaming. Now, I have a hard time tolerating any time waste or useless grinding that doesn't feel worthwhile or more than filler.  This game has a big open world with lots of npcs everywhere doing their own thing and honestly one of the most immersive, "Real" feeling worlds out there.  It was a bit too much for me in some ways, just the time spent alone was insane for a single player game, not a flaw for some but for me, it means a lot of time was "wasted" running around and it feels like I only saw about 60-70% of what the game had to offer, what with all the other endings and all the choices you can make. I feel a bit sad to not be able to see everything in a game but it's simply not worth the time to play another round.  Things like gigs and npcd missions were designed to just waste time unless you're VERY interested in lore and random goings on in night city, but luckily they're not in your quest log and can be ignored easily.  I played on hard but honestly, the difficulty felt at best normal, especially once you get some levels and implants/cyberware, ultimately I was able to just run around not giving a crap about what weapon I used, hiding to avoid getting shot or anything else, just walking around shooting everyone, even bosses were far too easy, so I can just imagine how easy it'd be on a lower difficulty. I don't particularly care for dfficulty anymore as I do not want to waste time on dying hundreds of times but at the same time it kind of ruins the gameplay when things are so easy you simply don't need to even try.  To the very end, I was left clueless about the crafting system and upgrading iconic weapons if you even can and most other parts. Only the ripperdoc part and upgrading my cyberware to the max and using the talent tree was done. Using attachmets for weapons were poorly explained and crafting stuff weren't pushed in the slightest. I felt no need or desire to utilize any system in the game, which makes these systems a big waste of time. It was more than easy to just use random dropped weapons or job weapons and change them with new ones when there's a better one dropped.  I feel it's a big waste when there's no real incentive whatsoever to craft things. Looting things also felt like a waste of time, needless filler, because all it did was give you some extra pocket change and materials. Why is there even food in the game and various other junk that didn't seem to provide any signficiant benefit? I'm not eating random crap for small boosts and wasting time in the menu for that when it's completely unnecessary. Hacking was fun but aslo felt useless most of the time unless you want to roleplay. Gaining skill points in certain things like body to get new dialogue choices never seemed to affect the outcome in any real way. I also really, really want to question the choice of only giving you two slots for quick actions, one grenade/extra action slot and one for healing items. Especially the extra one/grenade one. I had a bunch of different grenades but never got to use any of them, only using the cyberware projectiles. Why wasn't there a quick switch at least? A way to throw grenades in addition to using arm projectiles?  So many questionable decisions. Buying houses and cars were also mere filler for people who enjoy grinding, there was no incentive to buy anything in general except cyberware.  I'd say a lot in this game is poorly designed even if it's still a huge and rather impressive game world with a good story. Like they took too big a challenge and couldn't properly tie everything together.  I hated the endings, to be honest, pretty much all of them. Seems that's the point, like no ending can truly be a great one. I quite enjoy immersing myself as the protagonist and not being able to get a satisfying ending made me a bit frustrated and honestly somewhat sad towards the end, it's all so melancholic and pretentiously dramatic, some people get off on that, I don't in the slightest. I want a good ending for myself even if everyone else has to burn for it, sadly even that wasn't really an option here. I don't particularly think it's good game design to not leave ANY good endings to cater to my crowd when there are so many endings to be had. I don't mean some kind of flowers and rainbows ending where night city becomes day city, all the drug addicts and people are enlightened and become buddhists, the corps become moral pillars that try to better humanity and no one dies anymore as everyone transcends their mortal shell and lives on forever in joy and harmony, I just mean an ending where the PROTAGONIST gets a relatively happy ending, like putting johnny in another body and somehow solving your own issue and living a good, full life even if it has to be on the grave of a lot of other people as only the winners get to live a good life in night city...  Phantom liberty was the best part of the game. It felt much better put together, perhaps because it also took place in a much smaller area and had a more solid, put together and rapid quest line? It was better written and just more interesting, although I didn't like the ending there either, just too melodramatic for my taste.  I do not regret buying the game, it was a pretty fun experience, it just takes itself too seriously with some poor design choices. It's definitely one of the best games in modern times, even if I would personally prefer a lot of other games to this as it's not really my cup of tea, though cool.  Oh, and I'm real happy to finally be done. Was getting real sick and freaking tired of all the crashes, sometimes even locking me out from continuing until I lowered the resolution to 1080p. The game crashed on average every hour I'd say, sometimes it'd crash every 15 minutes, sometimes 30 minutes, sometimes it'd run for a few hours but every single day when I played this, it'd crash at least 3 times. Worst was 20 times.  Seriously annoying, I think I wasted about 5 hours easily just trying to get back into the game after crashes, maybe more, especially if you include troubleshooting, so maybe 10 hours.   Happy to finally have played the game I heard so much about, even if a lot of it was because it was a buggy mess. I still laugh thinking about reed in phantom liberty skipping like a girl in a flower field while pushing a garbage bag in front of him towards an elevator and finally the bag exploded as he, the whole time, talked in an extremely serious voice. Wish I had recorded it.

Cyberpunk 2077 is a beautiful game. Visually, artistically, and atmospherically, it is one of the most impressive open-world titles I’ve played.  Let me be clear — the story itself is good, but not something extraordinary. It’s not a once-in-a-generation narrative experience like Red Dead Redemption 2. It doesn’t aim for that emotional depth. However, what it does, it does exceptionally well in its own way.  Night City feels real. Not just big — but alive. Driving around the city at night, with the neon lights reflecting off wet streets, traffic moving naturally, ambient conversations happening in the background — it genuinely feels immersive. Sometimes I would just drive around without a mission, purely to take in the atmosphere.  I know the game had a very rough launch. Performance issues, bugs, poor optimization — it was widely criticized at release. But I played it after the 2.0 update, and the experience was completely different. The overhaul improved the mechanics, systems, and overall polish significantly.  Technically, I played with path tracing enabled along with DLSS Frame Generation (2x), and the visual experience was phenomenal. The lighting, reflections, and shadows transform the city into something next level. Every gunfight felt cinematic.  Speaking of combat — the Adam Smasher fight was absolutely top tier. The intensity, the destruction, and the final moment when he goes down — especially the explosion and overall presentation — were executed perfectly. It felt earned.  Cyberpunk 2077 may not have the deepest story ever told in gaming, but as a complete package — visuals, atmosphere, combat, and world design — it is exceptional. It has carved its own identity.  If you’re playing it post-2.0, you’re getting the game as it was meant to be experienced.  A flawed launch, but an outstanding comeback.

Amazing game, there really isn't another game like it which is very disappointing.  This review may look negative but trust me there is far more positives to outweigh the negatives I list  To start, I'd highly recommend installing the "New Game+" mod from Nexus, as this game does not have a new game plus mechanic.  I would also like to warn you that when it comes to missions in this game, they are chronologically awful. They use mission tokens that can be received only after finishing select missions, however these tokens are not directly tied to said missions so you may not receive the next part of a quest line for like 3 in game days. There is a mod that allows you to force the mission token so you don't have to be waiting hours on end. The mods name is Content Token Activator  The story and sub stories are amazing, my only issues with it are:  1) Lack of expansive content:  This is not to say the game does not have a lot of content, there's a decent amount of missions, however none of the missions really stand out to you, none of them I really found myself enjoying (aside from the relationship questlines). There isn't a lot to any of the questlines for that matter and once you finish them there really isn't anything to do. Ideally most players would want a lot more content or at least the have the community provided with better mod tools so the players can continue to expand the game.  2) Lack of difficulty:  The games really easy, even on it's hardest difficulties. This is all I really have to say about this and I'd definitely recommend adding some form of combat or enemy overhaul mod.  3) Lack of creativity:  The game itself is a creative masterpiece, however when it comes down to combat/enemies/missions nothing really feels unique. All of the enemies have the same attack patterns, mechanics, etc. The missions are pretty predictable and all feel the same just with slight twists. There's no real sense of urgency with any of the missions and they're mostly all just "kill this group of people" type missions. Would have definitely been nicer to see a more extensive set of quests and game mechanics.  P.S: The driving mechanic is kinda clunky I don't think much time was put into it  ----  The entire CP2077 community share the same sentiment with wanting more content for this game which we unfortunately will not be getting as CDPR have started working on the next Cyberpunk game. They have stated that when they started working on CP2077 that this is not the game they intended on making, however I'm glad they did because it's truly a masterpiece.  This being said, this is and likely forever will be my favourite game (unless the second game is even better) and I highly recommend it because it's definitely an experience.

Cyberpunk 2077: A Neon-Drenched Masterpiece  It is a rare and beautiful thing in the gaming industry when a title not only redeems itself but completely eclipses its original promises. Playing Cyberpunk 2077 in 2026 is an entirely different experience than it was at its initial launch. Through relentless patching, sweeping system overhauls, and the masterful Phantom Liberty expansion, CD Projekt Red has forged one of the most immersive, breathtaking open-world action RPGs of this generation.  Cyberpunk 2077 is an absolute must-play experience today.  A City Like No Other Night City is arguably the main character of the game, and it stands as a marvel of virtual architecture and atmosphere.  Unmatched Immersion: From the towering, rain-slicked corporate skyscrapers of Corpo Plaza to the dusty, sun-baked badlands outside the city limits, the world feels incredibly dense and alive. You can spend hours simply cruising the streets, listening to the meticulously curated radio stations.  Granular Detail: Continuous updates—right up to the latest 2.3 patch—have introduced fully functioning transit systems, AutoDrive features, and expanded weather dynamics like acid rain and sandstorms. The neon-lit alleys, shifting crowd densities, and towering megabuildings make this one of the most believable dystopian settings ever crafted.  Deep, Rewarding Gameplay The core gameplay loop has been completely rebuilt since launch, evolving into a phenomenally satisfying sandbox of destruction, hacking, and stealth.  Total Freedom in Combat: You are not locked into a single playstyle. You can be a hyper-mobile cyber-ninja deflecting bullets with a katana, a hulking solo with Gorilla Arms tearing heavy machine guns off their turrets, or a netrunner frying enemies’ cyberware from the shadows without ever drawing a weapon.  Meaningful Progression: The overhauled perk and cyberware systems ensure that every skill point you spend fundamentally changes how you approach encounters. Installing "chrome" at a Ripperdoc actually feels impactful, balancing your immense new powers against the limits of your character's physical capacity.  Narrative Brilliance Where the game truly cements its legacy is in its writing, voice acting, and intricate quest design.  Emotional Resonance: V’s desperate fight for survival, complicated by the digital ghost of rockerboy-terrorist Johnny Silverhand (played brilliantly by Keanu Reeves), is deeply gripping. The companions you meet—like Panam, Judy, and River—feel incredibly human, flawed, and memorable.  The Spy-Thriller Peak: The Phantom Liberty expansion elevates the storytelling to new heights. It introduces Dogtown, a ruined, walled-off district, and delivers a tense, espionage-driven storyline featuring Idris Elba. Furthermore, the game's side gigs rarely feel like filler; they are rich, tangled moral dilemmas that force you to make tough, lasting choices.  The Verdict Cyberpunk 2077 is a triumph of persistence, artistic direction, and creative vision. It manages to balance high-octane, visceral action with quiet, introspective moments exploring identity, extreme corporate greed, and the commodification of the human body. Whether you are experiencing it on a high-end PC or through the impressively optimized modern console versions, it is a stunning, deeply rewarding RPG that fully delivers on the fantasy of being an edgerunner trying to become a legend.

Once in a while, a bright star shines in the gaming firmament, gifting us with a gem like Cyberpunk 2077. I haven't seen such a well-made game in a very long time—and I've seen a lot.  Yes, I was late to the party and can't say much about the bugs that were reported at release. But in its current state, the game is a steroid-fueled rollercoaster ride. Pure cinematic magic.  I love the execution and the sheer audacity that CD Projekt Red has shown with this game. The legend is woven slowly and lovingly, only to mercilessly throw the player back into the cyberpunk setting at the next opportunity. The German voice acting features many well-known and truly great voices, which immediately gave me a big-screen feel. And I'm sure my next playthrough in English will be just as captivating. I still have a few achievements to unlock.  The modding community has showered the game with love because the possibilities are wide open – replayability and fun have always been the primary focus, rather than monetization.  Let's see if the sequel maintains these qualities and – I sincerely hope so – includes an online mode.  11 out of 10 – not because it's flawless or perfect, but because it tells a story that stands out so wonderfully from the bland uniformity so common today.

Playing Cyberpunk 2077 felt like stepping into a city that never truly lets you breathe. From the moment I started, there was this constant sense of tension — like everything around me was bigger, louder, and more dangerous than I was. Night City isn’t just a setting; it feels oppressive, seductive, and strangely beautiful all at once.  What struck me the most was how personal everything felt. Conversations didn’t feel like simple dialogue options — they felt loaded. Some choices left me sitting there for a second, actually thinking about the consequences. There were moments of chaos and gunfire, sure, but the quiet scenes hit just as hard. Driving alone at night with the neon lights reflecting on the streets gave me this strange mix of loneliness and freedom.  Combat felt satisfying in different ways depending on how I approached it. Sometimes I went in loud and reckless, and other times I slowed down, hacked cameras, and watched everything unfold from the shadows. That freedom made every encounter feel like my own story instead of a scripted sequence.  What really stayed with me, though, was the atmosphere. The music, the lights, the crowds, the small details in random alleyways — it all builds this world that feels alive but also decaying. There’s glamour on the surface, but underneath it all, there’s desperation. And the more I played, the more I felt like I was becoming part of that machine.  It’s one of those experiences that pulls you in slowly. The longer I stayed in Night City, the harder it was to leave.

I avoided this game for years because of all the bugs. When I finally picked it up in 2024, my first thought was that why had I not played this sooner!  The world in Cyberpunk 2077 is incredibly detailed and fleshed out. There are so many stories and bits of lore hidden in every corner that I couldn’t stop exploring. The characters are well written and feel alive, thanks to the 10/10 voice acting from the cast.  The game mechanics are pretty cool. You can hack your way through enemies, go in guns blazing, play stealth like a ninja, or smash everything with brute strength. However, the difficulty balancing feels a bit skewed, as mobs become ridiculously easy once your gear is strong enough. The boss fights still kicked my ass though.  The main story felt shorter than most games, I reached the final mission in about 30 hours. However, the game has so many side missions with unique stories that you can easily get over 60 hours of playtime out of them (while ignoring the final mission, of course).  Cyberpunk is one of those games you keep on your PC and boot up occasionally for nostalgia. Not a masterpiece, but it stays with you for a long time. Kudos to the studio for this banger. I’ve never played a game that makes the character you’re playing feel like a real part of the world and an important character in the story. The way characters talk to you and interact with you with their unique expressions is amazing. Sometimes when you’re just running around the city doing nothing or completing side quests, someone suddenly calls your phone to talk to you or offer a quest. The transition between cinematic moments and gameplay is also incredibly smooth. It doesn’t feel like a cutscene at all. As far as I know, I’ve never seen another game do it this smoothly. This is the first time I’ve experienced something like this. Even walking around after finishing a quest using walking mode feels very natural. The feeling is honestly hard to explain. Every wall, every room feels different. The city feels busy, colorful, and alive — not empty.  If this game became the standard for AAA open-world games, that would be insane, especially if developers keep pushing the limits even further with more freedom and fewer limitations on what players can do. Cyberpunk 2077 is a game that impresses on a technical and artistic level but struggles to maintain emotional and mechanical satisfaction. The world of Night City is visually extraordinary: neon lighting, vertical city design, and dense environmental storytelling create one of the most detailed sci-fi urban settings in gaming. However, beneath that visual mastery, the world sometimes feels more like a cinematic backdrop than a living, evolving ecosystem. The game leans heavily toward dystopian atmosphere rather than deeply explained scientific or sociopolitical worldbuilding, which can make the setting feel aesthetically convincing but narratively underdeveloped if you prefer hard sci-fi logic behind world design.  The narrative structure is heavily driven by existential urgency. The central plot device, involving the relic and Johnny Silverhand, creates a constant psychological pressure on the player. While this is intended to create emotional weight and tension, it can also conflict with open-world RPG design principles. Open-world games typically reward exploration and patience, but Cyberpunk’s story constantly reminds you that the protagonist is dying. This can produce narrative dissonance. You are encouraged to complete side content, yet emotionally you feel pushed to rush through the main story to find a cure. This creates, at least for me, fatigue and emotional stress rather than engagement.  Gameplay itself is competent but not revolutionary. Combat primarily revolves around standard shooter mechanics combined with ability upgrades. Character builds do provide some variety, but the moment-to-moment gameplay loop can become repetitive over long play sessions. If a player expects gameplay evolution similar to highly praised open-world RPGs where mechanics dramatically transform over time, this game may feel mechanically static after extended play.  The character writing is strong in certain areas. Johnny Silverhand serves as a narrative foil and philosophical counterweight to the player character. However, his constant presence can feel intrusive rather than compelling if the player does not emotionally connect with him. Instead of enhancing immersion, he can sometimes feel like a persistent narrative interruption, especially during exploration or gameplay-focused segments.  The game’s endings reinforce its philosophical tone rather than offering traditional RPG closure. Cyberpunk 2077 is built around tragic or bittersweet outcomes rather than heroic triumph. This design choice aligns with cyberpunk genre traditions, but it can feel unsatisfying to those who prefer narrative payoff and emotional resolution. Compared to RPGs where tragedy is balanced by legacy, continuation, or revenge arcs, this game emphasizes inevitability and systemic failure over individual victory.  Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 is best described as a game you admire rather than necessarily love. It excels in presentation, atmosphere, and thematic ambition, but may feel exhausting if you value world immersion driven by agency, scientific plausibility, or emotionally uplifting narrative arcs. It is a strong example of modern narrative gaming, but not universally appealing to players who want awe, progression satisfaction, and cathartic storytelling.

Nothing about it is scaled down - its setting is vast in a way that other games can only hint at, yet it is "confined" (if that is the right word) to a medium sized city somewhere in the West of what was once the USA. One can spend hours just driving around in it and not find a repeated landscape or city street.  I'm not going to comment on the mechanics of the gameplay. I'm not enough of a gamer to be qualified to do that. To my not-very-tutored eye they seem reasonably standard for an FPS type adventure/RPG, with lots of details and choices to ponder, make, and sometimes regret. The thing that has caught and held me with Cyberpunk is its brutally accurate depiction of a late capitalist society that has been hollowed out by externally imposed disasters and its own moral decay. Some of this depiction may be accidental - for example, if you're a bad driver of computer game cars, the chances are the police will decide you're public enemy number 1 and start shooting at you. Forget proper arrest and due process - it doesn't happen. Hell, I even caused a shootout when I obeyed a "cross now" symbol at a crossing and got bowled by a police car. I suspect that this is probably just a coding issue, but if it's deliberate, it fits the vibe. Trash-choked streets; graffiti-covererd walls; drugged-out citizens tottering down the footpaths, vomiting in the alleyways and spasming on the ground as a result of some strange narcotic; video billboards advertising sex of various kinds; weapon shops selling all kinds of firerarms; and quest lines where your character, V, has to steal, lie, and kill lots and lots of people to survive.  And that's what I think is so compelling about the game. There's no pretence at a moral justification or noble cause in which the player is acting. We ain't slaying dragons or ridding the world of monsters here. Yes, one can try to be kind, but often the imperatives of survival force the player to be brutal. And (spoiler alert) the two main quest endings I have experienced so far have seen the player both winning and losing everything. I'm pretty sure that choices I made in the game conditioned those endings, but I'm also willing to bet that there's no such thing as a "happy ever after" in the cyberpunk universe for V.  I bought the game when it was on special. It's been years since its first release, but to me I think it might be seen in the future, for all its faults and foibles, as a game that broke the mould. I'm glad I bought it. So far, it's been worth every penny.  Rate up

Today, I finished [b] Cyberpunk 2077[/b] and its expansion [b] Phantom Liberty[/b]  on PC through the [b] Cyberpunk 2077: Ultimate Edition[/b]  package on Steam, and with a multitude of QoL, aesthetic mods and very extra content from a very passionate fanbase. It finished to near total completion, and it took a total of around 143 hours according to a tracker that may or may not have glitched out, or counted some dead time in a report screen; a total of around 96 hours, according to the in-game tracker, and a total of 66 hours, according to a very untrustworthy tracker in Steam.  When I first started my trek through the dark alleyways of Night City, all I had in mind were the initial horror stories of the initial release of the game, the constant advertisement of the massive star-power involved, and a vague idea of its shooting-oriented gameplay loop.   When the city finally spat me out, forever changed, my mind reeled with much more: how much it meant to live through such a gorgeous, gorgeous experience; the constant musings and ponderings about philosophy, morality, and identity the many, many stories put me through at every step of the way; and an aching sense of loss for the fictional lives that passed me by, fully formed that I left behind.  Cyberpunk 2077 can be thought of as an open world first person shooter with very pronounced RPG elements, with a lot of mechanics, play-styles, sprawling choices and items galore that I will probably never experience fully, because I somewhat didn't care to.  The gameplay is snappy, emergent, at times simplistic, and not always fully functional, with the driving mechanics being a particular point of contention for most; the performance of the game in my admittedly medium-range gaming laptop was spotty at best, and highly crash prone; and a lot of its world-building elements wear their inspirations on their sleeves, most times fairly derivative, sometimes cliched, and at certain points bordering on rip-offs.  Yet, even as all these elements and problems in isolation paint a grim picture, the sum of its parts reaches higher highs than most games even aspire to, all thanks to the bow that ties around this mess of a box: its earnest, painfully real story, its charming dialogue and beautifully uneven delivery that definitely borders on Lynchian, and the most well-realized player characters, supporting characters, side-characters, and even background characters that any narrative can offer.  Particular praise must be offered to the impressive integration of its DLC expansion, Phantom Liberty, which almost (due to its two amazing bookending title and credits sequences) seamlessly integrates itself into the main experience with such finesse that I cannot imagine the game as a whole without it, telling a story of its own that complements the main one, if not, fully elevate it beyond its original scope.  After every unstable crash, after every frustration with some of its mechanics, after every odd interaction, glitch and immersion-breaking groan-inducing quirk in between missions, after every exhaustive nearly futile attempt to progress side content that failed to trigger over and over again, I somehow always came back, wanting, and hungry for more, feeling like I left a little bit of myself in it every day, a little bit of my thoughts, of my choices, my hopes, dreams and doubts. The game is not perfect, as hardly anything is, it's painful, it's frictional, uneven, persistently unsatisfying, sometimes borderline hateful, but it's also tender, sweet, sincere, cool, edgy and it's so much more, but more than all of that, it's alive.  The game is not perfect, but it's mine.  [b]AWESOME ◆◆◆◆[/b]

Cyberpunk is an absolute masterpiece. I am glad that CD Projekt Red took the time to fix its bad launch, improve upon the systems, and add an amazing DLC story to this game.   Night City feels like a living entity and one of the main characters in this game. The depressing, dystopian setting is well fleshed out and has enough detail and lore to feel like a real city. As I played, the cynical part of my brain drew parallels between this world and our own making it easier to imagine what events may have lead to such a society. It is an easy world to be immersed in, also thanks to the beauty of the visuals.  The characters really make this game and the setting backs this up well. Conversations in Cyberpunk are as smooth as can be and feel like genuine conversations with real people. It's not difficult to have empathy for a lot of the characters after experiencing the world they inhabit. The visuals enhance this. In some games, no matter what dialogue is being spoken, poor facial animations make it feel like you are talking to a robot and can break immersion. Not the case here. I know that I am going to miss those deep conversations with Johnny Silverhand.   Gameplay has a lot to offer, there are multiple valid playstyles that can make combat engaging. I fell into the generic rifle character as I do so often, but caught a glimpse of the different, more creative combat options and may do a deeper dive into them on a subsequent playthrough. I played on the "Normal" difficulty and, to be honest, it was very easy pretty much the whole way through. I think playing on the more advanced difficulties may improve the experience by encouraging further exploration into the different combat and build possibilities.  The story is well done. I was engaged and motivated throughout to keep pushing forward, which again lends to the depth of the characters involved. I would recommend playing through each of the endings, as they all seem to reveal different information and I found them interesting enough to warrant running through the final mission multiple times.  The DLC, Phantom Liberty, is absolutely this game at its best. It improves on gameplay systems like introducing a separate skill tree for the relic. Dogtown as a location, I did not find as interesting as Night City, then again its 15% of the size so it was at an unfair disadvantage. The characters, story and endings to this DLC are a must see. Some of the best moments in the game come from conversations involving the new characters and debriefing the situations you find yourself in with Johnny. After each of the endings, there is a conversation with Johnny reflecting on the outcomes and decisions you made, and these were probably my favorite moments from the game.  Overall, definitely cemented as one of my favorite games of all time. Highly recommend, I think its worth the full price tag, although now its regularly on sale for less than $30. Play this game, you will not regret it.  95/100 on the tacometer.

My 90 hours on record consist of a partial playthrough a couple years ago, and then a full playthrough that I just completed in Feb 2026.  I never played this game in its original buggy state.    The original Deus Ex is on of my favorite games of all time, and I think this is a good game too, but it doesn't wear the same mantle in my book.  It has a fun combat system, good character skill and cyberware development, an interesting story, driving, shooting, sex etc. etc.  But unfortunately it feels like so much of the good stuff is squandered.  Perthaps Cyberpunk could benefit from more focus.  I'm not sure the open world structure really works here, because most of the world is not interactive.  It's more just to establish a setting and mood.  But I think the game could've used a higher quantity and quality of specific missions, because otherwise all the cool cyberware, perks, stats, and equipment just aren't fully utilized.  I mean, most of the combat involved seems to just be with random grunts hanging out in a back alley somewhere.  So a lot of it goes to waste.  There are a bunch of things you can buy like apartments and cars and clothes, but a lot of that seems fairly useless, too.  I really was craving challenging scenarios that would force me to make full use of my build, but they were rare.  Very unfortunate...  And there are parts of this game that just DRAG.  I appreciate some good roleplaying and interesting conversations between characters, but some of that was just excessive.  I mean, if I have to press X to sit down in a chair, and then press X again to stand up one more time, I'm going to sonic shock myself to death, I swear.  There are many, MANY segments that are basically just cut scenes, but where you are required to press buttons to "do things" that are not optional.  Very irritating, and makes the idea of playing through the game again unpleasant.  Towards the end of my full playthrough, I was really feeling anxious to just be done with the whole thing already.  I was getting tired of V falling to his knees to cough up blood, and tired of him and Silverhand bickering back and forth.  I think some themes in this game are just beat to death with a hammer, and it gets fatiguing.  There is a fine line between making something feel epic, and making it feel painfully prolonged.
